intro:
**The Defense of the Vulnerable and the Social Fabric**

Al-Nisāʾ, "The Women," is the fourth chapter of the Qur'an, spanning 176 verses of rich Medinan legislation. It derives its title from its unprecedented and pervasive concern with the legal rights, familial status, economic autonomy, and social protections accorded to women. Classical scholars categorized it as one of the seven long sūrahs (*al-Sabʿ al-Ṭiwāl*) that establish the institutional foundation of Islamic civilization. Where prior pagan and imperial societies treated women and minor dependents as chattel or legal nonentities, Sūrah al-Nisāʾ systematically dismantled patriarchal hegemony, legislating compulsory shares of inheritance for women, establishing consent and financial endowments (*mahr*) in marriage, criminalizing the usurpation of widows' property, and instituting strict judicial oversight over the estates of orphans. Far from being a mere dry legal code, the sūrah grounds every legal obligation in the absolute sovereignty of Allah and the sanctity of common human origin, reminding humanity in its very first breath that the entire species was engendered *“from a single soul”* (4:1).

**The Structural Fabric of the Sūrah**

The architecture of al-Nisāʾ unfolds in several interlocking legislative and political movements. The opening movement (1–14) lays the domestic bedrock: the rights of orphans, guardianship ethics, marriage contracts, and the mathematically rigorous distribution of inheritance estates, closed with solemn divine warnings that consuming orphan wealth is tantamount to swallowing fire into one's belly. The second movement (15–35) tackles sexual morality, incest prohibitions, legal repentance, property theft, domestic discord, and arbitration, emphasizing mutual consultation between spouses. The third movement (36–59) synthesizes individual piety with civic duty, mandating benevolence to parents, kin, orphans, neighbors, and wayfarers, while confronting religious envy and ordaining the fundamental charter of governance and judiciary: *“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice”* (4:58). The fourth movement (60–104) examines national security, the psychology of cowardice and hypocrisy, the duty of military mobilization, protective intelligence handling, the tragedy of accidental manslaughter, and the rules of engagement during warfare, famously interrupted by the sublime prescription for the Prayer of Fear (*Ṣalāt al-Khawf*, 4:102) to show that liturgical communion must never be abandoned even in the trenches. The fifth movement (105–136) turns to judicial integrity, immortalized by the case of a Jewish man falsely framed for theft by a Muslim clan, whereupon revelation descended to clear the innocent outsider and forbid the Prophet from advocating for deceitful partisans (4:105–107), culminating in the monumental command to uphold justice even against oneself, parents, or kin (4:135). The final movement (137–176) exposes hypocritical alliances, corrects extreme Christian doctrines about Jesus and the Trinity, and concludes with a definitive legal postscript on lateral inheritance (*al-kalālah*).

verses.1:
> O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women. And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties. Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you

**A Single Origin That Undercuts All Claims of Rank**

This opening places the entire sūrah on a single foundation before any law is given. Mankind is addressed together — *yā ayyuhā al-nās* — not as tribes, clans, or ranks, but as the offspring of one soul and its mate. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may know one another”* (49:13), and again *“He created you from a single soul”* (39:6). By beginning legislation about orphans, women, inheritance, and marriage with creation, the verse teaches that law does not invent equality; it remembers it. Every claim that one lineage is higher than another collapses at the first sentence. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the purpose of reminding the audience of a common parentage at this exact point is to soften hearts for the duties that follow, because a person who feels his link to others is more likely to guard their rights. That psychological link matters here: the sūrah will command protection for the weakest — the orphan girl, the widow, the heir with a small share — and it grounds those commands not in pity but in kinship. If all spread from one soul, then wronging another is wronging one’s own extended family.

**From One Soul and Its Mate to Countless Men and Women**

The phrase *min nafs wāḥidah* — from a single soul — is understood by the vast majority of exegetes to mean Adam, with the mate understood as Ḥawwāʾ. The Arabic word *nafs* is grammatically feminine while *zawj* is masculine, yet commentators do not see a problem in the pairing, because the terms describe roles in creation rather than grammatical genders. What the verse stresses is sequence: singularity, then duality, then multiplicity. One became two, and two became countless. That pattern mirrors how the Qur’an elsewhere describes the spreading of humanity as a sign of divine power. Some modern readers have asked whether *minhā* — from it — means from the same substance or from the same kind. The majority read it as indicating that the mate was created from the same nature as the first soul, consonant with the usage of *min anfusikum* in other passages to mean of your own kind (3:164; 9:128; 16:72). Al-Rāzī observes that the Qur’an does not narrate the mechanism of Ḥawwāʾ’s creation in detail; the ḥadīth literature mentions creation from a rib, but the Book itself keeps the language brief, keeping attention on the moral point rather than the biology.

**The Womb-Tie and the Name of Mercy**

*Al-arḥām* — family ties, literally wombs — comes from the same root as *raḥmah*, mercy, and the divine Name *al-Raḥmān*, the Compassionate. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs devotion to God with goodness to kin, as in *“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents and relatives”* (4:36).

**Watchful Over You Even When No One Else Is**

The verse closes with *inn Allāha kāna ʿalaykum raqībā* — surely Allah is ever Watchful over you. The Name *al-Raqīb* gathers seeing, guarding, and reckoning. It is not only that God knows what people do behind closed doors; it is that He keeps watch like a guardian keeps watch over a ward. That closing fits the sūrah’s character as a book of law for the vulnerable. Guardians of orphans, holders of dowries, distributors of estates — all handle property that the owner cannot yet claim or cannot defend. No court can see every handover. The verse answers that gap with a single assurance and warning: the Watcher is already present. Elsewhere the Qur’an says *“Allah is Witness over all things”* (4:33; 58:6), and the same idea returns at the end of the orphan test in verse 6 with *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6). That thread links creation to accountability. The God who spread countless men and women from one soul is not distant from the countless transactions among them; He observes each one, and what is entrusted to people in this world will be measured with precision in the next.
verses.2:
> Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺, and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables, nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own. For this would indeed be a great sin

**Restoring What Was Never Yours**

The command is direct: give orphans their wealth. The Arabic *ātū al-yatāmā amwālahum* does not say hold it longer or invest it indefinitely; it says hand it over when the owner is ready. An orphan in Qur’anic usage is a child who has lost the father who would have guarded his property, and the community steps in as trustee, not as new owner. The verse treats that trust as real ownership by the child. The guardian is a keeper, and the wealth remains titled to the one who cannot yet defend it. That is why the same sūrah will later say *“Test the orphans until they reach a marriageable age”* (4:6) and only then return what is theirs. Between command and return lies a period of management, and this verse governs its ethics. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs justice to orphans with justice in measure and worship itself, as in *“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans”* (4:36), showing that how the strong handle the property of the weak is a measure of faith, not a footnote to it.

**Do Not Mix Their Wealth With Yours to Consume It**

The second prohibition *wa lā taʾkulū amwālahum ilā amwālikum* — nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own — addresses a subtler form of taking. Instead of an open exchange, the guardian merges accounts, spends freely from the combined sum, and tells himself the orphan’s share is still in there somewhere. The Qur’an calls that eating — *akl* — a word it uses elsewhere for illicit gain, as in *“Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29). Eating suggests both pleasure and disappearance; what is eaten does not return. The verse warns that mixing makes eating easy because boundaries blur. After this verse was revealed, some guardians became so scrupulous that they separated food, pots, and even cooking fires, fearing any mixing would count as sin. The hardship that followed was eased by a later clarification: *“If you intermingle with them, they are your brothers”* (2:220), which permits shared living with fairness, while this verse forbids shared living as a cover for consumption. The distinction is intention and accounting. Living together remains allowed; living off the orphan does not. The clause *innahu kāna ḥūban kabīrā* — for this would indeed be a great sin — uses a rare word, *ḥūb*, which the linguists connect with a grave crime that weighs heavily. By calling the act a great sin rather than merely a mistake, the verse places misappropriation of orphan wealth among major wrongs, alongside the other major sins the sūrah will later say to avoid to earn forgiveness for lesser ones (4:31). The occasion of revelation recalled by commentators sharpens the point: a boy whose parents had died was under his uncle’s care; when he grew and asked for his property, the uncle refused, and the matter was brought to the Prophet ﷺ.

**Guardianship as a Test of Character**

The verse does more than regulate a transaction; it defines what guardianship means in this faith. A guardian is not rewarded with the orphan’s wealth for his trouble, except for the modest provision the next verses will allow to a poor guardian who is doing real work (4:6). The standard case is service without compensation, witnessed at return (4:6), and watched by God (4:1). That structure turns guardianship into a visible proof of *taqwā*, which is exactly how the sūrah opened. If humanity shares one origin and God is watchful over all, then the treatment of a child who cannot hire a lawyer becomes the clearest mirror of whether that awareness is real. The Qur’an elsewhere promises double reward for justice to the weak and severe penalty for exploiting them, as in *“Those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth consume fire into their bellies”* (4:10). This verse sets the rule; that later verse sets the consequence.
verses.3:
> If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their ˹due˺ rights ˹if you were to marry them˺, then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four. But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice, then ˹content yourselves with˺ one or those ˹bondwomen˺ in your possession. This way you are less likely to commit injustice

**Two, Three, or Four — A Limit, Not a Target**

The phrase *mathnā wa thulātha wa rubāʿ* — two, three, or four — sets an upper bound, not a recommended number. Before this sūrah, there was no Qur’anic ceiling stated in this form; pre-Islamic custom allowed a man to take many wives without fixed limit. By capping the number at four, the Qur’an limited what was earlier open-ended, just as it elsewhere limited retaliation, divorce pronouncements, and waiting periods. The choice of two, three, then four with the conjunction *wa* was understood by grammarians to mean any number up to four, singly or in combination, not eight or nine. The same sūrah later adds the inner condition that makes the outer number meaningful: *“You will never be able to be perfectly just between wives, even if you try”* (4:129).

**The Meaning of Not Committing Injustice**

The verse closes with *adhālik adnā allā taʿūlū* — this way you are less likely to commit injustice. The verb *taʿūlū* was read by most early lexicographers as to act unjustly or to deviate, related to *ʿawl* as oppression, while a minority read it as to be overburdened with dependents. Both senses converge: limiting wives keeps a person nearer to justice and farther from being overwhelmed. That dual sense matches the sūrah’s broader pattern of keeping law inside human weakness. Two verses later it will say *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak”* (4:28), and here it already lightens the load by telling the anxious man to take one. The Qur’an does not treat the desire for more as shameful in itself; it treats the risk of wronging others through that desire as the decisive factor. A man is asked to judge his own case honestly before acquiring new duties.

**A Reading That Protects Consent and Dowry**

The widespread report from ʿĀʾishah ties this verse to verse 127, where the Qur’an returns to the same group: *“They ask you about women. Say, Allah answers your query about them, and what is recited in the Book about orphan girls whom you do not give what is ordained for them though you desire to marry them”* (4:127). That later verse was presented as clarification: men were withholding the prescribed bridal gift from orphan girls under their care while wanting to keep them. Read together, verse 3 and verse 127 draw a consistent boundary: the guardian’s authority over property does not extend to discounting the woman’s due at marriage. The dowry belongs to her, as verse 4 will immediately confirm: *“Give women their due dowries graciously”* (4:4). The connection also shows how the Qur’an reforms a power asymmetry step by step. First it orders return of wealth, then it redirects marriage away from exploitation, then it secures the woman’s personal gift, ensuring that at no point does the guardian’s stewardship become ownership of the person. The sequence is intentional and cumulative.

**Justice as the Sūrah’s Steady Measure**

This verse makes justice — *qisṭ* and *ʿadl* — the measuring stick for family formation. The same standard will recur for inheritance shares where male and female each receive a fixed portion (4:7, 4:11–12), for treatment of wives where kindness is commanded even when affection wanes (4:19), and for arbitration where mediators are sent from both families (4:35). By opening the marriage discussion with a warning about orphans, the verse teaches that entry into marriage is not only about attraction or alliance but about aptitude for fairness. That aptitude is not assumed; it is to be examined. The Qur’an pairs permission with caution in a way that keeps the law humane: what is allowed is immediately bounded by whether it can be done justly, and what is just is measured by whether the weakest party’s right remains intact. A man who hears *“two, three, or four”* and hears only an allowance has misheard; the sentence began with fear of injustice to a girl who could not argue her own dowry, and it ends with the choice that stays nearest to avoiding that wrong.
verses.4:
> Give women ˹you wed˺ their due dowries graciously. But if they waive some of it willingly, then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience

**A Gift That Belongs to the Woman Herself**

The command *ātū al-nisāʾ ṣaduqātihinna niḥlah* — give women their dowries graciously — establishes a property right that cuts against the customs around it. *Niḥlah* deepens that sense: a free gift, given warmly and without grudging, not a bargain extracted under pressure. The Qur’an elsewhere confirms that wealth a woman receives through dowry, inheritance, or earnings remains hers to manage, as reflected in the very next laws where women are named as heirs alongside men (4:7) and where their property is not to be handed to those unable to manage (4:5) without proper terms. Al-Ṭabarī reads *niḥlah* as a gift with no return expected, which distinguishes it from a loan or a conditional transfer.

**From Guardian Control to Personal Ownership**

Read after verse 3, this verse completes a movement from stewardship to ownership. By naming women directly — *al-nisāʾ* — as recipients, the verse bypasses intermediaries. It does not say give it to their families or to those who arrange their marriages; it says give it to the women. The sūrah will later reinforce that a husband who has given a great amount and then wishes to replace one wife with another may not take back any of it, *“even if you have given the former a stack of gold”* (4:20). It asks *“how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment?”* (4:21).

**What Coercion Looks Like in Practice**

The condition of willingness invites careful attention to real life. Consent is not only a signature; it is a state of heart at the moment of giving. Pressure can be open — threats, anger, withdrawal — or quiet — repeated hints, appeals to loyalty, or making the wife feel that refusal equals disloyalty. The verse’s wording excludes all such pressure, because *ṭīb al-nafs* cannot coexist with fear or embarrassment. Jurists drew from this a practical rule: if it becomes clear that the wife gave while feeling straitened, the husband should return it, even if she voiced consent. The principle extends beyond dowry to any gift between spouses. The Qur’an elsewhere describes marital wealth in mutual consent generally, as in *“not in fornication”* but through lawful marriage sought *“with your wealth”* (4:24), and the same consent standard governs trade in *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but trade by mutual consent”* (4:29). The dowry rule is so one instance of a larger ethic where lawful enjoyment depends on the other party’s genuine willingness, not merely on a formal yes.

**The Wholesome Enjoyment That Follows**

The permission to enjoy what is freely given teaches that property in marriage is not a zone of constant suspicion. The sūrah will later set careful limits for those unable to manage wealth (4:5) and testing for orphans (4:6), but here it speaks about the ordinary case where a wife, content and unpressured, chooses to share. In that case the Qur’an does not require witnesses or paperwork; it says *eat it as pleasant and wholesome*, language that signals moral ease. Two ideas meet in that ease: her autonomy is preserved, and his use is then blessed. The pairing matters for the sūrah’s overall vision of family wealth, where men and women each have shares (4:7, 4:11–12), each has obligations, and kindness is commanded alongside calculation. A household where the dowry was honored freely becomes a place where later sharing is also more likely to be free. The verse therefore does more than settle a single transfer; it shapes a habit. It trains the husband to receive only what is given with an untroubled heart on the other side, and it trains the community to see a woman’s wealth as hers to keep, to keep whole, or to give — as she herself decides.
verses.5:
> Do not entrust the incapable ˹among your dependants˺ with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you—but feed and clothe them from it, and speak to them kindly

**Who Are the Incapable**

The term *al-sufahāʾ* — the incapable, often translated the feeble-minded — was explained by the early authorities as those unable to manage property soundly, whether due to youth, inexperience, weak judgment, or a condition that impairs prudence. The word is masculine plural, and commentators who considered that grammar concluded it does not single out women as such. That matters, because verses 2 and 4 have just secured women’s ownership of property, and verse 6 will return that property to orphans when they show sound judgment, regardless of gender. To read *sufahāʾ* as women in general would contradict that immediate context, and the sūrah’s later inheritance laws that name women as obligatory heirs (4:7, 4:11–12). The sounder reading, held by the majority including al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, is that the term covers any dependant whose judgment is not yet reliable for guarding wealth — minors, those with cognitive impairment, or those whose habits show they would scatter funds quickly. Some added that the term also warns against handing financial control to those outside the faith who would not observe the limits the sūrah is laying down, such as the prohibition of consuming wealth illegally (4:29), though the primary reference remains within the household.

**Your Wealth and Their Wealth**

The phrasing *amwālakum* — your wealth — has been discussed carefully. Does it mean the guardian’s own wealth, or the wealth of the incapable that is legally theirs but presently in the guardian’s hands? Both readings have support, and both lead to the same care. If it is your wealth, the verse warns a provider not to hand the household’s capital to a member who will dissipate it, because the whole household will then need help. If it is their wealth held in trust, the verse warns not to hand it over prematurely, which would simply undo the protection the sūrah has been building since verse 2. The sūrah will clarify that orphans’ wealth must be returned only after testing and when sound judgment appears (4:6), with witnesses and with *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) as the closing audit. This verse sits between those two points and supplies the principle that timing matters as much as ownership. To recognize that someone owns a thing is not the same as deciding he is ready to manage it today. The law can affirm the first while delaying the second for his own protection.

**Speak to Them Kindly**

The third element, *wa qūlū lahum qawlan maʿrūfā* — and speak to them kindly — adds a dimension that law alone cannot enforce. *Qawl maʿrūf* is speech that is decent, familiar, and recognized as good — words that acknowledge the person while managing the delay. The Qur’an pairs this speech elsewhere with kindness at distribution time to non-heirs present (4:8), and with equitable speech when imagining one’s own children left behind (4:9), showing that how the community speaks in financial transactions is part of justice itself. Ibn ʿĀshūr observes that the command to speak kindly prevents two harms at once: the guardian becoming harsh or contemptuous toward the incapable, and the dependant feeling humiliated and then acting recklessly to prove independence.

**Keeping Law Inside Human Weakness**

This verse keeps the sūrah’s legislation humane by acknowledging weakness without exploiting it. The same chapter that will say *“humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens”* (4:28) already acts on that truth here. Weak judgment is not mocked, it is managed with provision and kindness until strength appears. The approach differs from two equal errors: handing everything over immediately out of sentimentality, which harms the weak by giving him what will ruin him, and withholding everything indefinitely out of mistrust, which harms him by denying him his right. The middle path — preserve the standing support, provide ongoing care from its yield, and accompany the delay with decent words — honours both ownership and welfare. It also prepares the reader for the testing that follows.
verses.6:
> Test ˹the competence of˺ the orphans until they reach a marriageable age. Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment, return their wealth to them. And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up ˹to demand it˺. If the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation; but if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision. When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses. And sufficient is Allah as a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner

**Do Not Eat It Before They Can Ask**

The warning *wa lā taʾkulūhā isrāfan wa bidāran a yakbarū* — do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up to demand it — exposes a temptation that grows as the test nears its end. A guardian who senses the handover approaching may spend quickly, telling himself that small withdrawals will not be noticed or that the orphan will not know what was there. The words *isrāf* — wastefulness — and *bidār* — haste — name two distinct motives: spending beyond need, and spending ahead of time to pre-empt the claim. The Qur’an links both to eating — *akl* — as it did in *“do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables”* (4:2) and *“consume nothing but fire into their bellies”* (4:10), keeping the image of illicit gain as consumption that will later be consumed as fire. The clause *a yakbarū* — before they grow up to demand it — is psychologically precise. The sin depends on the victim’s inability to speak; once he can speak, the opportunity closes. By naming that window, the verse teaches guardians to treat the approaching adulthood not as a deadline to exploit but as a trust to complete. The best guardian is one who, as the account grows, feels more cautious, not more entitled.

**When the Guardian May Take and When He Must Refrain**

The rule *wa man kāna ghaniyyan fa al-yastaʿfif, wa man kāna faqīran fa al-yaʾkul bi al-maʿrūf* — if the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation; but if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision — balances two risks. The sūrah elsewhere commands *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29) and permits only what is by mutual consent; here, where consent cannot be fully given by a child, the law substitutes a standard of fairness judged by the community and watched by God.

**Sufficient Is Allah as Reckoner**

The verse closes with *wa kafā bi Allāhi ḥasībā* — and enough is Allah as vigilant Reckoner. *Ḥasīb* gathers counting, reckoning, and sufficing; He counts precisely and He suffices as judge when human accounting is imperfect. That closing follows every stage that came before: testing, sensing sound judgment, refraining from hasty eating, taking only what is fair, and calling witnesses. After all visible steps are taken, the final audit belongs to God, who saw the small transfers no witness recorded and the intentions behind the timing. The same divine Name returns throughout the sūrah as a refrain for entrusted wealth, matching *“Allah is ever Watchful over you”* (4:1) at the opening and *“Allah is a Witness over all things”* (4:33) later. The repetition creates a frame: what was entrusted by creation is measured by reckoning at return, and the one who kept watch at the beginning is the one who reckons at the end.

**From Guardianship to Ownership Without Harm**

Taken together, verses 2 through 6 trace a full arc of trust. Return the wealth (4:2), do not exploit marriage to discount it (4:3–4), do not place it prematurely in weak hands while still meeting daily needs with kindness (4:5), and then, after testing, return it fully, without haste, with witnesses, and with God as the final auditor (4:6). The step *“test until they reach a marriageable age”* ensures that age is not a mechanical trigger and that judgment is not assumed; the phrase *“if you feel they are capable of sound judgment”* makes the guardian answerable for his perception, not only for a date. That balance protects both sides: the orphan from being handed what would ruin him, and from being held indefinitely under tutelage when he is ready. The sūrah therefore teaches a guardianship that ends well. The last image is not a child forever dependent, but a young adult, tested and found capable, receiving his property back in the presence of witnesses, with a clear record and an enough Reckoner over all.
verses.7:
> For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave—whether it is little or much. ˹These are˺ obligatory shares

**A Fixed Share for Both Sexes**

This verse establishes a principle that prior custom had denied: both men and women have a fixed portion in what parents and close relatives leave. The Qur’an states it twice in one sentence, once for men and once for women, with the same wording *naṣīb mafrūḍ* — an obligatory share — closing the verse. Repetition here is legislation. In the pre-Islamic order only adult men who could bear arms and produce revenue were counted as heirs; women and young children were excluded on the ground that they did not fight and did not earn. The Qur’an set that reasoning aside and assigned entitlement by kinship, not by military utility. Commentators link the revelation to the case of a widow with daughters who were left without support because male relatives took the estate. By saying *whether it is little or much*, the verse prevents the dismissal of small estates as not worth sharing; even a modest amount carries the same obligation. The Qur’an elsewhere confirms the same ethic with precise fractions for daughters and parents (4:11) and for spouses and siblings (4:12), but this verse is the foundation: no heir of either sex is erased from the ledger.

**Why the Verse Repeats the Same Formula**

The parallel phrasing — *lil-rijāl naṣīb... Wa lil-nisāʾ naṣīb* — does more than grant; it equalises the language of entitlement. Both have a *naṣīb*, a share that is known and assigned, not a gift left to generosity. The closing *naṣīban mafrūḍan* was read by grammarians as emphasizing obligation from above; *farḍ* in the Qur’an means what God fixes as duty, as in the limits that will be called *ḥudūd Allāh* two verses later (4:13–14). By naming women’s portion with the same noun and the same adjective as men’s, the verse teaches that the share does not depend on the goodwill of male relatives after death; it arrives as law.

**Little or Much — No Estate Too Small to Divide Justly**

The clause *mimmā qalla minhu aw kathur* — whether it is little or much — closes a loophole that frugality might have opened. In a large estate, sharing is expected; in a small one, heirs might argue that division would scatter what needs to stay together, or that the widow and daughters can be provided for informally while the core property stays with the men. The Qur’an rejects that economy of excuse. If the amount is small, the share remains, and the division must still be just. That rigor protects the most vulnerable heirs precisely when the temptation to consolidate is strongest. The sūrah will reinforce this by ordering that even bystanders at distribution be offered something and spoken to kindly (4:8), and by warning guardians to imagine their own helpless children left behind (4:9). The principle across those verses is consistent: presence creates a claim, kinship creates a share, and the size of the pot does not nullify either. A community that honours small shares trains itself to honour large ones without fraud.

**An Obligatory Share, Not a Favour**

The words *naṣīban mafrūḍan* carry legal weight that the sūrah will specify in fractions two verses later. Jurisprudence built on this verse a whole science of inheritance — *ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ* — where fixed heirs receive fixed portions after debts and gifts are settled. That science later contributed to the development of algebra, because its calculations require precise proportional reasoning, a historical detail that shows how a verse about family rights generated tools for mathematics. The deeper point is religious. Upon death, property returns to God, *“and to Allah belongs the heritage of the heavens and the earth”* (3:180), and He redistributes it by His own ordinance.
verses.8:
> If ˹non-inheriting˺ relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution, offer them a ˹small˺ provision from it and speak to them kindly

**When Those Without a Fixed Share Are Present**

This verse imagines a scene that still repeats at every estate division: relatives who do not inherit a fixed portion, along with orphans and the needy, are present when property is being apportioned. The law has already assigned obligatory shares to primary heirs in the verse before (4:7) and will quantify those shares in detail after (4:11–12), but this verse pauses at the moment of presence itself. *Wa idhā ḥaḍara al-qismata ulū al-qurbā wa al-yatāmā wa al-masākīn* — if they are present at the distribution — does not say if they have a legal claim under inheritance law; it says if they are there. Presence alone generates a duty of generosity.

**The Status of the Command**

Commentators differed on whether this verse remains legally binding, was abrogated by the fixed shares of 4:11–12, or refers to gifts made before death up to one-third of the estate. Many authorities, including al-Ṭabarī, held that it remains recommended and praiseworthy, even if widely neglected, and that the choice to give and how much rests with the legal heirs. Others treated it as abrogated in the strict legal sense but preserved as an ethical ideal. The sūrah itself seems to anticipate that neglect by adding the second half — speak to them kindly — which would be unnecessary if the gift were always given. That addition suggests the verse aims to shape behaviour even where the gift is small or where the estate cannot bear much. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs giving with gracious speech and warns against following charity with hurtful reminders (2:263). Here the same pairing appears in reverse: if you give, give with kindness; if you cannot give much, at least speak well. The moral weight therefore does not rest on the amount; it rests on not making those present feel erased while others receive.

**A Distribution That Remembers the Community**

The verse sits deliberately between the principle that men and women have obligatory shares (4:7) and the detailed arithmetic for those shares (4:11–12). By placing generosity to bystanders between principle and calculation, the sūrah teaches that law and largesse belong together. The fixed shares protect heirs from being denied; this provision protects the wider circle from being forgotten. That balance reflects the Medinan context in which al-Nisāʾ was revealed, where a new community of migrants and hosts was learning to handle wealth without clan seizure. The Qur’an elsewhere praises those who give relatives, orphans, and the needy from what they love (2:177), and it lists providing for orphans and the needy among the signs of true piety. Here that same triad — relatives, orphans, needy — reappears at the very table where estates are divided, as though to say: let your first act with new wealth be to notice who is present. A distribution that begins with that notice is less likely to end with resentment.

**Learning the Habit Before the Fractions**

For modern readers the verse trains a habit that remains before any estate exists: to think of property as a trust that is divided by rule and softened by kindness. The heirs who have just received a share are immediately asked to become givers, even if only with a small provision and a kind word. That move prevents the new owner from hardening into a claimant who sees only his portion. The next verses will return to precise fractions and severe warnings about consuming orphans’ wealth (4:10) and about knowing who is more beneficial to you (4:11). This interim verse ensures those powerful passages are not heard in a mercenary spirit. A person who has learned to offer something to the relative who has no fixed share, to feed the orphan who came to watch, and to speak decently while doing so, is more ready to handle the arithmetic that follows with a heart that counts people as well as portions. The verse therefore does not interrupt the sūrah’s legal sequence; it humanises it.
verses.9:
> Let the guardians be as concerned ˹for the orphans˺ as they would if they were to ˹die and˺ leave ˹their own˺ helpless children behind. So let them be mindful of Allah and speak equitably

**Imagine Your Own Children Left Behind**

This verse asks the guardian to reverse perspectives. *Wa al-yakhsha alladhīna law tarakū min khalfihim dhurriyyatan ḍiʿāfan khāfū ʿalayhim* — let the guardians be as concerned for the orphans as they would if they were to die and leave their own helpless children behind. The image is specific: not children in general, but *dhurriyyatan ḍiʿāfan* — weak offspring, small children who cannot yet stand on their own, whose future depends on how others will treat them. Every guardian knows the fear that image brings. The Qur’an takes that natural fear and turns it into a rule for conduct. Deal with the orphan in your care the way you would want strangers to deal with your children tomorrow. That single substitution — put your child in the orphan’s place — does more work than a list of penalties, because it recruits love and worry on behalf of justice. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not kill your children out of fear of poverty”* (17:31) and praises those who prefer others over themselves, but here the appeal is quieter: remember your own vulnerability, and let that memory govern your hand when it holds another’s wealth.

**Be Mindful of Allah**

The command *fa al-yattaqū Allāh* — so let them be mindful of Allah — returns the sūrah to its opening word. Verse 1 began with *ittaqū rabbakum* — be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul — and verse 1 closed with *Allah is ever Watchful over you* (4:1). This verse’s call to *taqwā* therefore completes a short arch: creation to kinship to accountability. For the guardian, *taqwā* is not an abstract piety; it is caution in accounting, restraint in spending, promptness in testing and returning, and care in wording at distribution. The sūrah has already detailed those steps: return wealth without substitution (4:2), do not use marriage to discount dowries (4:3–4), do not hand wealth prematurely while still providing generously and speaking kindly (4:5), test and return with witnesses under God as Reckoner (4:6), honour fixed shares for both sexes (4:7). Offer provision to those present with decent words (4:8). This verse gathers those particulars into a posture. To be mindful of God here is to handle the orphan’s affair as one who knows he is watched while others cannot watch him.

**A Standard the Community Can Apply**

The verse’s test is portable beyond individual guardians. A judge settling an estate, a committee dividing a legacy, a family meeting to agree on shares — each can ask the same question: if these were my children left weak, what would I want the table to decide? That question does not replace the fixed shares of 4:11–12, but it governs the discretionary spaces around them — timing, valuation, generosity to those present, tone of words, and speed of return. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Allah is a Witness over all things”* (4:33) and *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6), and this verse places that watchfulness inside human imagination. Before the next verse warns that consuming orphans’ wealth is eating fire (4:10) and before the long arithmetic of inheritance begins, the sūrah secures the disposition that will make the arithmetic honest. It asks for fear that leads to *taqwā*, and for *taqwā* that leads to straight speech, and for speech that leads to action where the weak child, whether yours or another’s, is left neither unprotected nor unheard.
verses.10:
> Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies. And they will be burned in a blazing Hell

**Eating What Will Become Fire**

The image is stark and physical. *Inna alladhīna yaʾkulūna amwāl al-yatāmā ẓulman innamā yaʾkulūna fī buṭūnihim nāran* — those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth consume nothing but fire into their bellies. The Qur’an uses the verb *akala* — to eat — for illicit wealth elsewhere, as in *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29), but here the metaphor completes itself: what is eaten as wealth in this world will be present as fire in the stomach in the next. The restriction *ẓulman* — unjustly, wrongfully — is essential, because guardians do handle orphans’ property legitimately when they preserve it, invest it, and spend from it for the child’s need (4:5–6). What the verse condemns is consumption that is *ẓulm*, the putting of a thing where it does not belong, the use of a trust for the trustee’s own appetite. The sūrah has spent eight verses defining that trust — return without substitution (4:2), marriage without exploitation (4:3–4), provision without premature handover (4:5), testing and witnessing under divine reckoning (4:6–9) — and now it states the inner reality of violating that trust in a single picture. What felt like food will be felt as fire.

**What Counts as Unjust Consumption**

The qualifier *ẓulman* excludes legitimate management. Feeding and clothing the child from his property while keeping the principal as a standing support (4:5), investing with care, paying a fair provision to a poor guardian who works on the estate (4:6), and spending within what is recognized as fair — all of that is not eating unjustly. What remains forbidden is waste, haste before the child grows to claim his right (4:6), substitution of bad for good (4:2), and any use that serves the guardian’s household at the orphan’s expense. Jurists detailed many forms: taking a loan from the orphan’s funds without intent to return, selling his property cheaply to oneself, or charging an inflated fee for custody. The common element is benefit to the strong that corresponds to loss for the weak without the weak’s considered consent.

**The Second Half — Burning in a Blazing Hell**

The closing *wa sa yaṣlawna saʿīrā* adds the external fire to the internal one. *Saʿīr* — blazing, fierce — describes a fire that is already kindled and intense. The sūrah pairs this with *sa yaṣlawna* — they will be burned, they will roast — a verb that suggests direct contact, not distant punishment. The two fires — in the belly and in the blaze — mirror the two stages of the sin. First, the guardian made the orphan’s wealth his own food; then, that food becomes his own punishment. The Qur’an elsewhere warns *“do not kill yourselves”* and *“whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire, and that is easy for Allah”* (4:29–30), and this verse specifies one path to that Fire. The sūrah’s next movement will turn to the constructive counterpart — precise shares for children, parents, spouses, and siblings (4:11–12) — but it earns that turn by first clearing the ground of exploitation. No fair division can thrive where one party has already been eaten. By naming the meal as fire, the verse makes return and restraint feel not only lawful but self-preserving.

**How the Sequence Trains the Heart**

Read with what came before, verse 10 closes the opening guardianship cycle that began with *“be mindful of your Lord”* (4:1) and *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1). Verses 2–9 built the practices — give, do not mix, do not exploit marriage, sustain with kindness, test and witness, share, remember bystanders, imagine your own children — and verse 10 states the inner truth of failing them. That order matters for how law shapes character. The sūrah does not begin with fire; it begins with a common origin and a call to awareness, then details, then motive, and only then the stark image. By the time the reader hears *“they consume fire into their bellies,”* he has already been given every tool to avoid it.
verses.11:
> Allah commands you regarding your children: the share of the male will be twice that of the female. If you leave only two ˹or more˺ females, their share is two-thirds of the estate. But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half. Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring. But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third. But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. ˹Be fair to˺ your parents and children, as you do not ˹fully˺ know who is more beneficial to you. ˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**A Divine Command, Not a Family Suggestion**

The verse opens with *yūṣīkum Allāhu fī awlādikum* — Allah commands you about your children. The verb *yūṣī* carries the sense of a binding directive, a gift that the speaker expects to be carried out. By framing shares as something God commands, the Qur’an removes them from the realm of preference, negotiation, or clan custom. The community had just heard that men and women have obligatory shares whether little or much (4:7), and that the division should be witnessed and watched by God (4:6) and softened by provision for bystanders (4:8). The verse closes with *farīḍatan min Allāh* — an obligation from Allah — matching its opening and making clear that these portions are not advice about fairness; they are the fair measure set by the One who knows.

**After Gifts and Debts — The Standing Order**

The repeated clause *after the fulfilment of gifts and debts* appears three times across verses 11 and 12, anchoring the whole inheritance system in a clear order. A person’s debts travel with his estate before any heir is considered; the Qur’an elsewhere warns against harming heirs through a will, and the addition *ghayra muḍār* — without harm — in the next verse (4:12) makes that explicit. A gift that favours one heir over others, or that exceeds one-third when it reduces fixed shares, is counted as harm and therefore invalid. The phrase *“you know not which of them are nearer to you in benefit”* (4:11) explains why God fixed the shares rather than leaving them to affection.

**You Do Not Know Who Is More Beneficial**

The clause *ābāʾukum wa abnāʾukum lā tadrūna ayyuhum aqrabu lakum nafʿan* — your parents or your children, you do not know which are nearer to you in benefit — was read as both religious and practical. Theologically, benefit includes intercession, supplication, and the good deeds that continue after death; a child’s prayer or a parent’s loyalty may outweigh present utility. Practically, fortunes change, and the child who seemed least able may become the most supportive, or the parent thought independent may later need care. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse therefore asks the testator to surrender the illusion of foresight and to trust the division of the One described as *ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — All-Knowing, All-Wise. Those two Names close the verse for a reason. Knowledge covers every family configuration the law anticipates, and wisdom covers why the portions differ across tiers. The sūrah will repeat the same pair of Names after the spouse shares (4:12, 4:17, 4:26), creating a refrain that what seems intricate to people is known and wise with God. That refrain is not decoration; it is reassurance that the law is not arbitrary even where it is not immediately intuitive.

**An Obligation That Generates Knowledge**

The specificity of these verses produced a discipline. Because the fractions must be applied without error — halves, thirds, sixths, eighths, two-thirds — Muslim jurists developed the science of the shares, *ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ*, whose calculations require finding common denominators and handling residuary portions, a practice that contributed to the growth of algebra. The historical point matters because it shows how a verse read for family settlement generated tools for mathematics itself. More immediately, the verse taught the community that piety includes precision. Worship is not only prayer but also measuring correctly when emotion tempts to round up or round down. The sūrah will follow these shares with a promise — Gardens for those who keep God’s limits — and a warning — a humiliating punishment for those who transgress them (4:13–14) — showing that the arithmetic is also an act of obedience. A household that divides by these portions after debts and gifts, with witnesses and with *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) still echoing, has turned a potential quarrel into an act of submission. Has honoured both the parents and the children without claiming to know better than the One who assigned each a share.

**How the Shares Came Down**
The reports give the question behind the verse. The widow of Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ, one of the Helpers who was killed at Badr, came to the Prophet with her daughters: the family's property had been taken by the clan, and the girls had been left with nothing, since the custom of the Arabs gave the inheritance to the men who could ride and fight rather than to women and children. The verses of the shares came down, and the daughters received their two-thirds, the parents their portions, and the widow her own share. The sūrah states the change in its own words when it says that men and women both have a rightful share in what parents and relatives leave, whether it is little or much (4:7), a sentence aimed at the same custom. The law did not adjust the old division; it cancelled its principle and replaced the clan's discretion with fixed portions.

**The Third, and the Limit of a Bequest**
The clause that the shares come into force after a bequest and a debt was read with the Prophet's words to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who asked whether he might will away his whole property. The Prophet allowed him a third and said that a third was much, and that to leave his heirs rich was better than to leave them dependent on people's charity (al-Bukhārī). The schools took the third as the outer limit for a will to a stranger, while a group of the early scholars read the Book's mention of the bequest as a duty owed; whatever the difference, the order the verse states is fixed — debts first, then the will, then the portions the verse has named. The closing names, All-Knowing and All-Wise, answer every case a reader cannot work out for himself: the One who set the portions knows the families the portions will fall among.
verses.12:
> You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless. But if they have children, then ˹your share is˺ one-fourth of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless. But if you have children, then your wives will receive one-eighth of your estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister ˹from their mother’s side˺, they will each inherit one-sixth, but if they are more than one, they ˹all˺ will share one-third of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm ˹to the heirs˺. ˹This is˺ a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing

**Shares for Spouses After the Children’s Shares**

This verse completes the fixed portions begun in the previous one by turning from children and parents to spouses and siblings. The husband inherits one-half of his wife’s estate when she leaves no child, and one-fourth when she leaves a child; the wife inherits one-fourth of her husband’s estate when he leaves no child, and one-eighth when he leaves a child. The pattern is consistent: the presence of offspring reduces the spouse’s share because the offspring themselves have the larger fixed claims detailed in *“Allah commands you regarding your children”* (4:11). The Qur’an counts grandchildren through a son among children for this purpose, and it directs that where there is more than one wife — the sūrah having limited wives to four (4:3) — the one-fourth or one-eighth is divided equally among them. That last point matters because it shows how the sūrah’s earlier permission is immediately bounded by arithmetic. A man who takes an additional wife does not create an additional estate share; the existing share is partitioned. The fractions are therefore not only about entitlement but about keeping the household’s expectations inside a known economy.

**After Gifts and Debts — Without Harm**

The refrain *min baʿdi waṣiyyatin yūṣā bihā aw dayn* — after gifts and debts — appears for a third and fourth time, with the addition *ghayra muḍār* — without harm to the heirs — attached to this verse. The sūrah’s earlier command to be mindful of God when handling orphans’ wealth (4:9) and its warning that consuming it is eating fire (4:10) find a legal counterpart here: the estate is not a private hoard to dispose of at whim; it is a measured trust whose portions are already set.

**Why the Shares Differ Between Husband and Wife**

The difference between half and quarter, and between quarter and eighth, at times raises the same question as the two-to-one share among children: why not equal? The husband is charged with maintenance — *“Men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially”* (4:34) — and his larger share corresponds to the larger ongoing obligation he bears after the estate is divided. The wife’s share, while smaller, is hers alone, to keep and to dispose of as she wishes, and the sūrah has already secured that autonomy with *“Give women their due dowries graciously”* (4:4) and with the protection of her property in guardianship rules. The closing Names — *“Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing”* (4:12) — frame that structure with knowledge of every household’s needs and forbearance toward those who find the division difficult to accept.

**A Commandment That Closes With Forbearance**

The verse ends with *waṣiyyatan min Allāh wa Allāhu ʿAlīmun Ḥalīm* — a commandment from Allah, and Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing. To call the fractions a *waṣiyyah* from God places them beside the human gifts just mentioned but above them. A person’s gift is his wish; God’s *waṣiyyah* is law. Yet the Name that follows is not only All-Knowing but also Forbearing — *Ḥalīm* — the One who does not hasten to punish. That forbearance is directed at recipients who may struggle with the division, especially the intense moment when a spouse or sibling is present and the reduced share feels personal. The sūrah will immediately follow with *“These are the limits set by Allah”* (4:13) and the promise of Gardens for keeping them and Fire for crossing them (4:13–14), showing that forbearance does not remove accountability. It simply marks that the lawgiver knows the difficulty and still asks for compliance. In that light, the precise arithmetic of half, quarter, eighth, sixth, and third becomes more than calculation; it becomes the measured way a community that began from a single soul (4:1) learns to part with wealth at death without parting from one another.

**The Shares and the Principle Behind Them**
The verse fixes the shares of the husband and the wife and then turns to the brothers and sisters on the mother's side, and the rules it lays down follow a system rather than a set of numbers. The whole passage arranges the inheritance in order of nearness: the children first, then the parents, then the spouse, then the uterine siblings, with the residue going to the nearest male relative. The jurists built the science of inheritance on this passage and on the verse of the shares in the same sūrah (4:11), and they named the obligations it settles as the fixed portions that no will may reduce beyond a third.
**What the Verse Adjusts**
The verse gives the husband half if there is no child and a quarter if there is one, and the wife a quarter if there is no child and an eighth if there is one, and it treats the uterine siblings as sharers who take equal portions regardless of sex, which differs from the treatment of full siblings in the previous verse. The commentators noted the difference and explained it as the Book's own arrangement rather than an inconsistency, and the schools worked out the cases of combination — a wife with a child and parents, a husband with brothers, and so on — from the arithmetic of the two verses read together.
**The Occasion and the Care Taken**
The reports connect the passage with the years in Madinah, when the community had property, widows and orphans to provide for, and the Book went into the detail because the subject had already caused disputes. The sūrah opens with the command to give the orphans their property (4:2) and it warns the guardians in the strongest terms about eating it (4:10), and the verses on the shares follow immediately. The Book's arrangement puts the duty to the weak before the arithmetic of the estate, and the law of inheritance in the community has been read in that order ever since.
verses.13:
> These ˹entitlements˺ are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. That is the ultimate triumph

**Gardens Under Which Rivers Flow as the Appropriate Reward**

The description *jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā* — Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever — appears across the Qur’an as the counter to the quarrel over portions. The inheritance code divided fixed pools; the Garden is described as water that does not need to be divided because it flows continuously and suffices all. The sūrah elsewhere promises that avoiding major sins leads to being absolved of lesser ones and admitted to a place of honour (4:31), and this verse shows one concrete major limit whose keeping leads to that honour. The language of permanence — *khālidīna fīhā* — staying forever — answers the impermanence of estates. What a person surrendered in this world — a fraction he thought was his, a gift he was tempted to write to harm others — returns as a dwelling that does not shrink or expire. The Qur’an elsewhere contrasts the brief enjoyment of this world with the lasting home of the next (4:77), and the same contrast operates here. The limits on wealth today secure wealth that never needs dividing tomorrow.

**That Is the Ultimate Triumph**

The closing *wa dhālika al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm* — that is the ultimate triumph — names the outcome as success on the largest scale. *Fawz* in the Qur’an is not only entering a pleasant place; it is being delivered from the Fire and admitted to the Garden, as the next verse will make explicit by describing the opposite. The phrase appears elsewhere for those who obey and keep trusts, and it gathers both the inner and outer dimensions of triumph: right relation with God and lasting well-being for the self. By placing that phrase immediately after the fractions, the verse teaches that the triumph is not in securing a larger share through pressure, but in receiving the share God assigned and trusting His promise about what follows. Al-Rāzī observes that the sūrah deliberately links the technical laws of inheritance to the highest religious promise, so that no one treats them as secondary or worldly. What looks like civil law is placed on the same ledger as faith and worship. A person who divides an estate while mindful that *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1) and that *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) is already living the triumph the verse names.

**Why the Promise Comes Here Before the Threat**

The sūrah gives the Garden before the Fire, the reward before the warning. The list of shares was demanding in a context where Male relatives had taken full estates; to hear first that keeping the limits leads to perpetual Gardens makes the demand feel like guidance rather than burden. The sūrah will shortly add *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak”* (4:28), and this promise already lightens the specific burden of parting with wealth by showing what parting correctly secures.

**The Limits That Hold the Community Together**

Read with verses 7 through 12, this verse seals the sūrah’s first legal suite with theology. Creation from a single soul taught that all are kin (4:1); trust laws taught that the strong must guard the weak (4:2–10); inheritance laws taught that every close heir has a named portion after debts and gifts (4:11–12). Now the sūrah lifts those portions and says they are *ḥudūd* — limits — whose keeping is obedience and whose breach is disobedience. The following verse will state the other side — humiliating punishment for crossing them — but this verse is allowed to stand first and to linger. It suggests that a community that respects divine limits in its most sensitive moment — when grief and greed meet over a loved one’s goods — builds a habit that steadies every other limit. Gardens under which rivers flow, forever, is the sūrah’s way of saying that what is surrendered at the division table is not lost; it is transformed. The measurer who gave each his due and sought no more has kept faith with the limits, and with the One who set them.
verses.14:
> But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds their limits will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever. And they will suffer a humiliating punishment

**The Other Side of the Limits**

The previous verse named the shares *ḥudūd Allāh* — limits set by Allah — and promised Gardens for those who obey Allah and His Messenger in those limits (4:13). This verse states the counterpart without softening: *wa man yaʿṣi Allāha wa rasūlahu wa yataʿadda ḥudūdahu yudkhilhu nāran khālidan fīhā* — whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds His limits will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever. The verb *yataʿadda* — to exceed, to overstep — pictures a foot crossing a marked line. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“whoever transgresses Allah’s limits has wronged his own soul”* (65:1), and that self-wrong is made visible here as a lasting abode.

**Abiding Forever and a Humiliating Punishment**

The threat is doubled in a way that matches the promise before it. The promise spoke of Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay forever, and called that the ultimate triumph (4:13); the warning speaks of Fire, to stay forever, and calls it a humiliating punishment — *ʿadhābun muhīn*. The adjective *muhīn* — humiliating, debasing — was chosen because the sin itself was a try at self-exaltation. The heir who seized more did so to appear stronger, to keep the estate consolidated, to show that custom outweighs revelation. The recompense humbles precisely that pride. Commentators noted the symmetry: the one who kept the limits was honoured with rivers and permanence; the one who exceeded them is debased with fire and permanence. The sūrah has been training that posture since *“be mindful of your Lord”* (4:1) and *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1); this verse states what becomes of a person who lives as though no watch was kept.

**What Exceeding the Limits Looks Like**

Exceeding the limits is not a single form. It includes refusing to pay the daughter or sister her share, reducing the wife’s quarter or eighth on the pretext of expenses, inflating a debt to shrink the estate before division, writing a gift beyond one-third to disadvantage fixed heirs, or taking from an orphan’s portion before it is returned (4:10). Prophetic tradition invalidated gifts that favour a fixed heir, precisely to block the most pious-seeming way of exceeding — the deathbed gift that rewrites God’s fractions. The sūrah will later warn generally *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29) and will say that doing so sinfully and unjustly leads to being burned in the Fire, where *“that is easy for Allah”* (4:30). This verse is the specific application of that general warning to the inheritance code. It tells the family gathered around the estate that the line they are tempted to move is not theirs to move. The fractions after gifts and debts (4:11–12) are not a starting offer; they are the limit. To cross them is to take what was not assigned, and the verse gives that taking its final name.

**Disobedience to the Messenger in a Legal Matter**

The addition *wa rasūlahu* — and His Messenger — deserves attention because the shares were among the most detailed laws recited by the Messenger ﷺ. His role was not only to convey the verses but to show how to apply them: which relatives count as child, which siblings count as kalālah, how debts precede gifts, how the residue is handled, how witnesses secure the handover (4:6). To disobey in these details is therefore to refuse the very explanation that makes the limits practicable. The Qur’an elsewhere links guidance and clarification — *“Allah wishes to make things clear to you and guide you to the noble ways of those before you”* (4:26) — and this verse shows what follows when clarity is rejected. A community that accepts the Messenger’s clarification finds its divisions manageable; a person who sets it aside finds the division becomes a quarrel and then a sin. The sūrah’s repeated closing Names — All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26), All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12) — frame that clarification as knowledge coupled with forbearance, so that the warning here is not abrupt but earned. Clarity was given; limits were drawn; recompense was named.
verses.15:
> ˹As for˺ those of your women who commit illegal intercourse—call four witnesses from among yourselves. If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them

**Four Witnesses and Testimony**

The number four was explained as demanding direct sight, not hearsay, inference, or circumstance. Jurists detailed that the witnesses must have seen the act itself in a way that leaves no ambiguity, a standard so high that it is rarely met, which is itself the point. The law makes the crime grave, the proof grave, and the consequence of false testimony grave, so that the social fabric is protected on both sides. The witnesses must be *minkum* — from among you — which the majority understood as upright members of the Muslim community, not outsiders with unknown motives. The sūrah will shortly turn to repentance for those who act ignorantly and then repent soon after (4:17), showing that even where proof might exist, the door to return is not closed arbitrarily.

**Confinement Until Death or Until Another Way**

The sentence *fa in shahidū fa amsikūhunna fī al-buyūt ḥattā yatawaffāhunna al-mawtu aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* — if they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die or Allah ordains a different way — sets a holding measure rather than a fixed corporal penalty. Early authorities understood this confinement as a stage in legislation. At this point in the Medinan period, the community was ordered to keep the women in their homes, both as protection for society and as prevention of further transgression, while awaiting what God would ordain as a way — *sabīl*. Commentators relate that the different way came later through verses on lashing for fornication (24:2) and through Prophetic clarification for adultery where marriage has occurred. The phrase *aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* therefore signals that the law is not yet in its final form; it is awaiting a clarified path. That language of waiting is characteristic of the Qur’an’s gradual legislation, where a ruling is given, held, and then completed. The sūrah will soon emphasize that Allah wishes to make things clear and to guide to the ways of those before, and to turn to you in mercy (4:26), and this temporary confinement is one place where clarity arrived in stages.

**Why Confinement and Why a Way Out**

Confinement to homes — *amsikūhunna fī al-buyūt* — was read in two lights. The until clause — *ḥattā yatawaffāhunna al-mawtu aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* — holds two possibilities open: life-long seclusion if no new ruling comes, or a new ordained way if God provides it. The sūrah elsewhere commands *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and describes God as ever Merciful (4:29), and even in this severe matter it leaves the future open to mercy through another way.

**Between Justice and Mercy**

Placed after the inheritance code and before the verses on repentance, this verse shows how the sūrah holds justice and mercy together without confusing them. The act is named without euphemism, the proof is set at the highest bar, the interim sanction is custodial rather than corporal, and the future is left explicitly to what God will ordain. That structure prevents two equal errors: treating a grave breach as if it were trivial, and treating accusation as if it were proof. The next verses will broaden the picture: both parties who commit the sin are to be disciplined and then relieved if they repent (4:16), and repentance itself has a time and a limit (4:17–18). This verse focuses on one side of the pair and on the evidential threshold that must be crossed before any sanction applies. By insisting on four and by naming the confinement as until death or until another way, the Qur’an keeps the law both firm and open — firm enough to protect the family, open enough to await the completion of its own legislation. Throughout mindful that the One who ordains the way is the One who is All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26).

The Qur’an elsewhere warns that accusing chaste women without four witnesses brings the accusers themselves to punishment (24:4).
verses.16:
> And the two among you who commit this sin—discipline them. If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them. Surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful

**What Discipline Meant at This Stage**

Commentators described *ādhūhumā* as verbal reproach, harsh words, striking with sandals, or other forms of public disapproval that make the offenders feel the community’s rejection without exceeding what the law authorizes. The purpose was deterrence and moral signalling: the household and neighbours see that the act is not treated as private taste but as *fāḥishah* that damages lineage and trust. At the same time, the discipline was not meant to become a second injustice. The sūrah’s broader ethic of *qawlan maʿrūfā* — speaking kindly where due (4:5, 4:8) — remains the norm for ordinary relations; here, a different register — *adhā* — applies because the act itself breached the trust those kind words normally protect. The distinction matters. The community is not asked to be harsh generally; it is asked to be clearly disapproving where a boundary that guards families has been crossed. The Qur’an elsewhere commands *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and elsewhere describes God as ever Merciful (4:29), so even this disciplinary moment is framed as protection, not cruelty.

**Ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful**

The closing *inn Allāha kāna tawwāban raḥīmā* — surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful — gives the reason for relieving. *Tawwāb* stresses repetition: the One who accepts repentance again and again, not once. *Raḥīm* stresses the mercy that follows acceptance. The pair appears together where the Qur’an wants to emphasize that God’s mercy is not reluctant. The sūrah elsewhere says *“Allah wishes to turn to you in mercy, but those who follow desires wish you to deviate entirely”* (4:27), and *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak”* (4:28). Those wishes frame this verse’s command to relieve.

**A Ruling Held Until a Way Was Ordained**

As with the previous verse’s *“until Allah ordains a different way for them”* (4:15), this verse’s disciplinary measure was understood as an interim stage. Later revelation specified *“As for the fornicatress and the fornicator, lash each of them with a hundred lashes”* (24:2), and Prophetic practice clarified the penalty for the married adulterer, showing that the community had been held in a preparatory discipline until the final way — *sabīl* — was given. Recognizing that progression prevents two misreadings: that the early verse’s confinement or the second verse’s *adhā* remains the final law, or that the later penalties negate the mercy that these early verses displayed. The progression is additive: the early verses taught procedural caution, shared accountability, measured social discipline, and an open door to return; the later verses kept that caution and added precise penalties where proof and conditions were met. The through line is consistent. The law guards lineage from the act, guards the accused from unproven accusation, and guards the repentant from endless shaming.

**Shared Fault and Shared Mercy**

Read together, verses 15 and 16 form a careful balance. One verse sets a high evidentiary bar and a custodial measure for women, with a future way awaited; the next sets shared discipline for the pair and a clear exit when repentance and mending appear. Both verses refuse to treat illicit intercourse as trivial, and both refuse to treat the offender as beyond return. The sūrah’s surrounding chapters on wealth and marriage show why that balance matters here. Family property is guarded by witnesses and reckoning (4:6); family honour is guarded by witnesses as well (4:15); both guards exist because trust is easy to break in private. Yet trust can also be restored. The command to relieve those who have repented and mended teaches that restoration has a form: stop the harm. That form becomes a habit the sūrah will extend beyond this case, into speaking equitably (4:9), trading by mutual consent (4:29), and appointing mediators when a split is feared (4:35). In each, the law asks not only for justice against wrong but for a path back when wrong is amended, because the One who judges is ever Accepting, Most Merciful.
verses.17:
> Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repent soon after—Allah will pardon them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Allah Will Pardon Them**

The promise *fa ulāʾika yatūbu Allāhu ʿalayhim* — Allah will pardon them — places the act of turning on God’s side as well. The same root *t-w-b* is used for the servant’s repentance and for God’s acceptance; the servant turns to God, and God turns to the servant with pardon. The doubling shows that forgiveness is not earned by a formula but received as a turn from the other side. The verse does not require the penitent to offer a ransom or to perform an exact counterweight; it requires ignorance acknowledged, speed in returning, and mending where mending is due, as the previous verse added *wa aṣlaḥā* — and they mend their ways (4:16). When those appear, God’s turn follows as a matter of His own commitment, expressed as *ʿalā Allāhi* — upon Allah — a phrasing that signals a promise He has laid upon Himself in mercy. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Allah loves those who constantly turn to Him”* (2:222), and the same love is implied here where the return is accepted soon. That love is not indiscriminate; it distinguishes the one who returns quickly from the one who persists until the final hour.

**All-Knowing, All-Wise**

The closing *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise — gives the measure by which repentance is judged. *ʿAlīm* knows the state of the heart when the sin was committed — whether it was heedlessness, arrogance, or confusion — and knows the sincerity of the return — whether it was immediate or delayed, full or partial. *Ḥakīm* places that knowledge inside wisdom: not every regret is wisdom, and not every delay is pardonable. The pair appears after the inheritance shares (4:11) and will appear again after the clarification of law (4:26) for the same reason.

**Ignorance and the Broader Pattern of the Sūrah**

The sūrah has been defining ignorance not as lack of intelligence but as acting without the restraint that knowledge should bring. That is why it pairs this verse with earlier pictures of hasty consumption before the orphan grows up (4:6), mixing wealth to make use easier (4:2), and inheriting women against their will (4:19) — all acts where the actor knows the roster of right yet follows appetite. The remedy is not more information alone but a quick return — *min qarīb* — while the heart is still soft. The Qur’an elsewhere describes the believer’s speed: *“those who, when they commit an indecent act or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins”* (3:135), and that remembering is presented as immediate. The same immediacy is asked here. A community that learns to turn soon — to stop the act, to amend, to seek forgiveness — builds the reflex that keeps smaller wrongs from becoming the major sins whose avoidance secures forgiveness for lesser ones (4:31). The verse therefore trains a habit more than it defines a threshold. The threshold will be defined by death in the next verse; the habit is defined here as soon.

**A Promise That Invites Speed**

Read with what follows, this verse is an invitation to hurry toward mercy. The next verse will close the window for those who persist until they are dying and only then say now I repent, and for those who die as disbelievers (4:18). The promise is not conditional on human witnesses or on the discipline being lifted by the community (4:16); it is a direct turn from God to the servant. The same One who set limits around property and family (4:13) and who is ever Watchful (4:1) is the One who is ever Accepting when the return is real and soon.

The Qur’an elsewhere describes wrongdoing as done out of ignorance and then followed by repentance and reform (6:54), showing that the category is broad enough to include many who will later be forgiven.
verses.18:
> However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, “Now I repent!” nor those who die as disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment

**Nor Those Who Die as Disbelievers**

The verse adds *wa lā alladhīna yamūtūna wa hum kuffār* — nor those who die as disbelievers. Both end in the same preparation: *ulāʾika aʿtadnā lahum ʿadhāban alīmā* — for them We have prepared a painful punishment. The verb *aʿtadnā* — We have prepared — stresses that the recompense is not improvised at the moment; it has been readied, as Gardens were readied for those who obey limits (4:13). Two verses earlier, those who obey limits enter Gardens to stay forever; here, those who persist until death face a penalty already prepared and described as painful — *alīm* — because the wrong persisted was itself a cause of pain to others and to the soul that chose it. The sūrah elsewhere says *“whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire, and that is easy for Allah”* (4:30), and this verse specifies one of the easiest ways to fall into that Fire — by treating time as endless.

**Knowingly Persisting Versus Acting Ignorantly**

The contrast between 4:17 and 4:18 turns on the state during the act. Verse 17 spoke of *bi jahālah* — ignorantly, heedlessly — while 4:18 speaks of persistence — *yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāt* as a continuing practice until death arrives.
