Persisting was understood by early commentators not as a single grave sin committed once in ignorance and then regretted, but as a settled habit where the person knows what he does and keeps doing it while postponing return. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“they do not persist in what they did while they know”* (3:135), praising those who, when they err, remember and do not persist. That praise implies that the blameworthy pattern is knowing and persisting. The sūrah has already shown what persisting looks like in other domains: consuming an orphan’s wealth hastily before he grows up to demand it (4:6), mixing wealth to make use easier (4:2), inheriting women against their will and then pressuring them to surrender dowries (4:19). Each is a case where the actor knows the roster of right yet continues because the victim cannot yet speak or because death seems distant.

**Prepared Punishment and the Sūrah’s Pattern**

The closing *aʿtadnā lahum ʿadhāban alīmā* gathers this verse into the sūrah’s larger pattern of prepared recompense. Those who keep limits receive Gardens prepared and described as flowing water (4:13); those who eat orphan wealth unjustly are told they eat fire in their bellies and will burn in a blazing Hell (4:10); those who cross limits receive a humiliating punishment and abiding in Fire (4:14). This verse adds the temporal border to that pattern: the Garden remains open while repentance remains soon (4:17); the painful punishment becomes prepared when soon is replaced by until death. The lesson for the living is not to measure the exact length of soon but to remove delay as a plan. The Qur’an elsewhere praises *“those who, when they commit an indecent act or wrong themselves, remember Allah immediately and seek forgiveness”* (3:135), and the praise rests on immediacy. The sūrah’s earlier promise that *“if you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of lesser misdeeds”* (4:31) also depends on the habit of turning quickly from smaller faults before they harden into major persistence. Delay is the bridge between small and great; this verse cuts that bridge by naming its end.

**The Mercy That Remains While Breath Remains**

Read with the verses that opened the sūrah, this warning is also a mercy. The call to be mindful of the Lord who created all from a single soul (4:1), to return orphan wealth with witnesses under God as Reckoner (4:6). To accept discipline and then be relieved when mending appears (4:16) — all of this assumes that breath remains and that a turn is still possible. The sūrah does not treat a person who fell ignorantly as finished; it says Allah will pardon those who turn soon (4:17).
verses.19:
> O believers! It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will or mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry ˹as a ransom for divorce˺—unless they are found guilty of adultery. Treat them fairly. If you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing

The verse opens with a prohibition that corrects a pre-Islamic practice by naming it for what it was: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā yaḥillu lakum a tarithū al-nisāʾa karhan* — O believers, it is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will. The woman is not an asset to be divided after debts and gifts; she is a heir in her own right (4:7, 4:12) and a party to a covenant described as *“a firm commitment”* (4:21). After settling that wives have a fixed share and that dowries belong graciously to the woman herself (4:4), the sūrah must ensure that widowhood does not become a loophole where those rights are seized back through control of the person.

**Treat Them Fairly**

The positive command *wa ʿāshirūhunna bi al-maʿrūf* — treat them fairly, live with them in kindness — uses the same root *ʿ-r-f* that elsewhere describes decent speech and customary good — *qawlan maʿrūfā* (4:5, 4:8) and *qawlan sadīdā* (4:9). *Maʿrūf* here is not only avoidance of harm; it is active companionship that is recognized as good — provision without stinginess, conversation without contempt, and intimacy without coercion. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and describes God as ever Merciful (4:29); that mercy is to appear in the home as well. The command to live with women in kindness was read to include what the next verses will detail: giving the dowry, not reclaiming it unjustly, not marrying the former wives of fathers (4:22), and respecting the full list of prohibited degrees (4:23). To live with a wife *bi al-maʿrūf* is therefore to keep the whole marriage ethic the sūrah is building: consent in entry, generosity in maintenance, equity if there is more than one wife (4:3, 4:129), and fairness in separation where it comes. The short phrase carries a long practice, because what is recognized as good is what a faithful community would recognize, not what a private preference would justify.

**If You Happen to Dislike Them**

The verse adds a counsel that reaches the heart at its most private: *fa in karihtumūhunna fa ʿasā a takrahū shayʾan wa yajʿalu Allāhu fīhi khayran kathīrā* — if you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing. The same theme recurs elsewhere: *“perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you”* (2:216). The sūrah’s earlier refrain that *“humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and that God wishes to lighten burdens (4:28) is already anticipated here: dislike is a weakness. The law lightens it not by forcing immediate release through harm but by asking for fair companionship and by promising that what is kept for God’s sake may yield more than what is seized in haste.

**From Creation to Kind Companionship**

This verse returns the sūrah to its first note: *“He created you from a single soul, and from it its mate, and spread from both countless men and women”* (4:1), and *“Allah is ever Watchful over you”* (4:1). If humanity shares one origin and the Watcher is present in every transaction, then the widow is not an extra to be claimed and the wife is not a debtor to be squeezed. Both are the mate created from the single soul, the partner in spreading, the one whose womb-tie shares a root with mercy. To live with them *bi al-maʿrūf* is therefore not an additional virtue beyond law; it is the law’s completion. The sūrah has moved from dividing estates to dividing households, and it keeps the same standard: fixed rights honored, voluntary gifts left voluntary, and dislike handled with patience rather than pressure. A husband who finds himself disliking his wife is told to remain fair in company and to trust that God may place abundant good in what he currently dislikes. That trust is the counterpart to *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) for orphans and to *“Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing”* (4:12) for heirs.
verses.20:
> If you desire to replace a wife with another and you have given the former ˹even˺ a stack of gold ˹as a dowry˺, do not take any of it back. Would you ˹still˺ take it unjustly and very sinfully

**Why the Qur’an Uses the Wish to Replace**

The phrase *istibdāla zawjin makāna zawj* was read not as a recommendation to replace but as a description of a case that will occur. The Qur’an does not encourage divorce to marry another; elsewhere it describes divorce as a hated permitted matter and it sets careful procedure for it. What the verse does is attach a protection to that case when it happens. The man who has decided to replace speaks from a position of power: he is the one initiating change, and he holds the leverage of maintenance, housing, and social expectation. The sūrah, which began with *“be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul”* (4:1) and which has guarded the orphan’s wealth with witnesses (4:6) and the heir’s share with limits (4:13–14), now guards the wife’s wealth at the precise moment when the husband’s power is greatest.

**Dowry as Permanent Gift**

The thought that a large gift might be reclaimed rests on treating the dowry as a price for continued marriage rather than as a gift that seals a covenant. The Qur’an rejects that treatment with language that will follow in the next verse: *“how could you take it after you have enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment?”* (4:21). The word *ifḍāʾ* — intimate going through — conveys the privacy and completeness of married life, while *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — firm, weighty covenant — recalls the covenant language used for prophets and for God’s own bond with humanity. Between those two facts — shared intimacy and a weighty pledge — there is no room to treat the bridal gift as a conditional loan. The sūrah has consistently moved wealth toward its owner and then kept it there: the orphan’s property to the orphan (4:2, 4:6), the bystander’s provision from the estate with kind speech (4:8), the heirs’ obligatory shares (4:7, 4:11–12). Here it moves the dowry to the wife and keeps it there, even when the marriage ends and even when the amount is a heap. The consistency is the point. What God has made obligatory is not to be undone by a change of desire.

**Unjust and Very Sinful — Two Names for One Taking**

The verse’s double accusation — *buhtānan wa ithman mubīnan* — was explained as covering both the method and the substance. *Buhtān* covers the false justification: to take the gift, the taker must invent a fault, magnify a dislike, or claim a right that does not exist, especially after being told to live with a wife fairly even when dislike occurs and to trust that God may place abundant good in what is disliked (4:19). *Ithm* covers the taking itself: it violates the law that gave the dowry as *ṣaduqah* with *niḥlah* and that permitted return only with *ṭīb al-nafs* — a contented soul (4:4). The sūrah’s earlier warning that consuming orphans’ wealth is eating fire (4:10) and that exceeding limits brings humiliating punishment (4:14) belongs to the same pedagogy: the true name of the act deters where the desire invites.

**The Ethic That Holds Across Replaceability**

Read with the previous verse’s *“live with them fairly”* (4:19) and the next verse’s *“a firm commitment”* (4:21), this verse forms a short sequence that teaches how to act when attachment changes. The first says be fair while you live together, even when you dislike. The second says do not reclaim a heap when you decide to replace. The third asks how could you take it after intimacy and covenant. Together they form an ethic that does not depend on continuity of feeling. The gift was given sincerely — *ṣaduqah* — as a sign of truthfulness at the start; it must be left sincerely at the end, even when the start feels distant. That ethic extends beyond dowry to any entrusted wealth. The sūrah has been training the reader to handle property as a trust watched by God (4:1), reckoned by Him (4:6), and bounded by Him (4:13).
verses.21:
> And how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment

**A Firm Commitment She Has Taken From You**

The second fact *wa qad akhadhna minkum mīthāqan ghalīẓā* — and she has taken from you a firm commitment — reframes the dowry as part of a covenant, not a payment for a service. *Mīthāq ghalīẓ* — firm, weighty covenant — is language the Qur’an uses for the bond God took from the prophets and from the Children of Israel, a solemn pledge that is not set aside lightly. The gift that accompanied that word — the *ṣaduqah* with *niḥlah* (4:4) — shares its weight. Once that covenant has been040 entered and lived, the wealth transferred under it acquires a permanence that even a later wish to replace the wife (4:20) cannot dissolve.

**Intimacy and Covenant Together Close the Door**

The verse places two facts side by side to close every justification. *Afḍā* answers the thought that the marriage was brief or formal and therefore the gift can be reclaimed. Even a short shared intimacy creates a bond whose gift is not retrievable. *Mīthāq ghalīẓ* answers the thought that vows are light and that a heap of gold deserves reconsideration when circumstances change; the pledge was weighty from the start and remains so. Together they show that the dowry is not a deposit held against performance but a settled transfer that belongs to the woman whether the marriage continues or ends. The sūrah has guarded that transfer from the beginning: given graciously (4:4), not to be reclaimed by pressuring the wife to ransom herself (4:19), and not to be taken even when the husband wishes to replace his wife (4:20). This verse completes the guard by giving it a human and a legal reason. The human reason is shared life; the legal reason is a firm covenant. Both say the same thing: what was given freely under a weighty pledge stays with the one to whom it was given.

**Why the Question Form Teaches More Than a Prohibition**

A direct prohibition — do not take it — would have sufficed legally, as the previous verse gave (4:20). It asks the husband to imagine the conversation where he asks for the heap back after months or years of *ifḍāʾ* and after a *mīthāq ghalīẓ* was accepted in front of witnesses. The scene itself exposes the request as shameful without needing to add a new penalty. Elsewhere the sūrah pairs law with an invitation to reflect on what is disliked possibly holding abundant good (4:19); here it pairs law with an invitation to feel the incoherence of demanding back a pledge gift after intimacy. That method is consistent with the sūrah’s earlier pedagogy of asking the guardian to imagine his own weak children left behind (4:9) before handling an orphan’s wealth.

**The Gift That Marked Truthfulness Remains True**

The root of *ṣaduqah* — truthfulness — helps answer the question. A dowry given as *ṣaduqah* was a sign that the husband’s word was sincere at the time. To reclaim it after intimacy and covenant is to act as though that sincerity can be withdrawn retroactively. The Qur’an treats truthfulness as a quality that, once shown in a covenant, should not be contradicted by later advantage. Other passages describe marital life as *“dwelling in tranquility”* with affection and mercy placed between spouses (30:21), and the same tranquility is injured when wealth given to mark truth is seized back. The verse therefore does more than settle a financial rule; it protects the meaning of the sign. A community that learns to leave the *qinṭār* where it was placed learns to mean what it pledged. That habit extends beyond marriage to every firm commitment the sūrah governs — witnesses at handover (4:6), limits in inheritance (4:13–14), and trade by mutual consent (4:29). In each, the pledge and the lived history make return or seizure incoherent. Here the pledge is the firmest named — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — and the history is the closest known — *afḍā* — so the incoherence of taking back is made most visible.
verses.22:
> Do not marry former wives of your fathers—except what was done previously. It was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice

**Why the Father’s Wife Is Singled Out**

The fuller list of prohibited degrees will follow immediately (4:23), naming mothers, daughters, sisters, aunts, nieces, foster-mothers and sisters, mothers-in-law, stepdaughters under guardianship where the mother’s marriage was consummated, sons’ wives, and two sisters together. This verse stands before that list as a separate, emphatic prohibition because the father’s widow had been treated differently from other relatives in custom. She was not seen as a mother, yet she held the father’s place in the household. The Qur’an treats her as inviolable for marriage to the son not because she is biologically a mother but because the father’s intimate covenant deserves reverence after his death. The same principle appears in the protection of dowries as a firm commitment (4:21); both teach that intimacy creates limits that outlive the moment. To marry the father’s former wife erases the distinction between father and son and turns the widow’s waiting period into an auction. By forbidding it with the three names, the verse restores the father’s honour, secures the widow’s freedom to be treated as a person with her own share and choice, and clarifies lineage for inheritance that depends on clear degrees.

**Except What Was Done Previously**

The clause except what was done earlier functions as clemency and as a limit. It tells those who had already contracted such a marriage before revelation that they are not to be punished retroactively, but they are to separate going forward. Jurists understood *mā qad salaf* here as annulling the continuity of such unions, requiring separation where the marriage still stood, while not treating the prior act as sin with worldly penalty where it was done in ignorance of the coming law. The same phrasing for two sisters together in the next verse (4:23) was read similarly, while the later clarification *“Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”* (4:23) confirms that repentance and correction are accepted. That pairing of prohibition and forbearance reflects the sūrah’s broader pattern of setting limits — *ḥudūd* — and then showing the path back for those who had crossed them before the limit was drawn. The sūrah has already linked limits to Gardens and Fire (4:13–14) and has defined soon repentance versus delayed words at death (4:17–18). Here it applies that pattern to family formation: the limit is now clear, the past is pardoned where it was done without that clarity, and persistence after clarity changes the moral status completely.

**Honouring the Father Without Inheriting the Woman**

The verse’s prohibition complements the earlier verse that forbade inheriting women against their will (4:19). There, the practice was to inherit widows as part of the estate; here, the specific form is the son taking the father’s widow. Both practices share the same error: treating a woman as transferable property rather than as a rights-bearing person who has her own obligatory share (4:7, 4:12), her own dowry (4:4), and her own choice. The sūrah’s opening — *“be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul, and from it its mate”* (4:1) — already frames women as the mate from the single soul, not as an item to be passed. The prohibition therefore does more than regulate marriage; it rehumanizes the widow at a moment when custom had depersonalized her. She is not to be claimed by a son, not to be blocked from remarriage, and not to be priced. Her future is to be decided by her own consent within the lawful degrees that follow, where her choice is respected and her dowry is again secured.

**A Shameless Path That Leaves No Good Behind**

The final phrase *sāʾa sabīlā* — evil way — warns that allowing this path harms more than the two persons involved. The sūrah’s later command to appoint mediators from both families when a split is feared (4:35) assumes families can mediate because roles are clear; a practice that confuses father and son destroys that clarity.
verses.23:
> ˹Also˺ forbidden to you for marriage are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal and maternal aunts, your brother’s daughters, your sister’s daughters, your foster-mothers, your foster-sisters, your mothers-in-law, your stepdaughters under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers—but if you have not, then you can marry them—nor the wives of your own sons, nor two sisters together at the same time—except what was done previously. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

The prohibitions rest on three distinct bonds, each treated as creating a sanctity. Blood ties — mothers, daughters, sisters, aunts, nieces — are inviolable because they share a common lineage that marriage would confuse; the sūrah has already rooted humanity in a single soul and its mate (4:1) and built inheritance on that lineage (4:7, 4:11–12). Nursing ties — foster-mothers and foster-sisters — are treated like blood ties, as Prophetic teaching clarified that nursing creates the same prohibitions as birth, so that a foster relationship is not a metaphor but a legal kinship.

**Except What Was Done Previously and All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The exception *illā mā qad salaf* — except what was done earlier — appears here for the bar on combining two sisters, as it did for the father’s former wife (4:22). It functions as clemency for marriages contracted before revelation, requiring separation where the bar now applies but not imposing retroactive worldly punishment for what was done without the light of the new limit. The closing *inna Allāha kāna ghafūran raḥīmā* — surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — gives the reason that correction is met with forgiveness when it is accepted. The sūrah uses the same pairing after defining repentance that must be soon (4:17, 4:26) and after the command to lighten burdens (4:28). Here it tells families that have to untangle prior marriages that the path back is mercy, not humiliation. That mercy does not reopen the prohibited degree; it forgives the past while holding the limit firm for the future. The pattern matches the sūrah’s treatment of limits — *ḥudūd* — elsewhere (4:13–14): the limit is clear and crossing it deliberately has consequence, but turning back when the limit becomes clear is met with pardon.

**Marriage Within Limits, Not Without**

The verse does not only forbid; it implies what remains lawful. The next verse will note that beyond the named degrees marriage remains open when sought through proper dowry and chaste intent (4:24), confirming that outside the barred list the field is lawful when approached in the right way. That framing matters because the list could be read as restriction alone, while the Qur’an presents it as clarification that makes the lawful field safe to enter. A community that knows who is permanently outside choice can choose inside the lawful field without confusion about lineage, which the inheritance laws depend on, and without rivalry between mothers and daughters, sisters, or foster kin. The sūrah’s earlier training in handling wealth as a trust (4:2, 4:5–6) finds a parallel here in handling persons as trusts. Just as wealth has fixed shares and guarded handovers, family has fixed bars and guarded entrances. Both guards come from the same source: the One described as All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26), who knows which ties, if crossed by marriage, would injure the household, and who is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful when the community realigns its marriages to the map He has drawn.
verses.24:
> Also ˹forbidden are˺ married women—except ˹female˺ captives in your possession. This is Allah’s commandment to you. Lawful to you are all beyond these—as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication. Give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries. It is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Lawful Beyond These, Sought in the Right Way**

The verse then opens the lawful field: *wa uḥilla lakum mā warāʾa dhālikum a tabtaghū bi amwālikum muḥṣinīna ghayra musāfiḥīn* — lawful to you are all beyond these, as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication. Two conditions define the lawful path. First, it is sought *with your wealth* — *bi amwālikum* — meaning through dowry and maintenance, the same wealth the sūrah has taught to guard as a standing support (4:5) and to give graciously as *ṣaduqah* with *niḥlah* (4:4). Marriage is therefore a commitment of provision, not a seizure. Second, it is as *muḥṣinīna* — seeking chastity, protection — not as *musāfiḥīn* — fornicators who pour out desire without bond. The contrast *muḥṣin / musāfiḥ* frames marriage as the shelter for desire rather than its mere outlet. The sūrah will repeat that shelter language for those who marry believing bondwomen, requiring chastity and avoidance of secret affairs (4:25). Here the same standard applies to all: the wealth is spent to build a lawful, protective tie, and the act is chaste. That pairing of wealth and chastity keeps the law from becoming a list of names alone; it makes the method of seeking part of lawfulness.

**Give Those You Have Consummated Marriage With Their Due Dowries**

The command *fa mā istamtaʿtum bihi minhunna fa ātūhunna ujūra-hunna farīḍah* — give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries — restates the dowry as an obligation — *farīḍah*. The word *istimtāʿ* — enjoyment, consummation — refers to the completion of marriage’s intimacy, the same *ifḍāʾ* that the sūrah called a firm commitment’s context (4:21). Once that stage is reached, the dowry is not a promise to be debated but a portion due. The Qur’an already secured the dowry as the woman’s gracious gift (4:4) and forbade reclaiming even a heap when wishing to replace a wife (4:20–21). Here it secures the dowry again at the point where the lawful field is opened, so that opening is not mistaken for licence to seek without commitment. The dowry is not a fee for access; it is the sign of seriousness — *ṣaduqah* — that makes the shelter real. The sūrah has guarded that sign at entry, during marriage, and at replacement; this verse guards it at consummation, marking the moment when the obligation hardens. The insistence on *farīḍah* also explains why the verse repeats what was said before: the rule needs to be present wherever marriage is sought, including where new lawful matches are being considered.

**All-Knowing, All-Wise at the Gate of the Lawful**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise — appears here where the entire list of prohibitions ends and the lawful field is opened. The pairing matches its use after the inheritance shares (4:11) and after the promise to make things clear (4:26). Knowledge covers every degree that, if crossed, would injure lineage and affection; wisdom explains why marriage is tied to wealth spent in chastity rather than to wealth spent for display. The Name *ʿAlīm* also watches the private adjustments to the set dowry, where mutual graciousness could be genuine or pressured, while *Ḥakīm* places that watch inside wisdom that seeks to protect the shelter marriage is meant to be. The sūrah will immediately follow with guidance for those who cannot afford a free believing wife and may marry a believing bondwoman with permission and fair dowry (4:25), showing that the same Two Names govern the easier path as well. The command written upon the community — *kitāba Allāhi ʿalaykum* — is therefore not a hard wall alone. It is a gate whose bars are known and whose opening beyond the bars is lawful when sought with wealth, with chastity, and with the woman’s due given as an obligation that may then be softened only by true mutual grace.
verses.25:
> But if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, then ˹let him marry˺ a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you. Allah knows best ˹the state of˺ your faith ˹and theirs˺. You are from one another. So marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness, if they are chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs. If they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women. This is for those of you who fear falling into sin. But if you are patient, it is better for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**A Lawful Path When Means Are Limited**

This verse opens a second door for those who cannot reach the first. *Wa man lam yastaṭiʿ minkum ṭawlan a yankiḥa al-muḥṣanāt al-muʾmināt fa mimmā malakat aymānukum min fatayātikumu al-muʾmināt* — but if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, then let him marry a believing bondwoman had by one of you. *Ṭawl* — means, capacity — was read as wealth to pay the dowry and provide maintenance for a free wife. The verse does not command such a marriage; it permits it — *fa mim mā malakat* — as a mercy for those who lack means and fear falling into unlawful intercourse. The sūrah has already limited polygamy to four and tied it to justice (4:3), listed the prohibited degrees (4:22–23), and described lawful seeking as spending wealth in chastity (4:24). Here it acknowledges that lawful spending may be beyond some, and it provides a path that still meets the sūrah’s core requirements: faith, permission, dowry, and chastity. The Qur’an elsewhere encourages freeing slaves as an act of piety and as expiation, and this permission sits inside that larger movement toward liberty, where the bondwoman is not a casual liaison but a wife entered through covenant, with a named owner’s permission and a known gift.

**You Are From One Another**

The phrase *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi īmānikum baʿḍukum min baʿḍ* — Allah knows best the state of your faith, and yours, you are from one another — addresses the social barrier that might have kept such marriages from happening. In a society where free and enslaved carried different rank, the Qur’an equalises by faith and by origin. *Baʿḍukum min baʿḍ* — you are from one another — recalls the single soul from which all were spread (4:1) and tells the suitor that the bondwoman who believes shares his humanity and his covenant. Elsewhere the Qur’an says *“a believing bondwoman is better than a polytheist woman even if she pleases you”* (2:221), and the same ranking operates here: where a free polytheist might be sought for status, the believing bondwoman is offered as the lawful, faithful alternative for the man of limited means.

**For Those Who Fear Falling Into Sin**

The restriction *dhālika li man khashiya al-ʿanata minkum* — this is for those of you who fear falling into sin — frames the permission as tied to need and to fear of transgression, not as an ideal to be preferred over marrying a free woman where means exist. The sūrah therefore keeps its earlier advice — if you fear you cannot be just, then one (4:3) — and adds here that if you cannot afford a free wife and you fear sin, the believing bondwoman is lawful, but patience may still be better. That counsel fits the sūrah’s repeated wish to lighten burdens (4:28) while keeping moral shelter intact.

**All-Forgiving, Most Merciful Over Means and Restraint**

The closing *wa Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm* — and Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — gathers this detailed law into divine forbearance. The forgiveness covers both the difficulty that led to limited means and the imperfections in choosing the lesser path. The mercy covers the provision of a lawful way where otherwise only hardship or sin would remain. The sūrah began by spreading humanity from a single soul (4:1), guarded the orphan’s wealth with witnessing and reckoning (4:6), fixed shares for heirs (4:11–12), and guarded marriage with lists and dowries (4:22–24). Here it shows that guarding marriage also means guarding those who cannot afford its usual form, by giving them a form they can afford that still requires permission, dowry, chastity, and accountability, and by reminding the free community *you are from one another*. A household entered through that door, with half penalty where sin occurs and with patience still named as better, is not a second-class contract in faith, even if it is a second choice in means.
verses.26:
> It is Allah’s Will to make things clear to you, guide you to the ˹noble˺ ways of those before you, and turn to you in mercy. For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**And to Turn to You in Mercy**

The third purpose *wa yatūba ʿalaykum* — and turn to you in mercy — shows that clarity and guidance are directed toward pardon. *Yatūba* here is God’s turning, His acceptance, as when the sūrah earlier promised *“Allah will pardon them”* for those who repent soon after acting ignorantly (4:17). The sequence matters: first He makes clear, then He guides to the path, then He turns to those who take it. Clarity without mercy would be exposure; guidance without acceptance would be demand without help. The sūrah therefore presents law as a means to mercy, not as its opposite. The same verse that promises to make things clear also promises to accept the return of those who had earlier blurred the lines — whether by consuming orphan wealth hastily (4:6), reclaiming dowries (4:20–21), or marrying where it was hateful (4:22). The sūrah will repeat that desire to turn in grace in the next verse — *“Allah wishes to turn to you in grace”* (4:27) — and will add that He wishes to lighten burdens because humankind was created weak (4:28). Here the turn is already offered as the outcome of understanding: once you see the distinction, walk its way, and you will find Him turning toward you.

**All-Knowing, All-Wise Over Detail and Time**

The closing *wa Allāhu ʿAlīmun Ḥakīm* — for Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise — matches the two purposes that came before. *ʿAlīm* knows every family configuration, every temptation to treat a widow as inheritable property (4:19), every pressure to reclaim a heap of gold (4:20), and every case where means fail and a believing bondwoman becomes the lawful choice (4:25). That knowledge is what makes the distinctions precise; the law is not guesswork about what might harm lineage but knowledge of what will. *Ḥakīm* places that knowledge inside wisdom: the distinctions are not only accurate but beneficial, producing households where trust can be kept and where wealth can be divided without rancour. The same pair closed the inheritance shares (4:11) and the dowry flexibility (4:24), showing that both arithmetic and mercy belong to the same wisdom. The sūrah’s detailed legislation could have been heard as burdensome without that closing; with it, the detail itself becomes assurance. The One who knows each tie’s sensitivity is the One who draws its limit, and He draws it so that the path of those before you becomes walkable for you, and His turning toward you becomes near.

**A Verse That Holds the First Third Together**

Read after twenty-five verses, this verse gathers the opening third of al-Nisāʾ into a sentence about divine intent. It tells the reader that the laws about a single soul and womb-ties (4:1), about testing orphans and witnessing handovers (4:6), about obligatory shares after debts and gifts (4:11–12), about disgust for marrying a father’s widow (4:22). About lawful seeking with wealth in chastity (4:24–25) are not a collection of disconnected rulings but a single clarifying, guiding, and pardoning will. The sūrah has moved from creation to trust to property to family formation, and this verse names the thread: Allah wills to make all of it clear, to place you on the noble way others walked, and to turn to you when you do. That naming prepares the next two verses, which contrast that will with the wish of those who follow desires to see you deviate completely (4:27) and which add that weakness is the reason burdens are lightened (4:28). Clarity, precedent, and mercy together form the ground on which the lighter burden can be borne. Without the will to make things clear, the law would remain opaque; without guidance to the ways before, it would feel rootless; without the turn in mercy, it would feel unattainable. With all three, the community is given both the map and the help to walk it.
verses.27:
> And it is Allah’s Will to turn to you in grace, but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely ˹from Allah’s Way˺

**Two Wills Facing One Another**

This verse places two intentions side by side in one sentence. *Wa Allāhu yurīdu a yatūba ʿalaykum* — and it is Allah’s Will to turn to you in grace — repeats the promise of the previous verse that He wishes to make things clear, guide to the noble ways, and turn to you in mercy (4:26). The repetition is not redundancy; it isolates the turning as the focus. Immediately beside it stands a contrary wish: *wa yurīdu alladhīna yattabiʿūna al-shahawāt a tamīlū maylan ʿaẓīmā* — but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate completely from Allah’s Way. The verb *yurīdu* — to will, to want — is used for both, making the contrast a contest of wills. On one side is the will that clarifies limits and then pardons those who keep them; on the other is the will that blurs limits and draws people into gross deviation. The Qur’an elsewhere says that Satan wants to lead astray and that human whims invite to the same. The sūrah has shown what that deviation looks like in practice: consuming orphan wealth (4:10), exceeding inheritance limits (4:14), treating women as inheritable (4:19), reclaiming dowries by slander (4:20), and marrying where God said do not. Those who follow desires benefit from each blur, because in each the strong gain at the weak’s expense. The verse tells the believer that the line he keeps is not a private preference but a front between two larger intentions.

**Turning in Grace Against the Pull of Deviation**

The contrast between *yatūba* — to turn in grace — and *tamīlū* — to tilt, to deviate — is spatial. One turn brings the community upright; the other tilts it off balance. The Qur’an uses *mayl* elsewhere for tilting toward one wife at the expense of another where justice is required, cautioning *“do not incline completely toward one, leaving another suspended”* (4:129), and that caution shows how *mayl* operates in family life as well. Here the tilt is entire — *ʿaẓīm* — a comprehensive swerve from the noble ways just mentioned. The sūrah’s answer to that pull is not to deny desire but to place it inside limits where it can be chaste and sheltered. The lawful field beyond the prohibited degrees — sought with wealth, in protection, not in fornication (4:24) — and the permission for a believing bondwoman where means fail (4:25) — already showed that desire has a lawful home.

**Why the Verse Repeats Allah’s Will to Turn**

Repeating *Allah wishes to turn to you* immediately after saying He wishes to make things clear and guide to the ways before (4:26) isolates grace as the purpose of law. Law without the promise of turning would be heard as burden alone, and the next verse will say explicitly that Allah wishes to lighten your burdens because you were created weak (4:28). Here the lightening is already implied: to be turned toward in grace after clarification is to be given a way back when the law has been broken. That way back was already detailed: repent soon after acting ignorantly (4:17), repent and mend and be relieved (4:16), give back what was taken, and speak equitably (4:9). The wish of the followers of desire is to keep people from that return by normalizing deviation until the return no longer seems needed. The sūrah has already defined the failed repentance that comes only when death is present (4:18); the deviators’ wish is to keep people persisting until that failure becomes inevitable. By naming both wishes together, the verse makes the choice urgent. One will has prepared a painful punishment for persistence (4:18) but has also prepared Gardens for keeping limits (4:13) and forgiveness for soon return; the other will has no garden to offer, only the satisfaction of seeing others swerve greatly with them.
verses.28:
> And it is Allah’s Will to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak

**A Will to Lighten**

After saying that Allah wills to make things clear and guide to the noble ways and turn to you in mercy (4:26). That those who follow desires wish you to swerve greatly (4:27), the sūrah adds a third divine will: *yurīdu Allāhu a yukhaffifa ʿankum* — and it is Allah’s Will to lighten your burdens. The verb *yukhaffif* — to lighten, to make less heavy — was understood as easing the legal and moral load to what people can bear, without removing the limits that protect them. The context shows where that easing appears. The prohibition on marrying former wives of fathers was softened with *except what was done earlier* (4:22). Combining two sisters carries the same exception (4:23); the field lawful beyond the prohibited degrees is opened widely when sought with wealth in chastity (4:24). The bar of inability to afford a free believing wife is eased by permission to marry a believing bondwoman with permission and fair dowry (4:25); and the set dowry itself is made adjustable by mutual graciousness (4:24). Each of those details is a lightening inside a limit. The verse gathers them and says the pattern is intentional: the limits are fixed, but the way of keeping them is made lighter.

**For Humankind Was Created Weak**

The reason given — *wa khuliqa al-insānu ḍaʿīfan* — for humankind was created weak — was read as comprehensive. Weakness covers several domains that the sūrah has touched. Physically, people need shelter and maintenance, which marriage provides when it is *muḥṣin* — protective. Sexually, desire is strong and persistent, which is why unlawful intercourse is called *fāḥishah* and why chastity is protected by requiring four witnesses and by disciplining the pair and then relieving them when they mend (4:15–16). Intellectually, people know the right but act ignorantly under impulse, which is why repentance is accepted for those who act in ignorance and turn soon (4:17) and not for those who persist until death is present (4:18). Socially, kin groups press individuals to favour custom over revelation, as with inheriting women against their will (4:19) and reclaiming dowries (4:20–21). To be created weak in all these directions is not an insult; it is an explanation that makes easing a mercy rather than an indulgence. The sūrah elsewhere says *“Allah does not charge a soul beyond what it can bear”* (2:286), and this verse is the social law counterpart: the soul that is weak is not charged with what would crush it.

**How Lightening Works in This Sūrah**

Lightening does not mean erasing. The orphan’s wealth must still be returned with witnesses and reckoning (4:6). The guardian who is well-off is asked to abstain while the poor guardian may take what is fair, and the test for *rushd* — sound judgment — allows return when readiness appears rather than at a single arbitrary age (4:6). The inheritance shares remain fixed — half, quarter, eighth, sixth, third, two-thirds — after debts and gifts (4:11–12), but gifts themselves remain permitted up to one-third and mutual graciousness about dowries is allowed (4:24). Prohibited degrees are fixed, but the past is pardoned and the lawful field beyond is broad. Fornication is not permitted, but marriage is made reachable even where means fail, with the concession for the believing bondwoman where fear of sin is real and patience still named as better (4:25). In each case the law keeps its bar and widens its door, which is exactly what lightening inside limits looks like. The sūrah therefore answers the deviators’ claim that limits are harsh (4:27) not by removing limits but by showing how many lawful paths exist to live well inside them.
verses.29:
> O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent. And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you

**Do Not Devour One Another’s Wealth Illegally**

The address *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — O believers — reappears to mark a new, general principle after the detailed family laws. *Lā taʾkulū amwālakum baynakum bi al-bāṭil* — do not devour one another’s wealth illegally — uses the same verb *akala* — to eat — that earlier described consuming orphans’ wealth as eating fire (4:10) and that warned against mixing orphan wealth with one’s own to consume it (4:2) and against hasty consumption before the orphan grows up (4:6). *Bi al-bāṭil* — illegally, by falsehood — covers every means where consent or right is absent: theft, fraud, usury where increase is taken without trade, gambling where property changes hands without productive exchange, bribery, and taking by coercion. The sūrah has spent its first thirty verses guarding wealth at its most sensitive points — orphan property, dowries, inheritance shares, and the estate around which relatives, orphans, and the needy gather (4:8).

**Do Not Kill Each Other or Yourselves**

The second prohibition *wa lā taqtulū anfusakum* — and do not kill each other or yourselves — was read in two linked senses, both supported by the wording *anfusakum* — yourselves, your own selves, one another. The other sense is social: in a community described as being from a single soul (4:1) and as *you are from one another* (4:25), killing another is killing the collective self, and devouring another’s wealth illegally is a slow killing of the community’s life as well. The sūrah has already warned that exceeding God’s limits in inheritance leads to abiding in Fire with humiliation (4:14) and that failing to repent until death is present leads to a prepared painful punishment (4:18). This verse adds the direct threat that follows illicit devouring and killing in the next verse: *“whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire”* (4:30).

**Surely Allah Is Ever Merciful to You**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna bikum raḥīmā* — surely Allah is ever Merciful to you — gives the reason that both prohibitions are mercy themselves. The mercy is not only in forgiving those who have done wrong and then turn soon (4:17); it is also in forbidding the wrong that would destroy them and others. A market where *bāṭil* is allowed quickly becomes a place where the weak — the very orphans, women, and needy the sūrah has been protecting — are devoured; a community where killing is tolerated cannot keep any of the family limits the sūrah has drawn. By prohibiting both, God spares the community the fire that illicit gain already is (4:10) and the Fire that deliberate injustice leads to (4:30). The Name *Raḥīm* here matches its use after the concession for bondwomen where patience is better (4:25) and after the promise to make things clear and lighten burdens (4:26–28). In each place mercy appears as the character of the lawgiver who both draws the line and eases the path inside it. The sūrah has said He wills to turn toward you (4:27) and to lighten because you are weak (4:28); this verse shows that turning and lightening include clear prohibitions that keep the weak from being eaten.

**A Guard That Holds Property and Life Together**

Placed after the verses on weakening and lightening burdens, this double prohibition holds the community’s two most basic trusts together. The sūrah began with creation from a single soul and watchfulness over womb-ties (4:1), moved through guardianship of orphans with witnessing and reckoning (4:6), fixed inheritance after debts and gifts (4:11–12), and governed marriage with dowries and chastity (4:24–25). Now it says, in the market and in the street, keep the same guard: do not take wealth by falsehood, and do not take life at all without right. Both takings are framed as eating and killing that rebound on the taker — here as burning in the next verse, earlier as eating fire (4:10), and always under a Reckoner who suffices (4:6).
verses.30:
> And whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire. That is easy for Allah

**Whoever Does This**

The pronoun *hādhā* — this — refers to the two prohibitions just named: devouring one another’s wealth illegally and killing one another or yourselves (4:29). The verse does not repeat those acts in detail; it gathers them as a single *this* and adds the condition that determines its recompense. The sūrah has spent its opening chapters defining what counts as *bāṭil* — mixing orphan wealth with one’s own (4:2), substituting bad for good, hastily consuming before the orphan grows up (4:6), reclaiming dowries by slander (4:20), exceeding inheritance limits (4:14) — and what counts as lawful trade by mutual consent (4:29). Now it says that doing *this* — the devouring or the killing — with two additional qualities leads to a named end. The brevity matters. After a long sequence of family and market laws, the warning is condensed to a single sentence so that it can be remembered in the market and at the estate table. A person who handles a sale or a legacy can recall *whoever does this* and know immediately which acts are meant, because the sūrah has already shown their many forms.

**That Is Easy for Allah**

The closing *wa kāna dhālika ʿalā Allāhi yasīrā* — and that is easy for Allah — was read as both warning and reassurance. As warning, it says the punishment is not difficult for God to execute; the barrier is not capability but forbearance, which is why the sūrah elsewhere calls Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:25–26) and Most Forbearing (4:12) yet still names the burning as sure for the deliberate overstep. The orphan whose wealth was eaten, the heir whose share was withheld, the victim of a killing — none needs to produce the Fire; the One who is Reckoner (4:6) and Witness over all things (4:33) and ever Merciful to believers (4:29) will see that what is easy for Him is done. What is easy for Him does not require a large apparatus; it requires only His will to recompense, which the sūrah has already said He wills to turn toward you in mercy when you keep limits (4:27) and wills to punish when you persist.

**A Bridge Between Property and Life**

Placed between the double prohibition and the promise that avoiding major sins leads to absolution of lesser ones (4:31), this verse functions as a bridge. It gathers the property and life violations together under one recompense, showing that both strike at the same trust: the community as *yourselves* — *anfusakum* — a single self-hood (4:29). The sūrah began with that selfhood as creation from one soul (4:1) and has returned to it repeatedly — *you are from one another* (4:25), *do not kill yourselves* (4:29). The sūrah does not leave that guard as threat alone; the very next verse offers a lighter path — avoid the major sins forbidden, and lesser faults will be absolved and you will enter a place of honour (4:31).

**When Ease Should Deter**

The practical force of *that is easy for Allah* is deterrence through proportion. A person weighing whether to falsify a measure or to pressure a widow to surrender a dowry may weigh the immediate gain against the likelihood of being caught by people. The verse shifts the scale to being caught by God, for whom it is easy. That shift was already prepared by *“Allah is ever Watchful over you”* (4:1) and *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) and *“Allah is a Witness over all things”* (4:33). Each of those Names makes detection certain; this clause makes recompense certain as well. At the same time, the qualifier *ʿudwānan wa ẓulman* keeps the deterrence from becoming despair. A person who slipped, who devoured out of ignorance and then turned soon (4:17), is not the one the burning addresses; the burning addresses deliberation and injustice persisted in. That distinction lets the weak who err take the next verse’s promise as their own, while those who calculate overstep read this verse as addressed directly to them.
verses.31:
> If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your ˹lesser˺ misdeeds and admit you into a place of honour

**Avoiding the Major to Be Forgiven the Lesser**

The verse offers a precise bargain: *in tajtanibū kabāʾira mā tunhawna ʿanhu nukaffir ʿankum sayyiʾātikum wa nudkhilkum mudkhalan karīmā* — if you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your lesser misdeeds and admit you into a place of honour. The language was explained as God’s undertaking to handle the small faults for those who guard against the great ones. *Kabāʾir* — major sins — were listed by early authorities with variations. A core was consistent: associating partners with God, killing a soul, consuming orphan wealth (4:10), devouring wealth illegally and killing deliberately (4:29–30), disobedience to parents, false testimony, and the *ḥudūd* violations the sūrah has detailed such as illicit intercourse (4:15–16), exceeding inheritance limits (4:13–14), and reclaiming dowries by slander (4:20). *Sayyiʾāt* — lesser misdeeds, evil deeds that stain even if smaller — are the slips that weakness (4:28) makes inevitable. The sūrah has already said humankind was created weak and that God wills to lighten and turn toward you (4:26–28); here it gives the mechanism of that lightening: guard the great, and the small is effaced. The promise does not trivialize the small; it says the small is ankles covered when the great dam holds.

**What Counts as Major**

The sūrah itself supplies many examples without needing an exhaustive list. Eating orphan wealth is named as a great sin — *ḥūban kabīrā* (4:2) — and as eating fire (4:10); devouring wealth by falsehood and killing without right is met with burning where *that is easy for Allah* (4:30); exceeding God’s limits in shares is met with abiding humiliation (4:14). Illicit intercourse was described as *fāḥishah* with a high bar of four witnesses to prevent slander (4:15). Inheriting women against their will and pressuring them to surrender dowries is called not permissible (4:19) and then slander and clear sin (4:20). Each of those is a candidate for *kabāʾir* because each betrays a trust that God named as a limit. The sūrah elsewhere warns *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and describes God as ever Merciful to you (4:29), so the major sins are those that, if done *ʿudwānan wa ẓulman* — sinfully and unjustly (4:30) — show a hardened intent rather than a moment of ignorance followed by soon return (4:17). That distinction matters because not every slip is major, and the verse invites the believer to learn the difference. A community that can name its major boundaries is more likely to keep them.

**A Verse That Lightens Without Loosening**

Read with the verses on weakness and lightening, this verse shows how burden is lifted without law being loosened. *“Humankind was created weak”* (4:28) explains why lesser faults will occur; *“We will absolve you of lesser misdeeds”* explains how they are handled when the great is avoided. The law remains firm where it must — the orphan’s wealth with witnesses (4:6), the fixed shares after debts (4:11–12), the bar on reclaiming a heap of gold (4:20), the bar on killing and devouring (4:29) — but the moral economy around the law is merciful. The believer is not asked to be flawless; he is asked to be serious about the great and quick to return from the small. Prophetic tradition listed seven destructive sins and taught that avoiding them and maintaining prayer, paying alms, and seeking forgiveness secures that covering, which shows that the verse was heard as both comfort and discipline. Comfort, because perfection is not demanded; discipline, because the major is not negotiable. Between those poles the weak person can walk without despair and without complacency, knowing that the One who is All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26) knows which faults are major. That the One who is ever Merciful (4:29) has promised to cover the rest when the great is avoided, and to admit to honour those He covers.
verses.32:
> And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others. Men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women ˹equally˺ according to theirs. Rather, ask Allah for His bounties. Surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**Do Not Crave What Was Given to Another**

The prohibition *wa lā tatamannaw mā faḍḍala Allāhu bihi baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍ* — and do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others — addresses the envy that the sūrah’s distribution laws could stir. After fixing shares for men and women whether little or much (4:7), detailing sons and daughters, parents and siblings after debts and gifts (4:11–12), and describing trade by mutual consent (4:29), a listener might look at another’s portion — larger inheritance, larger dowry, larger earning — and wish it were his. The Qur’an names that wish as *tamannī* — craving, wishing — not as planning to earn but as longing to have what another was given. The verse was revealed in a context where some men wished they had the double share and some women wished they had the same share as men, and where people coveted the martial rewards of others. The answer gathers both sexes and says the division of favour — *faḍl* — belongs to God’s apportioning, not to envy. The sūrah elsewhere says *“We have allocated among them their livelihood in this world”* (43:32), and here it asks that allocation to be met with asking, not craving.

**Rather Ask Allah for His Bounties**

The positive command *wa asʾalū Allāha min faḍlihi* — rather, ask Allah for His bounties — redirects the energy of envy into supplication. *Faḍl* — bounty, surplus, favour — is the same word used for the apportioning among people; to ask Him for His bounty is to ask the Source rather than to resent the recipient. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“If you are grateful, I will give you more”* (14:7) and encourages asking from the same bounty that sustains trade and family. The sūrah has already taught that God is ever Watchful (4:1), enough as Reckoner (4:6), a Witness over all things (4:33), and ever Merciful to you (4:29); asking Him is therefore not a vague hope but a request to the One who sees, counts, and shows mercy. It also respects the division of roles the sūrah has described — men as caretakers tasked with support (4:34) and women as protected bearers of entrusted wealth — without freezing either. Asking for bounty can mean asking for lawful earnings, for knowledge, for patience to avoid major sins (4:31), and for the ability to trade by mutual consent (4:29). Each is a form of *faḍl* that can be requested without craving what another was given.

**A Cure for Comparison After Law**

Placed between the promise that avoiding major sins brings a honourable entry (4:31) and the reminder that heirs are appointed and pledges must be honoured (4:33), this verse cures the comparison that law can breed. Law that divides — obligatory shares, dowries, trade — invites the eye to compare. The sūrah answers that invite with a different economy: shares in the next life are by deeds, equally open to men and women, and bounty in this life is to be asked from God, not extracted by envying people. The counsel is practical. A woman who sees a brother’s larger inheritance is told her deeds are counted as hers; a man who sees another’s profitable trade is told to ask God for his own bounty rather than to devour by falsehood (4:29). The sūrah has already said humankind was created weak (4:28) and that God wills to lighten and turn toward you (4:26–28). Here it lightens the specific weight of envy by giving the weak a prayer that is always available. To ask rather than crave is itself a deed that earns a share, and the One who knows all things will not forget it.

The sūrah elsewhere promises that *“whoever does good, whether male or female, while faithful, We will give a good life”* (16:97) and that God never wrongs even an atom’s weight but multiplies good many times over (4:40).
verses.33:
> And We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin. As for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share. Surely Allah is a Witness over all things

**Heirs Appointed for What Is Left**

The verse states *wa li kullin jaʿalnā mawāliya mimmā taraka al-wālidāni wa al-aqrabūn* — and We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin. The pronoun *We* — divine appointment — matches the earlier framing of shares as an obligation from Allah (4:11) and as limits set by Allah (4:13). Inheritance is not a tribal negotiation left to custom; it is an appointment. The word *mawālī* — heirs, close kin, protectors — was read as those who inherit by fixed portions and those who inherit as residuary kin where fractions leave a remainder. The phrase *mimmā taraka al-wālidāni wa al-aqrabūn* gathers every estate, whether little or much (4:7), under the same appointment. The sūrah has already detailed children and parents, spouses and siblings after debts and gifts (4:11–12), and has promised Gardens for keeping those limits and warned of Fire for crossing them (4:13–14). This verse steps back and says the whole system is appointed; no heir is an afterthought. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“to Allah belongs the heritage of the heavens and the earth”* (3:180, 57:10), so that appointment is also a redistribution of what already belongs to Him, which explains why the portions are obligatory rather than suggested.

**Between Fixed Law and Voluntary Pledge**

The pairing of appointed heirs and pledged associates displays the sūrah’s balance between what God fixes and what people undertake. Fixed heirs — *mawālī* — are not chosen by the deceased; they are appointed by the verse and quantified in the fractions that follow. Pledged associates are chosen; they are the result of *ʿaqadat aymānukum* — what your right hands have tied. Both generate a *naṣīb* — a share — that must be given. The first share is obligatory by divine appointment; the second is obligatory by personal commitment kept before God. Together they show that property moves by two just means — law and promise — both of which exclude seizing by desire or by *bāṭil* — falsehood — condemned just before (4:29). Trade by mutual consent (4:29) and the dowry given graciously (4:4) already taught that willingness makes transfer lawful; this verse adds that a pledge made willingly also makes transfer obligatory. The sūrah therefore trains the reader to see wealth as moving along clear tracks: appointed shares where kinship is the track, and pledged shares where contract is the track, with neither track to be diverted by envy (4:32) or by devouring (4:29–30).

**Surely Allah Is a Witness Over All Things**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿalā kulli shayʾin shahīdā* — surely Allah is a Witness over all things — supplies the watcher for both tracks. *Shahīd* — witness, present observer — matches *Raqīb* — ever Watchful (4:1) — and *Ḥasīb* — enough as Reckoner (4:6) — and *ʿAlīm* — All-Knowing (4:11, 4:26, 4:32). The difference is that *Shahīd* stresses presence at the act of transfer. The apportioning of an estate often happens in a family home without a judge; the fulfilment of a pledge often happens between two persons without an audience. The verse says the division and the fulfilment are already witnessed. That matters for the heirs appointed — the parents, children, spouses, siblings — whose shares could be trimmed if no one sees, and for the pledged person whose share could be denied if the pledge is forgotten after death. Elsewhere the Qur’an says *“Allah is Witness over what you do”* (10:46) and requires witnesses at the orphan’s handover (4:6); this verse is the general principle behind that requirement. What is witnessed by God need not be witnessed by many people to be binding, but human witnesses remain the community’s way of aligning its practice with the divine watch.
verses.34:
> Men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially. And righteous women are devoutly obedient and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with. And if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them ˹first˺, ˹if they persist,˺ do not share their beds, ˹but if they still persist,˺ then discipline them ˹gently˺. But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them. Surely Allah is Most High, All-Great

**Caretakers, Not Controllers**

The verse opens with *al-rijālu qawwāmūna ʿalā al-nisāʾ bi mā faḍḍala Allāhu baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ wa bi mā anfaqū min amwālihim* — men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially. The word *qawwām* — caretaker, maintainer, one who stands and keeps upright — is stronger than a claim to superiority; it describes a role of standing guard, providing, and managing affairs so that the household remains upright. That role is grounded in two facts, not in a claim of greater worth. First, *bi mā faḍḍala Allāhu baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ* — as God has provisioned some over others — which the sūrah earlier framed as bounty to be asked for rather than envied (4:32), and which elsewhere appears as differences in strength and in means. Second, *wa bi mā anfaqū min amwālihim* — and as they spend from their wealth — the financial maintenance the sūrah has already secured through the dowry as a gracious gift (4:4), the prohibition on reclaiming it (4:20–21), and the inheritance fractions that assign the larger share to the party bearing maintenance. The verse therefore ties authority to responsibility: the caretaking is not license to dominate but assignment to provide. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not crave what Allah has given some over others”* (4:32), and here it directs that what was given — provision and spending — be used to keep the other standing.

**Three Steps When Ill-Conduct Is Sensed**

The counsel *wa allātī takhāfūna nushūzahunna fa ʿiẓūhunna wa ahjurūhunna fī al-maḍājiʿ wa aḍribūhunna* — if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them first, if they persist, do not share their beds. If they still persist, then discipline them gently — sets a graded response to *nushūz* — rising up, ill-conduct, breach of marital harmony. The first step *ʿiẓūhunna* — advise, admonish — is speech that reminds of God, of limits, and of the covenant as a firm commitment (4:21). The sūrah elsewhere commands *“live with them in kindness”* (4:19) and says to appoint mediators when a split is feared (4:35), showing that the aim is amendment and reconciliation, not punishment for its own sake.

**Surely Allah Is Most High, All-Great**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿaliyyan kabīrā* — surely Allah is Most High, All-Great — places the household under a higher authority than either spouse. *ʿAliyy* — Most High — and *Kabīr* — All-Great — remind the caretaker that his standing over maintenance is itself under a greater standing. The sūrah has used similar closings to temper power: All-Knowing, All-Wise over shares (4:11, 4:26), Most Forbearing over division (4:12), Witness over pledges (4:33), and here High and Great over domestic authority. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse therefore warns the husband who might misuse *qiwāmah* — caretaking — that there is a higher *qiwām* — a higher Maintainer — who sees. That reminder is not abstract. The Prophet’s teaching that the best of men are best to their wives makes the standard concrete. The sūrah’s next verse — appoint a mediator from his family and one from hers when a split is feared (4:35) — shows that the home is not a private realm where power is unchecked but a community matter where families are called in. To be caretaker is therefore to be accountable to the Most High, and to know that the authority given to keep the household upright will itself be weighed. The sūrah’s ethic holds: as God has provisioned some over others, let that provision be spent to keep the other standing, and as God has guarded, let what is guarded in absence be kept faithfully, with admonition and pause before any discipline, and with no injustice once the way has returned.
verses.35:
> If you anticipate a split between them, appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers. If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware

**Bring the Two Families In**
When a husband and wife are heading for a split, the verse does not tell the community to look on and wait for the divorce. It tells it to appoint two arbiters, one from his family and one from hers, and to let them try to put the marriage back together. The Arabic word for the split is *shiqāq*, a word for a crack where each side goes its own way, and the remedy the verse chooses is the opposite movement: the two sides of the family come back into the room.

**Why One From Each Side**
The arrangement protects both parties. A man's relatives know his temper and his history; a woman's relatives know what she has been given and what she has been asked to put up with. The two arbiters are called *ḥakam*, which can mean judges, but their work here is reconciliation first: they listen, they advise, and they remind the couple of what the sūrah has already set down — that the marriage rests on a firm pledge (4:21), that a man must live with his wife on fair terms even when feeling cools (4:19), and that speech between people is to be equitable (4:9). The same sūrah has already given the steps for a man dealing with his wife's ill conduct: counsel her, then separate in bed (4:34). The verse in front of the reader steps in where those steps have failed, and it says plainly that the promise attached to the effort is real: if the two want to mend matters, God will bring their hearts together.

**The Two Names at the End**
The verse closes with God named as All-Knowing and All-Aware. The arbiters hear the story each spouse wants to tell; God hears the story each one brings and measures it against the facts. The sūrah has already spoken of the tie of kinship as something sacred, planted at the creation of the first human being (4:1), and it has spoken of pledges and of property held in trust and returned to its owners with witnesses (4:6; 4:33). The closing names belong to that setting: people may hide the dowry they took or the promises they made, but the One who sees the household from the inside is the One who knows. Mediation is the sūrah's preferred way to handle a marriage in trouble, and the verse gives it two arbiters, one purpose, and a God who knows everything. The command to mend a marriage sits inside the wider command the sūrah gives in the same passage: worship God alone, and treat parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbour, the companion and the traveller well (4:36). It sits too inside the sūrah’s rule about promises, that pledges made between people are to be honoured, and that God is witness over them (4:33).
verses.36:
> Worship Allah ˹alone˺ and associate none with Him. And be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, near and distant neighbours, close friends, ˹needy˺ travellers, and those ˹bondspeople˺ in your possession. Surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful—

**Worship Alone, Then Kindness Outward in Circles**

The verse begins with the foundation of all duty: *wa ʿbudū Allāha wa lā tushrikū bihi shayʾā* — worship Allah alone and associate none with Him. After thirty-five verses of law about orphans, dowries, shares, and marriage, the sūrah returns to the root that makes those laws worship rather than mere administration. Association — *shirk* — is not only bowing to an idol; it is placing any partner beside God in devotion, trust, or obedience, including wealth, lineage, or desire that the sūrah has shown can rival revelation. The command is followed immediately by kindness in expanding circles: *wa bi al-wālidayni iḥsānan wa bi dhī al-qurbā wa al-yatāmā wa al-masākīn wa al-jāri dhī al-qurbā wa al-jāri al-junub wa al-ṣāḥibi bi al-janb wa ibni al-sabīl wa mā malakat aymānukum* — be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, near and distant neighbours, close friends, needy travellers, and those in your possession. The sūrah has already guarded each of those groups separately: parents with a fixed third or sixth (4:11), orphans with return and witnesses (4:6), the poor and needy present at distribution (4:8), and bondspeople with permission, dowry, and half penalty (4:25). Here they are gathered in one ethic of *iḥsān* — kind, beautiful doing — that flows from worship without association.

**Why Parents Follow Worship Without Gap**

The pairing *wa bi al-wālidayni iḥsānan* directly after worship was explained as showing that gratitude to the Creator is followed by gratitude to the means of creation. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Be grateful to Me and to your parents”* (31:14), and the same adjacency appears here. Parents are named first among people because the sūrah opened with *“He created you from a single soul, and from it its mate, and spread countless men and women”* (4:1), rooting family in creation; to be kind to parents is therefore to honour the channel of that spreading. The sūrah has already secured parents’ shares equally when offspring exist (4:11) and has told the child not to crave what another was given but to ask God for bounty (4:32); kindness to parents completes that picture with conduct, not only fractions. *Iḥsān* here was read as good companionship, gentle speech, provision without reminder, and obedience in what is lawful. The early Medinan community included migrants who had left parents in Makkah and hosts who embodied hospitality; both were asked to see *iḥsān* as more than material support. Kindness here is the moral counterpart to the fixed share there: one gives the portion, the other gives the manner.

**Relatives, Orphans, and the Poor Near the Heart of the Law**

The triad *dhī al-qurbā wa al-yatāmā wa al-masākīn* repeats the core of the sūrah’s first laws. Relatives were to be honoured as womb-ties sharing the root of mercy (4:1); orphans were to have wealth returned without substitution (4:2), tested and witnessed (4:6), and not consumed as fire (4:10); the poor and needy present at distribution were to receive provision with kind words (4:8). To list them together here as objects of *iḥsān* shows that the sūrah’s ethic is not episodic but sustained. The same persons who receive legal protection also deserve habitual kindness beyond the moment of settlement. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or west. That you believe and give wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveller”* (2:177), and that verse helps read this one: the donation at distribution (4:8) is a single instance of a larger generosity that does not wait for an estate to divide. A community that learns to give to relatives, orphans, and the poor when it has little will give justly when it has much, because the habit precedes the occasion. The sūrah therefore lifts the specific rulings into a character.
verses.37:
> those who are stingy, promote stinginess among people, and withhold Allah’s bounties. We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment

**Arrogant and Boastful Made Visible Through Stinginess**

This verse completes the portrait begun at the end of the previous one: *inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu man kāna mukhtālan fakhūrā* — surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful (4:36) — those who are *alladhīna yabkhalūna wa yaʾmurūna al-nāsa bi al-bukhl wa yaktumūna mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlihi* — stingy, promoting stinginess among people, and withholding Allah’s bounties. The sūrah has just commanded *iḥsān* — kind, beautiful doing — to parents, relatives, orphans, poor, neighbours near and distant, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36). It keeps what was given as standing support — *qiyāman* (4:5) — for the household and the community locked in the hand, rather than letting it circulate as provision, dowry, inheritance shares, and trade by mutual consent (4:29). The verse therefore draws a straight line from worship without association (4:36) to openness of hand; to associate oneself with God in pride is to close the hand that worship should open.

**Withholding What Allah Gave of His Bounty**

The third trait *wa yaktumūna mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlihi* — and withhold Allah’s bounties — uses *katama* — to conceal, to hide — the same verb the sūrah uses for Jews who were given a portion of the Scripture and trade it for misguidance (4:44) and who conceal knowledge. Here the concealment is of bounty — *faḍl* — the surplus God gave to be spent, shared, and acknowledged. *Faḍl* in this sūrah has appeared as the apportioning among people not to be craved but to be asked for (4:32), and as the bounty of Gardens for those who keep limits (4:13). To hide bounty is both to hide wealth itself — not spending it where *iḥsān* would — and to hide gratitude — not admitting it came from God. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“if you are grateful, I will give you more”* (14:7), making gratitude the condition for increase; concealment is the opposite, a denial that the gift needs acknowledgment. That is why the verse ends with a prepared humiliating punishment for the ungrateful who cover. The humiliation matches the earlier warning for exceeding limits (4:14) and for devouring wealth deliberately (4:30); in each, the person who sought to appear larger by withholding is reduced. The sūrah has already said God is ever Merciful to you (4:29); the stingy person acts as though mercy will not return if he gives.

**A Community Trained to Circulate**

Placed between the comprehensive ethic of kindness (4:36) and the warning against spending to show off without belief (4:38), this verse identifies the inner disease that blocks that ethic. The sūrah has taught the community to circulate wealth at every sensitive point — return the orphan’s wealth with witnesses (4:6), give women dowries graciously (4:4), divide estates after debts and gifts (4:11–12), offer provision to bystanders with kind speech (4:8), trade by mutual consent (4:29). Ask God for bounty rather than crave another’s (4:32). Each act requires a hand that opens. Stinginess closes that hand, and promoting stinginess closes others’ hands as well. The verse does not only threaten; it diagnoses. The one who does not like to give is the one who loves to be seen as high — *mukhtāl fakhūr* — and who believes bounty is his own achievement to be hidden rather than God’s gift to be shared. To heal that, the sūrah offers the opposite practice: worship without partner, which humbles the self before God, and *iḥsān* that moves outward in circles until it reaches the traveller and the servant. A community that learns those two moves will find stinginess unnatural, because the hand that has been opened in worship does not easily close when a relative, orphan, or neighbour is in need.
verses.38:
> Likewise for those who spend their wealth to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever takes Satan as an associate—what an evil associate they have

**Spending to Be Seen**

The verse adds a second example of disliked giving to complement stinginess: *wa alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum riʾāʾa al-nāsi wa lā yuʾminūna bi Allāhi wa lā bi al-yawmi al-ākhiri* — likewise for those who spend their wealth to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. The previous portrait was the hand that never opens — the stingy who promote stinginess and conceal bounty (4:37); this portrait is the hand that opens only for eyes. *Riʾāʾ* — show, display — was read as doing a deed so that people see and praise, rather than so that God accepts. The act itself — spending — may look generous; orphans might be fed, neighbours might receive, trade might flow, yet the motive empties it. The sūrah has just commended *iḥsān* — kind, beautiful doing — to parents, relatives, orphans, poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36), and has warned against devouring wealth by falsehood (4:29). Showing off corrupts *iḥsān* at its source, because the recipient becomes a prop for reputation rather than a person honoured for God’s sake. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not nullify your charities with reminders and hurt, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people”* (2:264).
