The people who say "we obey" and then work against it are left where the chapter has already placed them, standing in front of a God who hears everything.

**What the Chapter Had Said About Those People**
The chapter described those people directly: they say one thing in the meeting and do another thing at night (4:81 describes them). And it said that whatever good a person receives comes from God, while the harm he suffers comes from his own conduct (4:79 states both), which is the answer to the people who blamed the Messenger for their own troubles.

**The Wider Frame the Chapter Gave**
Around all of this, the chapter kept two facts in view. It said that God's will in this Book is to make matters clear (4:26 states it). And it opened by addressing all people as created from one soul and spread across the earth (4:1 gives the address).

It also set out the two camps in the middle of the chapter by what they fight for (4:76 names both causes). So the verse stands at the end of an argument that began with the unity of humanity and ended with the differences between people who have been shown the same truth.
verses.81:
> And they say, “We obey,” but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said. Allah records all their schemes. So turn away from them, and put your trust in Allah. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

> And they say, “We obey,” but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said. Allah records all their schemes. So turn away from them, and put your trust in Allah. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**The Obedience They Announce**
The verse describes the men who had just been told that obeying the Messenger is obeying God (4:80). They answer with the word of submission: we obey. Then they leave the room, and a group of them spend the night working out the opposite of what they said. The Arabic verb for that night work is *tabyīt*, the shaping of a plan after dark, out of sight of the people who heard the promise. The verse says God writes it all down. The sūrah has already described the same wordplay: men who twist the greeting they use with the Prophet and turn it into an insult (4:46), men who turn away when they are called back to the Book (4:61), and men who arrive with a solemn reference to good intention when the matter is finished (4:62).

**The Record Nobody Escapes**
The verse's answer to the night meeting is not an argument but a ledger. God records what they plan. The sūrah has already named that knowledge in several ways: God is watchful over the people in a way no one escapes (4:1), He is a sufficient reckoner for what is held in trust (4:6), He is witness over all things (4:33), and He never wrongs anyone by the weight of an atom, multiplying good instead (4:40). The men who keep their schemes quiet should know that the Book has also said God knows best who the community's enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45) and that He knows what is inside hearts (4:63). The verse tells the Prophet that the double game is not a hidden variable; it is already written, and it will be produced.

**Trust in Place of Anger**
The verse ends with an instruction: leave them, and put your trust in God, who is enough to handle a person's affairs. The chapter has given the same instruction where the opposition was open and obvious.

It described the people who wanted their case judged by a tyrant's court (4:60 describes them). It described the people who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61 describes them). And it described the people whose fine words covered a decision they had already taken in private (4:62 describes them). Faced with all of that, the instruction is not to argue harder but to hand the matter over.

**What the Chapter Reminded the Prophet**
The chapter also reminded him what the same people lost by their own choices. Those who could have believed and given in charity would only have gained by it (4:39 states it), and God multiplies every good deed (4:40 states it).

The believers were told to march with whatever they had (4:71 gives the command), and the person who fights is promised his reward whether he is killed or whether he wins (4:84 states both). The community was also warned against spreading every report of fear or safety without checking it first (4:83 gives the rule).

**Who the Verse Is Describing**
The people the verse describes are the same people the chapter has been following from the start: the ones who say one thing in the room and another at night (4:72 describes them), the ones who hold back what God has given them (4:37 describes them), and the ones who fight for the cause of false powers when they do fight at all (4:76 describes them).

Against all of that, the chapter set two things. It set the plain command to accept the Prophet's ruling and to submit to it (4:65 gives the command). And it set the reminder that everything good comes from God, while a person's troubles come from his own conduct (4:79 states both). The verse turns the Prophet's response from confrontation to trust, and its closing name repeats the premise the whole chapter rests on: God knows what happens in the room after the meeting ends.
verses.82:
> Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies

**A Book That Does Not Contradict Itself**
The verse asks the men who were contradicting the Prophet in private a simple question: why do they not think over the Qur'an? Then it gives the test. If this book had come from anyone other than God, they would have found plenty of contradictions inside it. The argument is one a reader can check: the Book sets out family law, war, money, prayer and inheritance in the same opening sūrah, and the rules do not pull against each other.

**What the Sūrah Has Asked Them to Think About**
The question follows the men who said "we obey" and then spent the night working out the opposite (4:81). The Book offers them a long list to reflect on: the creation of humanity from one soul and the duty to guard the ties of kinship (4:1), the return of the orphan's property as it was handed over (4:6), the fixed shares for sons and daughters (4:7) and the fuller rules for heirs (4:11; 4:12), marriage entered with wealth and restraint rather than appetite (4:24) together with the protection of women who have no family behind them (4:25), the statement that God wants to make things clear and to forgive those who turn back (4:26), trade by agreement instead of devouring other people's money (4:29), the command not to envy what others hold (4:32), the promise that an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40), and the rules for prayer and cleanliness (4:43).

**Why the Two Pictures Cannot Come From One Human Author**
The sūrah has also recorded the harder half of the community's life: the men who want their cases judged by a tyrant's court (4:60), the men whose fine words arrive after the matter is closed (4:62), the command to take precautions and march out (4:71), the command to fight for the men and women and children who cry for help (4:75), the difference between the two causes men fight for (4:76) and the plea of the faint-hearted for a delay (4:77). It has answered the grumblers who blamed the Prophet for their troubles (4:78) and told the community to check serious news before passing it on (4:83). A law made by a man would bend wherever his interest or his mood bent; the Book answers all of it in one voice, and the verse hands that fact to the reader as the proof. The inheritance rules state the shares (4:11) and then handle the cases where the family is more complicated than the first list covers (4:12).
verses.83:
> And when they hear news of security or fear, they publicize it. Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan—except for a few

**News Carried Without Checking**
The verse describes a habit that could break a community at war: reports of safety or of danger reach them, and they pass them on at once. It then gives the remedy, which is the same remedy the sūrah has already given for disputes: take the report back to the Messenger and to the people in the community who understand it, and they will find out whether it is sound. The people who can weigh a report are described as those who can search out the truth of it, and the verse says plainly that if God's grace had not been with the community, most of them would have followed Satan instead.

**Why the Habit Was Dangerous**
The sūrah has just told the believers to take their precautions and march in groups or all together (4:71), and it has shown the man who held back and then called his absence a blessing from God (4:72). A false report also does work on the side of the enemy, and the verse joins it to that man's behaviour (4:81) and to the complaint of the faint-hearted who said they feared people as God should be feared, and asked why fighting had been prescribed for them (4:77). It sits alongside the community's duty to obey God, the Messenger and the men in authority among them (4:59) and to refer their disputes to God and the Messenger, since messengers are sent only so that people obey them by God's permission (4:64). Every one of those duties assumes that the community hears the truth, and this verse protects the supply.

**The Knowledge and the Grace Behind It**
The verse's closing words keep the community humble. Reports are checked because human judgment is incomplete, and the checking itself depends on God's help. The sūrah has already said that God gives His bounty to whom He wills (4:55), that He lightens burdens because human beings were made weak (4:28), and that the men who are given knowledge are tested by it. The instructions around this verse give practice in exactly that discipline: return what is entrusted to its owners and judge with fairness (4:58), keep the two prayers and this one (4:43), and use the prayer time of a journey or illness as God allows (4:28 again in that surrounding passage). It has shown the two causes men fight for and how weak the second cause is (4:76), and it has told the community that good and hardship both come by God's decree rather than from the man who delivered the message (4:78). A community that checks its news before it speaks is a community that can be trusted with a battle, and the verse gives it both the method and the mercy that keeps the method working. The sūrah has already said that if the people had done what they were advised it would have gone better for them (4:66), and the verse before this one asked them to think the Book over and look for contradictions in it (4:82).
verses.84:
> So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺. You are accountable for none but yourself. And motivate the believers ˹to fight˺, so perhaps Allah will curb the disbelievers’ might. And Allah is far superior in might and in punishment

**Fight, and Answer for Yourself**
The verse addresses the Prophet alone after a passage full of hesitant men. It tells him to fight in God's cause, and then it draws the line of responsibility: he is accountable for himself and not for those who hang back. The community had been given the command to go out in groups or together (4:71) and had been told that the fighters either die or win and that both are gain (4:74). Some of them had asked for the order to be delayed (4:77), and some had stayed behind and counted their absence a favour (4:72). The verse tells the Prophet that his duty does not wait on them.

**You Are Not Responsible for Their Choices**
The sūrah has said repeatedly that the Prophet is a warner and not a keeper (the point made at 4:80). The men described in the surrounding verses had answered the call with night meetings (4:81), with excuses after the fact (4:66), and with turning away when they were invited back to the Book (4:61). The verse leaves them out of the Prophet's ledger: he carries out the command, and the men carry what they chose. What they chose has been spelled out in the same sūrah, from the law about money and marriage (4:26) that they were reluctant to accept, to the burdens God lightened for them (4:28), to the promise of gardens for those who obey (4:57), and the witness the Messenger will be called to give over his people (4:41).

**Urge the Believers**
The second command is social: stir the believers up. The Prophet is told to keep calling them to the fight in the hope that God will hold back the strength of the men who reject the faith (4:76 is the verse that divides the two causes), and the sūrah has shown what that urging looks like in practice: the men who tell others to go out, the fighters who sell this life for the next (4:74), and the men standing for the weak who cry out (4:75). Those who obey are promised a straight path (4:68) and are told that their good is not lost (4:79). The verse closes with the reminder that God's strength and His punishment are greater than anything the other side can bring, and the sūrah has been saying the same in one form or another: guidance is His to give (4:68), goodness comes from Him (4:78), and the report about a community is checked before it is believed (4:83). The sūrah has said that messengers are sent to be obeyed by God’s permission (4:64) and that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God (4:80).
verses.85:
> Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. And Allah is Watchful over all things

> Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. And Allah is Watchful over all things

**A Share in What You Support**
The verse sets a rule about influence. A person who speaks up for a good cause — who urges someone to give, to fight, to make peace, to do right — takes a share of the good that comes from it. A person who speaks up for a bad cause — who urges someone to hold back, to keep what is not his, to harm another — carries part of the burden of what follows. The wording puts both on the same footing, and then the verse closes with the statement that God watches what people do in all of it.

**The Causes the Sūrah Has Named**
The sūrah has given the community a great deal to support and to resist. On one side stand the mediators who mend a marriage (4:35), the men who return what is entrusted and judge fairly (4:58), and the men who answer the oppressed who cry out for help (4:75) and fight for God's cause (4:74). On the other side stand the men who encourage others into miserliness (4:37), the men who urge people away from the Book (4:44 is that passage), the men who want their cases judged by a tyrant's court (4:51 is the verse about taking false powers), and the men who inflame panic by spreading every report they hear (4:81 and 4:83 together describe that traffic). The verse tells both groups that nobody stands outside the outcome of a cause he has helped along.

**Where the Verse Is Placed**
The verse follows the command to urge the believers to go out and fight (4:84 gives the command), and it generalises the lesson. Urging someone towards a good act is a form of support, and support carries a share of the reward. Urging someone towards a harmful act carries a share of the burden instead.

So the verse turns a chapter about armies and battles into a rule about ordinary influence, and it ends by saying that God sees who backed what.

**What the Chapter Had Said About Support**
The chapter had already described the two ways people use what they have been given. Some give from it and some hold it back (4:71 describes both). It told the community not to let the grumblers dictate its course (4:72 describes them), and it named the people whose wish was for a delay and the answer they were given (4:77 describes the wish, and 4:79 gives the answer).

It also set out what supporting the right cause earns. It promised the obedient the company of the blessed (4:69 names that company). It said that an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40 states it). And it said that the people who did what they were advised have a great reward waiting for them (4:67 states it). It also set out the two causes people fight for, so that the reader can tell which side he is supporting (4:76 names both).

**The Other Side of Support, in Full**
The chapter showed the other side of this in full. It described the people who wanted their case judged by a tyrant's court (4:60 describes them). It described the people whose wish for a share of the spoils appeared only when the outcome was being counted (4:73 describes them). It described people fighting for false powers rather than for God (4:76 describes them), people blaming the Messenger for the trouble their own hands had brought (4:79 describes them), and people spreading every report through the community before anybody had checked it (4:83 describes them).

Read together, the two sides make the verse's point concrete. Backing a cause is not a small private act. It adds weight to whatever it supports, and the reward or the burden that follows is shared.
verses.86:
> And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things

> And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things

**The Greeting and Its Answer**
The verse gives the community a rule for ordinary encounters. When someone greets you with peace, answer with a better greeting or at least the same one. The greeting itself in the Muslim community is the word of peace, and the verse attaches it to a reminder that God keeps count of everything.

**A Rule for a Community That Meets Constantly**
The sūrah had gathered a mixed society: immigrants from Makkah, hosts in Madinah, believers, doubters, and the men whose loyalty was for sale. The greeting became one of the small daily tests of that society. The sūrah has already told its readers to treat parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the neighbour, the companion and the traveller well (4:36), and the greeting is the smallest coin of that duty. The men who had been told to go out and fight (4:71) and whose news was checked before it was spread (4:83) were the same men who met each other in the street every day, and the verse keeps the ordinary courtesy inside the same moral world as the law. The sūrah has also warned that the man who holds back what God gave him is a miser (4:37) and that the man who gives to be seen is not giving for God (4:39), and it has promised that an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40). A greeting given well and answered better is part of that multiplication; a greeting refused is the miserliness of the tongue.

**What the Rule About Greetings Says**
The rule has a practical edge. A greeting must be answered with one at least as good, so that no greeting is left hanging. And the verse adds that God keeps count of everything, which means the answering of a greeting is not a trivial matter in His sight (4:86 states both the rule and the accounting).

**How Easily Words Were Used as Weapons**
The chapter has already shown how easily words were used as weapons in that community. It described the men who twisted their greeting into an insult when they met the Prophet (4:46 describes them). It described the men who came with impressive talk only after the matter was closed, and whose hearts God knew (4:63 states it). And it described the men whose words spoken at night undid what they had said in the day (4:81 describes them).

Against all of that, the rule here sets a floor and a ceiling: equality at the very least, and kindness at best.

**Why the Book Gives a Whole Rule to a Greeting**
The fact that the Book bothers to legislate a greeting shows how far the brotherhood of believers is meant to reach. The chapter opened by addressing all people as one family created from a single soul (4:1 gives the address), and it treated marriage as a bond that makes people relatives to one another (4:25 describes those ties).

So the person who greets with a lie is still answered with peace, and the person whose loyalty is doubtful is still answered with peace. The reckoning for what is behind the greeting is left to the One who keeps the count (4:40 states the same reminder about the exact weighing of deeds).

**What the Chapter Had Asked of the Community**
The rule sits well beside the other commands the chapter gave the community. It told people to pass on what they are entrusted with (4:87 records the lesson about the household and the promises made to them), and it called on the community to keep its agreements (4:73 shows how the obligation appears in the middle of a passage about the hesitant). It asked for fair speech (4:9 gives the instruction), and it warned against the mischief that spreads from passing on false reports (4:82 states the rule, and 4:83 handles the reports themselves).

And the two verses that follow apply the same standard to real fighting and real dealing, where the greeting of peace given by a man with his flock becomes the test case (4:94 describes it).

**The Weighing Behind It**
The chapter has told the community that God lightens what it cannot carry (4:28 states it). It described the man who held back and who will wish on the day of return that he had been with the others (4:73 describes him), and the man who counted his absence from the fight as a favour to the community (4:72 describes him). It also said that a person carries a share of whatever good he has helped along (4:85 states it).

Read with the greeting rule, that last point explains why a small courtesy is worth legislating. Every kindness a person supports, he carries a share of, and every greeting he answers is part of the record kept by the One who counts everything.
verses.87:
> Allah, there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt. And whose word is more truthful than Allah’s

**There Is No God Except Him**

The verse opens with *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa* — Allah, there is no god worthy of worship except Him — the same declaration that the sūrah placed at the root of worship: *worship God and associate none with Him* (4:36) and *association is not forgiven* (4:48). The sūrah has shown what association looks like in practice — belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51), seeking judgment of false judges though commanded to reject them (4:60), and saying to one who offers peace *you are no believer* for gain (4:94). To say *lā ilāha illā huwa* is to deny those rivals at the level of worship, judgment, and truth. The phrase follows the command to answer greeting with better or same and the reckoning of all things by the Vigilant Reckoner (4:86) to remind that the Reckoner is the only God to be worshipped. The sūrah elsewhere pairs *lā ilāha illā huwa* with *there is no helper* (4:48) to show that the One who alone is to be worshipped is the One who alone suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). Here the declaration stands as the premise for what follows: He who alone is God is the One who will gather.

**He Will Certainly Gather You on the Day of Judgment**

The promise *la yajmaʿannakum ilā yawmi al-qiyāmati lā rayba fīhi* — He will certainly gather all of you together on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt — was read as the gathering that the previous witness scene required. *Yajmaʿannakum* — will gather you — with emphatic *lām* and *nūn* was explained as the muster where a witness is brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his (4:41), where those who denied and disobeyed will wish to be dust and will not hide any statement (4:42). Where every soul that tasted death — even in towers (4:78) — is brought. The Day was called *yawm al-qiyāmah* — Day of Standing — because all stand before the Reckoner who counts even a better greeting (4:86) and an intercessor’s share (4:85). *Lā rayba fīhi* — no doubt about it — was stressed as removing the doubt that made a group fear people as God and ask *why have You ordered us to fight, delay us* (4:77) and that made laggers call absence a blessing (4:72). The One who is Vigilant Reckoner over all things (4:86) is the One who will certainly gather all things.

**About Which There Is No Doubt**

The clause *lā rayba fīhi* was linked to the Qur’an’s opening — *“this is the Book, no doubt in it”* — and to the sūrah’s question *do they not reflect on the Qur’an? Had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* (4:82). To have no doubt about the Day is the fruit of reflecting on the Book that has no inconsistency; the Book that governs inheritance whether little or much (4:7), dowry not reclaimed (4:20–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29) without contradiction is the same Book that promises the gathering without doubt. The sūrah has shown doubt’s practical fruit: publicising news of security or fear without referral (4:83), seeking *ṭāghūt* though commanded to reject it (4:60), and distorting *rāʿinā* (4:46). Each is a doubt about whether the Book and Messenger can handle the affair. To say *no doubt about it* is to answer that doubt at its root: the gathering where every atom is weighed and multiplied (4:40) is as sure as the Book’s coherence, because both are from the same One.
verses.88:
> Why are you ˹believers˺ divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites while Allah allowed them to regress ˹to disbelief˺ because of their misdeeds? Do you wish to guide those left by Allah to stray? And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way

**Why Are You Split Over Them?**
The verse asks the believers why they had divided into two groups about the hypocrites — one group treating them as Muslims still to be helped, the other treating them as enemies already. The verse's own answer is the heart of it: God has turned those men back into their unbelief because of what they did, and no one can guide a person whom God has left to wander. The question was not a request for information. It told the community that the argument itself was the problem.

**What the Dispute Was**
The sūrah has already given the evidence on both sides. These men claimed faith by day and worked against it at night (4:81). They wanted their cases decided by a tyrant's court and still called themselves believers (4:60), and they turned away as soon as they were called back to the Book and the Messenger (4:61). They came with fine words after the matters were settled (4:62), and their loyalty followed their advantage (4:72). On the other side, the community had been given clear instructions about how to treat them: check serious news instead of spreading it (4:83), return what is entrusted and judge fairly (4:58), answer a greeting with a better one (4:86), and remember that it was God's mercy that kept them from following Satan (4:87 states the same in the closing of that passage). A community with those instructions did not need to argue about the men; it needed to apply the rule and leave the judgment to God.

**The Men Who Cannot Be Guided**
The verse's last sentence is the one that settles the argument: those whom God has left to wander will find nobody to put them on the road. The sūrah has said what earns that state: taking false powers as authorities (4:51), inventing lies about God and treating them lightly (4:50), claiming a position God gives to whom He wills (4:53; 4:54 describes the family of Abraham and the gift given to them). It has also said what God does for the people who come to Him with a sound heart: He makes matters clear (4:26), He guides those who turn to Him (4:68), He gives His favour where He knows it belongs (4:54 again in the argument), and He is not unjust in the smallest degree (4:29 in the general sense). The two groups in the verse were arguing about men God had already described; the answer was to stop treating the enemy's friends as a matter of taste, and the verses that follow set out the rule for the men who wanted the safety of both sides (4:94 in this sequence, and 4:89 and 4:90 immediately after this verse). The sūrah has shown the same men twisting the words of their greeting (4:46) and ignoring the command to obey God, the Messenger and the men in authority among them (4:59). It has told the community to fight for the men, women and children who cry out for help (4:75), and it has said that the harm people suffer comes from their own conduct rather than from the man who brought the message (4:79).
verses.89:
> They wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. So do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take any of them as allies or helpers

**They Want You to Be Like Them**
The verse describes the wish of the men who had drifted back to unbelief (4:88): they wanted the believers to disown the faith as they had done, so that everyone would be level again. The Book has recorded that wish before in this sūrah: the men who follow their own desires want the believers to wander far away (4:27), and the men who were given a share of the Book traded guidance for error and want the same for the believers (4:44). What they wanted was for the community to abandon the rules that protected the weak and the obedience that joins a person to the company of the blessed (4:69).

**The Test: Take Them as Allies Only If They Move**
The verse gives a practical test for the community's relationship with them: do not take them as allies or protectors unless they leave their homes for God's cause, as the first believers had done when the command came (4:66). The same sūrah has praised the men who left their homes and endured the hardship of it (4:25 speaks of the believing women who migrated and the protection given to them), and it has told the community to march out and to fight for the men and women and children who could not defend themselves (4:75). The migration was the visible proof that a man had put the community before his clan.

**When They Refuse**
The verse's last part tells the community what to do with those who turn away after that test: they are to be treated as enemies in the field, seized and fought wherever they are found, and no one is to take them as ally or helper. The permission sits in the middle of a passage about war: the two causes men fight for (4:76), the command to the Prophet to fight even if others hold back (4:84), the men who only wanted the safety of both sides (4:91 describes that third group), and the rules that follow for a killing by mistake (4:92) and for a deliberate killing (4:93). The sūrah has also fixed the limits: men who come within a treaty with another people are not to be touched (4:90), those who want no part of the fighting are left alone, and the man who offers a greeting of peace is not to be called an unbeliever for the sake of a quick gain (4:29 is the general ban on taking what is not yours). The verse's severity has a boundary drawn around it in the very next line, and the community is not free to widen it. The sūrah has named the men who wanted the believers to go back with them (4:88), the men who took false powers as authorities (4:51), the men who denied the signs (4:56), and the men who were told to obey God, the Messenger and their leaders (4:59) but would not march when the order came (4:71) while keeping their eyes on the gains (4:73).
verses.90:
> except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people. If Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you. So if they refrain from fighting you and offer you peace, then Allah does not permit you to harm them

**The Exception That Holds the Line**
The verse follows a command to seize the men who wished the community to disbelieve with them (4:89), and it carves out two exceptions. The first covers men who have taken refuge with a people who have a treaty with the believers; the community is bound by that treaty in the same way a marriage is bound by its firm pledge (4:21 is where the Book calls the marriage agreement a serious covenant). The second covers men who have come to the believers with no stomach for fighting either against the believers or against their own people. The verse says that if God had wanted, He could have given those men the upper hand, and it ends with the rule that if they stay out of the fight and offer peace, the community has no way against them.

**Why the Rule Is Stated This Way**
The exception keeps the community's word. The sūrah began by commanding the return of everything entrusted (4:58 describes the trust command and the fair judgment that goes with it), and the Book treats a treaty as one of those trusts. To honour an agreement with one people means sparing the man who is under their protection, even when he shares the ideas of the enemy. The second exception takes account of real distress rather than loyalty: the verse describes men whose hearts are too tight to fight either side, and the sūrah has used the same word for the tightness that a person feels when a decision goes against him (4:65 is where the Book demands that the heart be free of that tightness in accepting the Prophet's ruling). These men are not pretending to a faith they do not hold, like the men who wanted a tyrant's court while calling themselves believers (4:60), and they are not the men who promised peace and then broke it. The sūrah has already forbidden the taking of other people's wealth by false means (4:29), and it treats a promise as a thing of the same kind, which is why it commands that a greeting of peace be answered with one at least as good (4:86).

**Where the Community Is Left**
The verse's last words are the most important: God has not given the community any way against these men. That closes the matter. The permission to fight in this passage applies to the men who wished the believers to disbelieve along with them (4:88), the men who turned back to hostility whenever they got the chance (4:89), and the men whose double-dealing had been exposed, whose hearts God knows (4:63). It does not apply to the man under a treaty, nor to the man who withdraws and offers peace. The Book elsewhere says that God watches over everything (4:45 is the reminder that God knows best who the enemies are), and the sūrah has taught the community to fight for the weak who cry out (4:75) and to answer the people who wanted peace with peace (4:28 again in the same spirit of lightening burdens). The verse keeps the two requirements together: the community defends itself against the men who attack it and keeps faith with the men who do not. The Book’s aim with the community is to make matters clear to them and to guide them (4:26).
verses.91:
> You will find others who wish to be safe from you and their own people. Yet they cannot resist the temptation ˹of disbelief or hostility˺. If they do not keep away, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. We have given you full permission over such people

**Men Who Wanted the Safety of Both Sides**
The verse describes a third group after the double-dealers (4:88) and the men who turned to hostility whenever the chance came (4:89). These men wanted to be safe from the believers and safe from their own people at the same time, and the verse says that whenever they were drawn back into the fighting, they plunged in headlong. The test the verse gives is the same as the one in the previous verses: if they stay clear of the fight, offer peace and hold their hands, then the community leaves them alone.

**Where the Test Comes From**
The community had been told to march when it was told to march (4:71) and to stand behind the men, women and children who were being crushed (4:75), and the Prophet had been told to keep urging the believers even when the community hung back (4:84). In that setting, the man who wants the protection of both sides is a danger to the weak he claims to stand with. The sūrah has already warned about half-loyalty: the men who came with fine words after the decision (4:61), and the men who claimed to believe and wanted a tyrant's judgment (4:58 describes the trust and the fair judgment that the community owed instead). The verse separates hesitation from duplicity: the man who cannot bring himself to fight is left in peace (4:90 is the rule that protects him), while the man who keeps rejoining the fight against the believers whenever he can is treated as what he is.

**Fighting When the Line Is Clear**
The verse ends with the community being told to fight these men wherever they are found, and it says the warrant for it is clear. The Book's word for the pressure that drives a man back to the wrong side appears three times in the Qur'an with three senses: as the fighting that keeps people from the faith (2:193 is the verse that commands fighting until that pressure ends), as a test that people are to each other (25:20 states the same), and as the trial that came to a people and their garden (68:17 is that parable). A man who returns to hostility every time the pressure rises has chosen his side, and the community is allowed to treat him accordingly. The permission is bounded by the three signs the verse names — keeping away, offering peace, holding the hand — and the sūrah has already drawn the limits of that fighting: the believer does not kill a believer by design (4:92 comes immediately after), and the man who withdraws entirely is not to be attacked (4:90). The verse before this one and the one after it together show that the Book prizes the community's safety and its word at the same time. The sūrah has spoken already of the ban on taking other people’s property (4:29), of the men who traded guidance for error (4:44), and of the fact that God knows best who the community’s enemies are (4:45).
verses.92:
> It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer unintentionally must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim’s family—unless they waive it charitably. But if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then a believing slave must be freed. And if the victim is from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money must be paid to the family along with freeing a believing slave. Those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months—as a means of repentance to Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**No Believer Kills a Believer**
The verse states a rule with one exception. It is not for a believer to kill another believer, unless it happens by mistake. Then it sets out what must be done about that mistake. A person who causes a death without meaning to frees a believing slave and pays compensation to the dead man's family, unless the family gives the money up as an act of charity. If the man killed was a believer living among a people at war with the community, then a believing slave is freed. If he was from a people bound to the community by a treaty, then compensation goes to his family and a believing slave is freed. If the person who caused the death has nothing to free and nothing to pay, then he fasts two months one after the other, and God accepts his turning back.

**Why the Rule Comes Here**
The verse sits inside a passage about fighting, and it puts a fence around it. The verses before describe men who kept going back to hostility and men who made peace and then broke it (4:90 describes the first group and 4:91 the second), and the sūrah allows the community to fight those men. This verse states what happens when a believer dies at the hands of his own people, whether through a mistake in the dark, in a crowded street, or in the confusion of a battle.

The Book calls the killing of a person a wrong that corrupts the earth, and it says that the killing of one soul is like the killing of all of humanity (5:32 states that). So the community was given a repair to make even when nobody intended the harm. The sūrah had already forbidden taking life and property by false means (4:29 forbids it), and it gave the rules of marriage and inheritance with the same seriousness, because the rights that hold a family together are the same kind of right as the safety of a life.

**The Compensation and the Family**
The rule protects the dead man's family as well as his life. The money goes to the family, and the family may give it up. The Book had already told the community to return what belongs to others and to judge honestly (4:58 states it), and it preserves the treaty even when the dead man was not a Muslim but lived under the community's protection.

The sūrah shows what freeing a slave meant in the community's own life. It turned one person's mistake into another person's freedom, and the Book uses the same remedy for a broken oath and for other wrongs (5:89 names it in the sūrah of the Table and 58:3 in the sūrah of the Dispute). The fast of two months is given to the person who has nothing, which fits the sūrah's habit of lightening burdens because people were made weak (4:28 states that), and the acceptance of a person's turning back stands at the end of the verse.

**What the Next Verse Shows**
The verse after this one names the deliberate killer, and it says that his repayment is the fire, with God's anger on him and a lasting punishment (4:93 states it). Together the two verses draw the line the sūrah has been drawing all along. A mistake has a repair, and a person who takes a life on purpose has taken something he cannot restore.

The community was told in the same chapter that a man may win a case by speaking better than his opponent, and the Prophet ﷺ warned that if he handed him his brother's right that way, he would be handing him fire (al-Bukhārī 2680 carries the report). This verse keeps the rights of the dead man's family in front of the community's life, and it shows what the community was expected to do with the power it had been given.

**Where the Rule Sits in the Chapter's Law**
The sūrah has been building a body of rules since its opening pages: the shares of a family in inheritance, the rules of marriage and divorce, and the limits that decide what belongs to whom. The killing of a believer by mistake is treated the same way, as a matter of who owes what to whom, because the Book does not separate the harm done to a person from the harm done to the community.

The two months of fasting for the man who cannot afford the remedy show the law's habit of leaving a way out for everyone, and the verse ends with God's acceptance of the person who turns back, because the mistake was never intended. The reader is left with a rule that treats a life as a debt that must be settled and a mistake as something that can be repaired. The sūrah had already set the rules for men who made peace and then broke it (4:91 describes them), and it had called the marriage agreement a serious covenant (4:21 states it).
verses.93:
> And whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward will be Hell—where they will stay indefinitely. Allah will be displeased with them, condemn them, and will prepare for them a tremendous punishment

**The Deliberate Killing**
The verse names the consequence for the man who kills a believer on purpose: the fire, staying in it, with God's anger on him, God's curse on him, and a massive punishment prepared for him. The Book joins the deliberate killing of a believer in several places to the worst human wrongdoing. The sūrah of the Criterion, for instance, puts the murder of a soul God has made sacred up against calling on other gods for help (25:68 states the three together), and the sūrah in front of the reader has already said that God does not forgive the man who dies joining others with Him (4:48 is that statement), and it has said that God is not unjust in the least degree (4:29 in the surrounding law, and 4:44 for the warning to the men who turn away from the Book).

**The Four Statements in the Sentence**
The verse stacks its four threats so that no reader can take the offence lightly: the fire, God's anger, God's curse, and a great punishment. The sūrah has used each of these in other contexts to make the contrast with the obedient: it promised the men who obey God and His Messenger the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69), it promised gardens that last (4:57 is the promise of the gardens under which rivers flow), it promised men and women who do good an honourable reward (4:13 is the promise attached to the limits of inheritance), and it opened the chapter's own account of the reward at 4:1 with the call to be mindful of God. Set against those promises, the four threats describe the exact opposite of the community the Book was building.

**The Argument the Teachers Made**
The early teachers argued about whether the deliberate killer had any route back. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse was among the last passages sent down on the subject and that nothing after it set its rule aside (Bukhārī; Muslim carry the report). The sūrah itself gives the men who follow the wrong way a warning in the same tone: they took false powers for judges (4:51 is that passage), they invented lies about God (4:54 relates to the same argument), and they were told that God's forgiveness is not offered to the man who dies in that state. The verse comes immediately after the rules for accidental killing (4:92) and immediately before the rule about the man who offers peace and is killed for his goods (4:94), and the placement is deliberate: the law protects blood, and it protects the words of peace. The sūrah has described the men cursed for their rebellion (4:118), the repentance that is accepted only before death arrives (4:17), the mercy that lightens burdens for people who were made weak (4:28), the men who traded guidance for error (4:44), the men condemned by God and left without a helper (4:52), the duty to fight for the oppressed (4:75) and the two causes for which men fight (4:76), the men who came back to hostility (4:89), and the double-faced men the community was allowed to fight (4:91).
verses.94:
> O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight. And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, “You are no believer!”—seeking a fleeting worldly gain. Instead, Allah has infinite bounties ˹in store˺. You were initially like them then Allah blessed you ˹with Islam˺. So be sure! Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what you do

> O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight. And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, “You are no believer!”—seeking a fleeting worldly gain. Instead, Allah has infinite bounties ˹in store˺. You were initially like them then Allah blessed you ˹with Islam˺. So be sure! Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**Check Before You Fight**
The verse tells the believers that when they set out to fight for God's cause they are to prove what they are doing before they act, and it names the case that prompted the rule. A man came to them offering the greeting of peace, and they told him he was no believer, because they wanted the property he had with him. The verse refuses that bargain and reminds them that God has plenty to give. It adds a second reason for restraint: the men it was written about had themselves been in the same position before God blessed them with faith. It closes with the instruction to make sure, and the reminder that God is fully aware of what people do.

**The Incident the Verse Answers**
The rule was not a theory. The reports describe a man from the tribe of Sulaym, named in some accounts as Mirdās, who greeted a Muslim patrol with the greeting of peace and was killed anyway so that the men could take his flock. The Prophet was grieved by it and recited this verse, and the two main collections carry the account (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4591; Muslim 3025 in similar wording for the same theme). The sūrah had already given the community the rule for words of peace: a greeting is to be answered with a better one or at least the same (4:86 is that command), and the man who offers peace in the field is not to be touched, whether he is the man who withdraws from the fighting altogether (4:90) or the man who would return to it if he could (4:91). The verse gives the community the discipline that makes those rules real: a claim of belief is not to be tested by the size of a man's herd.

**What the Reminder Adds**
The reminder in this verse about the community's own past is its gentlest argument. The people being addressed had themselves been unbelievers until God's favour reached them, and the Book says the same thing to the whole community elsewhere (3:103 reminds the believers how they stood on the edge of a pit before God brought them together).

The chapter has been making the same point from its opening pages. It told the believers not to take each other's property by false means (4:29 commands it). It warned them against wanting what other people hold (4:32 warns). It promised that even an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40 states it). And it described the people who wanted the believers to go back to disbelief alongside them (4:88 describes them).

**What the Verse Turns Into One Instruction**
This verse gathers all of that into a single instruction for a man travelling with a weapon: be sure of what you are doing. The same chapter has already said that the enjoyment of this life is small (4:77 states it), and that God has better stored up for the people who do right (4:95 names the ranks, and 4:96 names the forgiveness and mercy that follow).

**What Stands Around It**
The chapter has spoken of the burdens God lightens (4:28 states it), of the people who would rather the believers disbelieved with them (4:44 describes them), of the company promised to those who obey (4:69 names it), and of the rule that news of war is checked before it is spread (4:83 gives that rule).

The verses around this one carry the same theme of blood and its limits: killing by mistake (4:92 gives its rules), killing on purpose (4:93 gives its penalty), the rule this verse itself lays down (4:94 is the verse), the ranks of those who struggle in God's cause (4:95 names them), and the forgiveness and mercy they are promised (4:96 states them).
verses.95:
> Those who stay at home—except those with valid excuses—are not equal to those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind ˹with valid excuses˺. Allah has promised each a fine reward, but those who strive will receive a far better reward than others—

> Those who stay at home—except those with valid excuses—are not equal to those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind ˹with valid excuses˺. Allah has promised each a fine reward, but those who strive will receive a far better reward than others—

**Two Groups That Are Not Equal**
The verse states a plain fact before it states a rule: the believers who stay at home — apart from those who have a real excuse — are not on the same level as the men who struggle in God's cause with their money and their lives. The sūrah has already given the reason: the community had been told to go out in groups or all together (4:71), and it had been told that the men who sell this life for the next are the ones who fight, and that whether they die or win the reward is secured (4:74).

**The Addition That Came Afterward**
This verse was sent down in two parts. The blind Companion Ibn Umm Maktūm asked the Prophet what his position was, since he could not go out to fight, and the words "apart from those who have a real excuse" were added after the first revelation of the verse. The main collection records the report (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2832). So the verse does not grade people by willingness alone: it names the men who cannot go and leaves them out of the comparison. The sūrah has done the same with the man whose way was blocked by death on the road (4:100 covers that promise) and with the man whose excuse keeps him at home.

**The Two Things a Fighter Puts Down**
The verse names wealth and life as the two things the fighter gives up, and the chapter has named both before. It praised the man who spends from what God has given him (4:39 describes him). It warned the misers who hold back and press others to hoard as they do (4:37 describes them). And it said that God gave the family of Abraham the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom (4:54 states it).

The difference the verse is drawing is plain. The man who goes out spends his money and risks his life. The man who stays home spends nothing and risks nothing.

**What the Next Verse Promises**
The verse that follows names what the fighter is given: rank above rank (4:96 names it). The chapter has used that kind of language before, and always about what God gives rather than what a person claims for himself.

It promised the men who obey the company of the prophets and the truthful (4:69 names them) and a great reward (4:57 states it). It said that those who had done what they were advised would have been given something much better (4:66 states it). And it warned that the man who disobeys and crosses God's limits goes into the fire to stay (4:14 states it).

**The Complaints the Verse Answers**
The verse also follows a run of complaints and hesitations that the chapter has been recording: the men who grumbled when the fighting was commanded (4:77 describes them), the men who stayed behind and called their absence a blessing (4:78 describes them), and the community that split over the double-dealers (4:88 describes the split).

Against all of that, the chapter gives one standard. God knows where each person really stands, and the gift of knowledge and guidance that came to the Prophet came by God's favour rather than by anyone's claim (4:113 states it). The chapter had also promised the men who fight for the weak who cry out (4:75 records it) and ordered the community to check what it strikes before it strikes (4:94 orders it). It also said that God lightens burdens the community cannot carry (4:28 states it).
verses.96:
> far superior ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

> far superior ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Ranks, Forgiveness and Mercy**
The verse is the sequel to the statement that the fighters are not equal to the men who sit at home. God names what the men who struggle are given: ranks above the others, forgiveness, and mercy. The verse before it named the striver's two expenses, money and life (4:95). The rank is not a reward a man buys; the sūrah has said again and again that what God gives runs past what a person earns: He multiplies an atom's weight of good (4:40), He blots out lesser faults for the men who stay clear of the great ones (4:31), and He gives the great reward to the men who did what they were advised out of His favour (4:67). The Book's pattern with good work is to accept it and then give more than it deserved.

**The Same Two Names in a Harder Place**
The verse seals the promise with the pair of names that closes the passage about killing by mistake (4:92) and the reminder to the believers that they had once been as the unbelievers were until God favoured them (4:94). The sūrah has used the pair to cover several situations: men who err and turn back, men who fight and die, men whose faith is new and whose past is long. In all of it forgiveness does the same work: it takes the fault off the record. The sūrah has also said what God lightens for people who are weak (4:28), and it has said that He wrongs nobody by the weight of a thread (4:40 in the same argument about good and evil). Mercy here is not a mood; it is the thing that made the journey possible in the first place, as the emigrant finds havens he never built (4:100) and the men who fight for the oppressed are honoured whether they live or die (4:74).

**Ranks Given, Not Seized**
The last sentence of this verse repeats the two names the chapter has attached to its hardest laws: forgiveness and mercy.

The chapter had already handled the cases those laws cover. The person who kills a believer by mistake still owes a slave set free and money paid, and the door of turning back stands open to him (4:92 gives both). The person who kills on purpose is answered with anger and a curse (4:93 states it). And the person who sat at home with no excuse loses the rank that the fighter is given (4:95 states the difference).

So the ranks a fighter receives come from God's hand. They are not bought, and nobody seizes them.

**What the Fighters Under This Chapter's Rules Look Like**
The people who carry those ranks are the ones who fight by the rules the chapter set out. They verify before they strike (4:94 orders it). They protect the weak who cry out for help (4:75 records it). They answer the oppressor and then spare the person who offers peace and stops fighting (4:90 describes both).

Such people are not buying position. They are being handed it, and they carry it as a trust, which is where the chapter opened: it began with the ties that bind people to one another and to their Lord (4:1 gives the opening address).

**What the Chapter Said About Money and Position**
The chapter listed the ways a person can handle money. He can hold it back and call that wisdom (4:37 describes that) or give it only to be seen (4:39 describes that). He can also spend it where God has asked, which the Book compares to a seed that grows many times over (4:29 sets out the surrounding law on trade and property).

And the chapter made clear that much of what people hold was never earned in the first place: it named the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom given to the family of Abraham (4:54 states the gift). It said that good conduct leads a person to a straight path (4:68 states it) and that a person's trouble comes from himself (4:79 states it).

**What the Passage Counts**
The whole passage, running from the people who held back to the people who die on the road (4:97 describes the first group, and 4:98 and 4:99 give the excuse of the helpless), shows the reader what God counts and what He wipes out. The difference between the two groups is not social standing but conduct, and the ranks named in this verse are the visible result of that difference.
verses.97:
> When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves—scolding them, “What do you think you were doing?” they will reply, “We were oppressed in the land.” The angels will respond, “Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?” It is they who will have Hell as their home—what an evil destination

> When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves—scolding them, “What do you think you were doing?” they will reply, “We were oppressed in the land.” The angels will respond, “Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?” It is they who will have Hell as their home—what an evil destination

**The Angels at the Taking of the Soul**
The verse describes a scene that answers the men who stayed behind in Makkah and gave their weakness as the reason. The angels come to take their souls and ask them what they were doing; they answer that they were weak and oppressed in the land; the angels ask whether God's earth was not wide enough for them to move; and the verdict is given: their home is the fire, and what a terrible place to end up in. The taking of the soul in that way is the same gathering the sūrah has named in its reminder that God will bring everyone together on a day about which there is no doubt (4:87).

**The Claim and the Answer**
The answer the angels give is the hinge of the whole passage. The men blamed their surroundings; the Book asked them about the width of the earth. The sūrah has already established that the community moves: the men who are commanded to march out in groups or together (4:71), the men who go out for the weak who cry for help (4:75), and the men who leave their homes and then die on the way, whose reward is secured (4:100). It has also given the men who cannot move their due, in the two verses that follow this one. So the verse is not a judgement on weakness; it is a judgement on weakness used as a cover for staying with the powerful.

**What the Verdict Implies**
The chapter has said all along that hidden things are known. God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 states it), and He keeps count of everything (4:86 states it).

The people in this verse are the same people the chapter has described in several other places. They are the ones whose wish, when fighting is commanded, is for a delay (4:77 describes them). They are the ones who count their absence from the battle as a favour done to the community (4:79 states it). They are the ones who claim to believe while wanting a tyrant's ruling (4:60 describes them). And they are the ones who say "we obey" and then work against it after dark (4:81 describes them).

The verdict itself names the enemy of God as their shelter, and the chapter has already said that God knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45 states it). So the passage ends on the note that runs through the whole sūrah: the home a person arrives at is the one his own choices built.

**The Exception and the Mercy That Follow**
The two verses after this one provide the exception and then the mercy. First comes the exception for the helpless, the men, women and children who could not move and could not find a way out (4:98 names them). Then comes the hope held out for them, that God may pardon them (4:99 gives it).

And the chapter has already opened the door of forgiveness to the person who wrongs himself and then asks (4:110 states it). It also said that witnesses will be brought forward for every community on that day (4:41 describes them), and that the fire is enough as a punishment for those who turn away (4:55 states it).

**What the Chapter Promised the Fighters**
The chapter gave the men who do fight a different answer. It promised them rank above those who stay behind (4:95 gives the rank), and forgiveness and mercy on top of it (4:96 names both).

**What the Longer Passage Around It Settled**
The verses that surround this one carry the same theme of blood and its limits. The chapter set the penalty and the expiation for killing a believer by mistake (4:92 gives the rules), the punishment for killing on purpose (4:93 gives it), the order to verify what is struck before striking (4:94 orders it), and the ranks of those who struggle in God's cause (4:95 names them). Against all of that, this verse states what becomes of the people who had the strength to move or to fight, and chose to stay where they could not live their faith.
verses.98:
> Except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out—

> Except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out—

**The Exception: The Truly Helpless**
The verse names the people left out of the verdict just given: weak men, women and children who had no way to move and no means to work one out. The same class appears earlier in the sūrah, where the believers are told to fight for the men, women and children who cry out for help because they are oppressed (4:75). In that verse the helpless are a reason to fight; in this verse they are a reason to be excused. The Book holds both, and it is careful to say which people it means: not the man who could arrange a journey and did not, but the person whose movement depended entirely on others.

**Why the Barrier Is Named**
The sūrah has spent a great deal of its length protecting exactly the people this verse describes. It gave women their dowries as their own property (4:4), then gave them shares in inheritance and named what those shares are (4:7 to 4:11), and it set rules about the women whose families could not defend them (4:3). It told the community to return what is entrusted and to judge fairly (4:58), and it reminded the believers that they had themselves been weak once and that God had favoured them (4:94). A woman whose relatives would not let her travel, a slave with an owner watching him, a child with nobody to carry him out of Makkah — none of them is asked to do what they cannot do, and the Book says so before it says anything else about them.

**Two Truths Held Apart**
The verse keeps two truths from running into each other. The first is that the earth is wide, so a believer moves when he cannot live his faith where he is, which is the whole force of the verse just before this one (4:97 states the judgement).

The second is that God does not load a person beyond what he can carry. The chapter had already said it twice: it lightens burdens because human beings were made weak (4:28 states it), and it accepts the turning back of the person who does wrong in ignorance and then repairs it (4:110 states it).

So the helpless are excused on the second ground, while the people who had a way out are judged on the first.

**Who the Verse Names**
The verse names the men, women and children who were genuinely trapped: they could not find a way out and were not guided to one. These are not people who chose to stay. They are people who had no choice that the law can hold against them.

**How the Chapter Measured Commitment**
The chapter had already drawn the difference between a commitment made and a commitment kept. It ranked the person who fights, whether he dies or wins, above the person who stays behind without excuse (4:95 states the difference). And it named the people who were able to move and did not (4:97 names them).

**What Surrounds This Passage**
This verse states the exception, and it names the people it covers (4:98 is the verse itself). The mercy for the helpless follows in the next verse (4:99 gives the hope), and the invitation to move follows after that (4:100 gives the invitation).

Around the passage, the chapter warned the community against taking what belongs to others by false means (4:29 warns) and promised that those who avoid the great wrongs will have their smaller faults wiped out (4:31 promises it). Read together, the whole passage gives its reader a way to judge himself honestly: what could he have done, and what did he do with it?
verses.99:
> it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them. For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving

> it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them. For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving

**The Hope Held Out for Them**
The verse says that for these helpless people it is right to hope that God will wipe their fault away, since He pardons much and forgives. The sūrah has sealed other promises with certainty, and it names the same forgiveness elsewhere: it tells the men who stay away from the great wrongs that their smaller faults will be blotted out (4:31), and it promises the man who does wrong and then asks God's forgiveness that he will find God forgiving and merciful (4:110). Here the Book uses the language of hope, which the teachers explained as a sign that the pardon rests on God's choice rather than on a rule the reader can bank on.

**Who the Verse Is About**
The word "these" points back precisely to the weak men, women and children who could not devise a way out and had no path (4:98), and not to the men who had the means and stayed anyway (4:97). The sūrah has given the community other examples of the same care: the man on his deathbed making a will is the subject of a whole set of rules, and the community is warned against changing what he set down (4:92 relates to the duties that follow death, and the earlier rules about what is left behind appear in the inheritance section). It also accepts the prayer of a traveller or a sick person who cannot find water (4:43), which shows how the Book adjusts duty to capacity.

**The Hope Between Two Verses**
The hope given in this verse (4:99 is the verse itself) sits between a hard verse and a wide one. Behind it lies the judgement on the people who had the means to move and did not (4:97 states it). Ahead of it lies the promise made to the person who does move: he will find room in the earth and plenty, and if he dies on the road his reward is secured with God (4:100 states both).

So the passage runs as one unit: the judgement on those who could have gone, the exception for the helpless, the hope held out to them, and then the invitation to go.

**The Pattern the Chapter Uses**
The chapter applies the same pattern of mercy in several places. The people who fight are given ranks and forgiveness (4:96 gives both), and the person who does wrong and then turns back is given the same pair (4:92 states it). The people who obey God and His Messenger are promised the company of the prophets and the truthful (4:69 names that company), and the small good deed is multiplied many times over (4:40 states it).

The community was also told to stand up for the weak who cry out for help (4:75 records it), which is the same group of people the verse in front of the reader is describing from the other side.

**What the Book Does With People Who Could Not**
The pattern is consistent. What a person genuinely could not do is excused. What he could do is asked of him. And the door back stays open while he is alive. That is the shape of the whole passage, and the chapter had already said that God lightens burdens because human beings were made weak (4:28 states it).

So the verse in front of the reader is not a loophole. It is the completion of the law: the strong are required to move and to fight, and the trapped are covered by mercy while the invitation to escape stays open to them.
verses.100:
> Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth. Those who leave their homes and die while emigrating to Allah and His Messenger—their reward has already been secured with Allah. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Whoever Moves Finds Room**
The verse makes a promise to the man who leaves his home for God's sake: he will find in the earth many places to turn to and plenty of room. The sūrah has just recorded the question put to the men who stayed: was God's earth not wide enough for them to move (4:97)? This verse answers that question with what the mover actually finds. The Book's other accounts make the same offer in a different setting: the believers were told to go out for the men, women and children who cried for help (4:75), and the men who sold this life for the next were told they would be honoured whether they won or were killed (4:74).

**The Man Who Dies on the Road**
The second half of the verse covers the man who leaves and dies before he arrives: his reward is already settled with God, and God is forgiving and merciful. The Book treats the intention as the thing that counts here, because the migration is completed the moment it is undertaken for the right reason. The sūrah has been working toward this conclusion all along: it told the community that if they had done what they were advised it would have gone better for them and given them a great reward (4:66), and it has said that God multiplies every good deed (4:40). The emigrant who dies on the road is given the reward of the journey he intended.

**The Two Reports the Teachers Used**
The teachers read the verse with two reports in hand. The Prophet said that there is no migration after the conquest of Makkah, which ended the specific journey to Madinah as a duty (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3080; Muslim 1353), and he also said that the migrant is the man who leaves what God has forbidden, which keeps the wider migration open for every generation (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 10). Read together, the two say that the promise in this verse is not tied to one road: the believer who leaves what he must leave, or leaves a place where he cannot live his faith, is under the same promise of room to breathe. The sūrah has already shown what the community looked like when it stayed put in the wrong place: men who counted absence from the fight a favour (4:71 to 4:74 in the same passage on going out), men who took the side of the strongest when it suited them (4:91), and men whose loyalty followed their advantage (4:94). The verse in front of the reader offers the opposite road and names its two rewards: room in this world for the man who takes it, and a secured wage for the man who dies on it. The sūrah has opened with the creation of humanity from one soul and the ties that join them (4:1), has promised ranks and forgiveness to the men who strive (4:96), and has shown the two sides of the community: the helpless who are excused (4:98) and the men who hope for pardon (4:99). The verses that follow take the traveller through the journey itself: the shortened prayer (4:101) and the prayer said with weapons in hand (4:102). The sūrah has said that God lightens what people carry, because human beings were made weak (4:28).
verses.101:
> When you travel through the land, it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer—˹especially˺ if you fear an attack by the disbelievers. Indeed, the disbelievers are your sworn enemies

**Shortening the Prayer on a Journey**
The verse gives travellers permission to shorten the prayer, and it names the fear of attack as the setting in which the permission matters most: the men opposing the community are open enemies. The four-unit prayers are shortened to two, while the dawn prayer and the sunset prayer stay as they are. The practice is established: the Prophet shortened the prayer on his journeys even when there was no fighting, and when ʿUmar asked him why they shortened when they were safe, he answered that it is a charity God has given the community and that they should accept it (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 686).

**Why the Sūrah Turns to Prayer Here**
The verses just before this one were about war, movement and death on the road, and the verses just after it describe the prayer of fear, where one group prays and the other stands guard with weapons. The sūrah has been teaching the community to weigh what it can carry: it said that God lightens burdens because human beings were created weak (4:28), and it allowed a person who is ill or travelling and cannot find water to purify himself with clean earth (4:43). The permission to shorten the prayer belongs to the same way of dealing with people. The sūrah also warned, in the same stretch of verses, that the men the community was fighting wanted it to be careless with its weapons and its belongings so they could fall on it at once (4:102).

**The Fear and the Enemies Named**
The verse says that the men who refuse the faith are sworn enemies, and the sūrah has said the same about them in several ways: it called the men who wanted the believers to disbelieve with them a party to be treated as enemies (4:89), it described the double-dealers who went back to the fight at every chance (4:91), and it set out the cause for which each side fights (4:76). Their hostility is what explains the shortened prayer, the guard posted during the prayer, and the permission to keep weapons in hand while praying. The verse finishes the thought the community needed: the religion does not ask a traveller in danger to stand longer in prayer than his position allows, and the mercy is offered to him where he actually is (4:75 speaks of the weak who need help, and the same care runs through the whole passage). The sūrah has promised the man who moves for God's sake that he will find room (4:100), and it has named the enemies the community faces (4:90 for the men who withdraw, and 4:94 for the order to verify before striking). The sūrah has also given the same kind of ease in other places: a man who cannot find water may use clean earth (4:43), and burdens are lightened for people who were made weak (4:28). The sūrah has told the community that God knows best who its enemies are (4:45) and has set rules for dealing with a wife whose husband fears estrangement (4:128, where the Book again prefers settlement to hardship). The verses after this one show the prayer being prayed in the battle line (4:103). The sūrah has shown what a fair arrangement between people looks like where a dowry is settled by agreement (4:24), has told the community to be sure of what it strikes (4:94), and has described the men who stayed behind when they could have moved (4:97).
verses.102:
> When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer, let one group of them pray with you—while armed. When they prostrate themselves, let the other group stand guard behind them. Then the group that has not yet prayed will then join you in prayer—and let them be vigilant and armed. The disbelievers would wish to see you neglect your weapons and belongings, so they could launch a sweeping assault on you. But there is no blame if you lay aside your weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness—but take precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers

**The Prayer of Fear**
The verse describes the prayer said in a battle line. The Prophet leads one group while they keep their weapons with them; when that group finishes, the second group comes forward and prays while the first stands guard behind them; and the verse tells the men to keep hold of their weapons and their belongings. Then it gives the reason: the men who reject the message would like the community to leave its weapons and its baggage alone for a moment so that they could attack it in one rush. The verse ends by allowing the men to put down their weapons when heavy rain or illness makes it necessary, while still telling them to take care.

**How the Community Prayed It**
The main collections describe how the Prophet prayed this prayer: one group stood with him for one unit while the other group faced the enemy, then the groups changed places and the second group prayed a unit with him (al-Bukhārī 413 and Muslim 842 preserve the reports). The teachers of the community drew several arrangements out of these reports, because the wording allows the two groups to pray in sequence and allows one group to finish its whole prayer with the Prophet while the other stands guard and then prays alone. What every arrangement keeps is the principle the verse states: the community prays and keeps watch at the same time, and neither duty is dropped for the other.

**Prayer in the Middle of the Fight**
The verse is the Book's clearest statement that worship is not a break from the community's work. The sūrah had already told the believers to go out in groups or all together and to take their precautions (4:71 states both), and it had given the order to verify the target before striking (4:94 states that rule).
