The men the verse describes as wanting to catch the community off guard are the same men the sūrah has been describing all along, and the sūrah says their wish is for the community to slip back into what it left behind (4:89 describes that wish). The verse in front of the reader answers them with a community that keeps its appointments with God even while it is being watched by its enemies.

**The Other Prayers in the Same Passage**
The sūrah gives the community the prayer for every situation it could face, and the verse in front of the reader works with the two around it: the shortened prayer for the man on a journey (4:101 gives it) and the instruction to remember God standing, sitting and lying down, and to go back to the full prayer once the danger has passed (4:103 gives both). The sūrah also tells the community that a man who cannot find water may purify himself with clean earth (4:43 states the permission), and it tells the believer that God asks nothing beyond what a person can do (4:28 states it). The whole set shows the same care: the worship is never cancelled, it is adjusted to what the servant can manage.

**What the Verse Leaves With the Community**
The verse leaves the community with the picture of a prayer said with weapons in hand and a guard behind it. The men who prayed had marched all day and were standing in the open; they had lost brothers at Uḥud and they knew what the other side wanted. The verse tells them to keep their weapons and to say their prayer, and the sūrah's closing instruction after this verse tells them to remember God in every position. The verse also names the punishment prepared for the men who wanted to catch the community exposed, which is the answer to every plan made against the community's worship. The passage has already named the men who fight in God's way and the men who fight against the community (4:76 draws the two lines), so the prayer in the battlefield is the community's own statement of which line it stands on. The sūrah had named the man who migrates for God's sake and finds room in the earth (4:100 gives the promise) and the men who were settled and safe at home, and the verse in front of the reader shows the community on the road, praying under guard. The sūrah has also handled the request a wife may make when she fears her husband's coldness (4:128 records it), has named the wish of the men who follow their own appetites (4:27 states it), and has told the community to stand for the weak who cried out for help (4:75 gives that instruction).
verses.103:
> When the prayers are over, remember Allah—whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down. But when you are secure, establish regular prayers. Indeed, performing prayers is a duty on the believers at the appointed times

**Remember God When the Prayer Is Finished**
The verse follows the prayer of fear with an instruction that covers the hours around it. When the formal prayer is over, the men are to keep remembering God standing, sitting or lying down — in other words, in whatever position they happen to be, wounded or walking or resting. Then the verse gives the rule for the settled state: once they are safe, they are to establish the prayer in its full form. It closes by describing the prayer as a duty written for the believers at set times.

**The Three Positions and What They Cover**
The verse's three postures match the conditions the sūrah has just described. A man may be walking to the next position, sitting where he has been posted, or lying down because he was hurt. The sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān uses the same list for the people who remember God while standing, sitting and lying down and who think about the creation of the heavens and the earth (3:191). The community in the sūrah of the reader had been sick and travelling (4:43) and had been fighting for the weak who cried out for help (4:75), and the verse tells them that none of that shuts down the remembrance.

**The Duty Written at Fixed Times**
The last words of the verse turn the prayer into a fixed appointment: it is an obligation set out for the believers at named times. The Book states the same in the sūrah of the Cow, where the community is told to guard the prayers and stand before God with devotion (2:238). The sūrah in front of the reader has already made promises on the other side of that duty: the men who obey are given a great reward and a straight path (4:68 is the same passage of promise), the men who are asked to check their reports before spreading them are the same men who are expected to pray (4:83), and the men who are told to obey God, the Messenger and their leaders (4:59) are the men whose obedience is measured in ordinary practice. The Book also says that God is witness to what people do (4:94 in the same stretch of verses), which is what makes an appointment with Him something a man keeps or does not keep. The verse after this one returns to the battlefield and tells the community not to tire in pursuing the enemy (4:104 and 4:105 follow). The sūrah has promised the migrant room in the earth (4:100), has given the traveller his shortened prayer (4:101), and has taught the prayer of the battle line (4:102). The verses after this one return to the fight and to the courtroom: the community is told not to tire in the pursuit (4:105), the sūrah has said that God keeps faith with the men who return what they are trusted with and judge fairly (4:58), and it has described the community's enemies as men whose wish is to catch it off guard, and it has said that a witness will be brought from every community on the day of the return (4:41; 4:42).
verses.104:
> Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy—if you are suffering, they too are suffering. But you can hope to receive from Allah what they can never hope for. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

> Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy—if you are suffering, they too are suffering. But you can hope to receive from Allah what they can never hope for. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Do Not Tire of Pursuing**
The verse addresses a community that has just been given the shortened prayer, the guarded prayer of fear and the command to remember God in every position. It tells them not to slacken in chasing the men who are fighting them. It accepts that they are suffering, and then it says that the other side is suffering too. Then it gives the difference: the believers hope to receive from God what the others cannot hope for, and God knows everything and arranges everything wisely.

**What Makes the Two Sides Different**
The Book has placed the two hopes side by side in this sūrah with great care. On the believers' side stand forgiveness and mercy (4:96 is the promise to the men who strive), the havens and the plenty promised to the man who migrates (4:100), and, for the man who dies on the way, a reward already secured. On the other side stands the home that the men of the verse before the migration passage received (4:97 describes the men who stayed and were judged), the fear of a punishment they cannot stop (4:102 describes the wish of the enemies to catch the community off guard), and the loss of everything they were fighting for. The sūrah has said that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of a thread (4:40 is the same statement about good and evil) and that He knows the secret and the open alike (4:63).

**The Strain the Verse Acknowledges**
The verse does not tell the men that the pursuit is easy. It says plainly that they are suffering, and it reminds them that the other side is suffering too, so that the pain is not a sign that they have been abandoned.

The chapter has recorded the same tiredness in other places. It described the men who asked for the fighting to be put off (4:77 describes them), and the men who counted their absence from the battle as a favour done to the community (4:78 records that). It also described the community's own weakness in its early days (4:98 makes the exception for the helpless, and 4:99 holds out hope for them).

And it set the pain inside a larger frame. Whatever harm reaches a person comes from his own conduct (4:79 states it), God lightens what people cannot carry (4:28 states it), and the men who fight have their reward whether they are killed or whether they win (4:74 states both).

**What the Verse Gives the Tired**
So the verse takes the exhausted men and gives them the reason to keep moving: their hope is real, and God's knowledge and wisdom see to the rest.

**What the Chapter Had Put Around It**
The chapter told the community to go out in groups or all together (4:71 commands it) and to stand up for the weak who cry out (4:75 records that). It promised the men who fight that their reward is secured (4:74 promises it). It taught the community to check what it strikes before it strikes (4:94 orders it), and it set the rules of blood money and expiation for the man who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 gives the rules). It also told the community to remember God in every position and to keep the prayer at its fixed times (4:103 commands both).

The next verse turns from the battlefield to the courtroom (4:105 begins the case).

**The Same Truth Stated Elsewhere**
The Book says elsewhere that the days are turned over among the peoples, so that no community keeps a run of good fortune forever (3:140 records that), and that the men who reject God's signs should not think their delay is good for them (3:178 states it plainly). It also said that God does not give the man who follows his own desire a way to succeed over the community (4:27 states it), and it held out the promise that God will bring another turn after the community's effort (4:99 states the hope). And in the sūrah of the Spoils the community is told not to be like the men who left their homes boasting of themselves (8:47 warns).
verses.105:
> Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth to judge between people by means of what Allah has shown you. So do not be an advocate for the deceitful

> Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth to judge between people by means of what Allah has shown you. So do not be an advocate for the deceitful

**The Book Was Sent Down to Judge With Truth**
The verse tells the Prophet why the Book came down to him: so that he could judge between people by what God had shown him. Then it adds a warning that sits behind every court that has ever used a revealed law: do not take up the case of the men who betray their trusts. The sūrah had already commanded the community to give back what was entrusted and to judge with fairness (4:58), and it had told them to take their disputes back to God and the Messenger rather than to whoever they preferred (4:59), and it had exposed the men who wanted a tyrant's ruling while claiming faith (4:60).

**The Case Behind the Verse**
The reports connect the verse with a dispute over a stolen piece of armour. A man of the Banū Ẓafar was suspected of taking it, and the armour turned up with a Jewish neighbour; the family pushed the Prophet to clear their man and blame the Jew. The verse refused the pressure and told him to judge by what God had shown him rather than by the family's standing. The verse repeats the standard the sūrah gave for everyone else: the community was told to be fair when it judged (4:58) and to be careful about the enemy it suspected (4:94). Reading the two together, the Book makes no exception for a man who shares the community's faith, and it puts a limit on how far kinship or shared religion can bend a verdict.

**Judging by What God Shows**
The phrase about what God showed him marks out the limit of the Prophet's own knowledge. He judges by the Book and by the clarity God gives him, and not by private information about who really took the armour.

The chapter has already said as much in several places. God teaches a person what he did not know (4:113 describes that gift). He wants matters made clear to the community (4:26 states the will). And He knows best who the community's enemies are, and He is enough as guardian and helper (4:45 states all three).

**The People in the Case**
The men on trial are named in the verse as treacherous, and the chapter has shown what that treachery looks like in the community's own experience. It described the men whose loyalty followed their advantage (4:91 describes the men who wanted safety from both sides). It described the men whose fine words arrived only after the matter was settled (4:62 describes them). And it described the men who turn away when they are called to the Book (4:61 describes them).

The verse after this one takes the temptation to defend such men and turns it into a warning about what that defence earns (4:106 states it). It is followed by the case of the man the Prophet might be tempted to defend (4:107 describes it) and by the secret meetings of the guilty (4:108 describes them).

**What the Chapter Said Around the Case**
The chapter promised the person who moves for God's sake a home in the earth (4:100 states it) and set out the community's duties in prayer (4:103 gives the prayer) and in the pursuit of the enemy (4:104 gives it). It said that God lightens burdens (4:28 states it) and that the man who gives his wealth only to be seen gains nothing by it (4:38 states it). It said that God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 states it) and that He keeps the record of the night meetings where such men plan (4:81 states it).

**The Rule for Every Judge After Him**
The Prophet ﷺ described the limit of his own office in a report that governs every judge who came after him: I am only a human being, and disputes are brought to me, and some of the parties speak better than others, so if I give one of them what belongs to his brother because of his eloquence, I have handed him a piece of the fire (al-Bukhārī 2680; Muslim 1713). That report is the practical form of the phrase the verse uses, and it explains why the Book tells the judge to rule on what he is shown.
verses.106:
> And seek Allah’s forgiveness—indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Ask Forgiveness After the Warning**
The verse is short and it comes in the middle of a hard passage. The verse before it told the Prophet not to take up the case of the men who betray their trusts (4:105), and the verse after it repeats the warning in a broader form (4:107). Between the two, this verse tells him to ask God's forgiveness, and it names God as forgiving and merciful. The instruction is not only for the Prophet: the passage is about judging, and every judge and every reader who has ever leaned towards the side he preferred is addressed by the same command. The verse tells them where to take the fault.

**What the Sūrah Has Already Shown About Forgiveness**
The sūrah has opened this door several times. It told the man who does wrong and then turns back to God that he will find God forgiving and merciful (the same promise comes again four verses further on, at 4:110). It gave the man who kills a believer by mistake the freeing of a slave, the money paid to the family, and two months of fasting if he cannot manage that, and it described the whole arrangement as a turning back that God accepts (4:92). It allowed a man who cannot find water to purify himself with clean earth as long as he is ill or travelling (4:43), and it said that the men who wrong themselves and then come to the Prophet and ask God's forgiveness would find Him ready to accept their turning back (4:64). Even the prophet of the community is told to ask, which is the point: the mercy is not for one class of people, and the judge who fears that he has favoured his own kin needs it as much as anyone.

**The Two Names and Where They Belong**
The verse ends with the two names that have closed some of the heaviest passages in the sūrah. They are attached to the reward of the men who strive (4:96), to the promise made to the man who leaves his home and dies on the way (4:100), and to the hope held out for the helpless men, women and children who could not move (4:99). They are also attached to the law of the killing by mistake (4:92). The men who are judged by this passage include the thief, the men who pleaded for him, and the men the community was split over (4:88 describes that split). The verse puts the door of forgiveness beside all of them, and the two names repeat what the sūrah has said from its first page: God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63), and He is the one who settles the account (4:97 and 4:87 name the day of the gathering). The two verses around it show why the instruction is given here: the men in this case chose their words at night, thinking nobody heard them (4:108), and the door of forgiveness stands open to the man who admits what he did (4:110).
verses.107:
> Do not advocate for those who wrong themselves. Surely Allah does not like those who are deceitful, sinful

**Do Not Stand Up for the Men Who Wrong Themselves**
The verse repeats the warning given to the Prophet and widens it to everybody: do not argue the case of the people who betray their own souls, because God does not love a man who is treacherous and steeped in sin. The sūrah had already told the community that the man who takes the orphan's property is swallowing fire (4:10), and it had said that God is not pleased with a man who cheats and then covers it. The word for the pleading here is the same one used in the verse before, and the sūrah makes no distinction between the Prophet's court and any other court: whoever argues for a man who has betrayed his trust is standing on the wrong side.

**The Case That Prompted It**
The reports tie the passage to a piece of stolen armour. A man of the Banū Ẓafar was suspected of taking it, and it was found with a Jewish neighbour; the man's clan set about clearing their relative and putting the blame on the Jew. The verse refuses the arrangement. The Book's point is that a shared religion does not turn a theft into a favour, and the sūrah has said the same thing in other settings: it told the community not to take as allies the men who wanted it back in disbelief with them (4:89), and it forbade the men setting out to fight from calling a man who greeted them with peace an unbeliever so they could take his goods (4:94). Both of those verses are about the same mistake: letting advantage decide what the truth is.

**The Crime and the Trait**
The verse names the men twice over. They betray themselves, because the loss falls on the man who does the wrong; and they are treacherous and sinful, because what they are doing is not a single moment of weakness but a habit held in place by concealment. The sūrah has already described the same pattern: the men who met at night to work out the opposite of what they had said in public (4:81), the men who came with a solemn reference to good intention after the matter was closed (4:106 repeats the same charge of concealment), and the men whose loyalty followed their advantage (4:102 describes the guard they would let slip). It has also stated the standard for the community's own cases: report what you hear to the Messenger and to the men who can check it (4:83), return what you hold in trust (4:58), and judge by what God has made clear (4:105).

**What the Verse Closes**
The verse tells the community that the man who has already betrayed himself cannot be made clean by a clever argument. The sins it names are not errors that can be repaired by a later apology; they are the sins that the man chose and then hid. God will accept the man who owns what he did and turns back (4:17 says that plainly, and 4:92 lays down the path for the man who errs without meaning to), but He does not accept an advocate who makes the wrong look like a right, and the sūrah has said that God knows best who the community's enemies are (4:94), that He knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 in the earlier passage), and that He multiplies the smallest good (4:40). The verse after this one describes what the men in this case were doing while the community debated: they were holding their meetings at night, out of sight, and the Book tells them who was present (4:108). The verse after this one says where the loss lands: whoever commits a sin commits it against himself (4:111). The community had already been split into two camps over men like these, and the Book told them that God had left those men to go back to what they chose (4:88). The rule for a killing done by mistake shows how the Book treats an unintended wrong: a slave is freed, money is paid to the family, and a path of repair is opened (4:92). The Prophet described the limit of every court in a report that applies to this whole passage: I am only a human being, and disputes are brought to me; a Muslim who wins his brother's right by speaking better than him has been handed a piece of the fire (Muslim 1713).
verses.108:
> They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people, but they can never hide it from Allah—in Whose presence they plot by night what is displeasing to Him. And Allah is Fully Aware of what they do

**Hidden From People, Not From God**
The verse describes the men of the theft case at their work: they took care to hide what they were doing from other people, and they forgot that God was with them the whole time, listening to the words they chose in the dark. The Book puts the sentence in the middle of the passage and then closes it with the reminder that God is fully aware of what they do. The word for the night meetings is the same one the sūrah used earlier for the group that said "we obey" and then spent the night contradicting it (4:81). This verse tells the reader that the night had a witness.

**Why the Concealment Was the Whole Offence**
The men in this passage were not only thieves; they were arranging for someone else to carry the blame. Their meetings were about how to present the case, how to coach the witnesses, and how to steer the judge. The sūrah has said repeatedly that this kind of planning is done in front of God: He knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 is the statement the sūrah makes about the men who came with fine words), He hears the claim and the answer (4:58), and He keeps the record (4:82 asks the readers to think the Book over and see what it proves). The verse adds the detail that makes the crime worse rather than smaller: the men spoke their plans aloud, and God was in the room.

**The Presence the Verse Names**
The Book says that God is with people wherever they are (57:4 states it, and the sūrah of the reader names God as encompassing all things in knowledge at 4:126, and as the trustee who is enough for every affair at 4:132). The presence described here is not a physical one; the teachers explained it as knowledge and witness, the same way the Book says elsewhere that God is with the patient and the upright. The sūrah has also shown what the concealment earns: the men who say one thing and plan another in private are told that God writes it down (4:81), the men who turn away when the Book is read to them are shown to be seen (4:139 and 4:145 speak of the hypocrites and their waiting for the community's fortune to turn), and the community itself is warned that the men who hide are the men who will answer for it (4:110 is the open door, while 4:112 is the charge against the thrower). The verse turns the night meeting inside out: nothing was private, and the words chosen in the dark are the evidence in the case.

**What Follows From the Presence**
The sūrah draws the consequence in the next verses. The advocate who takes up the case in this life will not be there on the day of judgment (4:109 asks who will speak for them then, and 4:105 states the standard by which the Book judges). The wording of the verse is also a warning to the men who thought the plan was working: the sūrah has said that God does not love the treacherous (4:107), that He does not wrong anyone by a thread (4:40 is the same accounting), and that He is the one who will gather humanity on the day about which there is no doubt (4:87 states the gathering). The men were counting on the silence of a room; the verse tells them whose silence actually mattered. The Book answers men who plan in the dark by naming who was in the room. The Prophet was told to judge by what God had shown him (4:105); the judge was told to ask forgiveness after the pressure of a case like this one (4:106); the man who threw his fault onto a neighbour was told the load he was carrying (4:112); and the only private talk with any value was named: the talk that urges giving, kindness or reconciliation (4:114). God encompasses all things in knowledge (4:126), He is the trustee who is enough for every affair (4:132), and the men who wait to see which way the community's fortunes turn are known for what they are (4:145).
verses.109:
> Here you are! You ˹believers˺ are advocating for them in this life, but who will ˹dare to˺ advocate for them before Allah on the Day of Judgment? Or who will come to their defence

**Advocates in This Life, and Then What?**
The verse turns to the community that had taken up the thief's case. It says, in effect: here you are, arguing for them in this world — and then it asks who will argue for them in front of God on the day of judgment, and who will be their guardian then. The question has no answer, and the verse is built so that the reader feels the silence. The sūrah has already told the community what a court can and cannot do: a judge rules on what he is shown, and a clever speaker can win a case he should lose (4:105 sets out the standard the Prophet himself was given, and the report preserved from the Prophet makes the same point: he said he is only a human being, that disputes come to him, and that if he gives one man his brother's right because of his eloquence, he is handing him a piece of the fire — Bukhārī 2680).

**Why the Argument Works Here and Not There**
The sūrah answers the question of why people argue so hard in this life and do not think of the next: in this world the verdict depends on what can be seen and said, and in the next the record is complete. The Book has said that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of a thread (4:40), that the earth will be filled with the evidence of what people did, and that every community will be brought forward with a witness (4:41 describes that day, and 4:42 shows the men who denied the truth wishing they were dust). The community had been told to go out and fight for the men, women and children who cried for help (4:79 and the surrounding passage speak of the weak), to check what it strikes before it strikes (4:94), and to weigh the next life above this one (4:77 describes the men who asked for a delay because they preferred the present). The verse stands all of that next to the night meetings and lets the reader draw the line.

**The Guardian Nobody Else Can Be**
The second question asks who will take charge of them on that day, and the Book's answer everywhere is that no one can carry another person's load. The sūrah has said that God is the trustee who is enough for the men who rely on Him (4:132), and it has described the advocate's disappearance, since the sūrah before had said that a man's sins fall on him alone (4:110 and 4:111 follow immediately, one giving the door of forgiveness and the other the rule that the loss falls on the one who earned it). It has also reminded the reader that the community itself had been on the edge of the pit before God brought it together (4:94 and the surrounding passage on grace), that God keeps faith with the men who turn to Him (4:97 describes the men who were judged for staying), and that the day of the return brings out what was hidden (4:87). The verse leaves the advocates with the fact that the strongest court they can win is the one that closes with their own death.

**Where the Passage Goes Next**
The two verses that follow turn the passage from the courtroom to the heart. The first says that a person who does wrong and then seeks forgiveness will find God ready to forgive and merciful (4:110); the second says that whoever commits a sin commits it against himself (4:111). The sūrah has built the whole case this way: it names the crime, it tells the community to stop arguing for it, and then it opens the door for the man who will admit it. Alongside the door it keeps the warnings that the community needs: the men who hide what they do are known (4:108), the men who lie about the innocent carry a double load (4:112), and the men who were given a share of the Book and traded it for error were told plainly what they were doing (4:114 describes the good secret talk by contrast). The sūrah had already told the community not to plead for the men who betray themselves (4:107), and it had given the command to stand firmly on justice even when the case cuts against your own family (4:135). On the day the verse describes, the men who denied the truth will wish they were dust (4:42), and the record of the night meetings will be produced (4:81).
verses.110:
> Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

> Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Door That Stays Open**
The verse gives the rule that stands behind the whole passage: whoever does something wrong, or wrongs himself, and then asks God's forgiveness, will find God forgiving and merciful. The wording covers both kinds of fault — the wrong done against another person and the wrong done against one's own soul — and it names no exception. The verse sits between the men who were conniving at night and the statement that everyone carries his own load, and it is placed there deliberately: the door stands open in the middle of the crime report.

**How the Sūrah Has Prepared the Door**
The sūrah has said this before, in a different form. It said that God accepts the turning back of the men who do wrong without understanding and then put it right quickly (4:17), and it promised that the men who wrong themselves and then come to God asking will find Him ready to accept them (4:64). It gave the man who kills a believer by mistake a path back, with a slave freed, money paid and the family's loss acknowledged (4:93 is the rule for the deliberate killer, set beside it), and it described the man who errs in prayer and purifies himself with clean earth when he is ill or travelling (4:43). The sūrah has also warned that God lightens what people carry because they were made weak (4:28), and it has told the community to fight for the weak who cry out (4:75) and to keep its hands off other people's property (4:29). The forgiveness in front of the reader is offered inside a book that takes wrongs seriously, and that is the point.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**
The verse does not say that a man can keep the stolen goods and be forgiven; it says that the man who seeks forgiveness will find it. The difference is the difference between asking and pretending. The sūrah has already described the men who asked for pardon with their mouths while their plans ran in the other direction: the men who came with fine words after the matter was closed (4:62), the men who asked for a delay when fighting was prescribed (4:77), and the men who were split into two groups over the double-dealers (4:88). The verse's plain sense is that the man who comes back is received, and the sūrah has said that the man who migrates for God's sake finds room and a secured wage (4:100), and it has made the prayer a duty at fixed times (4:103). It also warns against the opposite road, where a man takes the wrong path and is left to it (4:115 and the passage before it state the result). The verse before the reader is the shortest complete statement of the Book's position on repentance, and it stands in the middle of a passage about a theft.

**The Two Names at the End**
The two names this verse ends with are the pair the chapter uses whenever mercy is the point. The man who strives and dies is given them (4:96 states it). The man who leaves home for God's sake is given them (4:100 states it). The helpless are given the hope of pardon (4:99 gives it). And the man who errs is given a way back (4:107 states it).

The chapter also describes the men who tried to hide their plans from people (4:108 describes them), and it makes the point that mercy is not a reward for secrecy. It is offered to the same people in the same sentence that exposes them.

**The Two Standards the Chapter Keeps**
God weighs every deed, even a weight as small as an atom (4:40 states it), and He knows best who the community's enemies are, and He is enough as guardian and helper (4:45 states all three).

The men in the theft case were offered the same door as everyone else, and the verse does not stop being true because of who happens to be standing in front of it.

**What the Chapter Expects of the Community It Forgives**
The chapter has laid out what it expects from the community that receives this forgiveness. The prayer said in the battle line (4:102 describes it), the prayer kept at its fixed times (4:103 commands it), the pursuit of the enemy that does not slacken (4:104 commands it), and the request for forgiveness that follows a hard case (4:106 records it).

God knows about the night meetings (4:108 states it) and about the arguing done in this life (4:109 states it). The person who commits a sin carries it himself (4:111 states it). And the talk that helps is the talk that urges what is good (4:114 names it).

The community had been told to return what it held in trust and to judge fairly (4:58 commands both), and it had been warned against taking as allies the people who wanted it back in disbelief (4:89 warns). Mercy, in this chapter, is never offered as an alternative to any of that.
verses.111:
> And whoever commits a sin—it is only to their own loss. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Every Sin Lands on the Man Who Earned It**
The verse states the rule that makes the whole passage work: whoever commits a sin commits it against himself, and God knows everything and arranges everything wisely. The sūrah has used this language of earning throughout. It promised that God multiplies every good deed many times over and adds a great reward (4:40), and it described the ranks given to the men who strive as something earned in a different currency (4:96). The same bookkeeping applies on the other side: the loss is booked to the account of the man who did the deed, and no advocate can move it.

**Why the Rule Matters in This Case**
The men in this passage had done two things: they had taken what did not belong to them, and they had arranged for another man to carry the blame. The rule in front of the reader closes the second manoeuvre. The sūrah has already named the load the thrower carries (4:112 says he carries slander and open sin), and it has said that the men who wrong themselves are not to be defended (4:107). It has also described what happens when a community tries to spread fault around: the people were split over the double-dealers and told that God had allowed them to go back to disbelief (4:88), the men who came with the fine words were told that God knows what is in their hearts (4:63), and the men who argued in this life were asked who would argue for them on the day (4:109). The verse in front of the reader is the sentence those questions were building towards.

**The Two Names at the End**
God is named here as All-Knowing and All-Wise, and the pair fits the two halves of the promise. Knowledge covers what the eye cannot see: the sūrah has said that God was with the men who chose their words at night (4:108), that He hears the claim and its answer (4:86), and that He knows exactly what the community does (4:94). Wisdom covers what people cannot arrange: the sūrah has told the readers that God gives the kingdom to whom He wills (4:104 and 4:105 speak of the gift and the judgment), and it has answered the men who argued about the division of His mercy that He distributes as He wills and raises some above others in rank (4:54 covers the gift to the family of Abraham, and the same point is repeated in the law on inheritance at 4:20 where the shares are fixed by God and not by the family). The verse closes the courtroom passage by returning the whole case to the One whose judgment includes what no human court can reach. The sūrah has shown the other side of the ledger: the man who leaves his home for God's sake finds room, and the man who dies on the road has his wage secured (4:100); the man who strives is ranked above the man who stays at home (4:95); the man who asks forgiveness finds it (4:110); and the judge is told to rule by what God has shown him (4:105). It has fixed the shares of inheritance by God's command rather than by the family's preference (4:20), it has said that whatever harm a man suffers comes from his own conduct (4:79), and it has given separate paths for the man who kills a believer by mistake (4:92) and the man who kills on purpose (4:93).
verses.112:
> And whoever commits an evil or sinful deed then blames it on an innocent person, they will definitely bear the guilt of slander and blatant sin

**The Fault Thrown Onto an Innocent Man**
The verse carries the case one step further. A man who has done wrong and then puts the blame on someone who had no part in it carries slander and a clear sin. The reports say this verse finished the armour case: the family of the Muslim who had taken it tried to make the Jewish neighbour answer for the theft. The verse tells the reader where the load ends up. The same language of earning was used in the verse before it, where the loss falls on the man who did the deed.

**What Slander Means in the Book**
The Book uses the word for the lie that leaves a person stunned and unable to answer. The sūrah has warned about the same kind of damage in several places: it told the community not to take another person's property by false means (4:29), and it forbade the men who set out to fight from calling a man who offered them peace an unbeliever in order to take what he had (4:94). The sūrah also warned the community about the opposite conduct, the good it should protect: the men who give and lend money and write the debt down are praised, and the Book tells the lender and borrower to keep the record straight (2:283 is the passage on writing down debts), and the sūrah of the Table commands the believers to stand firmly on God's side, bearing witness honestly even against themselves or their parents (5:8). Throwing a theft onto a neighbour is the exact opposite of both.

**The Double Load**
The verse says the man who does this carries two things — the slander and the plain sin — and it uses the picture of a load carried on the back. The same sūrah has used the picture of what a person carries in the other direction: the men who are rewarded carry ranks (4:69 speaks of the company of the prophets and the truthful), and the men who are punished carry humiliation (4:94 and the passage around it describe what the enemy's wish earns them, and 4:102 describes the guarded prayer that limits the damage they can do). The verse in front of the reader tells the man who has already earned one sin that he has now picked up a second, and the Book earlier described the men who plotted at night as men whose words were heard (4:108) and whose load was booked (4:40). The sūrah also warned that the man who keeps what is not his and hides it will find the record complete (4:105 gives the judge his standard, and 4:109 asks the unanswerable question). The verse ends the case with the two loads named, and the verse after it turns to the mercy that kept the Prophet from being fooled by the story (4:113). The sūrah had described the guard that men let slip when their loyalty follows the battle (4:102), the arguing done in this life by men who will find no advocate on the day (4:109), the door of forgiveness that opens for the man who asks (4:110), and the rule that every sin falls on the man who earned it (4:111).
verses.113:
> Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy, a group of them would have sought to deceive you ˹O Prophet˺. Yet they would deceive none but themselves, nor can they harm you in the least. Allah has revealed to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you never knew. Great ˹indeed˺ is Allah’s favour upon you

**God's Grace Kept the Judge Straight**
The verse tells the Prophet that if it had not been for God's grace and mercy, a group of those men would have led him off course. It then says what their plan actually achieved: nothing but harm to themselves, and no harm at all to him. And then it turns to what God had already given him — the Book, the wisdom, and knowledge of things he did not know. It closes with the statement that God's favour on him is great. The verse stands at the end of the theft passage and answers the question of what a judge can do when the pressure is applied by a family with a case.

**The Group and Their Plan**
The men the verse names are the clan of the accused man and the advocates who had taken up his case. The sūrah has described their work in the verses before this one: the night meetings where the words were chosen (4:108), the arguing in this life with an eye on the verdict (4:109), and the load of slander carried by the man who blamed the neighbour (4:105; 4:106). The Book had already told the community how to tell a good report from a bad one: take it to the Messenger and to the men who can examine it, and the men who know how to examine it will see what it is worth (4:83 covers that instruction). The verse says the plan failed, and the sūrah has said why: the Prophet was not left alone with the argument, because the Book was with him (4:105) and the Messenger is guarded by the One who sent him (5:67 states the protection of the message in the sūrah of the Table).

**The Gift Named in the Middle of the Verse**
The verse names three things God gave the Prophet: the Book, the wisdom, and knowledge he did not have. The sūrah has used the same pair for the family of Abraham, who were given the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom (4:54), and it has said that the community should think about what the Book proves rather than what the family claims (4:82). Wisdom here is the ability to see through a story: knowing which witness is lying, which man is protecting his cousin, and where a plea is actually a bribe. The sūrah has said that God teaches what people do not know (the same statement about teaching comes again in the passage where the sūrah names the gift of knowledge at 4:106 and the forgiveness the judge needs), and the verse before the reader makes the teaching part of the protection itself: the Prophet was not saved only by the revelation arriving, but by being taught how to use it.

**What the Verse Says About Pressure**
The verse is a lesson to every judge after the Prophet. The sūrah has told the community not to let its kinship pull it away from a fair verdict (4:58), not to take the side of a man who has betrayed his trust (4:107), and not to keep a man's goods on a technicality (4:92 and the wider law on property). It has said that the judge rules on what he is shown (4:105) and that the eloquence of a speaker can win a case that should be lost (the report from the Prophet on this point is Bukhārī 2680). The verse says that the strongest protection available to a man in that seat is God's own help, and it names the gift the Prophet received rather than the pressure he faced: the teaching, the wisdom, and the knowledge of things he had no way of finding out. The two names at the end of the passage — the forgiving and the merciful (4:106 and 4:110 use the same pair) — are the support that keeps a judge honest after a case has frightened him. The sūrah had given the traveller his shortened prayer (4:101) and the community its guarded battle prayer (4:102), and it names the night meetings where the words in this case were chosen (4:81). It has opened the door of forgiveness to the man who admits his fault (4:110), stated that sin falls on the man who earns it (4:111), named the load carried by the man who blames another (4:112), and set out the only private talk worth having (4:114).
verses.114:
> There is no good in most of their secret talks—except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does this seeking Allah’s pleasure, We will grant them a great reward

> There is no good in most of their secret talks—except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does this seeking Allah’s pleasure, We will grant them a great reward

**The Secret Talks Worth Having**
The verse sets a rule about private conversation. Most of it is of no use, it says, except for three kinds: talking somebody into giving, talking somebody into a kindness, and talking people back into agreement with each other. Then it promises a great reward to the man who does those things looking for God's pleasure rather than his own advantage. The verse comes after a passage about night meetings held to pin a theft on an innocent man (4:107 and 4:108), and it draws the line by what the talking is for.

**The Three Exceptions and Why They Are Named**
The Book names giving rather than hoarding, because the sūrah had warned the men who hold back God's gift and push others into holding back too (4:37). It names kindness, because the sūrah told the readers to treat parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the neighbour, the companion, the traveller and the people under their hand well (4:36). And it names reconciliation, because the sūrah had already shown two arbiters sent to mend a marriage that was cracking (4:35), and the Book's account of the same duty elsewhere in the sūrah names the men who make peace between people as the ones who do good work. The verse also speaks about the way a community talks: the sūrah had told the community to refer its news to the men who can examine it rather than spreading it around (4:83), and the Book of the Table says that whispering in a group and leaving one man out is the work of Satan (58:10 states that in another sūrah).

**What the Promise Requires**
The verse attaches the reward to two things: doing the good itself, and doing it for God's approval. That second condition is what separates the good secret from the bad one in the passage the reader has just read. The whole theft case was a piece of talk that produced a result: a neighbour accused and a family cleared. The three named items produce results too: money given, a hurt person helped, two men brought back together. The sūrah has already said that the man who gives in order to be seen gets nothing by it (4:38), that the men who strive with their wealth and their lives are ranked above the men who stay home (4:95), and that the reward for the men who do what they are told is great (4:100 and 4:96 state the ranks and the mercy). The promise in front of the reader is the same kind of reward, attached to the only conversations that leave something behind.

**The Same Three Things Said Elsewhere**
The Book gives the same three items in other words. The Prophet's own instruction says that helping a person with a word of good advice counts as a work of charity, and another well-known saying says that making peace between two people is a deed that earns a reward.

The chapter also made the principle behind this explicit in its law about property. The wealth a woman receives as her dowry belongs to her, to keep or to give away as she chooses (4:4 states it). That is the same principle of consent that runs through the verse in front of the reader, where the talk that matters is the talk that helps somebody.

**What the Chapter Had Taught About Talk and News**
The chapter warned the community to check its news before spreading it (4:94 orders it) and to keep its weapons about it during the prayer of the battle line (4:102 describes it), so that ordinary caution and ordinary worship stand together with ordinary speech.

**Where This Verse Falls in the Chapter**
The verse takes an everyday activity, people talking in a room, and gives it three purposes worth having: persuasion towards good, help for the weak, and peace between people. Everything the chapter has said about talk on either side of it is now measured against those three purposes.

On the one hand, the community was given its shortened prayer on the road (4:101 permits it) and its guarded prayer in battle (4:102 describes it). On the other hand, the night meeting where words are chosen is on the record (4:108 describes it), the advocacy people do in this life ends at death (4:109 describes it), and the person who blames another carries the load himself (4:112 states it). God's favour kept the judge from being fooled by the cleverest voice (4:113 states it).

The chapter also says later that the people who turn back from their wrong and set things right will be counted with the believers, and that God will give them their reward (4:146 states both).

**The Widening Frame**
Around this verse the chapter keeps the same practical concerns in view: the wishes of people who follow their own appetites (4:27 describes them), the burden God lightens for people who were made weak (4:28 states it), the permission to purify with clean earth when water cannot be found (4:43 permits it), and the compensation owed by a person who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 gives it). In all of it, the standard is the same. What a person says and does should leave other people better off, and the reward follows the deed rather than the intention behind it.
verses.115:
> And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell—what an evil end

> And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell—what an evil end

**Whoever Walks Away After the Road Is Clear**
The verse names the man who opposes the Messenger after the guidance has become plain to him and who follows a way other than the one the believers walk. It says what happens to him: God leaves him to the direction he has chosen, and his destination is the fire, and it is a terrible place to end up. The Book has used this root before in the same sūrah: God allowed a group of men to go back to disbelief because of what their own hands had earned (4:88). The teaching is the same in both: a man who keeps walking away is not chased.

**The Two Conditions in the Verse**
The verse attaches the result to two things rather than one. The first is opposition after the guidance has come, which means the man knew what he was rejecting; the sūrah has noted the difference between a mistaken man and a knowing one. The second is following a road other than the community's road, which sets the disagreement in public rather than in the man's own head. The sūrah has described the same two conditions several times: the men who took false judges while claiming faith (4:60), the men who turned away when they were invited back to the Book (4:61), the men who said one thing in the Prophet's presence and another after they left (4:81), and the men whose loyalty followed the turn of the battle (4:102). In each case the problem is not a lack of information.

**What It Means to Be Left to One's Choice**
The verse describes God handing the man over to what he chose. The sūrah has shown the patience that comes before that point: God accepts the man who does wrong and turns back (4:110), He gave the man who killed by mistake a way to repair the harm (4:92), and He keeps His favour on the community that came to the faith after being weak (4:99 and 4:100 describe the door held open). It has also shown the warnings that precede it: those who hide from people cannot hide from God (4:108), the man who blames another for his own fault carries the load (4:112), and the men who oppose the Messenger after being told plainly are the same men the sūrah has described as unwilling to accept a ruling against them (4:65). The verse says that the road out of the community is open, and the Book describes what is at the end of it.

**The Case the Chapter Was Building**
The verse after this one takes up the case the whole sūrah has been building. It states that God does not forgive a person who dies while joining a partner with Him, while He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills (4:116 states it). The chapter had said the same thing earlier (4:48 states it), so the ruling is not new here.

The verses on either side fill in the picture. Before this one, the chapter named the people who took up a false case (4:106 names them). After it comes the long passage on inheritance and on the standing of women and orphans (4:123 begins that passage), where the same standard of what a person earns is applied to men and women alike (4:124 states it plainly).

What this verse itself adds is its verdict on the person who turns away after the road has been shown to him. The Book says the same thing elsewhere in other words: those who turn away are left in their own darkness (6:110 states it), and those who fight God and His Messenger are cast out (8:13 states it).

**What the Chapter Put on the Other Side**
The chapter also placed a great deal on the other side of the scale. It promised the person who migrates for God's sake a home in the earth (4:100 states it). It described the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 describes it) and set out the limits of inheritance together with the reward for those who keep them (4:13 gives the limits). It told the believers to stand firmly for justice even when it cuts against themselves (4:135 commands it).

It named the punishment of those who cross the limits (4:14 names it), the clarity God wants for the community (4:26 states it), the wishes of those who follow their own appetites (4:27 describes them), and the exactness of the scale that weighs even an atom (4:40 describes it). It described the fire as the destination of those who refuse the signs (4:56 states it). It told the community to obey God, the Messenger and those in authority (4:59 commands it), and to take its precautions and go out (4:71 commands it).

It set the penalty for killing a believer on purpose (4:93 sets it), ordered the community to verify before it strikes (4:94 orders it), and described those who stayed behind in a place where they could not live their faith (4:97 describes them).
verses.116:
> Surely Allah does not forgive associating ˹others˺ with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills. Indeed, whoever associates ˹others˺ with Allah has clearly gone far astray

**The One Wrong That Is Not Forgiven**
The verse states the rule that gives the sūrah's warnings their ceiling. God does not forgive a person who joins other beings with Him in worship, but He forgives anything less than that for the person He chooses. The same statement was made earlier in the chapter (4:48 states it in almost the same words), and the placement here matters. It comes immediately after the verse about the person who walks away from the community's road (4:115 describes him), and it stands at the head of a passage that turns to inheritance and to the errors of the People of the Book about Jesus (4:171 gives the command to say nothing about God except the truth).

**What the Rule Covers**
The Book treats joining partners with God as the one fault that cannot be repaired after death, and the judgement follows from what the claim is. It is not a wrong done to a creature that can be paid back. It is a denial of the One on whom the whole creation depends.

The sūrah has already told its readers that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom and that He multiplies good (4:40 states both). It says that whoever earns a sin earns it against himself (4:111 states it), and that the door of asking forgiveness stands open for anything else (4:110 is the plain statement, and 4:97 shows the men who were judged for staying where they could not live their faith). It says in this sūrah that those who invent lies about God are the ones furthest away (4:50 describes the lie as a plain sin).

**The Exception the Verse Leaves Open**
The verse says that what is less than joining partners with God is forgiven for whom God wills. The teachers read this as a statement that mercy belongs to God to give, and that it is not something a person can count on as a right. The sūrah has shown the community where its own prosperity came from. God gave the family of Abraham the Book, the wisdom and a kingdom, and those who were given a share of the scripture traded it for error (4:54 and 4:58 appear in that argument about what is given and what is earned).

**The Promises Beside the Warning**
The sūrah also promises those who obey God and the Messenger the company of the prophets and the truthful (4:69 gives the promise, and 4:100 and 4:99 name the reward). It says that God knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45 states it) and that He is the one who settles every account (4:87 states the day of gathering).

So the verse leaves every reader with the weight of the Book's central claim. Whatever else a person brings, the one thing he cannot bring is a partner beside God. The sūrah has promised the person who migrates a home in the earth (4:100 gives the promise), has forbidden taking other people's property by false means (4:29 forbids it), has described those judged for staying where their faith could not be lived (4:97 describes them), and has held out hope for the truly helpless (4:99 names them).
verses.117:
> Instead of Allah, they only invoke female gods and they ˹actually˺ invoke none but a rebellious Satan—

> Instead of Allah, they only invoke female gods and they ˹actually˺ invoke none but a rebellious Satan—

**What They Call On Instead of God**
The verse says that the men who join partners with God call on nothing but female names, and that in the end they are calling on a rebellious devil. The Book is not describing a religion with a serious set of gods; it is describing names. The Arabs of Makkah called on al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, and the Book says elsewhere that the men who take protectors besides God say they worship them only to bring them nearer to Him (39:3 states the claim and the answer). The claim does not survive the question of what the names can do.

**What the Book Makes of the Names**
The sūrah has just described the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116), and this verse explains what the wrong looks like in practice: an act of calling directed at something that cannot answer. The sūrah has said that the men who were given a share of the Book took false powers as their authorities and then claimed faith (4:51), and it told the Prophet not to argue the case of the men who betray themselves (4:107) and not to be misled by the men who hold their meetings at night (4:108). The calling in this verse is the last item in that list of misdirections. The Book also says that the idols will deny the worship given to them on the day of judgment, and it reports that the idolaters themselves admitted that the names were no more than inventions of their fathers (see the argument in 16:58 for the contempt the Arabs held for daughters while assigning them to God).

**Where the Verse Sits in the Argument**
The passage has been moving through the reasons people give for the choices they make. They walked away from the community's road (4:115 describes it). They joined partners with God and wandered far from the path (4:116 describes it). And now the Book names the being they were actually serving.

The chapter had already answered the people who follow their own appetites, saying that they wish the believers to wander far away (4:27 states it), and it named the road of the people who fight for false powers rather than for God (4:76 names it).

**What the Verse Does in Two Moves**
This verse does two things at once. It reduces the gods to names that have no power in themselves, and it names the one actually standing behind them.

The verses that follow give that being his own speech. The curse laid on him is recorded first (4:118 records it), and then he states his programme and the promises he makes (4:119 gives them).

**What the Chapter Had Already Said About These Choices**
The chapter said earlier that the people invited to bring their disputes to the Book turn away instead (4:60 describes them), and that the people who trade their share of the scripture for error want others to leave the road with them (4:114 names the private talk that earns a reward, by contrast). It also recorded how the Arabs of the time despised daughters while assigning them to God (16:58 records it). That is the measure of the names being called on.

The chapter also showed what those appetites cost other people. The people who follow them want the believers off the road (4:27 describes them), and they think nothing of taking other people's property to get their way (4:29 warns against it).

And the chapter keeps the other side of the ledger visible. It says that God owns everything in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states it), which is why no name carries anything by itself. Where the names lead is stated next: the promises held out to the follower (4:120 names them), the end of the people who accept them (4:121 names it), and the home promised to the people who refuse them (4:122 names it).
verses.118:
> cursed by Allah—who said, “I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants

> cursed by Allah—who said, “I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants

**The Curse and the Speech After It**
The verse says the devil is cursed by God, and then it lets him speak: he declares that he will take a fixed share of God's servants. The Book gives the curse its setting elsewhere: the story of his refusal to bow when he was commanded, and his request for a delay until the day of the return (the account is given in the sūrah of the Heights, in the sūrah of the Rocky Tract, and in the sūrah of Ṣād, where God says the curse is on him until the day of judgment — 38:78). The verse in front of the reader takes the sentence from that scene and shows what he did with it.

**What the Devil Claims**
The claim is a share, a portion fixed and appointed. The sūrah has promised the men who strive in God's cause that they will receive their portion of ranks and mercy (4:96), and the emigrant that he will find room and a secured wage (4:100). Here the other side makes his appointment. The Book's answer to the claim is that it can only reach the people who choose him: the sūrah has described the men who followed their own appetites (4:27), the men who took the side of the strongest and went back to the fight at every chance (4:89), and the men who held their plans out of sight (4:108). Those are the men who answered his call, and the sūrah has already told its readers how weak the forces of that side are (4:76).

**The Curse and the Scale**
The verse stands between two statements in this chapter about exact justice. The first is that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 states it). The second is that the person who kills a believer on purpose is answered with anger, a curse and a great punishment (4:93 states it).

Placing the curse on the devil between those two statements keeps the punishment from looking arbitrary. The curse is not the fate of everyone the passage is describing. It is the fate of the one who refused and was expelled, and the share he claims belongs to the people who take him as their guardian.

**What the Verse Sets in Order**
This verse, read with the ones around it, sets out a sequence. The leader of the wrong way refused God's command and was expelled. The punishment is his, and the curse on him lasts until the day of judgment, a curse the Book records elsewhere in the same terms (38:78 records it). Then the verses that follow name the people who join him (4:119 gives his programme and his promises) and the destination they arrive at (4:121 names it).

The verse before this one described calling on names that cannot answer (4:117 describes them), and the verse after it gives the programme he announced to mislead people (4:119 states it).

**What the Chapter Had Said About the Same Ground**
The chapter had already covered the same ground from several sides. It said that the people who throw their faults onto others carry the load themselves (4:112 states it). It said that those who cross God's limits will burn (4:14 states it), and that those who trade the Book's guidance for their own advantage make the trade the scripture warned them against (4:44 describes them).

And it said specific things about the people in the middle of this argument. The people who plead for someone who has betrayed himself are standing on the wrong side (4:107 states it). The people who walk away from the road after it is clear are left with what they chose (4:115 states it). The wrong that cannot be forgiven is joining partners with God (4:116 states it). And among the people who claim to believe are some who have taken false powers as their authorities (4:51 describes them).
verses.119:
> I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah’s creation.” And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah has certainly suffered a tremendous loss

> I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah’s creation.” And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah has certainly suffered a tremendous loss

**What the Devil Promises to Do**
The verse continues the speech: he will lead them away from the road, fill them with hopes, and order them to cut the ears of cattle and to change God's creation. Then the sūrah gives the verdict on those who take him as a guardian instead of God: they have lost, and the loss is clear. The three items in his programme were not inventions; they were the religious practices of the Arabs around the community — the marking of animals for idols, the changing of the body for show, and the promises of the soothsayers.

**The Two Items That Were on the Ground**
The Book names the animals in the sūrah of the Table, where it describes the livestock dedicated to idols by old custom, with the ears slit and the names invented by men (5:103 states the practice and rejects it). The alteration of God's creation covers the customs the Book refuses and the claims the idolaters made about God's family, which the sūrah addresses a few verses later when it tells the People of the Book to say nothing about God but the truth (4:126 refers to the ownership of everything and the knowledge of God, and the argument continues at 4:172). The sūrah has already said that the men who followed their own appetites wish the believers to wander (4:27), and it has said that the men who are misled think they are in the right (4:115 describes that state). The programme in this verse shows how far the misguidance goes: it reaches the animals, the body, and the household's understanding of God.

**The Hopes That Are Not Hopes**
The verse names the delusion it is describing: empty hopes. What makes them empty is that they are promised by a being with no power to deliver anything.

The chapter has set real promises against them. It promised ranks and mercy to those who strive (4:96 gives both), room in the earth and a secure wage to those who migrate (4:100 gives both), and a hearing with God for those who spend quietly to please Him rather than to be seen (4:114 states it, and 4:38 describes the man who gives for show). It held up the way of Abraham as the best company a person can keep in religion (4:125 holds it up).

Against all of that stand the promises of the one who wants a share in human beings: that the idols will speak up for them, that the family will keep its standing, that money held back is safety.

**What the Chapter Says About Holding Back**
The chapter has already shown what that kind of trusting looks like in practice. It described the men who keep what God has given them and urge others to be as stingy as they are (4:37 describes them) and the men who give only so that people will see them (4:38 describes them).

The verse in front of the reader puts the two hopes side by side and says plainly what the second one is worth. The verse before it gave the curse and the opening words of the being behind them (4:118 gives them).

The verse after it sums up the whole programme in one line (4:120 does that) and then names the destination of everyone who accepted it (4:121 names it). The two verses after that name the promise being made (4:120 states it), the home of the people who accept it (4:121 states it), and the home of the people who do not (4:122 states it).

**What the Chapter Says on the Other Side**
The chapter has also described how God deals with the people He is addressing. It said that He lightens burdens because human beings were made weak (4:28 states it), that He knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45 states it), and that those who stand up for the weak who cry out are doing work the community owes them (4:75 records it).

It warned that the night meetings are recorded (4:108 warns), opened the door of forgiveness (4:110 opens it), named the knowledge God taught the Prophet (4:113 names it), and stated the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 states it). And the verse before this one named the beings the idolaters call on (4:117 names them), so the reader can see who is doing the promising.
verses.120:
> Satan only makes them ˹false˺ promises and deludes them with ˹empty˺ hopes. Truly Satan promises them nothing but delusion

> Satan only makes them ˹false˺ promises and deludes them with ˹empty˺ hopes. Truly Satan promises them nothing but delusion

**Promises That Come to Nothing**
The verse states the matter in two sentences: the devil makes them promises and fills them with long hopes, and everything he promises is a trick. The sūrah has shown what the tricks look like from the inside. There is the hope that a share of the Book can be traded for a better position (4:107 and the passage before it describe the men who argued the case for a thief), the hope that a greeting of peace can be used as an excuse to take goods (4:114 in the sense of the good talk the Book rewards), and the hope that the man who waits for the turn of the battle will be counted as a friend (4:109 asks who will stand for such men later). Each one looks like a small gain and ends in a loss.

**The Wishing the Sūrah Has Named**
The Book's language here is the language of wishing, and the sūrah has already used it for people rather than for the devil. It described the wish of the men who follow their own appetites that the believers would leave the road (4:27), the wish of the men who were promised long lives and easy outcomes by the being whose speech the sūrah has just recorded (4:119), and the wish of the man who had stayed at home when the fighters returned with bounty (4:73). The sūrah also warns about the man who keeps putting his turning back off until death arrives and then asks to be given another chance (4:18 states that no such turning back is taken). Wishing is the whole activity: it keeps a man busy while his time runs out.

**Where the Delusion Breaks Down**
The Book breaks the spell by naming what a person's real position is. The chapter said that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 states it), that whatever harm a person suffers comes from his own conduct (4:79 states it), and that the community was ordered to be sure of what it struck before it struck (4:94 orders it).

It also told the community what to do instead. Report news to the people who can check it (4:83 gives that rule). Talk in private in a way that urges good, speaks for the weak, or makes peace (4:114 names all three as the talk that earns a reward). And hold on to the promise that God's word is true (4:122 states it).

**Why the Promises Fail Their Own Tests**
The promises made by the one who wants a share in human beings fail every one of those tests, and the verse says so in a single sentence. The next verse names the place where the people who believed him end up (4:121 names it), and the verse after that names the home of the people who did not (4:122 names it).

**The Same Wishing Elsewhere in the Chapter**
The chapter has shown the same kind of wishing at work elsewhere. It described the people who held back when they were told to fight (4:77 describes them) and the people who wanted the believers to go back to disbelief with them (4:89 describes them). It also described the guard that gets set down when loyalty follows the course of the battle (4:102 describes it) and the load carried by the person who blames another for his own fault (4:112 names it).

The verses just before this one opened the being's speech (4:117 begins it), and the curse laid on him follows (4:118 gives the curse). So the reader sees the whole promise being made, and then sees it weighed.
verses.121:
> It is they who will have Hell as their home, and they will find no escape from it

**Their Home and the Way Out**
The verse says that the people who followed the promises will have the fire as their home, and that they will find no way to escape from it. The sūrah has used the word for home twice already: it is the destination of the men who stayed behind when the earth was wide enough for them to move (4:97), and it is the place of the men who walk away after the road has been made clear to them (4:115 describes that man and where he goes). The word itself means the refuge a person settles into, and the Book uses it for the garden as well, so the contrast is deliberate: the man who takes a guardian other than God has already chosen his shelter.

**What the Verse Leaves Out**
The verse names no escape route, and the sūrah has shown its readers where the escape routes actually were while they were alive. The first is the door of asking forgiveness, which the sūrah states for the man who does wrong and then turns back (4:110). The second is the road out of the place where the faith cannot be lived, which the man who takes it finds opened for him (4:100), along with the man who dies on the way, whose wage is secured. The third is the change of heart behind a private conversation that urges giving, kindness or reconciliation (4:114 promises the reward). The fourth is the correction a man makes of another man's harm, since the sūrah gives the man who kills by mistake a path of repair (4:92) and warns the man who blames another for his own fault what he is carrying (4:112). The verse in front of the reader describes a state that comes after all of those chances have passed.

**The Guardians Who Cannot Help**
The verse answers the wish that runs through the whole passage. The men in the theft case had advocates who argued for them during the case (4:109 asks who will argue for them later), the men in Makkah had the standing of their families and the names of their gods (4:117), and the men in the community had their own good opinion of themselves. The sūrah says that none of those is a guardian when the case is real: God knows best who the community's enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45), the men who cried out for help and had to be answered by the community (4:75), and the day of the return brings every claim with it (4:103 makes the prayer an appointment at fixed times, and the wider passage names the accounting). The verse names the fire as the home of the men who answered the wrong call, and the next verse names the home of the men who answered the right one (4:122). The sūrah has shown the two ends of the passage: the curse on the being who made the promise (4:118), his programme of misleading (4:119), and the promise itself, which is nothing but a trick (4:120). The home named here is the one the fire was called earlier in the sūrah (4:56 names the exchange of skins for the punishment) and the one the deliberate killer was given (4:93). The guard dropped in the battle prayer is part of the same story (4:102), and the next verse names the road the other group took (4:123).
verses.122:
> And those who believe and do good, We will soon admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true. And whose word is more truthful than Allah’s

> And those who believe and do good, We will soon admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true. And whose word is more truthful than Allah’s

**The Other Home**
The verse gives the reward of the people who believed and did good work: gardens with rivers running beneath them, and a stay that does not end. It closes with the statement that God's promise is true and asks who could be more truthful than God in what he says. The verse is the direct answer to the one before it, where the men who followed the promises they were given end up with no way out. The sūrah has been drawing this pair of destinations from its opening sections.

**What the Two Halves of the Description Mean**
Belief and good work are the Book's short description of the saved throughout the sūrah: the same pair is given as the condition for the gardens earlier in the chapter (4:57) and in the passage on the limits God set for inheritance (4:13). The Book has also named the people who believe and do good in the passage that answers the men who claim grace by belonging to a group, where it says that whoever does good, man or woman, and has faith will enter the garden and will not be wronged by the width of a date stone (4:124). The good work the sūrah has in mind is concrete: the talk that urges giving, kindness and reconciliation (4:114), the standing up for fairness even when it cuts against one's own people (4:135), the money spent from what God gave rather than hoarded (4:37 and 4:38 describe the two wrong uses), and the effort the men of the community put into the cause they had taken up (4:95 through 4:100 name the ranks and the reward).

**The Question the Verse Ends With**
The verse closes by asking who is more truthful than God, and the chapter has asked the same thing in another form: it stated that God's promise about the gathering of humanity is true (4:87 states it). The question is not an argument so much as the end of one, because the claim under discussion was a set of unverified hopes.

The chapter has answered that claim from several angles. It noted that the men who were given a share of the Book wanted to turn the believers back, and told them that God's decision was coming (4:54 describes the men who begrudged the gift to the family of Abraham). It told the men who mistook their own wishes for the truth that grace is not obtained by wishing (4:123 states the rule). And it said that the Book was sent to judge by what God shows (4:105).

**Truth Beside Wishes**
