This verse sets the two side by side. On one side are the wishes, and on the other is a promise from God together with a stay that never ends. The verse after it takes up the same argument about who actually receives the reward (4:123 continues it).

**How the Chapter Built the Argument**
Before reaching this point the chapter had moved through the whole sequence: the false gods (4:117), the curse on the being behind them and his programme of misleading (4:119), the promises that come to nothing (4:120), and the home of the men who believed those promises (4:121).

It had also set out what faith earns and what it costs. It promised the migrant room in the earth and a wage (4:100) and named ranks and mercy for the men who strive (4:96). It named the forgiveness waiting for the man who asks (4:110), the prayer said in the battle line (4:102), the prayer kept at its fixed times (4:103), and the pursuit of the enemy that does not slacken (4:104). It described the destination of the men who stayed behind in a place where they could not live their faith (4:97) and of the men who walked away from the road after it was clear (4:115).

It named the helpless people who are excused (4:99), the appetite of the men who follow their own desires (4:27), and the exact scale that weighs even an atom (4:40). And it named the penalty laid on the man who kills a believer deliberately (4:93). Against all of that, this verse states the promise that cannot be broken.
verses.123:
> ˹Divine grace is˺ neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book! Whoever commits evil will be rewarded accordingly, and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah

> ˹Divine grace is˺ neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book! Whoever commits evil will be rewarded accordingly, and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah

**Not by Wishing**
The verse refuses two claims at once: the claim of the Muslims that their religion would save them by name, and the claim of the People of the Book that their standing would do the same. Neither set of wishes decides anything, it says. Then it states the rule: whoever does an evil deed will be paid for it, and he will find no guardian and no helper besides God. The verse follows the passage on the devil's promises and the empty hopes, which is exactly the material it is answering.

**The Wishes the Sūrah Names**
The Book uses the same word for wishing that it used for the devil's promises (4:119 and 4:120). The sūrah has already shown human wishes doing damage: the wish of the men who follow their own appetites that the believers leave the road (4:27), the wish of the men who want the believers to go back to disbelief with the them (4:89), the wish of the men who want the community to leave its weapons for one careless moment (4:102 states that wish in the battle prayer), and the wish of the men in the armour case that the blame would settle on their neighbour (4:112 states the load carried by the man who blames another). Against all of that the verse says that the outcome is not decided by who wants what.

**The Rule Stated in the Verse**
The verse says that a man is paid for the evil he does, and the sūrah has stated the same rule in several ways: whoever earns a sin earns it against himself (4:111), the man who throws his fault on another carries slander as well (4:112 covers that heavier case), the deliberate killer is answered with anger, curse and punishment (4:93), and the men who cross God's limits end in the fire (4:14). The point of the rule is that it applies to everybody: the sūrah has just said that whoever does good, male or female, with faith enters the garden and is not wronged in the least (4:124 follows this verse), and it has said the same in the passage about the men who claimed grace by belonging: whoever works evil is paid for it, and whoever does good is paid for it, man or woman alike (4:124 is the same promise in the positive). The Book's other sūrahs state the rule for the People of the Book in the plainest terms, saying that whoever believes in God and does right has his wage with his Lord, with no fear and no grief (2:62 carries that statement), and that the reward of God is not decided by people's claims about themselves.

**The One Nobody Is Left With**
The verse ends by saying that the person who does evil finds no protector and no helper besides God. The chapter has already named the helpers its readers were relying on, and it has shown each of them failing. There were the families who would argue a case in this life (4:109 asks who will argue it for them later). There were the gods whose names were called on (4:117 names them). There were the men whose loyalty could be bought and dropped (4:102 describes the guard that gets set down). There were the men who took false powers as their authorities (4:51 describes them) and the road that looked better than the community's road (4:115 describes it).

And the chapter has named the One who is actually enough. God is the guardian who settles every affair (4:132 states it). He knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45 states it). And everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him (4:126 states it).

So the verse leaves a person with the rule, and with the only name worth relying on. The next verse states what that reliance produces (4:124 states it).

**The Door That Stood Open Before the Sentence Arrived**
The chapter had shown the way back before this sentence was passed. The person who does wrong and then asks forgiveness finds it (4:110 states it). The chapter named the home of the men who followed the false promises (4:121 names it) and the home of the men who believed and did good work (4:122 names it).

It also described the demand of the men who wanted a written revelation to come down on them from the sky (4:153 describes it) and the twisting of words by men who had the Book in front of them (4:46 describes it). It stated the duty of the community to answer the weak who cry out for help (4:75 states it). And it said that God weighs every deed exactly (4:40 states it).
verses.124:
> But those who do good—whether male or female—and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone

> But those who do good—whether male or female—and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone

**Whoever Does Good, Man or Woman, With Faith**
The verse states the other half of the rule. Whoever does good work, whether a man or a woman, and holds the faith, will enter the garden, and nothing they did will be lost, not even the tiny white speck on a date stone. The verse answers the claim of the men who thought that the reward followed their group and their family, and it removes the assumption that a woman's work counts for less.

**Why the Verse Names Both**
The Book names both sexes throughout the sūrah because the community it was building had customs that needed changing. It opened by saying that God created humanity from one soul and spread men and women across the earth (4:1), it made the shares of inheritance binding for men and women alike (4:7 and the fuller rules at 4:11), it set the rules for marrying the believing women who lack a protector (4:25), and it gave the helpless among the men, the women and the children a place of their own in the passage about moving to where the faith can be lived (4:98). The Book states the pairing of man and woman in the reward again in another sūrah, saying that whoever does right, male or female, and believes, will be given a good life and a reward better than what he or she did (16:97 carries that promise). Naming both here is not decoration; it is the answer to the men who thought the promise was theirs by right.

**The Work the Verse Means**
The good work is the work the sūrah has been describing: the private conversation that urges someone to give, to help, or to make peace (4:114), the standing for fairness even when it costs (4:135 gives that command), spending from what God provides rather than holding it back or showing off (4:37 and 4:38), the effort and the money the men of the community put into the cause (4:95 names the ranks), and the good opinion a person gives up when he stops elevating himself over others (4:49 warns the men who do that). The verse adds the condition of faith to the work, which the sūrah has stated elsewhere (4:136 commands the believers to keep their faith firm), and it warns that the men who joined partners with God lose the thread entirely (4:116). Both elements are needed: the work without the belief is a claim, and the belief without the work is a name.

**Not Even a Speck Is Lost**
The verse promises that nothing is lost, and it uses the smallest speck a person can see to make the point. The chapter had already used the same image for the other side of the scale, saying that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of a speck and that He multiplies good many times over (4:40 states both).

The verse also answers the dispute running through this passage. Two groups were arguing about who would be saved by belonging to whom. The Book names the actual conditions instead: belief, and doing what is right, for men and women alike. And it puts a speck on the scales to show how exact the accounting will be.

**The Rule the Chapter Stated on Both Sides**
The chapter stated the same rule in both directions. Whoever earns a sin carries it himself (4:111 states it). Wishes decide nothing, so ancestry and claims give nobody a free pass (4:123 states it). And whatever a person meets of harm comes from his own conduct (4:79 states it).

The chapter also named the two destinations the dispute was about: the home of the people who followed the false promises (4:121 names it) and the home of the people who believed and did good work (4:122 names it). This verse then states the conditions again in its own words (4:124 states them).

**What the Chapter Had Settled Around It**
The chapter fixed the shares of inheritance by God's command rather than by the family's choice (4:20 gives the shares). It forbade taking what belongs to others (4:29 forbids it) and warned against envying what other people hold (4:32 warns).

It described the people who begrudged the gift given to the family of Abraham (4:53 describes them), and it named the people who asked for the fighting to be delayed because they preferred the life of this world (4:77 describes them). Every one of those passages was about the gap between what people claim and what they actually do, which is the gap this verse closes.
verses.125:
> And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend

**Who Is Better in Religion?**
The verse asks a question and answers it in the same breath. Nobody is better in religion than the man who hands himself over to God, does good work, and follows the way of Abraham, who turned away from everything false. Then it says that God took Abraham as a close friend. The verse follows the argument about who will be saved, and it answers with a person rather than with a group.

**The Three Things Named**
The first is submission, the handing over of oneself to God. The sūrah has said that those who follow the way of Abraham are the ones God guided (4:68 names the path, and 4:54 names the family), and that God's will is to make matters clear and to guide people into the ways of those before them (4:26 states it). The second is doing good, which the sūrah has described in detail. It praises talk that urges giving, kindness and reconciliation (4:114 names it). It commands fairness even against a person's own side (4:105 sets the standard for the judge and 4:135 gives the wider command). And it warns the man who walks away after the road has been made clear (4:115 warns him).

The third is the way of Abraham, who turned from the worship of his own people to the worship of one God. That is exactly the position the sūrah has been arguing for, against the men who called on female names (4:117 describes them) and the men who were given a share of the Book and then hid it (4:47 gives the warning). The Book elsewhere calls Abraham neither Jew nor Christian but a pure monotheist (3:67 states the position plainly), and it records God's test of him and his fulfilment of it (2:124 names the trial and the covenant).

**The Friend God Took**
The last sentence names the honour given to Abraham: God took him as a close friend. The same word is used of this relationship in the Book's other passages. The companions wished that rank for the Prophet ﷺ, and he told them that if he were to take a close friend from among them he would take Abū Bakr, but that the close friendship of God belonged to his companion Abraham (al-Bukhārī 466 and Muslim 2383 carry the report). The rank shows that Abraham did not earn it by carrying a name or by being born into a line. The sūrah has already said that his family was given the Book, the wisdom and a kingdom (4:54 states the gift), and it has said that those who were given a share of the Book have been trading it for error (4:118 describes the deception).

**What the Question Settles**
The verse settles the whole passage. The reward is not decided by the group a person joins, as the verse before says (4:123 says it), and it is not decided by wishes and hopes, as the verses before that say (4:120 and 4:121 name the promises and their end). It is also not decided by the names a person's ancestors carried. It is decided by the three things named here. The Book shows its own consistency when it tells readers to weigh what they hear rather than argue from what they want (4:82 asks them to think the Book over). The sūrah has shown the men who had the truth in front of them and would not look at it (4:105 describes the judge told to rule by what God showed him), and it has told the community that the One who owns everything in the heavens and the earth is aware of all of it (4:126 states both).

So the debate about who is best ends with a person whose name the whole city honoured and whose way the Book commands. The sūrah promises the migrant room in the earth and a wage that is not lost (4:100 gives it) and describes the knowledge taught to the Prophet (4:113 describes it). It names the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 names it), the programme of the being who misleads people with hopes (4:119 describes it), and the rule for whoever does good work, man or woman, with faith (4:124 states it). The Book also says that Abraham stood firm in the truth and was not one of those who join partners with God (6:161 says it of the ancestral way).
verses.126:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is Fully Aware of everything

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is Fully Aware of everything

**Who Owns What Is in the Heavens and the Earth**
The verse states the fact that makes every argument in the passage pointless: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and God's knowledge surrounds all of it. The verse sits between the description of Abraham's way (4:125) and the passage on women and orphans that follows (4:127), and it is stated again in the same form further on in the sūrah (4:132 repeats the ownership, and the same claim is made at 4:170).

**Why the Verse Comes Here**
The passage before it was a fight over claims. The men wanted grace by belonging to a name (4:123 states the wish and refuses it), the men who had the Book claimed the reward (4:124 answers with the rule for whoever does good, man or woman, with faith), and the men of Makkah called on female names they had invented (4:117). The verse answers all three by saying whose the whole creation is. The sūrah has already made the same point in the earlier passage about the man who was given two gardens and relied on his wealth (4:172 and the surrounding verses speak of the Messiah and the angels as servants), and it has said that the One who made the single soul and its mate owns the people who argue about their standing (4:1).

**The Same Statement in the Sūrah's Other Arguments**
The Book uses this ownership claim as the ground for everything it has commanded in the chapter. The orphans' property is a trust because everything belongs to God before it belongs to their fathers (4:2 and 4:10 name the trust and the fire), the dowry belongs to the woman because the Book gives it (4:4), the shares of inheritance are fixed because God set them, not the family (4:11 and the rules that follow), the earth is wide enough for a man to move for his faith because its owner made it so (4:100 describes the room the migrant finds), and the prayer is short on the road because the One who set it is the one who lightened the burden (4:101 names the permission). The sūrah has also said that God is witness over everything (4:33), that He keeps the record of the night meetings (4:108), and that He knows exactly what the community does (4:94).

**The Knowledge That Surrounds Everything**
The verse closes by saying that God's knowledge takes in every single thing. The chapter keeps naming that knowledge as the reason behind its commands, and four of them follow from it directly.

God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 states it), so the men who bring fine words after the event are not hidden from Him. He knows what is said in secret and what is said openly, so the man who gives only in order to be seen has his reward already settled (4:38 describes that man). He knows the harm a person does when he blames another for his own fault (4:112 states the load). And because He weighs everything, the man who keeps faith with people who held back will not be wronged for it (4:40 states the exact weighing).

The same exactness runs through the chapter's law of inheritance, where the shares are fixed by God rather than settled by the family's preferences (4:20 gives those shares). So the chapter has been telling its readers that they are living inside something that belongs to someone else, and this verse states that in one line before it turns to the question about women (4:127 turns to it).

**What the Chapter Said on Either Side**
The chapter described the judgement given to the Prophet by what God showed him (4:105 records it) and the rule that every sin falls on the person who earns it (4:111 states it). It named the curse laid on the being who leads people away (4:118 names it), the programme by which he does it (4:119 describes it), and the home of the people who followed him (4:121 names it) together with the home of the people who did not (4:122 names it).

It said that whoever asks for the reward of this world will find the reward of the next world with God (4:134 states it). It told the community to return what it holds in trust and to judge fairly (4:58 commands both). And it gave the helpless their own place: the men, women and children who could not move are named as a group God has not forgotten (4:98 names them), and they are excused and given hope (4:99 gives it).
verses.127:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding women. Say, “It is Allah Who instructs you regarding them. Instruction has ˹already˺ been revealed in the Book concerning the orphan women you deprive of their due rights but still wish to marry, also helpless children, as well as standing up for orphans’ rights. And whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”

**The Question About Women**
The verse begins with a question the community had brought to the Prophet and answers it by pointing back to what God had already said: the instruction about women has already come down in the Book, along with the instruction about the orphan girls under a guardian's care whose rights are withheld while he hopes to marry them, and about the children who cannot press a claim of their own. It closes by telling the community that whatever good they do is known to God.

**What the Earlier Instruction Was**
The rules the verse refers to are at the beginning of the chapter. The sūrah told the community to restore the orphan's property and to hand it over when the child is grown (4:2 and 4:6 name the command and the testing), and it said that the man who fears he cannot deal fairly with the orphan girls in his care should marry elsewhere rather than take advantage of his position (4:3 states the instruction), and it told him to give the dowry to the woman herself as a free gift (4:4). Later in the same chapter, the Book sets the shares of inheritance so that a woman and a girl child receive what is theirs by name (4:11). The men who came asking about women were asking about a matter the Book had already settled, and the verse tells them where the answer is.

**The Two Classes Named With the Women**
The verse joins two other groups to the question of women: the orphan girls whose rights are withheld by the men who want to marry them, and the children who cannot ask for their due. The sūrah has said that the men who consume the orphan's property are swallowing fire (4:10 names that warning), and it has told the community to return what is entrusted and to judge fairly (4:58 sets the standard for every transaction), and it has told the Prophet to rule by what God has shown him rather than by the pull of a family (4:105 states the charge and 4:113 describes the protection that kept him straight). Standing up for orphans is therefore not a favour; it is the ordinary work of a community whose members are answerable for what they were given.

**The Closing Sentence**
The verse ends by saying that whatever good the community does is known to God, and the sūrah has made the same statement in the language of the account book: the smallest good is multiplied (4:40 states the promise), the man who does good work, man or woman, with faith loses nothing at all (4:124 uses the speck on the date stone for the same assurance), the man who follows the way of Abraham is named the best in religion (4:125). The sūrah has also said that God owns everything in the heavens and the earth and knows all of it (4:126), which is the line right before this verse and gives it its force. The community was told to check what it heard before acting on it (4:83), to keep the prayer at its fixed times (4:103), and to keep the law on blood and property straight (4:92 and the surrounding verses set the penalties). The verse in front of the reader ties the whole question about women back to the Book that had already answered it, and the verses that follow continue with the same subject, moving on to the wife who fears her husband's neglect (4:128). The sūrah has described the knowledge given to the Prophet (4:113) and the private talk that earns a reward (4:114), the programme of the being who misleads with hopes (4:119), the rule that the reward is not decided by wishing (4:123), and the command to stand firmly on justice even when the case cuts against one's own family (4:135). The command to hand the orphan his property when he is grown stands earlier in the chapter (4:6).
verses.128:
> If a woman fears indifference or neglect from her husband, there is no blame on either of them if they seek ˹fair˺ settlement, which is best. Humans are ever inclined to selfishness. But if you are gracious and mindful ˹of Allah˺, surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do

> If a woman fears indifference or neglect from her husband, there is no blame on either of them if they seek ˹fair˺ settlement, which is best. Humans are ever inclined to selfishness. But if you are gracious and mindful ˹of Allah˺, surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**When a Wife Fears Her Husband's Coldness**
The verse covers the marriage that has not broken but has gone cold. A woman senses that her husband is turning away from her or treating her harshly, and the verse says that if the two of them settle matters between them, there is no blame on either of them, and that settlement is better. It then adds a warning: people are naturally reluctant to give up what they consider their due, and if the two of them behave generously and are mindful of God, God knows what they do.

**What the Two Words Describe**
The first word describes the husband lifting himself above his wife in the way he deals with her; the second describes him turning his shoulder away — not supporting her as he should, not sharing her bed, leaving her hanging. The sūrah has already dealt with the harder version of the same problem, where the husband's bad conduct is answered with counsel, then separation in bed, and only then a firmer measure (4:34), and with the case where the split is so bad that two arbiters have to be brought in from the two families (4:35). This verse covers the state in between, where the couple can still mend the situation themselves, and the Book tells them to do it.

**Why the Permission Matters**
The verse makes settlement permissible rather than shameful. The sūrah had already said that the good private conversations are the ones that urge giving, kindness and reconciliation (4:114), and that the arbiters in a failing marriage are sent in with the same goal (4:35). It had also protected the woman's property so that a wife giving something up is giving what is hers and not what a man has a right to take: the dowry was hers from the start (4:4), and a husband was forbidden to reclaim it (4:20 states the rule). The verse in front of the reader is careful for the same reason. It allows a wife to give up part of what she is owed in order to keep the marriage, which the teachers read as a permission granted to her, not a claim held against her, because the Book has forbidden a man from holding a woman back in order to pressure her (4:19 covers that prohibition).

**The Reluctance the Verse Names**
The verse names a human reluctance to be generous, and the chapter has named it before. It described the men who hold back what God has given them and press others into the same stinginess (4:37 describes them), and it told the community not to neglect the kindness it owes to relatives, orphans and the poor (4:36 commands it).

The remedy this verse gives is the one the chapter gives everywhere else: do what is right, and be mindful of God.

**The Standard for Life Together**
The chapter made that the standard for the community's whole life together. The men who return what is entrusted to them and judge fairly are doing what God commanded (4:58 states it). The men who check a report before spreading it are protecting the community's safety (4:83 describes them). And the men who verify what they strike before they strike are keeping the same discipline (4:94 commands it).

The reward waiting for the men and women who do good work with faith is not lost (4:124 states it), and the best religion is the one that follows the way of Abraham (4:125 names it).

**What God Sees in a Closed Room**
God knows what the two of them do in the room, and that is the same knowledge the chapter has named throughout. It described the night meetings where words were chosen (4:108 describes them), and it said that God's knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states it).

**The Measure the Law Takes of People**
The kind of settlement this verse allows fits the way the chapter treats travel and war. The prayer may be shortened on the road (4:101 permits it), and weapons may be set down in rain or illness during the prayer of the battle line (4:102 permits it), because the law adjusts to what a person can actually carry. The chapter had said that God lightens burdens because human beings were made weak (4:28 states it), and it had warned the community against envying what others hold (4:32 warns).

**Where the Verse Stands in the Chapter**
The verse stands in a line of passages about the ties God has joined between people: the orphan girl whose guardian wants to marry her without giving her what is due (4:127 describes the case), the woman whose husband has gone cold (4:128 is this verse itself), the woman left neither cared for nor released (4:129 describes her), and the rule that every sin falls on the person who earned it (4:111 states it).
verses.129:
> You will never be able to maintain ˹emotional˺ justice between your wives—no matter how keen you are. So do not totally incline towards one leaving the other in suspense. And if you do what is right and are mindful ˹of Allah˺, surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**You Cannot Be Even, So Do Not Be Unjust**
The verse tells husbands a fact and gives them a rule. The fact is that no man can keep his heart perfectly even between his wives, however much he tries; the rule is that he must not lean so far to one that the other is left hanging, neither cared for nor released. Then it names the way out: if a man puts things right and is mindful of God, God is forgiving and merciful.

**The Fact the Verse States**
The Book states the limit honestly rather than pretending the difficulty does not exist. It has already said that a man must treat his wives fairly when he marries more than one (4:3 states the condition of justice and tells the man who fears he cannot manage it to marry one), and it has told the community that God's will is to lighten what people carry because they were made weak (4:28). The verse in front of the reader does not say that the feeling of preference is a sin; it says that letting the preference decide everything is.

**What Leaving a Woman Hanging Looks Like**
The verse's phrase describes a woman who is still married and no longer cared for. The Book has already forbidden the men who would keep a woman against her will (4:19) and has told the community that the men who were given a share of God's gift must not begrudge it (4:32 and 4:37 describe the men who hoard and the men who begrudge). The sūrah had also warned about the opposite mistake in the previous verse, where a wife senses her husband's coldness and tries to arrange a settlement (4:128). Between the two verses the Book closes both doors: a man may not hold a wife in place to punish her, and a man may not keep a wife only as a name. The verse also names the two things that keep a marriage working when love is uneven — putting things right and being mindful of God, which is the same pair the verse before it gave the couple in the case of coldness (4:127 covers the instruction about women, and 4:1 opened the whole chapter with the command to be mindful of the One who made the ties).

**The Two Names at the End**
God is named here as forgiving and merciful, which is the Book's answer to a difficulty it has just admitted is real. A man who cannot feel the same about two women is not being asked to pretend; he is being asked not to let the difference decide how he treats them, and the two names are there for the man who fails and comes back. The sūrah has used the pair for other human limits: the man who does wrong and then turns back (4:110), the man whose trouble comes from his own conduct (4:79 and the surrounding passage on the measure God gives), and the helpless people who could not do what the capable were asked to do (4:99). The Book names the same mercy beside the community's hardest rules: the men who plead for a thief and then need forgiveness (4:106 and 4:107 cover that passage), the man whose marriage is failing (4:35), and the two families that cannot agree (4:128). The verse before the reader tells a man what justice looks like when feeling is uneven, and the names at its end tell him where to go with what he cannot fix. The sūrah has described the guard that gets dropped when loyalty follows the battle (4:102) and the judgment that must be given by what God shows rather than by kinship (4:105). It has told the community not to plead for the men who betray themselves (4:107) and has named the private talk that earns a reward (4:114). It has named the wish of the men who follow their own appetites (4:27), the penalty of the deliberate killer (4:93), and it has said that God's knowledge surrounds everything (4:126).
verses.130:
> But if they choose to separate, Allah will enrich both of them from His bounties. And Allah is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise

**If They Part, God Enriches Both**
The verse gives the outcome of the last step. If the marriage does end, God will give each of them enough from His own plenty, and God's provision is wide and His arrangement wise. The verse follows a passage that had forbidden a husband to leave a wife hanging (4:129) and had allowed a couple to settle their differences between them (4:128), and it says what happens when neither of those things keeps the marriage together.

**The Promise Made to Both**
The Book promises the same care to each of them separately: the man who loses the marriage and the woman who loses it. The sūrah had already promised the man who leaves his home for God's sake that he will find in the earth many places to turn to and plenty of room (4:100), and it had used the same word for room in the verse before this one, where it says God gives from His spaciousness. It has also told the community not to fix their eyes on what God has given to others and to ask Him from His bounty instead (4:32), which is the same refusal to treat one arrangement as the last word. The Book elsewhere says the same of the community's security: the prayer is a duty at fixed times and God's provision covers His servants (4:103 is the verse on the prayer and the protection that comes with it).

**Why the Pair Is Named**
The closing words of the verse describe God as the one whose gift is wide and whose decisions are wise, and the sūrah has used the same pair for the community's arrangements: the shares of inheritance were fixed by God with wisdom (4:11 brackets the shares with the statement that God is knowing and wise), the community was told that God's will is to make matters clear (4:26), and the two names close the passage on the marriage that could not be saved. The Book never presents marriage or divorce as a defeat for one party: it tells the community to settle where settlement is possible (4:128), forbids cruelty where it is not (4:129), and then takes the whole arrangement into God's hands, saying that He will provide for both.

**The Ownership Behind the Promise**
The two verses that follow this one restate that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God (4:131 and 4:132), and the promise in front of the reader stands on the same foundation: the One who enriches both parties when they part is the One who owns everything they were dividing. The sūrah has used this ownership to answer every kind of claim in the chapter: the men who thought a family's standing would save them (4:123), the men who argued a case in this life and wanted an advocate in the next (4:109), and the men who kept their plans out of sight (4:108). The verse in front of the reader is the last word of the marriage passage and the promise it leaves with both parties: the arrangement may end, the provision does not, and the One who fixes the outcome knows what He is doing (4:134 follows with the statement that both rewards are with Him). The sūrah has named the talk that urges giving, kindness and reconciliation (4:114) and has said that God's knowledge surrounds everything (4:126).
verses.131:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, We have commanded those given the Scripture before you, as well as you, to be mindful of Allah. But if you disobey, then ˹know that˺ to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy

**Everything Belongs to God, and the Command Is the Same for Everybody**
The verse restates that whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth belongs to God. Then it says that God commanded the men who were given the Book before the community, and the community itself, to be mindful of Him, and it adds that if they refuse, the ownership does not change, because God is free of any need and worthy of praise. The verse follows the passage on marriage, settlement and separation, and it opens the passage on wealth and inheritance that comes after it.

**The Command Given to Both Communities**
The verse says that the same order was given to the earlier communities and to this one. The sūrah has made the same point about the prophets: the family of Abraham was given the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom (4:54), and the community was told that God's will is to guide people to the ways of the men before them (4:26). It has also told the community what happened when the earlier holders of the Book let their own preferences decide the law (4:44 describes the men who bought error with guidance), and it has warned the men who claim grace by belonging to a group that the reward is not decided that way (4:123 states the rule). The verse in front of the reader says that the order to be mindful of God is not new; it is the one thing that has been asked of every community that was given a Book.

**The Command Itself**
Being mindful of God is the phrase the sūrah opened with, where God told humanity to be mindful of the Lord who made them from one soul and made their ties of kinship sacred (4:1). It is the phrase that closes the marriage passage, where the wife who fears her husband's coldness is told to be mindful and generous (4:128), and the phrase that closes the verse about leaning too far to one wife (4:129 uses the same word). The sūrah has also used it as the standard for the community's dealings with money and trust: the orphans' property is handed back whole, and only after the child has been tested (4:2; 4:6), the dowry is given as a free gift (4:4), the shares are paid after debts (4:11 and the rules that follow), and the man who leaves his home for his faith finds room in the earth (4:100). The mindfulness the verse commands is the thread that runs through all of it.

**What the Refusal Means**
The verse says that if a person refuses, the ownership is unchanged: everything still belongs to God and He needs nothing from anybody. The sūrah has stated the same about the community's existence: God is able to remove a people and bring others, since He owns everything in the heavens and the earth (4:133 says exactly that in the next passage). It has also warned the men who held their meetings in secret that nothing escapes the One who owns the room (4:108), and it has said that God is the trustee who settles every affair (4:132). The verse in front of the reader leaves a man with the plain fact the whole chapter rests on: the command comes from the owner of everything, and the men who follow it are doing what the earlier communities were told to do. The two verses that follow repeat the ownership and name God as the one who takes care of every matter. The sūrah has said that the prayer is a duty at fixed times (4:103), has described the men who argued for the thief in this life (4:109), and has named the knowledge the Prophet was taught (4:113). It had told the community what the orphan girls under its care are owed (4:127) and has promised that God will enrich the couple who separate from His plenty (4:130).
verses.132:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**The Ownership Restated a Third Time**
The verse states that everything in the heavens and everything on the earth belongs to God, and that God is enough to take care of every matter. It is the third time the ownership is stated in this stretch of the chapter, and the repetition comes at the end of the passage on women, settlement and separation, before the passage on wealth that follows. The Book repeats a thing when it wants the reader to stop treating the surrounding commands as somebody's opinion.

**Why the Repetition Fits This Passage**
The commands just before this verse dealt with the weakest people in the household: the orphan girl whose guardian wants to marry her without giving her what she is owed (4:127), the wife whose husband has gone cold on her (4:128), and the woman left neither cared for nor released (4:129). The sūrah keeps placing the ownership statement beside those rules because the rules are not the household's private arrangements: the property, the marriage and the people in the house all belong to God before they belong to anybody else. The same ownership stands behind the earlier laws about the orphan's estate (4:2 and 4:10), the dowry (4:4), and the fixed shares of inheritance (4:11). The sūrah has also used the ownership statement to answer the claims of the men who called on names that could not answer them (4:117) and the claims of the one who said he would take a share of God's servants (4:118).

**God Is Enough as the One in Charge**
The second sentence of this verse says that God is enough as the one who takes charge of affairs. The chapter has made the same point in several places. It said that God is the guardian who settles every matter (4:81 states it). It told the men who were advised by a judge they did not like that God is enough as a guardian and a helper (4:45 states it), and it said that He is sufficient for the community against the men who stir up panic (4:45 states it again).

It also said that the One who owns everything hears and sees everything that is done, even in a closed room (4:134 closes that passage with the pair).

**What the Verse Asks of Its Reader**
So the verse gives its reader the instruction that runs quietly through the whole chapter. What people arrange among themselves is only the small part of the matter, and the One who holds the whole of it is the one whose care a person should be content with.

The verse before it made the same statement (4:131 states it). And the verses that follow turn to the community's own existence and tell it that God could replace it with others if He wished (4:133 states it).

**What the Chapter Has Laid Out Around It**
The chapter had already set out a great deal on this ground. It promised the person who migrates for God's sake room in the earth (4:100 gives it), gave the travellers their shortened prayer and the fighters their guarded prayer (4:102 describes both), and told the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 records it).

It described the men who argued a case in this life and will find nobody to argue it for them later (4:109 describes them). It named the promise made by the being who wants a share of God's servants (4:119 names it), the empty hopes he trades in (4:120 states them), the home of the men who believed him (4:121 names it) and the home of the men who did not (4:122 names it), together with the rule that the reward is not decided by wishing (4:123 states it).

It promised a couple who separate that God will enrich them both (4:130 promises it), and it told the believers to stand for justice even when the case cuts against their own family (4:135 commands it).
verses.133:
> If it is His Will, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and replace you with others. And Allah is Most Capable to do so

**If He Wished, He Could Replace You**
The verse says that if God wanted, He could remove the people He is addressing and bring others in their place, and that He is fully able to do it. The sentence is short and it belongs to a passage that has just restated God's ownership of the heavens and the earth (4:131 and 4:132), and it comes immediately before the passage about the community's own standing and the reward God holds for both this life and the next (4:134).

**The Point the Verse Makes to the Community**
The verse is a warning and it is left deliberately unspecified: the Book does not say whether it is aimed at the whole of humanity, at the community that received the Book, or at the men in the community whose conduct the passage has been correcting. The same statement is made elsewhere with the community named directly: the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān says that if the people turn away, God will bring others in their place who will not be like them (the same promise is stated in the sūrah of Muḥammad at 47:38). The sūrah in front of the reader has already used the same figure in another form: it said the men who were given the Book before had been told the same command to be mindful of God and that their refusal would not change the ownership he holds (4:131). The verse repeats the idea for the community that came after them.

**Why the Warning Belongs Here**
The passage around it has been removing the grounds on which a person might think he matters by belonging. The men of Makkah called on names they had invented (4:117), the men who had the Book claimed the reward by their own wish (4:123), and the community had been told that the reward goes to whoever does good work, man or woman, with faith (4:124). The verse says the same thing from the other direction: a community is not necessary to God, and the same call can be given to others. The sūrah has said as much in its account of the men who were given a portion of the Book and traded it for error (4:44), and the men who walked away from the road after it had been made clear to them (4:115). The Book also held out hope for the weak who could not do what the strong were asked to do (4:99).

**What the Verse Leaves Standing**
The verse leaves God's ownership and His ability untouched, and it leaves the reader with the question of what he is actually adding. The sūrah has shown what a person contributes: the talk that urges giving, kindness or reconciliation (4:114), the stewardship that returns the orphan's wealth and gives each heir his share (4:10; 4:11), the honesty of a witness who tells the truth against his own family (4:135 gives that command), and the gratitude that turns a gift into something other than a claim. The verse in front of the reader takes the community's importance out of its own hands and puts it where the Book has been putting it throughout: the One who could replace them with a word is the One whose command they are being asked to keep (4:135 follows with the command to stand for justice, and 4:134 names the reward in both lives). The Book states the same in the sūrah of Muḥammad, where it says that if the community turns away, God will bring another people in its place who will not be like it (47:38). The sūrah has promised the migrant room in the earth (4:100), has described the man who walks away after the road is clear (4:115), has named the promise of the being who wants a share of God's servants (4:119), and has dealt with the wife whose husband has gone cold (4:128) and the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129). It has promised that God will enrich the couple who separate (4:130) and has said that God takes care of every affair (4:132). It has said that every deed is weighed exactly (4:40) and that God knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45).
verses.134:
> Whoever desires the reward of this world, then ˹let them know that˺ with Allah are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing

> Whoever desires the reward of this world, then ˹let them know that˺ with Allah are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing

**The Two Rewards Are With God**
The verse says that whoever wants the reward of this life should be told that the rewards of this life and the life to come are both with God, and it closes by saying that God hears and sees everything. The verse stands at the end of a stretch on marriage, separation and provision (4:128 through 4:131) and near the command to stand for justice that follows it (4:135).

**What the Verse Is Answering**
The Book is not telling the reader that he should not want good things; it is telling him where to go for them. The sūrah has dealt with the man who wanted the reward of this world and nothing beyond it: the man who stayed behind when the fight was called and then, when the bounty arrived, wished he had been among the fighters (4:73), the man who was ready to deny a man who offered peace so that he could take what he had (4:94), and the man who thought his group's standing would carry him through on its own (4:123). The Book answers all of them with the same statement: the One who provides for this life provides for the next as well, and a man who asks for both from the same hand does not have to choose.

**The Provision the Sūrah Has Named**
The sūrah has shown what the two rewards look like. In this life the man who leaves his home for his faith finds many places to turn to and plenty of room (4:100), and the couple who separate are promised that God will enrich them both from His plenty (4:130). In the life to come the men who strive are given ranks and mercy (4:96), the men who believe and do good work enter gardens with rivers running beneath them (4:122), and the men and women who do good work with faith lose nothing, not even the width of a date stone (4:124). The sūrah has also said that the man who spends to be seen gets his payment in this world and nothing beyond it (4:38), which is the trap the verse is warning against: a person who takes his reward early has taken the small coin.

**Hearing and Seeing**
The verse closes with the statement that God hears everything and sees everything. The chapter uses that pair at the points where a person's real intention matters more than his words.

The pair stands behind the judge who must not let the more eloquent side win the case. The Prophet's own report on that is preserved through al-Bukhārī 2680, and the chapter's instruction to judge by what God shows him comes at 4:105. The pair also stands behind the community's duty to hand back what is entrusted and to judge fairly (4:58 records both duties). And it stands behind the case of the person who twists a greeting into an insult while thinking nobody is listening (4:46 describes him).

**What the Verse Says to Its Reader**
So the verse tells its reader that a person who wants credit for his efforts cannot hide what he was actually working for. The verse that follows gives the command that the two names support: stand for justice as a witness, even against yourself and your own family (4:135 commands it).

**What the Chapter Had Laid Out Around It**
The chapter had set out a good deal on the same ground. It made the prayer a duty at fixed times (4:103 states it) and told the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 records it). It described the people who argued a case in this life (4:109 describes them) and named the load carried by the person who throws his own fault onto another (4:112 names it).

It named the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 names it) and the promise made by the being who wants a share of God's servants (4:119 names it). It described the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129 describes her) and warned that God could replace a people if He wished (4:133 warns).

It also said that every deed is weighed exactly (4:40 states it) and described the people who asked for the fighting to be delayed because they preferred the life of this world (4:77 describes them). Read with the verse in front of the reader, the whole run says the same thing: nothing is lost and nothing is hidden.
verses.135:
> O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives. Be they rich or poor, Allah is best to ensure their interests. So do not let your desires cause you to deviate ˹from justice˺. If you distort the testimony or refuse to give it, then ˹know that˺ Allah is certainly All-Aware of what you do

> O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives. Be they rich or poor, Allah is best to ensure their interests. So do not let your desires cause you to deviate ˹from justice˺. If you distort the testimony or refuse to give it, then ˹know that˺ Allah is certainly All-Aware of what you do

**Stand for Justice, Even Against Yourself**
The verse gives the community its standard for testimony. Be firm in standing for what is right, and give your evidence for God's sake, even when it goes against you, against your parents, or against your close relatives. It does not matter whether the person affected is rich or poor, because God can look after the interests of both better than you can. Then it warns the reader not to let his own preference pull him off the truth, and it ends by saying that God knows exactly what people do, whether they bend their evidence or refuse to give it.

**The Severity of the Command**
The Book asks the witness to do something hard: to speak against the people he belongs to. The sūrah has been setting that standard all the way through. It told the community not to take the side of the man pleading for a thief (4:107), it told the Prophet not to let the family of an accused man bend his judgment (4:105), and it told the community to return what it held in trust and to judge fairly (4:58). It also told it to check what it heard before it acted (4:94). The verse in front of the reader turns all of that into a personal instruction: the man in the witness seat is the one who has to be straight, and the people he is testifying about are the ones he loves.

**Why Rich and Poor Are Named**
The verse names wealth because wealth is what a witness can be tempted by from either direction. In the armour case that runs through this sūrah, the accused man's family had standing and the neighbour was an outsider, and the pressure ran towards the man with the clan behind him (4:105 describes the case and 4:113 names the group that tried to mislead). The Book also warns the community against the rich man's expectation that his money settles a case: the sūrah had told the men who hold back what God gave them that their holding back will be hung around their necks (4:37 describes the misers and the thing they will find tied to them), and it had said that a man's standing is not decided by what his family has (4:123). The verse says plainly that the judge and the witness are not the guardians of either party; God is better at that than they are.

**The Pull That Bends a Witness**
The verse names the pull that ruins a witness, and the chapter has shown that pull in several forms. There is the wish of the people who wanted the believers off the road (4:27 describes them). There is the wish of the people in the armour case, that the blame would settle on the neighbour instead of on them (4:108 describes the night talk, and 4:112 names what it earned). And there is the wish of the people who walked away from the community's road after the truth had been made clear to them (4:115 describes them).

The same chapter has shown what happens when a court is fed that wish. The Prophet was told to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 records the instruction), and his own report on the matter says that a person who wins his brother's right because he speaks better than him has been handed a piece of the fire (al-Bukhārī 2680 carries the report).

**Where the Verse Sits in the Chapter**
This verse closes the chapter's long argument about the armour case. The verse that follows turns from conduct to the belief that makes good conduct possible, calling on people to have faith in God, in His Messenger, in the Book given to him and in the Books given before (4:136 records the call).

**What the Chapter Had Settled Around It**
The chapter made the prayer a duty at fixed times (4:103 commands it). It described the duty owed to orphan girls living under a guardian's care (4:127 describes it), and it dealt with the wife whose husband has gone cold (4:128 describes her) and the wife who must not be left neither cared for nor released (4:129 describes her).

It told the community that the command to be mindful of God was given to the earlier communities as well (4:131 states it). It named God as the one who takes charge of every affair (4:132 states it), warned that a people can be replaced (4:133 warns), and said that both rewards are with God (4:134 states it). And earlier in the chapter it had given the steps for handling a wife's bad conduct, from counsel to separation in bed (4:34 gives those steps).

So the verse stands at the end of a chapter that kept moving between the courtroom, the household and the battlefield, and it states the one quality without which none of those settings can be handled honestly.
verses.136:
> O believers! Have faith in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before. Indeed, whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has clearly gone far astray

> O believers! Have faith in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before. Indeed, whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has clearly gone far astray

**Believe, and Keep Believing**
The verse calls on the people who already believe to believe: in God, in His Messenger, in the Book He sent down to His Messenger, and in the Books He sent down before. Then it adds that whoever denies God, His angels, His Books, His messengers and the last day has wandered far from the road. The command to people who are already believers is deliberate: the Book is telling them that faith is a thing a person keeps up rather than a status he collects once.

**Why the Sūrah Turns From Conduct to Belief Here**
The verse follows the command to stand for justice as a witness, even against one's own family (4:135). The Book places the belief beside the conduct because the conduct is hard. A man who testifies against his own people does it because he believes he will answer for it to God, and the whole chapter has been showing what happens when that belief is thin: the men who came with fine words after the event (4:62), the men who held their meetings at night (4:81), the men who wanted a tyrant's ruling (4:60), the men who turned away when the Book was read to them (4:61), and the men who held their plans out of sight (4:108). The community is told in the same chapter that obeying the Messenger is obeying God (4:80), that messengers were sent so that people would obey them by God's permission (4:64), and that accepting the Messenger's ruling is what makes belief real (4:65).

**The Books Named Together**
The verse names the Book given to the Prophet and the Books given before it, and the sūrah has made the continuity of the message one of its themes. It said that God commanded the men who were given the Book before the community, and the community itself, to be mindful of Him (4:131), and it named Abraham and his family as the men who were given the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom (4:54). It also told the community what the earlier holders of the Book had done with what they were given: they twisted words (4:46), they traded guidance for error (4:44), and they claimed the reward by their own wish (4:123). Believing in the earlier Books is therefore not the same as agreeing with what their holders had made of them; the Book asks the community to believe in what was sent down, and it warns about the men who denied the message that came to them (4:116 states the wrong that cannot be forgiven, and 4:115 describes the man who walks away after the road is clear).

**What the Chapter Keeps Coming Back To**
That belief is the reason the chapter returns to the same few things. It named the day of gathering that God will certainly bring about (4:87), the witness He will bring forward for every community (4:41), and the angels who take the souls of those who wronged themselves (4:97). It described the man who walks away from the road after it has been made clear to him (4:115) and the men who go back and forth until they belong to neither side (4:137). And it set the promise against all of it: the men and women who believe and do good work enter the gardens (4:122), and no one who believes and does good loses anything (4:124).

**Where This Verse Sits in the Chapter**
The chapter has covered a great deal of ground before reaching this point, and almost all of it bears on what belief costs in daily life. It allowed the traveller to shorten his prayer (4:102) and told the judge to rule by what God has shown him (4:105). It named the private conversation that earns a reward (4:114), held up the way of Abraham as the best religion (4:125), and said that God's knowledge surrounds everything (4:126).

It answered the community's question about women (4:127), dealt with the wife whose husband has gone cold (4:128) and the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129), and promised that a couple who separate will be enriched (4:130), because God takes care of every affair (4:132). It warned that a people can be replaced (4:133) and said that both rewards are with God (4:134). It told the community not to sit with people who mock God's verses (4:140). And it described the wish of those who follow their own appetites (4:27) and commanded kindness to parents, relatives, orphans and neighbours (4:36).

So the verse lands at the end of a long teaching section, and it names the belief the whole section rests on. Everything the chapter has asked for, the fair verdict, the kept trust, the kindness at home and the guarded prayer, is work a person does because he believes in God, His angels, His Books, His messengers and the last day.
verses.137:
> Indeed, those who believed then disbelieved, then believed and again disbelieved—˹only˺ increasing in disbelief—Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Way

> Indeed, those who believed then disbelieved, then believed and again disbelieved—˹only˺ increasing in disbelief—Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Way

**Back and Forth Until the Heart Hardens**
The verse describes a pattern rather than a moment: men who believed, then disbelieved, then believed again, then disbelieved again, and each time added to their disbelief. The verse says that God will not forgive them and will not guide them to a way. The sūrah has already given the door of forgiveness to the man who does wrong and then turns back (4:110), and the verse before this one showed the state of the community that held its belief (4:136). The difference between the two is not the number of mistakes; it is that the men in this verse are not turning anywhere.

**What the Pattern Shows**
The Book describes the men who move back and forth because their belief was never something they were willing to pay for. They were in the community while it was safe and out of it when it was costly, which is the same man the sūrah described as being torn between the two sides and belonging to neither (4:143), and the man who waits to see which way the fighting turns before deciding whom he knows (4:141). The sūrah had already told the community that the men who take the false powers as their authorities while claiming faith exist among them (4:60), and it warned about the men whose walk away from the community came after the road had been made clear to them (4:115). The verse in front of the reader describes what happens when that becomes a habit: the person keeps stepping over the line and the line stops meaning anything.

**Why Forgiveness Is Not Offered Here**
The verse does not say that a man who sins twice cannot be forgiven; the sūrah had said plainly that the man who does wrong and then asks God's forgiveness finds Him forgiving and merciful (4:110), and it had given the man who errs a way to repair what he did (4:18 covers the man who delays until death and then repents, and 4:17 names the turning accepted from the man who corrects himself quickly). What this verse describes is a man who keeps leaving and coming back for reasons of his own and never once turns to God, and the Book answers with the state he has chosen. The sūrah has shown the same principle in the community's own history: God allowed a group of men to go back to their disbelief because of what their hands had earned (4:88), and the men who joined partners with God were told that they had gone far from the road (4:116).

**What the Verse Takes Away**
The verse withholds two things from the people it describes: forgiveness and guidance. Both are gifts the chapter has tied to a person's turning. The man who asks is forgiven (4:110 states it). The man who obeys God and the Messenger is placed with the prophets and the truthful (4:69 names that company). And the man who does what he is advised is given a great reward and guided to a straight path (4:67 and 4:68 state the pair).

The people standing in front of this verse had all of that available to them, and they kept trading it away. So the verse is the sentence the whole portrait rests on, and the verse after it names the group being described (4:138 does that).

**The Chapter's Portrait of Them**
The verses around this one paint the same group from several angles. They are the men who wait to see which way the community's fortunes turn. They are the men who try to trick God while the trick falls back on them, and they are the men who pray only to be seen doing it (4:142 describes both). They end in the lowest depth of the fire with nobody to help them (4:145 states it).

And they are the men who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers (4:139 names them). The chapter had already named the false names those idolaters called on (4:117 names them) and the programme of the being who promised them long lives (4:119 describes it).

**What the Chapter Offered Them Instead**
The chapter also set out what the same people were turning down. It promised the gardens to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122 states it). It refused the idea that reward comes by wishing (4:123 refuses it). It said that the command to be mindful of God was given to the earlier communities too (4:131 states it), and it told the believers to stand for justice even against their own family (4:135 commands it). It instructed the community not to sit with people who mock God's verses (4:140 instructs it).

It described the turning that is accepted from the person who corrects himself quickly (4:17 describes it) and the will of God to make matters clear and to forgive (4:26 states it). It named the wish of those who follow their own appetites (4:27 names it). And it kept the door of return open until the end.
verses.138:
> Give good news of a painful punishment to hypocrites

> Give good news of a painful punishment to hypocrites

**Good News of a Painful Punishment**
The verse tells the Prophet to give the hypocrites the news that a painful punishment is waiting for them. The instruction is ironic: the word used is the one for announcing glad tidings, and the thing announced is the opposite. The verse opens the chapter's portrait of the men whose loyalty could not be relied on, and the verses that follow fill in the picture.

**Who the Men Are**
The sūrah has named them all through the chapter without always using the label: the men who say "we obey" and then work out the opposite after dark (4:81), the men who want their disputes decided by a tyrant's court while claiming to believe (4:60), the men who turn away when the Book and the Messenger are mentioned (4:61), the men who arrive with impressive words after the event is settled (4:62), the men who held back from the fight and then called their absence a favour (4:72), the men whose loyalty moved with the battle (4:141), and the men who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137). The verse in front of the reader gathers all of them under one name.

**What the Ironic News Says**
The Book uses the announcement of good news as a weapon in other places too, telling the men who hoard their wealth what is being saved up for them. The point of the irony in this verse is that the hypocrites' own conduct is a kind of announcement: the man who sits in the mosque to be seen is announcing a faith he does not hold, and the verse answers his announcement with one of its own. The sūrah has shown what the men in this group lose in this life as well: they lose the trust of the community that would have stood with them and they end up belonging to neither side (4:143 describes that state), they are left with the wealth they held back (4:37 describes what that grip produces), and they are known to the One who hears every meeting they held (4:108). The Book has said that a man who talks about his faith while his conduct says otherwise has his reward already settled (4:38 describes the man who gives in order to be seen).

**A Warning Matched to the Offence**
The warnings in this chapter run on the same scale as the offences they answer. The men who devour an orphan's property are described as eating fire (4:10 states it). The men who cross God's limits go into the fire to stay (4:14 names that penalty). The man who kills a believer on purpose is answered with anger, a curse and a heavy punishment (4:93 lists the three). And the men who tried to mislead the community in the case of the stolen armour were answered with a load of slander and sin (4:112 states it).

The destination named for this group is the same kind of thing, stated in plain words: a humiliating punishment, and the lowest depth of the fire with nobody to help them (4:145 states it).

**Where This Verse Sits**
This verse is a single line at the head of that passage. The verses after it explain what these men were doing while the rest of the community fought, paid and buried its dead.

The chapter had already described the men who argued a case in this life (4:109 describes them). It named the best religion a person can follow (4:125 names it) and warned that a people can be replaced by others (4:133 warns).

**The Portrait the Verses After It Fill Out**
The verses that follow complete the picture. These are the men who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers (4:139 names them). They are the men who must not be sat with when they mock God's verses (4:140 instructs). They are the men who try to trick God while the trick falls back on them, and who pray only to be seen doing it (4:142 describes both).

They belong to neither side (4:143 states it), and they end in the lowest depth of the fire (4:145 names it).

**The Same Warnings Elsewhere in the Chapter**
The chapter had warned about the same kinds of people earlier, in other settings. It described the men who delay their repentance until death arrives (4:18 describes them). It warned against taking what belongs to others (4:29 warns) and against killing (4:30 warns). It described the community split into two groups over the double-dealers (4:88 describes the split), the men who wanted the believers back in disbelief (4:89 states the wish), and the men who go back to the fight whenever they get the chance (4:91 describes them).

So this verse stands in a line of warnings, and it names in one sentence what the rest of the passage explains at length.
verses.139:
> who choose disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour and power through that company? Surely all honour and power belongs to Allah

> who choose disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour and power through that company? Surely all honour and power belongs to Allah

**Taking the Other Side as Friends**
The verse describes the men who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers, and then asks them a question: do they expect to find honour and power by joining those people? The answer follows immediately: all honour and power belong to God. The verse follows the passage that named the men who kept going back and forth between belief and denial (4:137) and the announcement of a painful punishment for them (4:138).

**What the Alliance Was For**
The Book names the motive in the question. Men in the community were looking for protection, for standing, for a share of whatever advantage the stronger side could offer, and they thought the way to it ran through the men who rejected the message. The sūrah has shown the same calculation elsewhere: the men who wanted their disputes decided by a tyrant's court while claiming faith (4:60), the men whose loyalty followed the battle and who reminded the winners that they had been with them (4:141), and the men who took the false powers as their authorities (4:51 states the charge against them). It has also shown what the community was actually offered in exchange for its loyalty: the men who left their homes for God's sake found room in the earth (4:100), the men who held their ground were promised ranks and mercy (4:96), and the men who stood for the weak who cried out were doing the work the community owed (4:75).

**The Answer the Verse Gives**
The verse's answer is a statement of ownership rather than a prohibition: honour belongs to God, which means it is not a commodity the other side can hand out. The sūrah has made this point about every kind of power in the chapter: it said that God gives the kingdom to whom He wills (4:54 describes the gift given to the family of Abraham), it warned the men who thought they could share out God's mercy (4:54 again and 4:53 in the same argument), it said that God raises whom He wills (4:49 states it), and it said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God (4:126 and 4:131 through 4:134 repeat it). The verse in front of the reader takes the friends a man chooses and turns the question around: whatever they can give, the thing a person actually needs is held somewhere else. The sūrah also warns about the price of the alliance, saying plainly that the men who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers are giving God a case against themselves (4:144 states the warning) and that such men will find no helper (4:145 names the destination).

**The Last of the Chapter's Arguments About Loyalty**
This passage is the last of the chapter's long arguments about where a person puts his loyalty and where he looks for his standing. The chapter had already covered the same ground from several sides. It told the judge to rule by what God shows him (4:105). It warned the Prophet against pleading for a man who had betrayed himself (4:107), described the plotters who chose their words at night (4:108), and asked who would argue their case when the day comes (4:109).

It named the false names the idolaters called on (4:117) and the promises the being behind those names was making (4:119). It stated the rule that reward does not come by wishing (4:123) and held up the way of Abraham as the best in religion (4:125). And it gave the community its own instructions: obey God, the Messenger and those in authority (4:59), verify what you strike before you strike (4:94), and stand for justice even against your own family (4:135).

**Where the Honour Actually Sits**
The verse in front of the reader closes that sequence from the other direction. The men who chose the other side were looking for honour in a place where no honour exists, and the verse states where honour actually sits, which is with God alone (4:139 gives the claim and the answer).

The chapter had warned about the same choice throughout. It described the man who walks away from the road after it has been made clear to him (4:115), the men who join partners with God and wander far from the path (4:116), and the men who were promised long lives by the being whose words the Book records (4:120). Against them it set the men and women who believe and do good work and are admitted to the gardens (4:122).

**What the Chapter Said on Either Side of It**
The chapter said that the command to be mindful of God was given to the earlier communities as well (4:131) and that God takes care of every affair (4:132), and it said that both rewards are with Him (4:134). It described the men on the wrong side of the fighting (4:89), the men who withdraw from it (4:90), and the men who keep coming back to it (4:91). It named the wish of the men who follow their own appetites (4:27) and said that God knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45).

It pictured the man who stayed behind and then wished he had been with the fighters when the spoils were counted (4:73), and the men who turned back to the fight whenever the chance came (4:91). And the verse before this one describes the men who go back and forth until they belong to neither side (4:143).
verses.140:
> He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear Allah’s revelations being denied or ridiculed, then do not sit in that company unless they engage in a different topic, or else you will be like them. Surely Allah will gather the hypocrites and disbelievers all together in Hell

**Do Not Sit With Those Who Mock the Book**
The verse reminds the community of a rule they had already been given. When they hear God's verses being denied or laughed at, they are not to sit with the people doing it unless the conversation moves on to something else, because sitting there makes them like the people they are listening to. It adds that God will gather the hypocrites and those who rejected the message together in the fire.

**The Rule and Its Reason**
The objection is not to hearing a difficult argument. It is to attending a performance in which the message is ridiculed while the listener sits and says nothing. The instruction protects the reader from two things at once. It keeps him from looking like a man who has no objection, and it keeps the community's own reading of its own Book from becoming a joke in its own streets. The sūrah has said elsewhere that men twisted their words when they greeted the Prophet (4:46 describes it). It names the men who hold their meetings at night (4:108 names them) and the men who spread every report through the community before checking it (4:83 describes them). Silence in those settings was how the poison spread.

**What the Rule Does Not Mean**
The sūrah shows the community arguing its case in public throughout the chapter. It answered the claims of those who called on other names (4:117 answers them). It set out the proof that God owns everything (4:126 gives it). It named the best in religion (4:125 names him). And it told the community that its duty is to convey the message and not to force it, since the Prophet himself was not set over the people as a keeper (the same principle appears where the sūrah describes those who turned away at 4:80). What the Book orders is to leave the gathering when it turns into mockery.

The same chapter also tells the community to keep its distances in other matters. It warned against taking those who were fighting the community as allies instead of the believers (4:144 gives the warning), and it had already drawn the line between those who withdraw from fighting and those who go back to it at every chance (4:90 and 4:91 describe both). Leaving the room is itself a form of speech.

**The Gathering Named at the End**
The verse ends by saying that God will collect the men who doubted and the men who denied together. The Book describes the same gathering elsewhere, where every community is brought forward with a witness (4:41 describes the scene). It has named the destination of those whose loyalty was for sale: they will be in the lowest depth of the fire with nobody to help them (4:145 states it, and 4:138 gives the announcement).
