The sūrah also tells the community what to weigh instead. God knows everything in the heavens and the earth (4:132 states it). There is a day when people will be asked (4:87 mentions it). And the record leaves nothing out (4:94 sets the standard for what the community does). So the instruction about where a person sits is tied at the end of the verse to the largest of the Book's statements about the last day. Those who mock are the ones who will be gathered, and the verses that follow describe what they were waiting for while the community fought (4:133 and 4:134 name the ownership of everything and the two rewards).

**Other Threads in the Chapter**
The Book also warns against pursuing what a person has no knowledge of, and against suspicion and backbiting, in other sūrahs (17:36 and 49:12 carry those instructions). This sūrah gave the community the guarded battle prayer (4:102 gives it) and the command to judge by what God has shown (4:105 gives it). It named the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 names it) and the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 names it). The verse before this one described those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 describes them), and the verse after it describes those who kept watch on the outcome of the fighting (4:141 describes them). The verses that follow close the portrait of that group (4:143 closes it).

The sūrah has also said that God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 states it), that the day of gathering will come (4:87 states it), that the community must verify before it strikes (4:94 gives the rule), and that the angels took the souls of those who wronged themselves (4:97 reports it). The Book instructs the community not to sit with men who mock God's verses in another sūrah as well (6:68 carries the same rule). The promises of the being who wants a share of God's servants (4:120 names them), the home of those who believed him (4:121 names it), and the home of those who did not (4:122 names it) stand in the verses before, along with the ownership of everything (4:132 states it), the warning that a people can be replaced (4:133 states it), the promise that both rewards are with God (4:134 states it), and the command to stand for justice even against one's own family (4:135 commands it). The Book also warns the believers against suspicion and against speaking about one another behind their backs (49:12 states that instruction).
verses.141:
> ˹The hypocrites are˺ those who wait to see what happens to you. So if Allah grants you victory, they say ˹to you˺, “Were we not on your side?” But if the disbelievers have a share ˹of victory˺, they say ˹to them˺, “Did we not have the advantage over you, yet we protected you from the believers?” Allah will judge between ˹all of˺ you on the Day of Judgment. And Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers

**Waiting to See Who Wins**
The verse describes how men whose loyalty was uncertain behaved while the community was at war. They watched the outcome. When the believers were given a victory, they came and pointed out that they had been on the same side. When the other side got the better of a day, they reminded the winners that they had been friendly all along and had done what they could to protect them from the believers. Then the verse says that God will judge between them all on the day of the return, and that He will never give those who reject the message a way over the believers.

**What the Verse Is Describing**
The Book is describing the same people it names in the verses around it. They said one thing in the room and something else at night (4:81 describes them). They held back from the fight and then counted their absence a blessing (4:72 describes them). Their walking away came after the road had been made clear (4:115 describes it). And they went back and forth between belief and denial until they belonged to neither side (4:143 describes them). Their position was always the same: keep the friendship of whoever seemed to be doing better. The Book describes the same calculation in its account of the men who wanted their cases judged by a tyrant's court (4:60 describes them) and the men who took false powers as their authorities (4:51 describes them).

**The Two Things the Verse Gives**
The first is that a man's conduct in trouble shows what his earlier professions were worth. The sūrah shows this in its picture of the man who wants the reward of this world and nothing beyond it (4:134 describes him), and in its warning to those who asked for the fighting to be delayed and so showed what they preferred (4:77 warns them).

The second is the promise that those who reject the message will not be given a way over the believers. The sūrah says the same about the community's enemies elsewhere. It told the community that the fight against those who followed the wrong way would be fought on God's terms (4:76 states it). It gave the fighters their guarded prayer so that they could not be taken by surprise (4:102 gives it). And it told them that God is the guardian who settles every affair (4:81 states it). The promise does not mean that every battle goes well. It means the message will not be defeated, and the community will not be handed over to those trying to destroy it.

**The Judgment Named at the End**
The verse closes with the day of the return. The Book says that the account is not settled by which side had a better year. The sūrah names that day in other passages: God will gather humanity on a day about which there is no doubt (4:87 states it), every community will be brought forward with its witness (4:41 states it), and those who consumed the wealth of orphans will find what they swallowed (4:10 describes it).

The Prophet's ﷺ own report makes the same point about the limits of any human hearing. A man may win his case by speaking better than his opponent, and the Prophet said that if he gave one of them his brother's right that way, he would be handing him fire (al-Bukhārī 2680 carries the report). The verse leaves those who waited to see the outcome in the hands of the One who knows what was in their hearts while they waited (4:63 states that knowledge, and 4:108 says that nothing in the night meetings escaped).

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
The sūrah promises the migrant room in the earth (4:100 gives it), tells the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 gives the instruction), names the night meetings (4:108 names them), and describes the knowledge the Prophet was taught (4:113 describes it). It promises the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 gives the promise), says that God's knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states it), and says that He takes care of every affair (4:132 states it). It tells the believers to stand for justice even when the case cuts against their own family (4:135 commands it). It describes those who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137 describes them) and announces a painful punishment for those whose belief was a show (4:138 announces it), for those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 names them), and for those who sat with mockers (4:140 names them).

The verse after this one describes their prayer (4:142 describes it). The sūrah says that God's will is to make matters clear and to forgive (4:26 states it), names the wish of those who follow their own appetites (4:27 names it), says that whatever harm a man meets comes from his own conduct (4:79 states it), and describes the community that was split over the double-dealers (4:88 describes it) and the men who wronged themselves and were taken in death (4:97 describes them).
verses.142:
> Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them. When they stand up for prayer, they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people—hardly remembering Allah at all

> Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them. When they stand up for prayer, they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people—hardly remembering Allah at all

**The Men Who Try to Trick God**
The verse describes the men whose belief was a performance. They try to outwit God, it says, and He turns their trick back on them. When they stand for prayer they do it without any heart in it, and only to be seen by other people, and they remember God hardly at all. The verse follows the passage about the men who waited to see which side won (4:141), and it stands at the head of the verses that explain what those men were actually doing.

**What the Trick Amounts To**
The Book is describing a man who behaves as though there were somebody he could fool. He stands where people can see him, he says the words, and he keeps his real position to himself, thinking that the appearance is what counts. The sūrah has shown the same approach in other settings: the men who brought an oath that they had intended nothing but good after the decision had gone against them (4:62), and the men whose hearts God knows (4:63), the men who took the disbelievers as allies because that seemed the safer bet (4:139), and the men whose loyalty moved with the battle (4:141). The Book's answer in each case is the same: nothing they did was hidden.

**The Prayer Without Heart**
The verse names the form their hypocrisy took in the community's daily life: prayer performed for an audience. The Book had already shown the opposite picture in the same chapter. It gave the community the battle prayer, where men pray with weapons in hand and one group guards the other (4:102), and it told them to remember God standing, sitting and lying down, and to keep the prayer at its fixed times once they were safe (4:103). It gave the traveller a shortened prayer so that the duty could be met on the road (4:101), and it told the community that God lightens what people carry because they were made weak (4:28). The men whose prayer is described in this verse had all of that in front of them, and they turned the appointment into a performance. The Book had warned the community about the same error in the matter of money, where it described the man who gives only to be seen (4:38), and it had placed the prayer of the show beside the long list of duties owed to parents, relatives, orphans and neighbours (4:36).

**What the Trick Earns**
The verse says that God turns their trick back on them, which means that the men who think they are managing appearances are the ones being managed. The sūrah has shown what that looks like when the account is opened: the men who kept their meetings at night found them recorded (4:108), the men who blamed another for their fault found the load doubled on them (4:112), and the men who argued a case in this life were asked who would argue for them on the day (4:109). The Book's warning to the men in this group is stated in the verses that follow: they think nobody is watching, and the Book says that God keeps their account (4:142 is the verse, and 4:145 gives them their place in the fire). The sūrah has named the alternative in the same chapter: the men who return what they hold in trust and judge fairly (4:58), the men who stand for justice even against their own family (4:135), and the men and women who do good work with faith and lose nothing (4:124). The verse in front of the reader takes the outward show of religion and puts it beside the One who sees the inside, and it leaves the reader with the difference.

**How the Chapter Answers the Trick**
The chapter answers this kind of trickery elsewhere with the same plainness. It said that the men who break their promises will not be given a way over the believers (4:141 states it). It said that the men who walk away from the road after it has been made clear to them are left in it (4:115 states it), and that the men who join partners with God have gone far from the path (4:116 states it).

And it named the prayers the community was given, so that the contrast with these men is exact: the shortened prayer of the road (4:101 describes it), the guarded prayer of the battle (4:102 describes it), and the remembrance of God in every position (4:103 commands it).

The Book says in another sūrah that the men who plotted were answered by God's own plan (3:54 states it), which is the same answer this passage gives.

**Where the Verse Sits**
This verse closes the first movement of the passage about the men whose belief was a strategy they changed with the weather. The verse after it gives their description in one line: they belong to neither side (4:143 gives it).

**What the Chapter Had Said Around It**
The chapter told the community not to slacken in the pursuit of the enemy (4:104 commands it). It named the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 names it) and the promise made to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122 states it). It recorded the question the community was asked about women and orphans (4:127 records it), and it said that God takes care of every affair (4:132 states it).

It described the men who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137 describes them), announced the punishment of the men whose belief was a show (4:138 announces it), and named the men who sat with people who mock the Book (4:140 names them). It also said that God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 states it) and described the men who asked for the fighting to be delayed because they preferred the life of this world (4:77 describes them).

So the verse stands at the centre of a chapter that has shown, point by point, what sincerity costs and what pretending saves.
verses.143:
> Torn between belief and disbelief—belonging neither to these ˹believers˺ nor those ˹disbelievers˺. And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way

> Torn between belief and disbelief—belonging neither to these ˹believers˺ nor those ˹disbelievers˺. And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way

**Belonging to Neither Side**
The verse describes the men who were torn between belief and disbelief, belonging neither to the community nor to the men who rejected the message. Then it adds the sentence the sūrah has used more than once: whoever God leaves to wander will not find a way. The verse is the summary sentence of the whole passage on the men whose position was never settled.

**The Description and How It Was Earned**
The Book describes the state rather than the sentence, and the passage before it has shown how the state arrives. The men kept leaving and returning to the community until the going back stopped meaning anything (4:137), they took the disbelievers as allies because the alliance seemed to offer protection (4:139 states the calculation and gives the answer), they stood for prayer looking at the people rather than at God (4:142 describes the show), and they waited to see which side came out ahead in the fighting (4:141 shows the wait and the two speeches they had ready). The sūrah had already described the same community problem in its earlier passage: the men who were split into two groups over the double-dealers (4:88), the men who went back to the fight whenever the chance came (4:91), and the men who held back when the order to march came (4:71).

**The Second Sentence**
The verse closes by saying that whoever God leaves to stray will not find a road, which the sūrah had already stated in almost the same words about the men the community argued over (4:88 gives that sentence). The Book is not saying that a man is pushed off the road by somebody else; it is saying that a man who keeps choosing the direction himself is eventually left in it. The sūrah has shown the same principle in its account of the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116), in the man who walks away from the community after the road has been made clear to him (4:115), and in the men who go on trading their share of the Book for a small advantage (4:44 describes the trade). It has also shown the other side of the same statement, where the man who does the right thing is guided because God guides him (4:26 names the will to make matters clear and to guide).

**What Comes Immediately After**
The verse is followed by a direct address to the community: do not take the men who reject the message as allies instead of the believers, or you hand God a case against yourselves (4:144 states the warning in full). Then comes the place reserved for the men whose lives matched the description in this passage, the lowest depth of the fire with nobody to help them (4:145).

And then the chapter keeps the door open for the men who mend what they broke, describing them in the next verse (4:146 names the four conditions and the reward that follows).

**The Argument This Verse Ends**
This verse is the last word on an argument the chapter has been conducting for a long stretch: who receives God's grace, and on what grounds. The chapter has said that the reward is not a matter of belonging to the right family (4:123), not a matter of wishes (4:122 states the promise and asks whose word is more truthful), and not a matter of sitting in the right room while the heart is elsewhere.

So the verse gives the men who spent their lives in the middle of the road exactly where the middle of the road leads.

**What the Chapter Rose Through to Get Here**
The chapter has promised the migrant room in the earth (4:100). It has named the false names the idolaters called on (4:117), the curse on the being who promised them long lives (4:118), his programme of misleading them (4:119), and the promises that come to nothing (4:120), together with the home of the men who believed him (4:121) and the home of the men who did not (4:122). It has said that the reward does not come by wishing (4:123) and has described the men and women who do good work with faith (4:124), the best in religion (4:125), and the ownership of everything with the knowledge that surrounds it (4:126).

It has answered the community's question about women (4:127), dealt with the wife whose husband had gone cold (4:128) and the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129), promised that a couple who separate will be enriched (4:130), and stated the ownership of everything again (4:131). It has said more than once that God takes care of every affair (4:132). And it has recorded the instruction not to sit with people who mock God's verses (4:140).

> O believers! Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Would you like to give Allah solid proof against yourselves

**Do Not Take the Other Side as Friends**
The verse addresses the believers directly: do not take the men who rejected the message as your allies in place of the believers, and it asks them whether they want to hand God a clear case against themselves. The verse follows the passage that answered the same practice among the men who kept their loyalty flexible (4:139 and 4:141), and it is the plain instruction that answers those descriptions.

**What the Sūrah Has Already Shown**
The sūrah has shown what the community's friendship was supposed to look like. It told the believers to obey God, the Messenger and the men in authority among them (4:59), told them to answer a greeting of peace with a better one (4:86), told them to fight for the men, women and children who cried out for help (4:75), and told them to check what they struck before they struck (4:94). It has also shown what the wrong kind of alliance cost: the men who took a tyrant's court for their disputes were told that they were seeking judgment from a power the Book had already rejected (4:60), and the men who took the side of the fighters against the community at every chance were handled under the rules of war (4:91 covers that group). The verse in front of the reader makes the instruction general: the community's friendships are not a private matter, because the community is what a man's friends are.

**The Evidence a Man Hands Over**
The verse's second half asks the reader whether he wants to give God a case against himself, and the sūrah has used the language of evidence throughout. The Book speaks of the day when every community is brought forward with its witness (4:41 describes the scene), of the record that leaves nothing out of what a man does (4:94 sets the standard), of the men whose night meetings were written down (4:108), and of the Prophet who was told to judge by what God had shown him (4:105). The community has been told that the men who argue a case in this life will find nobody to argue it for them later (4:109), and that the man who blames another for his own fault carries a double load (4:112). A man who chooses the other side as his protectors has done the arguing for the prosecution himself.

**The Rule and Its Exceptions**
The Book does not tell the community to treat every man who is not a Muslim as an enemy, and the same chapter shows the limits clearly. It told the community to be fair when it judged (4:58), to answer a greeting of peace with peace (4:86), to treat parents, relatives, orphans, neighbours, travellers and those under its care well (4:36), and to spare the men who withdrew from the fighting and offered peace (4:90 names those who withdraw and the treaty that protects them). The rule in front of the reader concerns the men who are fighting the community and the men who want it back in disbelief, which is how the sūrah has described the group all along (4:89 and 4:91 describe the two kinds of enemies, and 4:75 names the weak the community was told to defend). The instruction is therefore about loyalty in a conflict and not about ordinary kindness, and the chapter proves the difference by naming the men who kept their agreements.

**The Destination Named Next**
The verse that follows this one names the place reserved for the people whose conduct the passage has been describing: the lowest depth of the fire, with nobody to help them (4:145 names it).

The chapter had already announced that punishment at the head of the portrait (4:138 gives the announcement). And it said the same about the other groups whose loyalty was for sale: the men who join partners with God have gone far from the path (4:116 states it), and the men who walk away from the road after it has been made clear to them are left in it (4:115 states it).

**What the Verse Asks of Its Reader**
This verse puts the community's choice in plain terms: do not take as allies the people who have rejected the message, in place of the believers. The verses after it show that the door back stays open for anyone who wants it (4:146 opens that door).

**What the Chapter Put on the Other Side**
The chapter promised the person who migrates for God's sake room in the earth (4:100 gives it) and taught the community the prayer of the battle line (4:102 describes it). It told the Prophet not to plead for the men who betray themselves (4:107 records that), and it said that God's knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states it) and that He takes care of every affair (4:132 states it).

It warned that a people can be replaced by others (4:133 warns), said that both rewards are with God (4:134 states it), commanded the believers to stand for justice even against their own family (4:135 commands it), and instructed them not to sit with people who mock God's verses (4:140 instructs them).

It described the men who kept watch on the outcome of the fighting to see which way it went (4:141 describes them) and the men who prayed only to be seen doing it (4:142 describes them). And the verse before this one described the men who belonged to neither side (4:143 describes them). Against that whole portrait, this verse states in one sentence what a believer's loyalty may not become.
verses.145:
> Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire—and you will never find for them any helper—

> Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire—and you will never find for them any helper—

**The Lowest Depth of the Fire**
The verse says that the men whose belief was a performance will be in the lowest level of the fire, and that nobody will be found to help them. It follows the announcement of a painful punishment (4:138), the description of the men who waited to see who won (4:141), and the instruction not to take the other side as allies (4:144).

**Why the Verse Names the Lowest Place**
The Book ranks the punishments and puts this group at the bottom, and the passage before it has shown why. The men it describes had the most and gave the least: they sat in the community, heard the Book recited, heard the Prophet speak, stood in the rows for prayer (4:142 describes that prayer), and used all of it as cover for a position they kept hidden. The sūrah has shown what that costs the community: the men who spread every report before it was checked (4:83), the men who turned away whenever they were called to the Book (4:61), the men whose loyalty followed the battle (4:141), and the men who held their meetings at night to work out how to beat a neighbour in a case (4:108). Their presence inside the community did the work their absence could not have done.

**The Helper Who Is Not There**
The verse says that nobody will be found to help them, and the sūrah has used that sentence for the men who trusted in the wrong support. It said the same about the men who took the wrong road and were left in it (4:115), about the men who committed a wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116), and about the men who argued a case in this life and will find nobody to argue it on the day (4:109). The Book has also said what the friends a man chose will do for him: nothing beyond the grave, which is why the chapter keeps telling its readers where honour comes from (4:139) and who takes care of every affair (4:132). The men described in this verse had the protection of families, the standing of clans, and the goodwill of whatever side seemed stronger; the verse names the day when all of that is gone.

**The Door That Immediately Follows**
The verse after this one names the exceptions and the road back: the men who turn from what they were doing, put their conduct right, hold firmly to God, and make their devotion sincere will be counted with the believers, and God will give the believers a great reward (4:146 states all of it). The sūrah has opened that door in many places and never closed it: the man who does wrong and then asks forgiveness finds God forgiving and merciful (4:110), the man who turns back and puts things right is counted with the believers (4:146 again in its own words), and the men who were given the worst descriptions in the chapter are still addressed as people who can come back. The verse before the reader is the hardest of the announcements, and the verse after it is the Book's standing answer: nobody is stuck where he was.

**The Two Ends Set Side by Side**
The chapter has placed the fire and the garden beside each other since its early pages, and the contrast in this passage is exact. The people who sold their loyalty are placed in the lowest level of the fire. Against them the chapter has set what faith earns: the company of the prophets and the truthful (4:69 names the groups), ranks and mercy for those who strive (4:96 names both), hope for the helpless (4:99 gives it), room in the earth and a secure wage for those who migrate (4:100 gives both), and the promise that the men and women who believe and do good work lose nothing (4:124 states it).

The verses closest to this one keep the same pattern. Those who step out of hypocrisy are promised the reward of the believers (4:146 states it), and those who stay in it are told where they end (4:145 is the verse itself).

The chapter has been arguing since its first page that the difference between the two ends runs through what a person does rather than through the label he carries.

**What the Chapter Put Around This Verse**
Around this verse the chapter has given the community the guarded battle prayer (4:102 describes it) and named the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 names it). It named the false names the idolaters called on (4:117 names them), the home of those who believed the promises they were given (4:121 names it) and the home of those who did not (4:122 names it), and it promised a couple who separate that God will enrich them (4:130 promises it).

It commanded the believers to stand for justice even against their own family (4:135 commands it), described those who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137 describes them), instructed the community not to sit with people who mock God's verses (4:140 instructs it), and left those who belonged to neither side without a road (4:143 states it).

It also said that God knows best who the community's enemies are (4:45 states it), that the believers were told to stand up for the weak who cried out (4:75 records it), and that those who wronged themselves were taken in death (4:97 describes them).
verses.146:
> except those who repent, mend their ways, hold fast to Allah, and are sincere in their devotion to Allah; they will be with the believers. And Allah will grant the believers a great reward

> except those who repent, mend their ways, hold fast to Allah, and are sincere in their devotion to Allah; they will be with the believers. And Allah will grant the believers a great reward

**Except the Men Who Come Back**
The verse names the exceptions to the sentence just passed on the men whose belief was a performance. Whoever turns from what he was doing, sets his conduct right, holds fast to God, and makes his devotion to God sincere will be counted with the believers, and God will give the believers a great reward. The four conditions are given in order, and the last of them reaches the thing that was wrong in the first place: the heart.

**The Four Conditions**
The first is turning back from the conduct itself, which the sūrah has asked of others in other places: the man who does wrong and then asks forgiveness (4:110), and the man who turns from his fault and puts things right (4:146 is the verse doing that work). The second is setting the conduct right, which is the repair the sūrah calls for rather than the apology: the man who carries a load of slander must make the accusation good (4:112 states the load), the man who kills by mistake must free a slave and pay the family (4:92 gives the remedy), and the community must return what it holds in trust (4:58 sets the standard). The third is holding fast to God, which the sūrah has named as the opposite of taking the wrong side as an ally (4:144 gives the instruction, and 4:139 answers the men who were looking for honour in the wrong place). The fourth is sincerity of devotion, which reaches the thing the whole passage was about, since the men whose conduct has been described prayed to be seen (4:142).

**What the Reward Is**
The verse says that such men will be with the believers and that God will give the believers a great reward, which is the same promise the chapter has made to the men and women who do good work with faith (4:124), to the men who obeyed God and the Messenger (4:69 names the company of the prophets and the truthful), and to the men who did what they were advised, who are given a great reward (4:67 states the promise and 4:68 names the path). The verse puts the man who was just described at the bottom of the fire into that company on one condition: that he comes back. The Book's pattern is consistent throughout the chapter: it names the sin and then names the door, and it never treats the sin as the man's final identity.

**Why the Door Stays Open**
The chapter keeps the door open because the people it is describing are the community's own members, and because their hypocrisy was a matter of what they chose each day rather than a label fixed on them at birth. The same chapter shows the community being given room in smaller matters: the men who came with fine words after the event (4:62), the men who held back from the fight and then wanted a share of the spoils (4:72), and the community that split into two camps over the double-dealers (4:88).

Against all of that the chapter sets a few steady instructions. Return what is held in trust. Stand for justice even against your own family (4:135). Keep the prayer at its fixed times (4:103).

**What the Verse Turns Around**
This verse turns the whole portrait of the hypocrite around and shows what the man who steps out of it looks like. The verse after it closes the passage with a question: what would God gain from punishing people who are grateful and who believe (4:147)?

**The Chapter's Other Portraits**
The chapter has promised the person who migrates for God's sake room in the earth and plenty (4:100). It has named the night meetings where the words were chosen (4:108) and the private talk that earns a reward (4:114). It has described the man who walks away from the road after it has been made clear to him (4:115) and the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122).

It has dealt with the wife whose husband has gone cold (4:128), the men who go back and forth until they belong to neither side (4:137), and the punishment announced for those whose belief was a performance (4:138). It has named the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139), the instruction not to sit with people who mock God's verses (4:140), the men who watched the fighting to see which way it went (4:141), and the men who joined neither side (4:143). It has named the place reserved for the men whose belief was a show (4:145).

It has described the two kinds of turning: the turning of the person who corrects himself quickly (4:17) and the repentance that comes only when death arrives (4:18). It has described the man who gives in order to be seen (4:38), the men who wronged themselves and were taken in death (4:97), and it will name the road of those who follow the light at the end of the chapter (4:175).
verses.147:
> Why should Allah punish you if you are grateful and faithful? Allah is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing

> Why should Allah punish you if you are grateful and faithful? Allah is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing

**What Would God Gain From Punishing You?**
The verse asks a question that closes the whole passage about the men whose belief was a performance: why would God punish you if you are grateful and believe? He is appreciative and knows everything. The question is rhetorical, and its tone is the opposite of the warnings around it. The Book does not need anybody's punishment, and the door in the verse before this one is open for the reader's sake rather than for God's.

**The Question and What It Implies**
The Book says elsewhere that God does not gain anything from a person's worship and does not lose anything from his refusal, and the same point stands behind several statements in this chapter. The sūrah has said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and that He is free of any need and worthy of praise (4:131 states it), that He could remove a people and bring others if He wished (4:133), and that the person who is guided is guided for his own good (4:26 speaks of God's will to make matters clear and to guide, and 4:79 says that whatever good comes to a person is from God). The verse in front of the reader draws the conclusion the whole sūrah has been working towards: the point of the law, the warnings, and the promises is the state of the human being rather than a need in God.

**The Two Conditions Named**
The verse names gratitude and faith, and both words carry the chapter's argument. Gratitude is the response the sūrah keeps describing: a person who uses what God gave him in the way God asked, spends from it rather than hoarding it (4:37 describes the alternative), and gives for God's approval rather than to be seen (4:38 states the contrast). Faith is the belief the sūrah asked its readers to keep up, when it told the people who already believed to believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136), and it is the condition attached to the reward for good work throughout the chapter (4:124 is the plain statement). Put together, the two words describe a man who has taken what he was given and is using it in the right direction.

**The Names and What They Mean**
The verse closes by describing God as appreciative and knowing everything. The first name means the small effort is noticed and paid; the sūrah has said the same in its promise that the smallest good is multiplied (4:40), that the man who does good work loses nothing (4:124 uses the speck on the date stone), and that the men who strive are given ranks and mercy (4:96). The second name means nothing is missed: the sūrah has shown that God was present at the night meetings (4:108), that He knows what is in people's hearts (4:63), and that His knowledge surrounds everything in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states the ownership and the knowledge together). The verse before the reader ends the chapter's portrait of the men whose belief was a show with a question about the point of it all: nobody is asked to be grateful for God's benefit, and everyone is asked because of his own.

**What Comes Next in the Chapter**
Two verses after this one return to the community's everyday speech. The Book tells the believers not to criticise people openly, with the exception of someone who has been wronged (4:148 gives that permission), and it tells them that whether they do good openly or in secret, or pardon a wrong, God pardons and is able to do everything (4:149 describes the open door).

Then the chapter closes with the rules on the inheritance of a man who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 handles that last case) and with a description of the people who follow the light (4:175 gives it).

So this verse is the pivot. It stands between the chapter's long argument about people whose loyalty was for sale, and its final instructions about ordinary words and ordinary deeds.

**What the Chapter Laid Out on Both Sides**
The chapter opened the door of forgiveness to the person who asks (4:110 states it) while saying that each sin falls on the one who earns it (4:111 states it). It described the knowledge the Prophet was taught (4:113 names it) and the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 names it). It named the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 states it), refused the idea that reward comes by wishing (4:123 refuses it), and held up the best religion (4:125 holds it up).

It said that God takes care of every affair (4:132 states it) and that both rewards are with Him (4:134 states it). It told the believers to stand for justice even against their own family (4:135 commands it). It described the people who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137 describes them), announced the punishment of those whose belief was a show (4:138 announces it), and described those who belonged to neither side (4:143 describes them).

It warned the community against taking the other side as allies (4:144 warns it). And it named both the place reserved for a performed belief (4:145 names it) and the door back for the people who mend what they broke (4:146 names it).

One promise from another sūrah belongs here too. God announced that if the people were grateful, He would give them more (14:7 states the promise). That promise is the ground under the question this verse asks.
verses.148:
> Allah does not like negative thoughts to be voiced—except by those who have been wronged. Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**Speaking Evil and the Man Who Was Wronged**
The verse says that God does not like evil words to be spoken openly, except by a person who has been wronged, and it closes by naming God as the one who hears and knows everything. The verse follows the question about what God would gain from punishing a grateful believer (4:147), and it turns the community's attention to the ordinary speech of its members.

**What the Rule Protects**
The Book draws a line around complaint. A man who has been wronged is allowed to state what was done to him; a man who has not is not allowed to spread evil talk about others. The sūrah has been dealing with the same kind of damage all the way through: the men who put the blame for a theft onto a neighbour (4:112 states the load carried by the man who does that), the men who whispered their plans at night (4:108), the men who twisted their greeting into an insult (4:46 covers that), and the men who carried every report through the community before anybody had checked whether it was true (4:83 states the rule for checking). The verse's exception is the safety valve: a man who has been robbed can say so, and the community is not told to silence him.

**The Good Talk the Book Sets Against It**
The verse before this passage named the kind of private conversation that earns a reward: the talk that urges someone to give, to help, or to make peace between people (4:114 states the three and the promise). The chapter keeps that instruction beside its warnings: it told the community to treat parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the neighbour, the companion and the traveller well (4:36), to settle a marriage that has gone cold (4:128), to keep a wife from being left hanging (4:129), and to give a greeting of peace and answer it with one at least as good (4:86). The verse in front of the reader protects the man who has been harmed from being told to keep quiet, and it still holds the community to the standard of useful speech.

**The Court and the Report**
The sūrah has given the community a legal path for a person who has been wronged, and the verse assumes it exists. It told the community to return what it held in trust and to judge fairly (4:58), told the Prophet to judge by what God had shown him rather than by the pull of a family (4:105), set the rules for a killing by mistake and for a killing on purpose (4:92 and 4:93), described the case of the man who threw a theft onto his neighbour (4:112), and told the believers to stand for justice even when the case cuts against their own relatives (4:135). The complaint the verse permits is the beginning of that process, not a substitute for it.

**The Two Names at the End**
God is named here as the one who hears and knows everything, which is the Book's answer to both parties in a quarrel. The man who was wronged may not be believed by the community, and the man who did the wrong may be confident that his story will hold; the verse says that the hearing took place. The sūrah has used the pair for the same purpose elsewhere: it is attached to the command to return what is entrusted and to judge fairly (4:58), to the warning that a man may win a case by speaking better than his opponent (the report of the Prophet on this point is preserved through al-Bukhārī 2680), and to the community's duty to verify what it hears before it acts (4:94). The verse before the reader teaches the community how to speak about a wrong, and the verse after it teaches it how to answer one: by doing good openly or in secret, or by pardoning (4:149). The sūrah has promised the migrant room in the earth (4:100) and has told the Prophet not to plead for the men who betray themselves (4:107). It has described the knowledge the Prophet was taught (4:113) and has said that both rewards are with God (4:134). It has said that God's will is to make matters clear (4:26), has described the men who hold back what God gave them (4:37), has told the community to stand for the weak who cried out (4:75), and has named the helpless among the men, women and children (4:98).
verses.149:
> Whether you reveal or conceal a good or pardon an evil—surely Allah is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable

> Whether you reveal or conceal a good or pardon an evil—surely Allah is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable

**Open Good, Hidden Good, and Pardon**
The verse gives the community three ways of dealing with a wrong: do good openly, do good quietly, or forgive the offence, and it closes by saying that God pardons and is able to do all things. The verse follows the rule about speaking evil and the exception made for the man who was wronged (4:148), and it takes the reader past the complaint to the response.

**The Three Options**
The Book does not ask a wronged man to pretend nothing happened. The verse before this one allowed him to say what was done to him, and this verse shows him what he can do next. The sūrah has been giving the community the same choice in concrete settings: it told the men who had been insulted in the street to answer with a word of peace (the instruction to answer a greeting well appears at 4:86), it told the couple whose marriage had gone cold to settle the matter between them (4:128), it told the man who feared his wife's conduct to live with her on fair terms regardless of his feelings (4:19 covers that instruction), and it told the community that the reward for the private conversation that urges good is with God (4:114). The verse in front of the reader names the three movements of the generous response, and the last of them, pardoning, is the one that reaches the person who did the harm.

**How the Sūrah Has Used These Actions**
The chapter has shown each of the three in the lives of the people it discusses. Doing good openly is the conduct of the men who stand for the weak who cry out for help (4:75) and of the men who fight in God's cause with their wealth and their lives (4:95). Doing good quietly is the conduct the Book praises when it says that the private talk that urges giving, kindness and reconciliation earns a reward (4:114), and it is the opposite of the men who give in order to be seen (4:38). Pardoning is what the Book asks of a man who has been robbed of his good name and knows who did it, and it is the same movement the sūrah names in the case of a woman who gives up part of what she is owed in order to keep a marriage together (4:128 permits the settlement). In each case the Book is describing a person who chooses what the situation could have made him do anyway, and chooses it for a reason.

**The Two Names at the End**
The verse closes with God described as pardoning and able to do everything. The first name is the one the Book uses for the person who has been wronged and chooses to forgive. The chapter promised the person who asks forgiveness that he will find God forgiving and merciful (4:110 states it), and it described the people who turn back and set their conduct right as those who will be counted with the believers (4:146 describes them).

The second name is the Book's reminder that the community's own arrangements are never the whole story. The chapter said that God weighs every deed exactly (4:40 states it), that He knows what is hidden (4:108 states it), and that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him (4:126 states it).

**The Three Things a Wronged Person Can Do**
This verse closes the chapter's long passage about people whose loyalty was for sale and about the community's duty to live honestly. And it leaves the reader with three things he can do when he has been wronged: give openly, give quietly, or let the matter go and leave it to the One who is able to do everything (4:148 gives the permission to complain, and this verse names the better option).

**What the Chapter Had Settled Around It**
The chapter promised the person who migrates for God's sake room in the earth (4:100 states it) and named the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 names it). It warned that a people can be replaced by others (4:133 warns), said that both rewards are with God (4:134 states it), and told the believers to stand for justice even against their own family (4:135 commands it).

It ended the portrait of the people whose belief was a show with a question about what the point of it was (4:147 asks it), and the verse before this one allowed the person who was wronged to say what had been done to him (4:148 gives that). It had also allowed a person who cannot find water to purify himself with clean earth (4:43 permits it), given the remedy owed by the person who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 gives it), and named the helpless who are excused (4:99 names them). So the chapter treats forgiveness as one item in a body of law that covers everything from ritual purity to blood money.
verses.150:
> Surely those who deny Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, “We believe in some and disbelieve in others,” desiring to forge a compromise

> Surely those who deny Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, “We believe in some and disbelieve in others,” desiring to forge a compromise

**Splitting the Messengers**
The verse describes men who reject God and His messengers together, and who want to draw a line between God and the messengers by accepting some and rejecting others. They say they believe in part and disbelieve in part, and the verse says the wish behind it is to find a middle way of their own making. The verse follows the passage about the men whose loyalty was for sale (4:143 through 4:149), and it turns to the People of the Book who were doing the same thing with the prophets.

**What the Verse Is Refusing**
The Book is not complaining that people find some messengers hard to accept; it is refusing the arrangement in which a person keeps the parts of the message he likes and drops the messenger who brings the part he does not. The sūrah has shown the same conduct among the believers who were being addressed: the men who wanted a tyrant's court while claiming faith (4:60), the men who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61), and the men whose fine words arrived after the decision had been made (4:62 — the excuse the Book answers). It has also told the community what belief actually means in this chapter: believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 gives the full list), which is the same refusal to pick and choose.

**The Men the Verse Is About**
The reports connect the passage with the Jews and Christians of Madinah, who told the Muslims they believed in their own prophet but not in the one who came after him, while claiming that their own position was the middle ground. The sūrah had already answered the same group's claim that they would be saved on the strength of their book, and it had set the rule that the reward is not decided by that claim (4:123 states the refusal), and it had named the earlier communities as those who were given the same command to be mindful of God (4:131). It had also shown what the holders of the Book had done with the prophets who came to them: they killed some and rejected others (4:155 describes that record). The verse in front of the reader names the arrangement for what it is: not a compromise between two faiths but a rejection of both, because the messenger is not separable from the One who sent him.

**The Two Verdicts That Follow**
The verses after this one state the two outcomes plainly. The people described in this verse are the real disbelievers, and a humiliating punishment is prepared for them (4:151 states it). The people who believe in God and in all of His messengers are given their reward, and God forgives them and shows them mercy (4:152 states it).

The chapter has been building that same pair of outcomes from its early pages: from the men who eat fire for taking an orphan's property (4:10 gives that image) to the men who follow the light that has come to them (4:175 closes the chapter on that note).

**What Accepting a Messenger Costs**
The chapter has shown what accepting a messenger costs and what refusing one costs. The people who take the Messenger as their judge, without tightness in the chest, are the ones whose belief is real (4:65 states it). And the people who turn away are told that the Prophet was not set over them as a keeper (4:80 states it).

So this verse is the sentence that closes the door on the pick-and-choose position, and the two verses after it name the two destinations.

**The Habits the Chapter Had Already Described**
The chapter had already drawn the portrait of the people this verse is answering. It named the men who twisted their words when they greeted the Prophet (4:46 describes them), the men who walked away from the road after it had been made clear to them (4:115 describes them), and the men who joined partners with God and went far from the path (4:116 describes them).

It described the best religion as handing oneself over to God and doing good work (4:125 names it), and it dealt with the couple whose marriage had gone cold and who settled matters between themselves (4:128 describes them). It described the men who went back and forth between belief and denial until the going back stopped meaning anything (4:137 describes them) and the men who watched the fighting to see which way it went before choosing a side (4:141 describes them).

It praised the private talk that urges giving and reconciliation (4:114 praises it), and it said that God's will in this Book is to make matters clear (4:26 states it). The people who wanted a compromise were offered clarity instead.
verses.151:
> they are indeed the true disbelievers. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment

**The True Disbelievers**
The verse gives the verdict on the men described in the verses before it: they are the real disbelievers, and God has prepared a humiliating punishment for them. The verse is short and it makes no room for the middle position that the men in the previous verse were looking for.

**Why the Verdict Is Stated This Way**
The Book has already answered the claim that a person can accept part of the message and reject the rest: it told the community to believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136), and it said that whoever denies God, His angels, His Books, His messengers and the last day has wandered far off the road. The verse in front of the reader states the other side of the same sentence, and it uses a strong word: these are not people who have a different understanding, they are the men who reject the message. The sūrah has used the same plainness with the men whose loyalty was for sale: it told the community not to take the other side as allies (4:144), named the place reserved for them (4:145), described the men who belonged to neither side and could not find a road (4:143), and gave them a prayer that was only for show (4:142).

**The Humiliation Named in the Verse**
The Book chooses the punishment to match the offence, and the offence in this passage is pride: the men who picked which messengers they would accept were doing it from a sense of their own standing. The sūrah has named the same trait in the community's own people, saying that God does not love a man who is arrogant and boastful (4:36 places that warning beside the command to worship God alone and to treat people well) and that God does not love the treacherous and the steeped in sin (4:107 states it of the men who wanted to blame a neighbour for a theft). It had also warned the men who elevated themselves, saying that it is God who raises whom He wills (4:49 states that). The verse in front of the reader answers that pride with the humiliation that the Book keeps for the men whose standing was the whole of their argument.

**The Two Formulae the Sūrah Uses**
The chapter uses the same ending for several of the groups it corrects. The men who think they can trade a part of the Book for a better position are told what they will find (4:105 names the standard the Prophet was given for judgment and 4:113 describes the protection that kept him straight), the men who gave only to be seen were told that their payment was already taken (4:142 describes that prayer), and the men who came from the wrong side of the battle were told where the account would be settled (4:141 states the day of the return). The verse in front of the reader adds the punishment to the verdict, and the next verse names the reward of the men who took the whole message instead (4:152).

**What the Passage Has Been Doing**
The verses around this one are the chapter's answer to the People of the Book, and the Book keeps the argument on the level of what was actually sent to them. It describes the demand for a written revelation to be brought down from the sky (4:153 states it), the stiff-necked history that followed the prophets of Israel (4:155 names the breaking of the covenant and the killing of the messengers), and the wrongs that were counted against them (4:156 and 4:157 name the slander against Mary and the claim about the crucifixion). The verse in front of the reader takes the men who were hearing all of that and choosing to believe in some of their own prophets and not others, and it gives the verdict its name. The sūrah has already told the community that the earlier Books and the Qur'an give the same command (4:131) and that God knows exactly what people do (4:113 describes the knowledge given to the Prophet). The sūrah has also given the community the prayer it was taught to keep in the middle of a battle (4:102), has named the home promised to the men who followed what they were shown (4:121) and the home of the men who did not (4:122), and has described the best in religion as the man who hands himself over to God and follows the way of Abraham (4:125). It has described the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139) and the men who sat with mockers of God's verses (4:140), and the verse before this one names the position the verdict here answers (4:150).
verses.152:
> As for those who believe in Allah and His messengers—accepting all; rejecting none—He will surely give them their rewards. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Faith in God and All His Messengers**
The verse gives the other half of the verdict. The men and women who believe in God and in all of His messengers, without dividing one from another, will be given their reward. God forgives and shows mercy. This answers the people described in the two verses before, who wanted to accept some messengers and reject others.

**What the Verse Asks For**
The condition is that a person takes the messengers as one body: believe in God and in every man He sent. The Book had given the community the same list already, naming God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 names the four). The line the community inherited is named earlier in the sūrah, since the family of Abraham was given the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom (4:54 records the gift). The sūrah has also named the best in religion, the man who hands himself over to God, does good work and follows the way of Abraham (4:125 names him). This verse puts that posture to work on the question the passage has been arguing about. The pick-and-choose position is not answered by ranking the messengers. It is answered by saying that they all brought the same message.

**The Wrong the Passage Answers**
The Book has been reciting the history of the people who were given the Books before. The next verse describes their demand for a written revelation to come down from the sky (4:153 records the demand). The verses after that name the covenant they broke, the signs they rejected and the prophets they killed (4:155 lists them). Two more add the slander against Mary and the boast about the crucifixion (4:156 and 4:157 record both). Against that record the Book sets the people who accepted all of the messengers. This faith is not an opinion about a person. It is the acceptance of what God sent, which the sūrah has been asking of the community from the start, and which it stated plainly when it told those who already believed to go on believing (4:136 appears again, with its warning about denial).

**The Reward Named Here**
The reward promised in this verse has been named several times in the sūrah. The men and women who do good work with faith enter the garden and lose nothing (4:124 states it). Those who obey God and the Messenger are with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69 names the company). Those who strive are given ranks and mercy (4:96 names both). The sūrah has also shown what the community lost by arguing over who would be saved. Those who claimed the reward by wishing were refused by name (4:123 records it). Those who thought their group's standing would carry them were told that whoever does good, man or woman, with faith, is the one who enters (4:124 says it again).

**The Two Names at the End**
The verse closes with God described as forgiving and merciful. The chapter keeps this pair for people who come back, not for people who were never wrong. The pair appears for the man who does wrong and then asks forgiveness (4:110 gives it), for the man whose conduct at home fell short of what he wished (4:129 gives it), and for the man who kills a believer by mistake and makes the payment owed (4:92 gives it). The verses that follow describe the demand for a written revelation and the breaking of the covenant (4:153 through 4:155 tell it), and the two names stay beside those failures so that people reading their own history know what is still open to them. The sūrah also warns about the men who would not accept a messenger's ruling even after the truth had reached them (4:65 describes them). It says that the good done openly or quietly, and any pardon given, are all known to God (4:149 states it).

**The Road Through the Sūrah**
The way of life this verse describes runs through the whole chapter. The sūrah gives room in the earth to the man who migrates for God's sake (4:100 names it). It praises the private talk that urges giving and reconciliation (4:114 praises it). It warns that joining partners with God is far from the path (4:116 warns of it), and it promises gardens to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122 promises them). It records the command to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book (4:131 records it), and it keeps both rewards with God (4:134 keeps them). It commands justice even against a man's own family (4:135 commands it).

The same chapter describes the men who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137 describes them). It announces the punishment of the men whose belief was a show (4:138 announces it) and names the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 names them). It forbids sitting with men who mock God's verses (4:140 forbids it), describes the men who waited to see who won (4:141 describes them), and names the prayer performed for an audience (4:142 names it). It describes the men who belonged to neither side (4:143 describes them), forbids taking the other side as allies (4:144 forbids it), and states where that road ends (4:145 states it).

Then the sūrah opens the door for the men who came back (4:146 opens it) and asks what God would gain from punishing anyone who is grateful (4:147 asks it). It allows a wronged man to say what was done to him (4:148 allows it) and praises good done openly or in secret along with the man who pardons (4:149 praises both). It names the pick-and-choose position as a wish for a middle way (4:150 names it) and gives the verdict on the men who held it (4:151 gives it). The same sūrah says that God sent writers to the prophets (4:163 records them), that His will is to make matters clear (4:26 states it), that men who follow their own appetites wish the community would go far astray (4:27 describes them), and that no deed escapes the exact account, not even the weight of an atom (4:40 states the scale).
verses.153:
> The People of the Book demand that you ˹O Prophet˺ bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven. They demanded what is even greater than this from Moses, saying, “Make Allah visible to us!” So a thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf for worship after receiving clear signs. Still We forgave them for that ˹after their repentance˺ and gave Moses compelling proof

**The Demand for a Book From the Sky**
The verse reports that the People of the Book asked the Prophet ﷺ to bring down a written revelation from heaven for them. Then it says they had asked Moses for something greater. They told him to show them God plainly, and a thunderbolt struck them for it. The verse then says that after that they took the calf as an object of worship while clear signs stood in front of them, and that God pardoned them and gave Moses clear authority. One sentence here gathers the whole history of the earlier community.

**The Demand and What It Shows**
The Book answers the demand by showing that it is not a request for evidence but a way of never having to settle. Those making it had the Book in their hands and a messenger speaking to them, and the sūrah has already shown what they did with what they were given. They traded their share of the guidance for error (4:44 describes that trade). They twisted words when they spoke to the Prophet (4:46 records it). And they wanted him to give up part of what he had received in order to reach an agreement (4:150 names that position in this passage). So the demand for a revelation written from heaven is a demand for a different arrangement, not for a proof.

**The History the Verse Recites**
The verse names three episodes from the community of Moses. The first is the demand to see God plainly, which was answered with the thunderbolt. The second is the worship of the calf after the signs they had been shown, which the sūrah of the Cow narrates at length and which this verse states in one line. The third is the pardon that followed and the authority God gave to Moses.

The same history is named in the verses after this one, where the Book records the covenant they broke and the mountain lifted over them (4:154 records it), the signs they rejected and the prophets they killed (4:155 records it), and the slander they spoke about Mary together with the claim they made about the crucifixion (4:156 and 4:157 record both). The Book recites the list not to shame a people from long ago but to show the community what happens when a group gets used to living with a message it has no intention of following.

**What the Verse Says to the Prophet**
The verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and the sūrah has been telling him throughout how to handle the pressure of these arguments. Judge by what God has shown you, and do not plead for men who betrayed their trusts (4:105 gives the instruction). A group tried to lead him off course, and God's favour kept him straight (4:113 describes it). He was told to ask forgiveness after a hard case (4:106 gives the instruction). And he was told to stand for justice even when the case cuts against his own family (4:135 commands it). This verse answers one more demand for credentials, and the Book's reply is the history of what the demanders had already done with what they were given.

**The Wider Passage**
The verses that follow carry the account further, then turn to those among the People of the Book who believed and did right, naming them by what they actually did. They study the Book, they believe in what was sent to the Prophet and to the prophets before him, and they are given their wages (4:162 states it). The chapter keeps the same distinction throughout. It judges people by what they do with what they were given, whether they are the community being addressed or the communities that came before.

The sūrah has already said that God's will is to make matters clear and to guide people into the ways of those before them (4:26 states it). It named the people who were given the same command as this community when it said that the earlier holders of the Book and this community alike were told to be mindful of God (4:131 records it). So the demand ends with the record of the demanders, and the sūrah moves on to those in the same communities who did otherwise.

**The Book's Version of the Same Story**
The account of the calf and the demand to see God is told in full in the sūrah of the Cow, which reports the command to turn back to the One who made them and the thunderbolt that took those who made the demand (2:54 and 2:55 carry both). The command to look at God plainly is recorded in its own verse (2:55 gives it).

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
This sūrah has already opened the door of asking forgiveness (4:110 opens it). It warns those who walk away from the road after it has been made clear (4:115 warns them) and names the wrong that is not forgiven (4:116 names it). It describes the names the idolaters call on (4:117 describes them) and the promises being made to them (4:119 names them), and it says that reward does not come by wishing (4:123 states it). It forbids the community to take the other side as allies (4:144 forbids it) and praises good done openly or in secret (4:149 praises it). It names the pick-and-choose position the passage is answering (4:150 names it) along with the reward of those who accept all of the messengers (4:152 names it). It says in the passage ahead that God bears witness to what was sent down to the Prophet (4:166 states it). It describes those who go back to fighting whenever they can (4:91 describes them) and names the helpless who are excused from the journey (4:99 names them).
verses.154:
> We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant and said, “Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility.” We also warned them, “Do not break the Sabbath,” and took from them a firm covenant

> We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant and said, “Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility.” We also warned them, “Do not break the Sabbath,” and took from them a firm covenant

**The Covenant, the Gate and the Sabbath**
The verse recites three things that the earlier community was bound by and then broke: the mountain lifted over them as a sign, the command to enter the gate bowing low, and the warning about the Sabbath, which came with a firm covenant taken from them. The verse follows the account of the demand for a revelation from the sky (4:153), and it lists the charges of the verses that follow.

**What Each Item Was**
The Book narrates these episodes in its own account of the people of Israel: the mountain raised over them so that they would take what they were given seriously, the entry into the city with humility and the request for forgiveness in the words they were told to use, and the rule of the Sabbath which they broke by fishing on the day they were not allowed to fish. The sūrah in front of the reader names the covenant as the frame around all of it, and the Book says elsewhere that God took the same kind of affirmation from the prophets and the community (4:154 uses the word for the covenant, and the sūrah's own passages on the promises people make appear at 4:21 for the marriage and at 4:154 again here). The point of naming the covenant is that the community was not being asked for something new: it had already agreed.

**Why the Sūrah Recites This History**
The chapter is answering the men who wanted a middle position between belief and disbelief (4:150 describes the wish that ran through the passage), and the Book answers them with what their own history shows. The men who broke the Sabbath, the men who wanted to look at God plainly, and the men who asked for a written revelation from the sky are the same kind of demand: give us something other than what we have been given. The sūrah has shown the same habit among the Muslims being addressed: the men who wanted their disputes decided by a tyrant's court (4:60), the men who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61), and the men who came with fine words after the event (4:62). The verse in front of the reader puts the community's story next to its own, and the lesson is the same in both.

**The Covenant, and What a Person Does With It**
The verse names the covenant as the thing that was broken, and the chapter has placed its whole weight on what a person does with what he has agreed to. It told the community to return what it holds in trust and to judge fairly (4:58 commands both). It named the marriage agreement a firm covenant, using the same word (4:21 names it). It told the believers to stand for justice even against their own relatives (4:135 commands it). And it said that God is a witness over what people do (4:33 states it).

**What the People of the Covenant Had**
The men whose history this verse recites had everything: a covenant, a mountain lifted over them, signs placed in front of them, and a messenger living among them. The chapter's verdict on them is the long list that follows, and it runs from the breaking of the covenant and the killing of the prophets to the slander they spread and the boast they made about the crucifixion (4:155 begins that list).

So this verse tells the community what to expect from a people with that record. And the verses after it turn to the people among them who did the opposite, describing those who believed and did right (4:162 names them).

**The Same Episode Told Elsewhere**
The Book tells the same episode in the sūrah of the Heifer, where the community is told to enter the gate bowing and to ask forgiveness in the words they were given (2:58 carries the command). And the sūrah of the Heights reports what became of the people who broke the Sabbath (7:166 records their transformation). Reading the three together, the reader can see that the grievance in this verse is not a one-off failure but a pattern the Book keeps returning to.

**Where the Chapter Had Already Been**
The chapter has given room in the earth to the person who migrates for God's sake (4:100 gives it), taught the community the prayer of the battle (4:102 describes it), and told the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 states it). It opened the door of asking forgiveness (4:110 opens it), named the names the idolaters call on (4:117 names them), and said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God with a knowledge that surrounds it (4:126 states it).

It recorded the command to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book (4:131 records it) and the care God takes of every affair (4:132 states it). It will say that God bears witness to what was sent down (4:166 states it). And it warns the community about a marriage treated lightly (4:29 warns) and about the record kept of every promise (4:154 is this verse itself, and the reader is being asked what his own record will say).
verses.155:
> ˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah’s signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and for saying, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”—it is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few—

**The Charges Against Them**
The verse lays out why the earlier community was condemned: they broke their covenant, they rejected God's signs, they killed the prophets without any right to do so, and they said that their hearts were covered over. The verse closes by saying what that statement meant: God sealed their hearts because of their disbelief, so that hardly any of them would believe.

**The Charges Named in Order**
The first charge is the covenant they broke, which the verse before it introduced as the frame around the whole history (4:154 names the covenant and the mountain that was lifted over them). The second is the rejection of the signs, which the Book names throughout its account of them: the cloud, the manna, the water from the rock, and the deliverance from Egypt. The third is the killing of the prophets, which the Book names in other places as the crime of the community that had been given the most guidance: it says elsewhere that they killed the men who came to them with what they themselves did not want (2:87 states the charge in the sūrah of the Cow). The fourth is the claim that their hearts are locked shut, which the verse answers by saying that God sealed them.

**How the Sūrah Has Used These Charges**
The chapter has placed the same four in front of its own readers, translated into their situation. It has described the men who trade their share of the Book for error (4:44), the men who twist words when they greet the Prophet (4:46 covers that), the men who want a middle position between belief and disbelief (4:150), and the men who want the community to go back to unbelief with them (4:88 describes the group the community was split over). The sūrah has also said what it does with people who go on like that: it told the Prophet that God allowed the doubting men to go back because of what they had earned (4:88 again), and it said that the men who are left to wander will not find a road (4:143 states it). The verse in front of the reader takes the history that the men of the earlier community were proud of and shows them the account of it.

**The Statement That Their Hearts Are Covered**
The verse answers a specific claim: the men said their hearts were enclosed, by which they meant that they could not be expected to take anything else in. The Book refuses the excuse and says the enclosure was God's doing and a consequence of what they did. The sūrah has said the same about the men in the community whose loyalty was for sale: God allowed them to go back to what they had chosen (4:88), and the men who claimed that their group's standing would carry them were told plainly that the reward is not decided that way (4:123). It had also named the men who withheld what God gave them and urged others to be like them (4:37), and the men who gave only to be seen (4:38), both of whom were treating their wealth and their standing as the important thing.

**The Faith That Would Not Come**
The verse's last words say that only a few of them would believe, and the passage after it names some of the ones who did. It says that the men among the People of the Book who are firmly established in knowledge, and who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and in what was sent down before him, and who keep the prayer and give the alms and believe in God and the last day, are the ones who will be given their wage (4:162 states all of it). The sūrah has kept the door open in the same way for the community's own men: it named the men whose belief was a show and then named the four conditions under which they could be counted with the believers (4:146), and it told the men who had been misled that the door of seeking forgiveness stands open (4:110). The verse before the reader records hard hearts as a consequence, and the chapter does not present them as the end of the story. The sūrah has also reminded the reader that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 states the scale) and that God knows what is in people's hearts (4:63). The sūrah has named the same stakes for its own readers: it warned about trading the share of the Book for a small profit while the consequence is fire (4:10 states the fate and 4:44 the trade), it described the man who throws his fault onto an innocent neighbour and carries the blame for it (4:112), it warned the man who walks away from the road after it has been made clear (4:115), and it left the question of what God gains by punishing a grateful believer to the reader (4:147). It named the reward of the men who accept all of the messengers (4:152), and it goes on to describe the demand for a written revelation (4:153) and the claim the community made about the crucifixion (4:157). It also set the penalty for a killing done on purpose (4:93 states the rule).
verses.156:
