> and for their denial and outrageous accusation against Mary

> and for their denial and outrageous accusation against Mary

**The Slander Against Mary**
The verse names two things together: their refusal to believe and the serious accusation they made against Mary. The verse is one line in the long list that begins with the covenant and ends with the boast about killing the Messiah (4:157), and it stands in the middle of the passage so that the reader takes the accusation as one item in a record, not as a remark in an argument.

**What the Accusation Was**
The Book does not repeat the slander here; it says only that it was serious. The claim was that Mary had been unchaste, which the sūrah of Mary answers directly when it reports her own words on the day she brought the child back to her people (19:27 and the verses around it name the charge and her answer). The Book had already told the community what such a charge means: it commanded four witnesses for the accusation of indecency and prescribed the punishment for men who make the charge without producing them (the rule is set out in the sūrah of Light, and the sūrah in front of the reader names the same protection of reputations when it tells the community not to spread evil reports (4:148) and describes the man who throws his fault onto an innocent neighbour (4:112)). The verse in front of the reader names the slander as one of the reasons the community in question was condemned.

**Why the Sūrah Names It Here**
The passage is the Book's answer to the men who wanted to choose which messengers they would accept. The sūrah has already answered their claim to hold a middle position: it said that these men are the real disbelievers (4:151), and it named the reward of the men who accept all of the messengers (4:152). The list that includes the slander against Mary is the evidence that the position was not a matter of scholarly disagreement: the same community had lived through the covenant, the signs, the prophets, and the slander. The Book says it elsewhere for the community in front of it: the men who twist their greetings (4:46), the men who traded their share of the Book for a small profit (4:44), and the men who wanted the community to go back to unbelief (4:88) were doing the same work.

**The Honour the Book Gives Mary**
The sūrah answers the slander without repeating it. It names Mary as the mother of the Messiah and describes her child as a servant of God, a word from Him, and a messenger (4:171 gives all three). And it says elsewhere in the Book that God chose her above the women of her time.

The sūrah also protects the reputation of ordinary people through the rules it gives about accusation and evidence. It told the community to stand for justice even against its own family (4:135 commands it), to return what it holds in trust and to judge fairly (4:58 commands both), and to verify what it strikes before it strikes (4:94 orders it).

**Where This Verse Sits in the Record**
This verse is one entry in a record the Book keeps of what was said and done. The verses after it name the last item on the list: the claim that they had killed the Messiah (4:157 states the claim). Then the sūrah gives the correction the whole passage has been building towards: they did not kill him and they did not crucify him (4:157 gives both), and God raised him to Himself (4:158 states it).

**What the Chapter Says to the Same People**
The Book also says that those among the People of the Book who believe in God and the last day and do what is right have their wage with their Lord, and have nothing to fear (4:162 states it). And the command to keep hearts and tongues straight appears in this sūrah's own instruction that God does not like evil words spoken openly, except by someone who has been wronged (4:148 gives the exception).

**What the Chapter Said About Accusations**
The chapter had already warned about the damage a false accusation does. It named the fire waiting for those who consume the property of orphans (4:10 names it), the private talk that earns a reward (4:114 names it), and the gardens promised to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122 promises them).

It answered the community's question about women and orphans (4:127 records it). And it has been reciting the record of the people it is addressing, from the demand for a written revelation to come down (4:153 records it) and the covenant with the mountain lifted over them (4:154 records it) to the charges that fill the verses around this one (4:155 begins them). The chapter will then name the messengers God sent to guide people and to warn them (4:163 names them).
verses.157:
> and for boasting, “We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.” But they neither killed nor crucified him—it was only made to appear so. Even those who argue for this ˹crucifixion˺ are in doubt. They have no knowledge whatsoever—only making assumptions. They certainly did not kill him

> and for boasting, “We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.” But they neither killed nor crucified him—it was only made to appear so. Even those who argue for this ˹crucifixion˺ are in doubt. They have no knowledge whatsoever—only making assumptions. They certainly did not kill him

**The Boast That They Killed the Messiah**
The verse reports the claim that they had killed Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of God. Then it corrects the claim in one sentence. They did not kill him and they did not crucify him; the matter was made to look that way to them. Then it says that those who disagree about it are in doubt themselves, with no knowledge to follow and only a guess to work from, because they did not kill him for certain.

**The Correction the Verse Makes**
The Book leaves the manner of what happened to God and states the fact that the men who boasted had not done what they said. The verse does not describe how Jesus was taken up. It says that the claim to have killed him was empty, and the next verse supplies the answer by saying that God raised him to Himself (4:158 states it).

The sūrah uses the same method in its other corrections. It answered those who made Mary's child a partner of God by naming him a servant (4:171 gives that description). It answered the demand for a written revelation from the sky by reciting the history of those who made the demand (4:153 describes the demand and what followed). This verse refuses the boast and the doubt about it in one movement. Those who claimed the killing were mistaken, and those who argue about it have nothing but a guess.

**What the Verse Leaves Out**
The Book says nothing about who was on the cross, and the teachers of the community have offered more than one explanation without any of them settling the matter. The verse's silence is deliberate. It says that the matter was made to resemble the truth to the people looking at it, which is a statement about their perception rather than a description of an event. The chapter keeps its interest in what people claimed and what their claims were worth. Those in front of the reader had built a boast on something that did not happen.

**The Doubt Named in the Verse**
The verse says that those who disagree about the matter are in doubt, with only guessing to work from. The Book names doubt as the state of other groups in the same chapter. It describes those whose loyalty moved with the battle (4:141 describes them), those who tried to trick God and prayed only to be seen (4:142 describes them), those who split into two camps over the double-dealers (4:88 describes them), and those who belonged to neither side because they kept going back and forth (4:143 describes them).

It also warned the community against pursuing what it had no knowledge of, which is the same instruction that stands behind this correction, and the sūrah says that God does not like evil words spoken openly except by the person who has been wronged (4:148 states it). So the verse tells the reader what a claim is worth when those making it have nothing to stand on. The chapter takes the same line with the community's own disputes. It told the Prophet to judge by what God had shown him rather than by what was argued (4:105 gives the instruction), and it told the believers to stand for justice even when the case cuts against them (4:135 commands it).

**What Follows**
The verse after this one gives the correction its positive form: God raised him to Himself, and God is mighty and wise (4:158 states both). The passage then turns to the People of the Book and says that every one of them will believe in him before his death, and that he will be a witness against them on the day of judgment (4:159 states both).

Then the Book names what was forbidden to the Jews because of their wrongdoing and their turning many people away from God's road (4:160 names it), and it names those among them who are firmly grounded in knowledge and who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and before him (4:162 names them). The sūrah keeps the same method all the way through the passage. It takes a claim that a community built its standing on and sets the record beside it, whether that claim is the demand for a written revelation (4:153 records it), the slander against Mary (4:156 records it), or the boast in this verse. Then it names the people in the same community who did the opposite, which is why it can say that the door was never closed on anyone.

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
The correction in this verse is tied to the community's own instruction about truthful speech. The chapter allows a wronged person to complain, and it forbids spreading malicious reports (4:148 permits the complaint, and 4:149 praises the person who pardons instead). It describes the people who hold meetings at night to work out how to beat a neighbour in a case (4:108 records them) and the knowledge given to the Prophet so that he could answer what they brought him (4:113 describes it).

It praises the private talk that urges giving and reconciliation (4:114 praises it) and warns those who walk away from the road once it is clear (4:115 warns them). It names the promises made to the people who took the wrong way (4:120 names them) and promises the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 promises them).

It names the pick-and-choose position on the messengers (4:150 names it) and the reward of those who accept every messenger (4:152 names it). It recites the charges the passage has been building, the breaking of the covenant (4:155 records it) and the slander against Mary (4:156 records it). And it will say that God bears witness to what was sent down (4:166 states it).

Behind all of this stands the wider point of the chapter: the people who twisted their words when they greeted the Prophet (4:46 describes them) are the same people whose words are being judged here, and God's will in this Book is to make matters clear (4:26 states it).
verses.158:
> Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**God Raised Him to Himself**
The verse gives the positive statement that answers the boast in the verse before it: God raised Jesus up to Himself, and God is mighty and wise. The verse is one line, and everything it does not say is as important as what it does: it does not describe the raising, it does not name a place, and it does not explain the manner.

**What the Verse Corrects**
The verse before it refused the claim that the men had killed the Messiah and said that the matter was made to look that way to them (4:157). This verse states what actually happened to him. The Book uses the same verb in another sūrah when it reports God's words to Jesus that He would take him and raise him to Himself and purify him of the men who disbelieved (3:55 states that promise). In both places the Book says what God did and leaves the mechanics alone, which is the same way it treats other matters it considers beyond the reader's reach in this chapter: it said that God taught the Prophet what he did not know (4:113 describes the gift), and it said that God's knowledge surrounds everything in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states the ownership and the knowledge).

**The Two Names at the End**
The verse closes with God described as mighty and wise, and the chapter has used the pair for the moments when human arrangements fail. The men who thought a group's standing would save them were told that the reward is not decided that way (4:123), the men who claimed the killing of a messenger were answered by the One who raised him, and the chapter had already told the community that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and that He takes care of every affair (4:132 states both). The pair also matches the two halves of what the verse is doing: the power answers the boast, and the wisdom explains the silence. The same pairing closes the chapter's account of the men who tried to mislead the Prophet in the armour case: they deceived only themselves and did him no harm, and God gave him the Book and the wisdom and taught him what he did not know (4:113 describes it).

**Where the Passage Goes After This**
The verse that follows says that every one of the People of the Book will believe in him before his death and that he will be a witness against them on the day of judgment (4:159). The Book then names the things that were forbidden to the Jews for their wrongdoing and their turning of others away from God's road (4:160 states it), and it follows that with the answer to the men who thought the prohibition was permanent: the same passage says that the men among them who are firmly grounded in knowledge and who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and what was sent before him, and who keep the prayer, give the alms and believe in God and the last day, are given their wage (4:162 names the whole list). The chapter's method in this whole section is to take the claims a community had built on and to replace them with what God actually did. The verse in front of the reader is the shortest statement in that series: the men boasted, and God raised His messenger.

**What the Verse Leaves With the Reader**
The Book's own instruction to the community in this chapter is to judge by what God has shown rather than by the weight of an argument (4:105 states the prophet's charge, and the report he left behind says that a man may win a case by speaking better than his opponent and be handed a piece of fire — al-Bukhārī 2680). The verse in front of the reader is the same lesson told from God's side: the powerful men who claimed a killing were answered by an act that none of them could touch, and the community reading the account two thousand years later has nothing but the sentence. The sūrah has said elsewhere that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 states the scale) and that the account is kept with exactness (4:134 says that both rewards are with God). The sūrah has praised the private talk that urges good (4:114), has promised the gardens to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122), and has warned that a people can be removed and others brought in their place (4:133). It has described the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139), has praised the good done openly or in secret and the man who pardons (4:149), and has named the covenant the earlier community was bound by and the mountain lifted over them (4:154). It will name the messengers sent to guide people and warn them (4:163) and will say that God bears witness to what was sent down to the Prophet (4:166). The chapter will name the messengers sent to give good news and warning (4:165).
verses.159:
> Every one of the People of the Book will definitely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Judgment Jesus will be a witness against them

**Every One of Them Will Believe in Him Before His Death**
The verse says that every one of the People of the Book will believe in Jesus before his own death, and that on the day of judgment Jesus will be a witness against them. The sentence is short, and the teachers of the community read it in two ways: as a statement about what happens at the end of each person's life, and as a statement about the day when every claim is settled.

**The Reading the Teachers Discussed**
The words can mean that nobody from the People of the Book will die without having believed in Jesus first, whatever he said while he was healthy. They can also mean that this will happen when Jesus himself returns and every claimant sees who he was. The Book supports the second reading when it reports his return in other passages. The main collections carry the report of the Prophet ﷺ that Jesus will come down before the hour and that the People of the Book will believe in him then (al-Bukhārī 3448 and Muslim 155 preserve the report). Either way the verse closes the argument the passage has been having. Those who boasted about killing him, and those who built their religion on a wrong idea about him, will both have to look at him.

**The Witness at the End**
The verse ends by naming Jesus as a witness on the day of judgment, and the Book gives messengers that role in other places too. It says that God will bring a witness from every community and bring the Prophet as a witness over his own (4:41 describes that scene). The same sūrah says that the Prophet's own testimony will be asked about the people he lived among (4:41 again). The Book also told the community that God will gather humanity on a day about which there is no doubt (4:87 states it), and it described the account of those who were taken in death while they wronged themselves (4:97 describes them). So the arguments about Jesus are not open forever, because the man at the centre of them is going to be there.

**What the Passage Has Built Toward**
This whole section corrects claims made about the messengers. The demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153 records it), the broken covenant and the rejected signs (4:155 records them), the slander against Mary (4:156 records it) and the boast about the killing (4:157 records it) all come from the same attitude: a people treating God's messengers as an argument to be won. This verse hands the whole matter over to the person they were arguing about. The sūrah has kept the same door open for those who stop pretending. It named the four conditions under which people whose belief had been a show could be counted with the believers (4:146 names them). It opened the door of asking forgiveness (4:110 opens it). And it said that those who believe in God and all of His messengers will be given their reward (4:152 states it).

**The Larger Frame**
The chapter goes on to name what was made forbidden to the Jews for their wrongdoing and for their turning many people away from God's road (4:160 states it). It then answers anyone who treats the prohibition as a complaint against God by naming those among them who believed, kept the prayer, gave the alms and believed in God and the last day, and saying that they are the ones who will be given their wage (4:162 names them).

The sūrah has already given the community the instruction it needs to hold all of this together. Stand for justice even when the case cuts against your own family (4:135 commands it). Keep your agreements (4:33 commands it). Return what was entrusted to you (4:58 commands it). And speak about a wrong done to you without spreading evil reports about others (4:148 allows it). The Book also says in this chapter that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 states the scale) and that He knows what is in people's hearts (4:63 states it), which is why the day of the witness is the day accounts are settled rather than a day of surprises. The sūrah also says that whoever God leaves to wander will not find a road (4:137 describes those who went back and forth, and 4:143 states the rule).

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
The sūrah records the command to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book (4:131 records it). It forbids sitting with those who mock God's verses (4:140 forbids it). It names the pick-and-choose position on the messengers (4:150 names it) and the verdict passed on those who held it (4:151 gives it). It says that God spoke to some messengers directly and raised some of them in rank (4:164 states it), and that He bears witness to what was sent down (4:166 states it). The passage ahead names the Messiah as a word from God placed in Mary and a spirit from Him (4:171 names him), and the chapter has already promised that God accepts the turning of the person who corrects himself in time (4:18 states the condition).
verses.160:
> We forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful to them for their wrongdoing, and for hindering many from the Way of Allah

**What Was Forbidden to the Jews**
The verse says that certain good foods were made forbidden to the Jews because of their wrongdoing, and because they turned many people away from God's road. It follows the account of the demand for a written revelation (4:153 records it), the broken covenant (4:155 records it), the slander against Mary (4:156 records it) and the boast about the killing (4:157 records it). What it names is one consequence of that history.

**What the Restriction Was**
The Book names the foods in another place, listing what was forbidden to the community of Israel before the Torah was sent down, and making clear that these restrictions were part of the law they were given rather than a burden placed on everyone. The Book also says elsewhere that all food was lawful to the people of Israel until the Torah came, with the exception of what Jacob gave up for himself (3:93 carries the account). This verse gives the reason for the restriction in the same sentence as the restriction: their wrongdoing and their turning others off the road.

**Why the Sūrah Names the Reason**
The Book keeps tying rules to the conduct of the people who were given them, and this chapter does it repeatedly. It says that God allowed a group of men to go back to their disbelief because of what their hands had earned (4:88 states it). It says that the men who traded their share of the Book for a small profit did so to keep their position (4:44 describes the trade). It names the same conduct among the community being addressed: men who hold back their wealth and urge others to do the same (4:37 describes them), men who give only to be seen (4:38 describes them), and men who want a middle position between belief and unbelief (4:150 describes them). This verse adds the charge the Book has used for this people throughout. They shut the road to God for other people as well as for themselves.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**
The verse does not say that the restrictions were unjust. The Book states in the same passage that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 states the scale). It also says that these restrictions belonged to a specific law given to a specific community, which is why the sūrah goes on to describe the men among them who believed and did right and are given their wage (4:162 names the belief, the prayer, the alms and the faith in God and the last day).

The same method appears in the chapter's own laws. The sūrah restricted divorce and the taking back of gifts (4:20 sets the limit), it limited marriage so that a man takes one wife if he fears injustice (4:3 states the rule), and it told the community to keep its promises even when the cost is high (4:58 sets the standard). The Book also says that the Prophet described in their own books will make lawful for them what is good and forbid them what is wrong (7:157 gives the description).

**Where the Passage Turns After This**
The verses that follow describe the men who eat the forbidden thing knowingly and the men who turn others away (4:161 states the charge). Then the chapter answers the whole section with the men among the People of the Book who are firmly grounded in knowledge and who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and before him, who keep the prayer, give the alms and believe in God and the last day, and it says that these will be given their wage (4:162 names the whole list).

The sūrah has ended several of its arguments this way, naming the people who got it right after the people who got it wrong. It had told the community that its own belief should take in the full message (4:136 states it), that the door back is open for anyone who mends what he broke (4:146 states it), and that God's will in the Book is to make matters clear and to guide people into the ways of those before them (4:26 states it). This verse names what a community lost by its conduct, and the verses after it name what a community in the same position gained by behaving differently. The chapter's closing movement, which sets out the last rules of inheritance, follows shortly after (4:175 and 4:176 carry the close), tying the discussion back to the practical life of the community. The wider claim stands in the same passage: to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states it), and He forgives whom He wills.

**The Rest of the Chapter's Road**
The sūrah has promised the migrant room in the earth (4:100 states it), has warned the men who walk away from the road after it is clear (4:115 warns them), has named the wrong that is not forgiven (4:116 names it), and has named the promises made to the men who followed the lying being (4:119 names them). It says that reward does not come by wishing (4:123 states it), describes the best in religion (4:125 describes him), names the reward of the men who accept all the messengers (4:152 names it), recites the covenant and the mountain lifted over the community (4:154 recites them), and names the messengers sent to guide people (4:163 names them). The verses ahead describe the men among the People of the Book who held back part of what they were given (4:167 states the charge). The sūrah has also said that God lightens what people carry because they were made weak (4:28 states it) and has described the men who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61 describes them).
verses.161:
> taking interest despite its prohibition, and consuming people’s wealth unjustly. We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment

**Two More Charges**
The verse adds two charges to the record of the community it has been discussing. They took interest after it had been forbidden to them, and they consumed people's property wrongly. The verse closes with the verdict the chapter has used for this group: a painful punishment has been prepared for those among them who rejected the message.

**What Interest Is**
Interest is a sum charged for the use of money over time, and the Book treats it as a claim on wealth that was never earned. The verses before this one named the foods forbidden to the community of Israel because of its wrongdoing and its turning people away from God's road (4:160 gives the reason), and this verse names the practices that went with it.

The Book repeats the warning about interest in its own words in the sūrah of the Cow, where it also forbids taking one another's property by false means and telling a judge a false story in order to take what is not yours (2:188 states both). This chapter had already said that consuming the property of orphans is eating fire (4:10 states it), and it told the community not to devour one another's wealth through falsehood (4:29 gives the rule). So the charge here belongs to a set of rules the community was given in every age.

**Consuming Wealth Unjustly**
The second charge covers everything from a rigged measure to a bribe to a claim pressed with a false story. The sūrah shows how careful the community was expected to be with money. It told the believers to hand back what was placed in their trust and to judge fairly (4:58 gives both). It prescribed the payment owed by a person who kills a believer by mistake (4:93 states it). It told the community to give a woman her marriage gift freely (4:4 gives the instruction). And it named the wrong of swallowing a neighbour's right in a case (4:112 describes that man). The Book's standard is stated plainly in the same sūrah when it says that no one is wronged by so much as the weight of an atom (4:40 states the scale).

**Why the Verse Names a Punishment for Some of Them**
The verse says that a painful punishment is prepared for those among them who rejected the message. This is the same construction the chapter used when it announced the punishment of those whose belief was a show (4:138 gives the announcement) and of those whose loyalty was for sale (4:145 names their place).

The Book keeps making one distinction: the punishment belongs to the rejection, not to a person's family tree. The next verse names those in the same community who believed, kept the prayer and paid their alms, and it says they will be given their wage (4:162 gives the whole list). The chapter had already praised the people who combined knowledge with faith, and it names the road of those who follow the light near its close (4:175 mentions it).

**Where the Chapter Has Placed This**
The verses around this one carry the last of the chapter's charges against the community that had been given the Book. The demand for a written revelation (4:153 records it), the covenant and the mountain (4:154 records them), the charges that follow (4:155 gives them), the slander against Mary (4:156 records it) and the boast about killing the Messiah (4:157 records it) are followed by the foods forbidden for the same wrongdoing (4:160 names them), and then by this verse about interest and wealth.

The sūrah keeps reminding its readers what the whole Book is for. The names the idolaters call on are only names (4:117 says it). Reward is not decided by wishes (4:123 says it). God owns everything and His knowledge surrounds it (4:126 states both). And private talk that urges good earns a reward (4:114 states it). The chapter also described those who traded their share of the Book for a small gain (4:44 describes them) and those who look for honour in the wrong company (4:139 describes them). It gave the community its own instruction to be mindful of God (4:131 records it).

**The Practical Rules Beside These Warnings**
The chapter's practical rules appear alongside the warnings. It gives the shortened prayer on a journey (4:101 describes it) and the guarded prayer of battle (4:102 describes it). It promises the person who migrates for God's sake room in the earth (4:100 gives the promise). It names the couple who separate and are enriched by God (4:130 names them). It passes its verdict on those who wanted a middle way between belief and denial (4:151 gives the verdict), and it says that God lightens what people carry because they were made weak (4:28 states it).
verses.162:
> But those of them well-grounded in knowledge, the faithful ˹who˺ believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you—˹especially˺ those who establish prayer—and those who pay alms-tax and believe in Allah and the Last Day, to these ˹people˺ We will grant a great reward

**The Men Who Got It Right**
The verse turns to the people in the same communities who did otherwise. It names those among them who are deeply grounded in knowledge. It names the believers who accept what was sent down to the Prophet and what was sent down before him. It names the men and women who keep the prayer, the men and women who pay the alms, and those who believe in God and the last day. All of these, the verse says, will be given their wage. They are named one by one so that nobody can claim the passage was a sentence on a whole people.

**Knowledge and Faith Together**
The verse puts knowledge first, and the Book has praised that combination throughout the sūrah. It named the book and the kingdom given to the family of Abraham and the line of David (4:53 records the gift), it told of the Prophet being taught what he did not know (4:105 sets the judge's standard and 4:113 describes the instruction), and it reports that those firmly rooted in knowledge say that what was sent down is the truth. The sūrah also warns that knowledge alone is not the point. The men who were given a share of the Book are criticised for trading it away (4:44 describes the trade), and men who argue about what they have not been given are sent back to the verses before them (4:150 describes that position).

**The Practices the Verse Names**
Three practices are named, and they show that faith is not a claim but a life. Keeping the prayer appears in the sūrah in every situation the community could face: shortened on a journey (4:101 records it), guarded in battle (4:102 records it), and at its fixed times once the danger passes (4:103 records it). Paying the alms is the duty the chapter puts beside the prayer when it describes the faithful. Belief in God and the last day is the pair the sūrah uses for the men who do good work with faith (4:122 describes them), for the men who turn back to God and hold fast to Him (4:146 describes them), and for the men and women whose deeds are never lost (4:124 states it). So the verse names the ordinary conduct the passage has been describing from its opening verses.

**What the Verse Adds to the Argument**
The whole passage has been answering a claim about belonging. It named the men who wanted a middle way between faith and denial (4:150 describes them), the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 describes them), the men who waited to see which side won and the men who performed their prayer for an audience (4:142 describes both). Against that the sūrah sets the people named here, whose learning produces prayer and giving. The chapter has also said that nothing is lost with God, not even the weight of an atom (4:134 says that both rewards are with Him, and 4:126 states that everything belongs to Him and that His knowledge surrounds all things).

**The Same Road in the Rest of the Chapter**
The sūrah has been pointing to this group from its early pages, and the promises it made there are the wage this verse names. The men who obey God and the Messenger are with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69 names the company). The men who strive are given ranks and mercy (4:96 states it). The men and women who do good work with faith enter the garden and lose nothing (4:124 states it again).

The chapter has also told the community what belief in the full message means, naming God, the Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 lists all four). It named the same holding fast when it described the men who came out of hypocrisy (4:146 describes them). Its list of duties runs alongside: verify what you strike (4:94 gives the rule), return what is entrusted to you (4:58 commands it), keep your agreements (4:33 commands it), and remember that God does not like evil words spoken openly except by the person who has been wronged (4:148 states it). The sūrah also warned the community not to treat marriage lightly (4:29 states the rule) and named the couple who settle their differences between themselves (4:128 names them).

This verse is the chapter's own answer to the question of who belongs to the community that will be given its wage, and it answers with learning, prayer, giving and faith in the day of account. The chapter has promised room in the earth to the man who migrates (4:100 states it), has praised the private talk that urges giving and reconciliation (4:114 praises it), and has described the best in religion as the man who hands himself over to God and follows the way of Abraham (4:125 describes him). It has named the reward of the men who accept all of the messengers (4:152 names it), has recited the charges against the earlier community that stand in the verses before this one (4:155 states them), and has named the interest they took and the property they consumed (4:161 names both).
verses.163:
> Indeed, We have sent revelation to you ˹O Prophet˺ as We sent revelation to Noah and the prophets after him. We also sent revelation to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants, ˹as well as˺ Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon. And to David We gave the Psalms

**The Chain of Revelation**
The verse says that God sent revelation to the Prophet just as He sent it to Noah and the prophets after him, and it names a long list of prophets: Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and it says that David was given a book. The verse connects the Prophet's message to the whole line that came before him and refuses the idea that the Qur'an is a new thing with no history.

**What the List Establishes**
The names in the verse are the founders and the heirs of the earlier communities. The chapter opened by addressing humanity through the One who created them and the one soul from which they were made (4:1 names the creation and the ties of kinship, and the family of Abraham is named at 4:54 in the same passage). The list continues into the prophets of Israel, and it puts Jesus in the same line, which is the point the passage has been working towards since the verses on the crucifixion. The verse after this one adds that there are messengers whose stories were told and others whose stories were not, and it says that God spoke to Moses directly (4:164 states both).

**Why the Book Names Them Here**
The passage has just recited the record of the community that was given the Book and the covenant: the demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153), the breaking of the covenant, the rejection of the signs and the killing of the prophets (4:155), the slander against Mary (4:156) and the boast about the crucifixion (4:157). The chapter's answer is to show that the Prophet stands in the same line as the men they claimed to follow, which is why it names the very prophets whose descendants they were. The same method runs through the sūrah: it said that God took the covenant from the prophets and from the men who followed them (the covenant appears at 4:154 in its account of the earlier community), it named the men who were given wealth and a great kingdom in the family of Abraham (4:54 uses David and his book as the example), and it said that the men who follow the light sent down with the Prophet are the ones who prosper (4:175 at the close of the chapter).

**David and the Book He Was Given**
The verse ends with David and the book he received, which the Book names elsewhere as the Psalms. The sūrah has already told the community that God gives His knowledge and His book to whom He wills (4:113 describes what the Prophet was taught, and 4:126 states that God's knowledge surrounds all things). The verse in front of the reader puts David in the line beside the Prophet and beside Moses, who speaks with God directly in the verse that follows, and it leaves the reader with a plain fact: the message given to the Prophet is the same message carried by men whose names the earlier communities knew.

**Where the Passage Is Going**
The verses after this one explain the purpose of the whole line of messengers: they came with good news and warnings so that people would have no excuse left once the messengers had come (4:165 states that purpose). The sūrah keeps the same frame around everything it reports, and the verses that carry these names also carry the chapter's promises and warnings: the men who believe and do good work are given their reward (4:152 states it), the men who look for honour in the wrong company will not find it (4:139), and the men who hold their meetings at night should know that everything is written if they fear being found out (4:108 describes those meetings). God's knowledge covers what is in the heavens and the earth, and He is the one who bears witness to what He sent down (the witness named at 4:166). The verse in front of the reader is part of the Book's plain answer to the men who argued that it had no pedigree: it names the chain. The sūrah has told the Prophet to judge by what God showed him (4:105), has described the best in religion (4:125), and has said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God with the knowledge that surrounds it (4:126). It has given the community the full list of what belief covers (4:136 lists God, His Messenger, the Books and the last day), has named the covenant taken from the earlier community (4:154), has said that God raised the Messiah to Himself (4:158), and has recalled the gift given to the family of Abraham (4:53 names the kingdom and the book).
verses.164:
> There are messengers whose stories We have told you already and others We have not. And to Moses Allah spoke directly

> There are messengers whose stories We have told you already and others We have not. And to Moses Allah spoke directly

**Messengers Both Named and Unnamed**
The verse says that there are messengers whose stories God has already told the Prophet, and messengers whose stories He has not, and it closes by saying that God spoke to Moses directly. The verse follows a list of names (4:163) and it opens the reader's view beyond the names he has been given.

**The Messengers He Did Not Name**
The verse tells the reader that the list he has been given is not the whole list. The Book names many prophets in its own passages and speaks of others by their communities rather than by name, and it does not treat the silence as a loss. The sūrah has taken the same attitude to other matters beyond its own account: it said that God taught the Prophet what he did not know (4:105 sets the standard for judgment and 4:113 names the instruction he was given), and it says that the Book was sent with God's knowledge (4:166 states it). The verse in front of the reader is a reminder that the reader's information is not the whole of the story, and it is placed next to a list of names so that the reader sees both the record and its limits.

**Moses and the Direct Speech**
The verse singles out Moses for speech with God, which is the distinction the Book gives him in other places as well. The community of Moses is the one whose history has filled the last section of this sūrah: the demand to see God plainly and the thunderbolt that struck them (4:153 states it), the covenant and the mountain lifted over them (4:154 names the covenant), the charge of killing the prophets (4:155 lists it), and the claim about the crucifixion (4:157 reports it). Against that history the Book sets the fact that God spoke to Moses plainly, which is the honour given to a prophet from the same people. The sūrah has kept the same balance with the men who followed the earlier Books: it named the men among them who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and before him and who keep the prayer (4:162 lists them), and it named the men who hold back what they were given (the passage ahead names them at 4:167).

**What the Verse Does in the Argument**
The chapter's whole argument with the People of the Book comes down to the question of who is speaking and who was sent. The verse in front of the reader answers it by placing the Prophet in the same line and by saying that some of the men in that line were not named to him at all. The sūrah has already said that God's messengers came with good news and warning (4:165 gives the purpose), and it had named the covenant that the earlier communities carried (4:154 uses the word), the instruction to be mindful of God that was given to the holders of the Book and to the community alike (4:131 states it), and the promise that the men who accept every messenger will be given their wage (4:152). The verses around this one keep the same two-sided message: the men who reject the message and hold others back from the road have gone far astray (4:167 says it of the group the verse after this one describes), and the men who believe in God and all of His messengers are promised their reward.

**Where the Passage Stands**
This verse comes after a list of prophets and before the statement of why they were sent. The chapter has been threading the same idea through its account of the community standing in front of it. Its own opening address to humanity (4:1) and its description of the family of Abraham (4:54) place the reader in the middle of a long story rather than at the start of one.

The chapter had also given the community its practical rules: what to do when a report reaches them before they act on it (4:83 states the rule), how to hand back what has been entrusted and how to judge fairly (4:58 commands both), and the guarded prayer for the battlefield (4:102 describes it).

**What the Verse Tells the Prophet**
The verse tells the Prophet that he is not alone in what he carries, and it tells the reader that he does not know the whole list of those who were sent. Its two halves match the two names given in the verse after it: the messengers who carried good news (4:165 names them) and the witness who knows exactly what was sent down (4:166 names him).

**What the Chapter Said Around It**
The chapter named the people who migrate for God's sake (4:100 describes them) and promised that a people can be removed and others brought in their place (4:133 states it). It said that both rewards are with God (4:134 states it). It promised the gardens to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122 promises them), and said that God's knowledge surrounds everything in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states it).

It also forbade the community to take the other side as allies (4:144 forbids it) and named the place reserved for the people whose belief was a show (4:145 names it). It told the believers to obey God, the Messenger and those in authority among them (4:59 commands it). So the verse stands in a chapter that keeps joining the long history of revelation to the small daily duties of the people receiving it.
verses.165:
> ˹All were˺ messengers delivering good news and warnings so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**Why the Messengers Were Sent**
The verse states the purpose of the whole line of messengers. They came with good news and with warnings, so that people would have no argument left against God once the messengers had come. It closes with two names of God: the mighty and the wise.

**Good News and Warning Together**
The Book never sends a warning without a promise, and this verse states that balance as the reason the messengers were sent. The chapter has used the same pair in its warnings about people whose belief was a show and people whose loyalty was for sale. It announced a painful punishment for the first group (4:138 gives the announcement) and named the place reserved for the second (4:145 names it). But it also named the door back for those who turned, set their conduct right, held fast to God and made their devotion sincere (4:146 gives the four conditions), and it asked what God would gain from punishing anyone who is grateful and believing (4:147 asks it). The point this verse makes is that nobody can claim afterwards that he was never told.

**The Argument That Is Removed**
The phrase about people having no argument left answers a claim the Book reports more than once: the excuse that no messenger had reached a person or his people. The sūrah answers that complaint in the case of the men who were taken in death while they had wronged themselves and who said that they had been weak (4:97 reports it, and 4:98 names the helpless among men, women and children). It also names the people who were left behind after the messengers, who are held to account only for what they could do. This verse closes that door. News has come, and the warning is part of the news.

**How the Sūrah Handled the Same Question**
The chapter shows the community how to receive a message that reaches it and how to carry it to others. It tells the believers to verify what comes to them before they act on it (4:83 states the rule for reports and 4:94 gives the rule for the field). It describes the men who hold others back from the road (4:167 names them) and the men who walk away from the road after it has been made clear to them (4:115 states their case).

It also warns against the attitude that turns the message into a matter for argument instead of conduct. It names the pick-and-choose position on the messengers (4:150 describes it), the verdict passed on those who held it (4:151 gives it), the reward promised to those who accepted all of them (4:152 gives it), the demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153 records it), and the covenant that came with the mountain lifted above them (4:154 records it). The verse gives the whole line its purpose, and the sūrah gives the community the same purpose in its own duty, telling believers to invite people to good (4:114 names the private talk that earns a reward) and to stand for justice (4:135 sets the standard).

**The Two Names at the End**
The verse closes with the mighty and the wise, the same pair the sūrah used when it said that God raised the Messiah to Himself (4:158 states it). The pairing matches the two halves of what the verse is doing: the power stands behind the warning, and the wisdom stands behind a plan that includes both news and caution. The chapter uses the same names in the same situations. The plotters were answered by God's own plan (3:54 gives it). Those who doubted the sending of their messenger were told that God raised him (4:158 again). And the community was told that everything belongs to God, who knows all things (4:126 states both).

The sūrah goes on to say that God bears witness to what was sent down and that His witness is enough (4:166 states it). It has already named what the holders of the earlier Book were given: the family of Abraham received the Book, the wisdom and a great kingdom (4:54 names the gift). And the men among the People of the Book who are grounded in knowledge and believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and before him are given their wage (4:162 lists them). This verse connects the two ends of the chapter: the men who were sent, and the community responsible for having heard.

**The Rest of the Chapter's Road**
The sūrah promises room in the earth to the man who migrates (4:100 gives it). It names the home of those who followed what they were shown (4:121 names it) and the home of those who did not (4:122 names it), and it refuses the idea that reward comes by wishing (4:123 refuses it). It handles the couple who settled their differences between themselves (4:128 describes them) and says that a people can be replaced (4:133 states it). It describes the prayer performed for an audience (4:142 describes it), forbids the community to take the other side as allies (4:144 forbids it), and records that every one of the People of the Book will believe in Jesus before his death (4:159 records it).

It names the interest the earlier community took (4:161 names it). It lists the prophets who carried the same message (4:163 lists them) and the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164 names them). It says that God's will in this Book is to make matters clear (4:26 states it), that every community will be brought forward with a witness (4:41 states it), and that men who go back to fighting whenever they can will be dealt with under the rules of war (4:91 gives the rule).
verses.166:
> Yet ˹if you are denied, O Prophet,˺ Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you—He has sent it with His knowledge. The angels too bear witness. And Allah ˹alone˺ is sufficient as a Witness

**God Bears Witness**
The verse answers those who deny the message by naming a witness who cannot be doubted. God bears witness to what He sent down to the Prophet, and He sent it with His knowledge. The angels also bear witness, and God is enough as a witness. The verse follows the account of why the messengers were sent (4:165 gives that purpose) and the list of messengers named and unnamed (4:164 lists them).

**What the Witness Means Here**
The people the sūrah has been answering did not ask for proof in the ordinary sense. They asked for an arrangement that suited them, and the answer is that the message has a witness whose testimony settles the matter. The sūrah says the same at several points in this chapter. It told the Prophet that God knows the community's enemies best and that He is enough as a protector (4:45 states it). It described the knowledge given to the Prophet so that he could answer the arguments brought to him (4:105 sets the standard of judgment and 4:113 names what he was taught). And it gave the community the rule that reports must be checked before they are acted on (4:83 states the rule). This verse puts the whole question of who has the last word into one sentence.

**The Angels as Witnesses**
The verse names the angels beside God, and the Book does the same when it describes the day of account. It says that every community will be brought forward with a witness, and that the Prophet will be brought as a witness over his own people (4:41 describes that scene). It says that the angels were present when the souls of those who wronged themselves were taken (4:97 reports their words). And it names the angels in the community's call to believe, so that faith covers the messengers, the books, the angels and the last day.

So the heavenly witness stands beside the human denial. Those who keep the record are named, and the record is the thing the men in this passage have been ignoring all along.

**What the Passage Has Built**
The verses before this one recited a long history of people who argued with messengers. There was the demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153 records it), the broken covenant (4:155 records it), the slander against Mary (4:156 records it), the claim about the crucifixion (4:157 records it), the forbidden foods (4:160 mentions them), and the interest they took (4:161 names it). The chapter answered that history with the witness it names here, and then turned to the people in the same communities who believed and did right (4:162 lists them). This verse is the point where the argument stops being about evidence and becomes about what a person does with the news.

**The Rest of the Chapter**
The verses after this one describe those who rejected the message and held others back from the road (4:167 states the charge), and those who wronged themselves and will be led to no path but the fire (4:168 and 4:169 give the two verses). Then comes the direct address to all humanity that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it) and the warning to the People of the Book against extremes in their faith (4:171 gives it).

The sūrah keeps the same frame around the whole section. It says that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, with knowledge that surrounds it (4:126 states both), and that no deed escapes the account (4:40 sets the scale). It says that private talk which urges good earns a reward (4:114 states it). It describes those whose plans are written down at night (4:108 describes them), those who look for honour in the wrong company (4:139 names them), those who perform a prayer for an audience (4:142 names them), those who belonged to neither side (4:143 describes them), and those who took the other side as allies (4:144 describes them). This verse answers every one of those positions with a single fact: what was sent down was sent with knowledge, and the One who sent it is watching the answer each person gives.

The sūrah had already named the people who keep their agreements and stand for justice (4:135 sets the standard) and those who hand back what was entrusted to them (4:58 commands it). It named the messengers who came with news and warning so that nobody would have an argument left (4:165 states it). It promises the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 gives the promise) and answers the community's question about women and orphans (4:127 addresses it). It records the instruction to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book (4:131 records it), says that God takes care of every affair (4:132 states it), and places both rewards with Him (4:134 states it). It names the pick-and-choose position on the messengers (4:150 names it), records that every one of the People of the Book will believe in Jesus before his death (4:159 records it), and lists the prophets who carried the message before the Prophet (4:163 lists them). It also describes those who go back to fighting whenever they can (4:91 describes them) and tells the community to verify before it strikes (4:94 gives the rule).
verses.167:
> Those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah have certainly strayed far away

**Rejecting the Message and Blocking Others**
The verse describes people who reject the message and then stand in other people's road, turning them away from the way of God. It says of them that they have gone far astray. The verse follows the witness named just before it (4:166 names the witness), and it names the second half of the offence. It is not only a refusal to walk the road, but a blocking of the road for everyone else.

**The Two Sides of the Offence**
The Book treats a person who misleads others as carrying something extra, and this chapter makes the point more than once. It says that a man who blames an innocent neighbour for his own fault carries a double load (4:112 describes that man). It says that a man who earns a fault and then throws it onto someone else carries both the slander and the plain sin (4:111 states it). This verse names the same doubling in another setting. Those who hold others back from God's road do harm twice: to themselves and to the people who would have listened to them.

The sūrah has already shown what that looks like inside a community. It describes men who take the other side as allies because it seemed safer (4:139 describes the practice), men who sit with those who mock God's verses (4:140 covers that instruction), men whose loyalty is flexible so that they belong to neither side (4:143 states it), and men who held back when the order to march came and then wanted a share of the gains (4:72 names them).

**Where the Chapter Names This Wrong Elsewhere**
The sūrah charges the same wrong to the earlier community in the passage just before. The verse that forbade certain foods gave the reason that they turned many people away from God's road (4:160 states the reason), and the verse before it named the interest they took and the property they devoured (4:161 gives both charges). It charges the same to the community standing in front of it when it describes men who wanted a tyrant's court to judge between them (4:60 states the case) and men who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61 names them). This verse sums up the whole attitude: a man who does not want the road for himself and does not want it for anybody else.

**The Verdict Stated**
The verse says that such people have gone far astray. The same language has been used for other wrong turns in this chapter. It was used of the men who reached the wrong destination through a chain of errors (4:116 names the wrong that cannot be forgiven), of the men who had the road made clear and then walked away (4:115 gives that case), and of the men who wanted the reward without the conduct (4:123 refuses the wish). The chapter also warns that such positions do not stay still. It says that God left the men who chose their own direction to it (4:115 again), and it says that a man who is left to wander will not find a way (4:143 states the rule).

**What the Chapter Keeps Beside This Warning**
Much stands beside this warning in the verses around it. The men who are grounded in knowledge and believe in what was sent to the Prophet and before him are given their wage (4:162 lists them). Those who accept all of the messengers are promised their reward (4:152 states it). Those who turn back and put things right are counted with the believers (4:146 names the four conditions). And the people excused from the journey are described with mercy, since God names the helpless among men, women and children (4:98 names them and 4:99 states their case).

The sūrah also reminds its readers what the whole Book is for. God's will in it is to make matters clear (4:26 states it). God owns the heavens and the earth and knows everything (4:126 states it). Both rewards are with Him (4:134 says it). And the people who were given the Book before were told the same thing the community is told (4:131 records the command). The chapter names the men among them who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and in what was sent before (4:162 appears again), and it says that the road of the people who follow the light is named near the close of the chapter (4:175 mentions it).

**Where the Passage Turns Next**
The two verses that follow state what happens to the people described here. They will not be forgiven, and they will not be guided to any path except the road of the fire (4:168 and 4:169 give the two verses). Then the chapter turns to all humanity with the news that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it) and to the People of the Book with a warning against extremes (4:171 gives it).

The sūrah names the people who did otherwise at every point where it names the people who did wrong. It names those who keep the prayer and pay the alms (4:162 lists them), those who migrate and find room in the earth (4:100 gives the promise), those who strive in God's way with their wealth and their lives (4:95 names the rank given them), and those who ask God only for what is good (4:134 says that both rewards are with Him). The verse says what happens when a person decides that his refusal has to be everybody's refusal.

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
Other threads run beside this one. The sūrah tells the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 gives the instruction). It handles the couple whose marriage had gone cold (4:128 describes them) and the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129 commands it). It gives the community the list of what belief covers (4:136 gives the list). It names the prophets who carried the message (4:163 lists them) and the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164 names them). And it states the purpose of the whole sending, which is that nobody would have an argument left (4:165 gives that purpose).
verses.168:
> Those who disbelieve and wrong themselves—surely Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to any path

**Not Forgiven and Not Guided**
The verse says that the men who reject the message and wrong themselves will not be forgiven and will not be guided to any path. The verse follows the account of the men who block others from the road of God (4:167) and it states the consequence in two parts: no forgiveness, and no road.

**What the Verse Is Not Saying**
The Book does not say that a man who has done wrong cannot come back, and the whole chapter contradicts that reading. The sūrah opened the door of asking forgiveness to the man who does wrong and then turns to God (4:110 states it), described the four conditions under which the men whose belief was a show could be counted with the believers (4:146 lists them), and asked what God would gain from punishing anyone who is grateful and believing (4:147 gives the question). The verse in front of the reader is about men who did not ask, did not turn, and did not stop holding others back: the wrong they did to themselves is the thing that kept them where they were.

**The Wrong Done to Oneself**
The Book describes sin as a wrong done to the person who commits it, and the sūrah has used the phrase before: it named the men who were taken in death while they had wronged themselves and who called themselves weak (4:97 reports it and follows with the men, women and children who were genuinely helpless at 4:99). It told the community that whoever earns a fault has earned it against himself (4:111 states it), and it described the man who does a wrong or a sin and then throws the blame on an innocent person as carrying the slander and the plain sin (4:112 gives that picture). The verse in front of the reader names the same fact: the men who reject the message are not harming God by it, and the chapter has said as much when it said that a people can be removed and others brought in their place (4:133 states it).

**The Road That Is Withheld**
The verse says that such men will not be guided to any path, and the sūrah has shown what guidance means in the chapter's own terms: it named the men who were guided for their own good (4:26 speaks of God's will to make things clear and to guide), it said that God does not wrong a soul by the weight of an atom (4:40 sets the scale), and it named the men whose hearts are kept from the truth because of what they chose (the sūrah's account of the earlier community says that God sealed their hearts as a consequence). The verse in front of the reader states the same principle with two negations. The men in the passage had the message in front of them, the witness named (4:166 states that God bears witness to what was sent down), and their own history to read (4:157 records the claim about the crucifixion and the correction that followed).

**What the Chapter Has Placed Opposite**
The sūrah has set the other road beside this one in the verses immediately around it: the men and women who believe in God and the last day and do good work are given their wage (4:162 lists them), the men who accept all of the messengers are promised their reward (4:152 states it), the men who turn back and mend what they broke are counted with the believers (4:146 names the conditions), and the men who follow the light sent down with the Prophet are named at the close of the chapter (4:175 states their road). The chapter keeps the same two columns from its early pages: the men who believe and do good work (4:122 names the gardens) against the men who look for honour in the wrong company (4:139 states the answer), and the men who ask forgiveness (4:110 opens the door) against the men who keep the road closed to others (4:167 gives the charge). The verse in front of the reader belongs to the second column, and the verses after it turn to the widest address in the chapter: the call to all humanity that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it). The sūrah has described the knowledge given to the Prophet for the arguments brought to him (4:113) and has warned the man who walks away from the road once it has been made clear (4:115). It has described the men who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137), has named the interest the earlier community took (4:161), and has named the helpless who are excused because they had no way out (4:99).
verses.169:
> except that of Hell, to stay there for ever and ever. And that is easy for Allah

**The Road of the Fire**
The verse states what the people described in the verses before it are guided to: the road of hell, where they will remain. It adds that this is easy for God. The verse follows the statement that such people will not be forgiven or guided (4:168 states it) and completes the sentence with the destination (4:169 gives it).

**What the Verse Names**
The Book describes the two destinations as two roads, and it places each person's journey on one of them. This chapter names both roads in its own way. It names those who follow the light sent down with the Prophet as the successful ones (4:175 states their road). It names those who obey God and the Messenger as the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69 names the company). And it names those who are taken in death while they have wronged themselves as people whose dwelling is hell (4:97 reports their state). This verse states plainly the other end of the road, and it comes at the close of the passage about those who kept others off the way of God.

**Remaining There**
The verse says that the people on this road will remain in it. The Book uses the same word for the reward of those who did good, describing the gardens that believers will be given (the sūrah states the same permanence for the reward of the men and women who believe and do good work at 4:122).

The point is not the length of the punishment but the finality of the choice. The people in this passage had the message, the warnings, the record of their own history, and the door that stays open in this life (4:146 names the conditions and 4:110 opens the door of asking). The sūrah says the same about the earlier community whose hearts were sealed by their own conduct (4:155 states the consequence) and about those who were left to the direction they chose (4:115 gives that case).

**Ease for God**
The verse closes by saying that this is easy for God. The sūrah uses the same phrase elsewhere for what God does without trouble. It says that God is able to remove a people and bring others in their place (4:133 states it). It promises the couple who separate that God will enrich each of them from His abundance (4:130 gives the promise). It states that the wrong which is not forgiven will not be forgiven (4:116 gives the rule). And it names the fire as the destination for those who consume the property of orphans and for those who kill a believer on purpose (4:10 and 4:93 name the two). So this verse closes a passage that has run from the slander against Mary to those who block the road, with a reminder that the matter is not hard for the One who keeps the account.

**Where the Chapter Goes From Here**
The verse after this one turns to all humanity. The Messenger has come with the truth, so believe for your own good. And if you reject, remember that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, who knows all things and is wise (4:170 states all of it). The chapter then addresses the People of the Book directly, warning them against extremes in their faith and telling them to say nothing about God but the truth (4:171 gives the warning), and it names the Messiah as a messenger of God, a word placed in Mary, and a spirit from Him. The sūrah closes with the rules for the person who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 handles that last case).

**The Two Roads, Kept in View**
The chapter keeps the reader's attention on the two roads all the way through. It names those who ask forgiveness after doing wrong (4:110 names them) and those who turn back and hold fast to God (4:146 names them). It describes those whose faith was a show (4:142 describes them) and those who waited to see who won (4:141 describes them). It names those who were taken while they wronged themselves (4:97 names them) and those among the People of the Book who believed and did right and are given their wage (4:162 names them). This verse says where one of the two roads ends, and the verse after it invites every reader to take the other.

The sūrah has named the home of those who followed what they were shown (4:121 names it) and the gardens promised to those who believe and do good work (4:122 names them). It places both rewards with God (4:134 states it) and names the place reserved for those whose belief was a show (4:145 names it). It passes its verdict on those who wanted a middle way (4:151 gives it), describes the demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153 describes it), and names the interest the earlier community took (4:161 names it). The verses around this one name those who block others from the road (4:167 names them) and those who guard what they were given (4:172 names them). The sūrah also says that God's will is to make matters clear (4:26 states it), warns the community about a marriage treated lightly (4:30 warns of it), and names the helpless who are excused (4:99 names them).
verses.170:
> O humanity! The Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe for your own good. But if you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**An Address to All Humanity**
The verse turns from the argument with the People of the Book and speaks to everybody. The Messenger has come with the truth from your Lord, so believe, because that is better for you. And if you reject, remember that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, who knows all things and is wise. The verse follows the statement of the two roads (4:168 and 4:169 give them) and it opens the chapter's final address.

**Why the Address Is Universal**
The Book widens the frame here because the argument of the passage was never only about one community. The chapter opened by addressing all people through the One who created them from a single soul and made families and kinship from it (4:1 states it). Then it dealt with believers, doubters, hypocrites and the holders of earlier Books all the way through. This verse says that the invitation is addressed to everyone, and it gives two reasons. The message brings the truth, and accepting it is good for the person who accepts it.

The sūrah made the same point when it described the reward as a wage rather than a favour (4:100 gives the promise to the man who migrates, and 4:40 sets the scale of every deed).

**Believe for Your Own Good**
The phrase about believing for one's own good matches the question the sūrah asked earlier, what God would gain from punishing a grateful believer (4:147 asks it). The Book says plainly elsewhere that a person's faith adds nothing to God and his refusal takes nothing from Him. The chapter has stated the ownership that stands behind this: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and His knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states both), and He can replace one people with another (4:133 states it). So the decision belongs to the reader, and the verse tells him whose interest is at stake in it.

**The Names at the End**
The verse closes with the knowing and the wise, the two names the chapter uses at the moments when an argument settles. It named them when it said that God raised the Messiah to Himself (4:158 states it). It named God as knowing what is in the hearts of those whose words changed at night (4:63 gives the knowledge). And it named those who were given knowledge and faith as the ones whose understanding is complete (4:162 lists them). Placing the two names at the end of a universal invitation carries its own meaning: the One who knows everything is inviting people to what benefits them, and there is no hidden reason behind it.

**What the Chapter Built Toward This Address**
The verses before this one carried the whole case. There was the witness who cannot be doubted, since God bears witness to what was sent down (4:166 states it). There were those who block the road (4:167 names the charge), those who are not guided because they choose it (4:168 states it), and the road where that choice ends (4:169 names it). Before them came the list of messengers (4:163 lists them), the purpose of the sending (4:165 states it), the knowledge given to the Prophet so that he could judge (4:105 states the charge and 4:113 names what he was taught), the charges against the earlier community (4:161 names the interest they took), and those in that community who believed and did right (4:162 lists them).

The chapter had also given the community its own duties. Verify before you strike (4:94 gives the rule). Return what is entrusted to you (4:58 commands it). Keep your agreements (4:33 commands it). Stand for justice even against your own family (4:135 commands it). Remember God in every position (4:103 gives the instruction). The verse after this one addresses the People of the Book and warns them against extremes (4:171 gives the warning). The chapter then closes with the rules for the person who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 gives them), naming the road of those who follow the light (4:175 names it).

**The Door of Mercy, Kept Open**
The sūrah keeps the door of mercy in view throughout: those who ask forgiveness after doing wrong (4:110 opens it), those who turn back and mend (4:146 names the conditions), the men and women who do good work with faith (4:124 names them), the helpless who are excused (4:99 names them), and those who migrate and are given room in the earth (4:100 gives the promise). So the widest of the chapter's invitations comes at the end of the longest of its arguments.

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
The sūrah says that every sin falls on the person who earns it (4:111 states it). It promises the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 gives the promise). It promises the couple who separate that God will enrich them (4:130 gives the promise). It records the instruction to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book and to the community (4:131 records it). It gives the list of what belief covers (4:136 gives the list), names the pick-and-choose position on the messengers (4:150 names it), and names the reward of those who accept all of them (4:152 names it). It names the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164 names them) and says that no deed escapes the exact account (4:40 states it).
verses.171:
> O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes regarding your faith; say nothing about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger of Allah and the fulfilment of His Word through Mary and a spirit ˹created by a command˺ from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers and do not say, “Trinity.” Stop!—for your own good. Allah is only One God. Glory be to Him! He is far above having a son! To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

> O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes regarding your faith; say nothing about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger of Allah and the fulfilment of His Word through Mary and a spirit ˹created by a command˺ from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers and do not say, “Trinity.” Stop!—for your own good. Allah is only One God. Glory be to Him! He is far above having a son! To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**Do Not Go to Extremes**
The verse addresses the People of the Book and warns them against extremes in their religion, telling them to say nothing about God but the truth. It then explains who the Messiah is: a messenger of God, a word He placed in Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and in His messengers, it says, and do not say that there are three; stop, because that is better for you. God is one God, far above having a child, and to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and He is enough as a guardian.

**What the Warning Is About**
The verse is not asking anyone to be careless with his religion; it is telling him not to load it with claims that the truth cannot carry. The sūrah has been correcting one such claim in the verses before it: the slander against Mary (4:156 names it), the boast about the crucifixion (4:157 reports the claim and corrects it), and the statement that God raised him to Himself (4:158 states it). The verse in front of the reader answers the claim that grew out of that history, which is the claim that the Messiah is more than a servant and messenger.
