The sūrah's list of messengers in the same passage puts Jesus in the line with Noah, Abraham and the others (4:163 names them), which is exactly where the verse leaves him.

**The Three Things the Verse Says About Jesus**
The verse names him the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, then gives three descriptions. He is a messenger of God; he is a word from God placed in Mary, which means he came to be by God's command rather than through the ordinary course; and he is a spirit from Him, a life given by God's command. The Book described the same beginning in another sūrah when it reported the angel's announcement to Mary (66:12 states it), and the same chapter says that nothing about this is hidden from God. The verse then says that believing in God and in His messengers is the way to stop the argument, which is what the chapter has asked of its readers all along: it told them to believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 lists them), it named the men who accept all the messengers and are given their reward (4:152 states it), and it named the men who wanted to choose among them (4:150 describes the position).

**The Command to Stop**
The verse tells the men it addresses to stop, and it gives the reason: it is better for them. The chapter has used the same plain instruction at other points where a wrong idea had taken hold: it told the community not to step over the limits in the matter of marriage and orphans (4:127 answers the question about women, and the chapter's rules on marriage begin at 4:3), it answered the claim about a group's standing carrying them into the garden (4:123 refuses the wish and 4:124 names the condition), and it refused the pick-and-choose attitude to the messengers (4:150) and (4:151 give the position and the verdict). The verse in front of the reader stops the argument at its root: the claim is not a small detail of language, because it puts a creature where the Creator belongs.

**God Is One and Above Having a Child**
The verse states that God is one God, far above having a child, and that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and that He is enough as a guardian. The sūrah has stated the ownership in the same terms several times: it said that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and that His knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states both), that He is the only one who takes care of every affair (4:132 gives that), and that He is able to replace a people with others (4:133 states it). The verse's last phrase about His being enough answers the fear that lies behind the claim: nobody needs a mediator between himself and the One who already owns everything.

**What the Chapter Does With This at Its Close**
The chapter's closing verses carry the same two themes to the end. The address to humanity in the verse before this one tells everyone that the Messenger has come with the truth, and that belief is for the believer's own good (4:170 states both). The closing verses then handle the last of the inheritance questions, the case of a man who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 gives that rule).

The chapter has also named the people who follow the light sent down with the Prophet as the successful ones (4:175 states their road). And it kept the practical duties in view all the way through: the guarded prayer of the battle line (4:102 describes it), the alms and the prayer of the people grounded in knowledge (4:162 lists them), the weight of every deed (4:40 sets the scale), and the command to stand for justice even against one's own family (4:135 commands it).

**What This Verse Corrects**
This verse corrects the last claim that stood between the People of the Book and the message, and it uses the simplest possible words: one God, and a messenger who was a human being.

The chapter had prepared the ground for that correction. It told the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 records it), named the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 names it), and promised the gardens to the men and women who believe and do good work (4:122 promises them).

**Why the Messengers Were Sent**
The chapter also recorded the instruction to be mindful of God (4:131 records it), gave its verdict on the people who wanted a middle way (4:151 gives it), and stated the purpose of sending messengers, which is that no one should have an argument left against God (4:165 states it).

It said that God bears witness to what was sent down (4:166 states it). And it told the community to stand up for the weak who cried out for help (4:75 records it).
verses.172:
> The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels nearest to Allah. Those who are too proud and arrogant to worship Him will be brought before Him all together

**The Messiah Is Not Too Proud to Be a Servant**
The verse says that the Messiah would never consider himself above being a servant of God, and neither would the angels who are closest to Him. It adds that those who are too proud and refuse to worship will all be brought before Him together. The verse follows the warning to the People of the Book against extremes (4:171 gives it) and answers the claim corrected in the verse before by naming service to God as the highest honour there is.

**What the Verse Establishes**
The Book's answer to the elevation of a prophet is not to lower him but to name what he is. The verse puts the Messiah and the nearest angels in one sentence and says that neither thinks himself above serving God. Service, then, is the ground on which the greatest creatures stand. The sūrah names the Messiah in the same line as the other prophets on its list (4:163 lists Noah, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the rest, and 4:164 names the messengers whose stories were not told). It names him as a messenger of God, a word placed in Mary, and a spirit from Him (4:171 states the three descriptions). This verse adds the posture that goes with all of it.

**Why the Sūrah Names the Angels**
The verse mentions the angels nearest to God because they are the creatures whose rank nobody disputes, and it shows that rank and worship belong together. The chapter had already named the angels in its account of the day of account. It says that humanity will be gathered on a day about which there is no doubt (4:87 states it), and it reports that the souls of those who wronged themselves were taken while the angels asked them what they had been doing (4:97 records their words). It also says that God bears witness, and the angels bear witness, to what was sent down (4:166 states the witness). This verse takes the highest of the angels and pairs them with the Messiah, to show that the creatures closest to God are the first to worship Him.

**The Fate of the Proud**
The verse says that those who are too proud and refuse to worship will be brought before God all together. The chapter has warned about pride in several settings. It describes those who held their meetings at night and thought nobody was watching, and it says that nothing in those meetings escaped God (4:108 states it). It refuses the position of those who chose which messengers they would accept (4:150 describes their wish and 4:151 gives the verdict). It names those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 states the answer) and those who sat with mockers of God's verses (4:140 records the instruction). This verse gathers all of those positions into one picture: those who would not bow will be brought in front of the One they refused.

**Where the Chapter Stands at This Point**
The verses around this one are the chapter's closing arguments with the People of the Book, and they keep the tone of correction rather than insult. The verse before describes the Messiah as a servant and messenger (4:171 gives both), and the verse after this one states the reward of those who believe and do good work and the punishment of the proud (4:173 gives both halves).

The sūrah has used the same shape at other points in the chapter. Those who believed and did right were promised their wage while those who held back were told what their conduct earned (4:162 gives the list of the first). Those whose belief was a show were told where they end, and the door back was opened in the very next verse (4:145 and 4:146 give the two).

**The Ties That Make Pride Absurd**
The chapter had also reminded its readers of the ties that make pride absurd. God created humanity from a single soul (4:1 states it). He owns whatever is in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states it). And those who knew this best were the ones whose learning showed itself in prayer and giving (4:162 appears again).

The sūrah names the curse that the being promised a share of God's servants brought on himself (4:118 records it). It describes the best in religion as the person who hands himself over to God and follows the way of Abraham (4:125 describes him). It names the covenant taken from the earlier community (4:154 names it), the slander spoken against Mary (4:156 records it), and the messengers whose stories were not told to the Prophet (4:164 names them).
verses.173:
> As for those who believe and do good, He will reward them in full and increase them out of His grace. But those who are too proud and arrogant, He will subject them to a painful punishment. And besides Allah they will find no protector or helper

**Reward for the Believers, Punishment for the Proud**
The verse states the two outcomes that follow from the description in the verse before. Those who believe and do good work will be paid in full and given more out of God's grace. Those who are too proud to worship will be given a painful punishment, and they will find no protector or helper besides God. The verse closes the chapter's long argument with the People of the Book and with everyone who thought his standing would carry him.

**The Reward Stated First**
The verse puts the reward first, which is the chapter's habit whenever it sets out the two destinations. The men and women who do good work with faith are told that they will not be wronged by so much as a speck on a date stone (4:124 gives the promise). Those who strive are given ranks and mercy from God (4:96 names both). Those who migrate for God's sake are given room in the earth and a wide provision (4:100 gives the promise). And those who believe and do good work are promised gardens with rivers flowing beneath them (4:122 names the destination).

This verse adds that the reward is not only paid in full but increased, which is the same generosity the sūrah names when it describes those who hold fast to God and are admitted into His mercy (4:175 states it).

**The Punishment and the Pride Behind It**
The punishment is attached to pride, and the chapter has named pride as the reason a person refuses what he knows. It describes those who refused to go out to fight and said their brothers would not have died if they had stayed (4:72 reports that claim in its account of those who stayed behind). It reports the case of men who were too important to be judged by anyone but their own favourites (4:60 reports the case of those who wanted a tyrant's court). And it names those whose group standing made them sure of the garden (4:123 refuses that wish and 4:124 names the actual condition). This verse gives the proud their sentence, and the next verse turns to address all humanity with the news that decisive proof has come from their Lord (4:174 states it).

**Nobody to Help**
The verse says that the proud will find no protector and no helper besides God, and the sūrah has used that sentence for those who trusted in the wrong support. It said that those who take the other side as allies will find no helper (4:144 gives the instruction and 4:145 names the place). It asked those who argued a case in this life who would be their advocate on the day, putting that question to those who pleaded for the thief (4:109 records it). And it told the community that God alone is the guardian who settles every affair, since He knows the community's enemies best and is enough as a protector and a helper (4:45 states both). So the verse names the emptiness of every shelter that is not God, and it names God as the one shelter that remains.

**The Duties Kept in Front of Readers**
The chapter never leaves its readers with warnings alone, and the duties it gives run through the same pages. Verify before you strike (4:94 gives the rule for the field). Stand for justice even when the case cuts against your own family (4:135 sets that standard). Treat parents, relatives, neighbours and the traveller well (4:36 gives the list). Remember God in every position (4:103 gives the instruction). And keep your agreements, as the passage names the servants of God who do exactly that (4:172 names them, and 4:129 handles the marriage left hanging).

**The Chapter's Closing Threads**
The sūrah also names those who were given knowledge and faith, whose learning does not stop them from praying and giving (4:162 lists the conditions). It warns the community against the wish of those who follow their own appetites (4:27 names the wish, and 4:40 sets the exact scale of every deed).

This verse is the last of the chapter's verdicts before the call to all humanity, and it holds the same balance the sūrah has kept from the beginning: reward for those who do the work, and no shelter for those who think they do not need one. The sūrah described the knowledge given to the Prophet for the arguments brought to him (4:113 describes it). It named the false names the idolaters call on (4:117 names them) and the promises the lying being made to them (4:119 names them). It handled the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129 addresses her case) and placed both rewards with God (4:134 states it). It described those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 describes them), named those who block others from God's road (4:167 names them), and corrected the claim that the Messiah was more than a servant (4:171 corrects it). It said that no deed escapes the exact account (4:40 states it) and told the community to stand for the weak who cried out for help (4:75 gives the command).
verses.174:
> O humanity! There has come to you conclusive evidence from your Lord. And We have sent down to you a brilliant light

**Clear Proof and a Bright Light**
The verse addresses all humanity with the news that decisive proof has come from their Lord, and that a clear light has been sent down. It follows the two verdicts of the verse before it (4:173 gives them) and it opens the last movement of the chapter before the final inheritance rule.

**What the Proof Is**
The Book calls the message itself the proof, and that is the same claim the passage has been making against those who asked for something else. They asked for a written revelation brought down from the sky (4:153 reports the demand), and they argued about the claims of their own history (4:154 names the covenant and the mountain lifted over them). The sūrah answers all of it by naming the messenger and the Book. The same chapter had already said that the prophets came with good news and warnings so that nobody would be left with an argument after them (4:165 states that purpose). And it said that God bears witness to what He sent down (4:166 states it), which leaves the reader with the proof and with its witness.

**The Light the Verse Names**
The light is the guidance the Book gives to the person who reads it, and the chapter describes what that light does. It says that God guides by it to the ways of peace and brings people out of darkness by His permission, as another sūrah states, and this chapter names those who follow the light sent down with the Prophet as the successful ones (4:175 states their road). It says that God's will in the Book is to make matters clear and to guide the reader into the paths of those who came before (4:26 states that will). And it names those who were given knowledge and faith as the ones who understand what was sent (4:162 lists them). The light, then, is not hidden or private. It has been sent to the reader.

**What the Chapter Has Asked of the Reader**
The chapter has been asking the same thing since its opening pages, and the call in this verse is its plainest form. The sūrah began by addressing humanity through the One who created them from a single soul (4:1 states it). Then it named every group in the community it was addressing: those whose belief was a show (4:142 describes their prayer), those who waited to see which side won (4:141 describes the habit), those who blocked others from the road (4:167 gives the charge), and those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 states the answer). Against all of them it named the people who did the work: those who migrate for God's sake (4:100 names them), those whose knowledge shows in prayer and giving (4:162 names them), those who turn back and hold fast to God (4:146 names them), and the men and women who do good work with faith (4:124 names them). This verse calls everyone to the proof that has already arrived, and it tells the reader what he is asked to do with it.

**Where the Light Leads**
The verses after this one name the destination of those who take the light. God will admit those who believe in Him and hold fast to Him into His mercy and grace, and guide them to Himself along a straight path (4:175 states all of it). The chapter then closes with the ruling for the person who dies leaving neither parent nor child (4:176 gives the case).

The sūrah has kept two ideas together all the way through, and it stated them in the middle of the chapter when it said that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 uses the speck on a date stone). It also warned about the wish of those who follow their own appetites (4:27 names it) and about a marriage treated lightly (4:28 speaks of the burden God lightens, and 4:29 forbids taking property by false means). Its instruction concerning the weak was stated plainly when it told the community to stand for the men, women and children who cried out for help (4:75 gives the command, and 4:99 describes the helpless who are excused).

**The Rest of the Chapter's Threads**
The verse gathers the whole chapter into two words, proof and light, and the reader is told what to do with both. The sūrah gave the community the prayer in every situation it could face (4:103 gives the instruction), told the Prophet to judge by what God showed him (4:105 gives the instruction), and described the knowledge he was given (4:113 describes it). It praised the private talk that urges giving and reconciliation (4:114 praises it), named the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116 names it), named the promises the lying being made to the idolaters (4:120 names them), and promised the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 gives the promise). It said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, with knowledge that surrounds it (4:126 states both). It handled the couple whose marriage had gone cold (4:128 addresses them), said that a people can be replaced (4:133 states it), and listed the prophets who carried the same message before the Prophet (4:163 lists them). It addressed all humanity with the news that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it), corrected the claim about the Messiah (4:171 corrects it), and named the helpless who are excused from the journey (4:99 names them).
verses.175:
> As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into His mercy and grace and guide them to Himself through the Straight Path

**Those Who Hold Fast to God**
The verse names the men and women who believe in God and hold fast to Him, and it promises them three things. God will admit them into His mercy and grace, and He will guide them to Himself along a straight path. The verse follows the call to humanity with the proof and the light (4:174 gives both), and it describes the people who take hold of what has been sent.

**What Holding Fast Means**
The phrase describes a person who has taken hold of something and will not let go. The chapter used it earlier for the people who came out of hypocrisy: those who turned from what they were doing, set their conduct right, held firmly to God and made their devotion sincere, who are counted with the believers (4:146 gives the four conditions). The same sūrah told the community to obey God, the Messenger and those in authority among them, and to take any disagreement back to God and the Messenger. What this verse describes is the posture the whole chapter has been asking for: not a claim about belonging to a group, but a grip on the message.

**The Mercy and the Grace**
The mercy and grace promised here are the same pair the sūrah used earlier, where it said that the men and women who do good work with faith will enter the gardens and be wronged by no more than the speck on a date stone (4:124 states it). It also promised those who migrate for God's sake that they will find room in the earth and plenty (4:100 gives the promise). And it named those who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and in what was sent before him, who keep the prayer and pay the alms, as the ones who will be given their wage (4:162 lists them). What a person receives for holding fast, then, is forgiveness he did not earn and generosity that is not counted.

**The Straight Path**
The verse ends by naming the straight path, the road the whole chapter has been describing since its opening pages. The sūrah names the people who walk it: those who believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 lists the four), those who ask forgiveness after doing wrong (4:110 opens the door), those whose devotion to God is sincere (4:146 names that condition), and those who were given knowledge and faith (4:162 appears again). The road is not a puzzle. Those who take hold of God are placed on it.

**What the Chapter Keeps Around This Promise**
The chapter closes with this promise and with one more practical ruling. The verse before it addresses all humanity with the proof and the light (4:174 states both), and the verse after it gives the inheritance ruling for a man who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 gives the ruling). The sūrah keeps the same two subjects together through its closing pages, the call to believe and the rules for ordinary life. It gave the community the prayer in every situation it could face (4:103 gives the instruction), and it named the payment owed by a man who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 states it). It names the helpless who are excused from the journey (4:99 states their case) and the people of the earlier community who believed and did right (4:174 names the ones called and 4:163 lists the prophets who carried the message). It also states the principle that the call is for the reader's own good and not for God's benefit (4:147 asks what God would gain by punishing a grateful believer).

This verse brings the chapter's account of belief to its plainest form, and the last verse of the chapter returns to the law that governs a family after a death. The sūrah has also described those who walked away from the road once it had been made clear to them (4:115 states their case) and those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 gives the answer), so that the reader can see the difference between holding fast and letting go. Its instruction not to waste what a person has been given stands in the same sūrah, and those who hold fast are named as people whose hearts were kept steady (4:26 speaks of the will to make matters clear and to guide). The sūrah tells the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 gives the instruction), promises the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 gives the promise), and places both rewards with God (4:134 states it). It lists the prophets who carried the message before the Prophet (4:163 lists them), names the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164 names them), corrects the claim about the Messiah (4:171 corrects it), describes the servants who are not too proud to worship (4:172 describes them) and states the two outcomes for the believers and the proud (4:173 states them). It also names the payment owed by the man who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 states it).
verses.176:
> They ask you ˹for a ruling, O Prophet˺. Say, “Allah gives you a ruling regarding those who die without children or parents.” If a man dies childless and leaves behind a sister, she will inherit one-half of his estate, whereas her brother will inherit all of her estate if she dies childless. If this person leaves behind two sisters, they together will inherit two-thirds of the estate. But if the deceased leaves male and female siblings, a male’s share will be equal to that of two females. Allah makes ˹this˺ clear to you so you do not go astray. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**The Last Ruling on Inheritance**
The verse answers a question put to the Prophet ﷺ about a person who dies leaving neither parent nor child, and it sets out the shares. If a man dies childless and leaves a sister, she takes half of his estate. If she dies childless and leaves a brother, he takes all of it. Then it gives the case of two sisters, who take two thirds between them, and the case of brothers and sisters together, where each man takes the share of two women. The verse closes by saying that God makes the matter clear so that the community will not go astray, and that He knows all things.

**Why the Chapter Ends With This**
The chapter opened with the rules of inheritance for children, parents and spouses, and it gave them with a warning attached: those who obey are admitted to gardens, and those who disobey are punished (4:11 and 4:12 give the shares, and 4:13 and 4:14 give the two destinations). Then it dealt with the inheritance of the widow and the orphan, whose rights were being swallowed (4:10 names the fire for those who consume an orphan's property, and 4:7 states the shares due to men and women alike). The sūrah returns to the same subject at its close because the community kept asking about cases the earlier rules had not settled, and this verse answers the last of them.

**What the Kalālah Case Is**
This is the case of a person who leaves neither a parent nor a child, and the ruling covers the dead person's brothers and sisters. The verse gives three arrangements. One sister alone takes half of the estate. Two sisters share two thirds. And when brothers and sisters inherit together, each brother takes twice the share of each sister. The rule follows the same principle that runs through the chapter's earlier shares for sons and daughters, and the Book states here the reason it gives for all of it: God makes His ruling plain so that the community will not wander.

**How the Rule Works With the Earlier Ones**
The sūrah had already set the shares for the closest relatives and told the community what to do about a will and about debts (4:11 and 4:12 set the shares, and 4:12 speaks of what is left after a will and debts are settled). It also answered the community's question about women and orphans, telling them to give the orphan his property and not to trade the good for the bad (4:127 deals with the question, and the chapter's earlier verses forbid consuming what belongs to the weak).

The sūrah keeps the whole set of rules together by giving them the same closing sentence: whoever obeys God and His Messenger is admitted to gardens, and those who overstep the limits that have been set are punished (4:13 and 4:14 give both sides). So the chapter ends on the same note of exactness with which it began, and this is the last of its answers about the family.

**What the Chapter Leaves With the Reader**
The chapter moves from the rules of the family to the rules of the community and back again, and it keeps the same frame around everything. It told the community to return what was placed in its trust and to judge fairly (4:58 gives both). It told the believers to stand for justice even when the case cuts against their own family (4:135 sets the standard). Its rules about women and the weak stand in its verses on the family, and it named those who took the rights of the weak for their own advantage (4:160 records the charges against the earlier community and 4:161 names the interest they took).

The sūrah's last words are the same as its method throughout: God states the law plainly, and He knows every case. The verse before this one follows the call to humanity with the proof and the light (4:174 states both) and the promise to those who hold fast to God (4:175 states the three gifts), so that the chapter closes with the law and the light together. Along the way the sūrah also reminded its readers that God's knowledge surrounds everything in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states it) and that no deed escapes the account (4:40 sets the scale). So the chapter's final sentence leaves the reader with a law that names every case it was asked about, and with the assurance that the One who gave it knows the cases nobody has asked about yet.

**The Rules the Chapter Set Out Along the Way**
The sūrah named the destination of those who overstep the limits God set for the family (4:14 states it). It stated the shares due to men and women alike in the middle of its rules (4:7 names them). It closed its account of the earlier community with the charges against it (4:160 names the foods that were forbidden), and the passage just before this one calls all humanity to the proof (4:174 gives the call). The chapter also said that God's will in this Book is to make matters clear (4:26 states that will).
